Rescue Team 6 retains most of the barebones time management gameplay of its predecessors, but it also tries to spice itself up with some new elements and puzzle-like levels, with varying success.
Rescue Team 6 feels more like an expansion pack than a new instalment, since it barely touched any of the assets and core mechanics introduced back in Rescue Team 4: the goal is still gathering resources with our tireless workers to clear obstacles, rescue civilians, and rebuild their homes and production buildings.
Like many expansion packs, RT6 also tries to shake things up with some added elements. The most obvious is the new worker type, rescue dogs; they even get a unique headquarters, resource (doggie treats), and a special kind of civilian building only they can enter.
Furthermore, the game uses a few tricks in level design. We have puzzle-like stages that require many resets before figuring out their required order; stages with multiple headquarters that can be a bit dizzying to manage; and stages where the great walking distances can lead to rather tight timing.
Although these changes can lead to some unneeded frustration, especially in normal mode, Rescue Team 6 still manages to stay inside the comfortably mediocre territory, so if you like the series thus far, there is no point in skipping this one either.

While graphically nice, thats about as much as this game has to offer. This game starts off very easy, and gradually gets harder. you know, like any other game. Well the way Sonic Lost Worlds executes it is wrong.
There is not a level you will not die in in this game, no matter how good at video games you are. You will die at least once.
Why?
There is a fine line for challenge in gaming. theres "oh boy thats pretty challenging, I'll get it next time" and then theres ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t challenge, where instead of being a challenge its just straight up near impossible, and requires quite a bit of raw luck.
The first half of the game is straight forward. Run through the levels, die a few times, yada yada no big deal.
Well the second half just screws you over 100% of the time. They introduce new gimmicky things on each level without even explaining what or how to do it.
Towards the end of the game, the levels stretch out way too long, to the point where you just get bored and frustrated. On top of this a lot of things one hit kill you despite you having rings, which negates the point of even having rings in the first place.
Then after you get game over, its back to the beginning of the level for you, wasting all that progress which took way too long, and you just straight up give up
Bosses:
the bosses stir up quite a bit of controversy because theyre all "way too easy". Well, its true. I had more challenges with the regular badnicks you find in the level than the bosses themselves. They literally take only 2 hits to beat. Hell, some badnicks take more than 2 hits.
So overall, unless you like games that will make you want to snap your controller in half, no, I would not recommend this game to anyone.

For a game that, for many people, was under the radar in 2013, Gunpoint certainly made a good impression on me. Unique and charming, this action puzzler was a fun breath of fresh air for me, although there were a few issues which barely prevented it from hitting my personal Game of the Year list.

The story of Gunpoint is, honestly, too convoluted for its own good. Strangely enough, the game actually addresses this fact with a few self-defacing comments later in the game. I wasn’t aware at first that the storyline was advancing with my dialogue choices, and I’m still not completely sure if the outcome of the game is heavily affected by my actions. Once I realized that my choices were making an impact on the characters that I was interacting with, I had a moment of panic and considered starting over with the intentions of paying more attention to what I was doing. In the end, I was satisfied with my actions, but I have a feeling something could have unintentionally gone very wrong (such as when I played Spec Ops: The Line).

Speaking of dialogue, the writing here is top-notch, reminding me of how witty old-school adventure games were years ago. It isn’t afraid to incorporate some noir grit as well, but never becomes overly dark or saturated with drama. It’s a script that would work in a Joss Whedon movie.

Gameplay is fun, and the game loads very quickly after failed attempts, which I feel is required for games that have very fast deaths, or else the gamer quits out of frustration. Every now and then I would earn a one-hit failure that would leave me cursing at the controls, but overall the entire package is just fine.

However, Gunpoint is the gaming equivalent of blue balls. Once everything clicks and you have all the gameplay elements presented to you and you’ve used them in a mission, the game is over. I was actually surprised to find how quickly I reached the game’s conclusion, and looked up online to make sure that I was indeed nearing the end. I would have happily played a game that was twice as long as this one, which is a compliment that I really haven’t said about that many games lately.

Recommended, for anyone really. It’s a fast, fun game that everyone should power through once.

I bought this before it had Steam workshop support and felt lukewarm about it having a level editor where you couldn't share, but coming back to it and seeing it has Steam workshop support I highly, highly, recommend getting it!
The storyline itself is generic. You're a spy and you break into places. Nothing to write home about. I do like the fact that you're a bad spy and have to fix your mistakes but not the fact that your actions cause somebody to commit suicide. That bothered me for a while that you couldn't prevent that. There's also an excessive of swearing; and a lot of the dialogue feels like it was written trying to be edgy by swearing every other word, but really it's just not.
The dialogue trees are beyond shallow -- but that's forgivable because this is not a game you buy for the story. It's a game you buy for the puzzle system. Which in my view is fantastic. There's something endless satisfying about wiring a light switch to shock a guard; or creating infinite loops of lights that turn each other on and off and watching guards run about in confusion.
As to the game itself, the levels have a generous learning curve and I was able to solve the final puzzle without much trouble. There's a few tricky moments where you learn new tricks (delayed wiring) but nothing that a casual player would find overly taxing.
Again the real reason to get this game is that with steam workshop you have nearly unending amounts of puzzles you can play through. A good puzzle takes about 10 minutes to solve, and so there's several thousand ways to spend those ten minutes you have in between things doing something enjoyable.
Pros
+ Steam Workshop
+ Easy learning curve
+ Clever puzzle mechanic
Cons
- Fairly short
- Excessive swearing
- Poor story

The second part of every night is where you actually fight the werewolves and other nasties, making sure your traps function properly... and you'll know if they don't.
Admitedly, the last level (boss) frusterated me quite a bit, but after...  A dozen tries, and looking up a walktrhough I managed to get it.  I'll go ahead and spill the beans on that, to prevent frustation for any future players;
That being said (even with that minor frusteration), this game is certainly worth taking a look at, and was fun and frusterating (in a good way) - after all, if a game's no challenge, what's the point?

Tales From The Borderlands is such a well written and comical story from the beginning to the very end.  There was never a dull moment, and it never seemed as though the writters were scrambling to come up with something.  Several aspects were enjoyable in Tales From The Borderlands, but I think the one that stood out the most, for me anyways, was the soundtrack.  They did an excellent job writting and composing the songs.  I dont know if it was one person doing all of the work there, or several, however, it is brilliant.  A close second goes to "Gortus" :)  And even though the soundtrack was my favorite part of Tales From The Borderlands, I still very much enjoyed the story, the writting, the gameplay, the graphics and many other things.
The gameplay was more like a visual novel with choices that made a difference in the end.  The outcome of your Vault Team will depend on what choices you make and how you handle each situation.  Some do not effect outcomes at all, but most of them will.  And you can only make so many choices, so the game does have a little bit of replaybility.  I would find it equally enjoyable running through it one or more times, it was a fun and entertaining experience.
The graphics follow the same theme as previous versions of Borderland games.  The illustration like graphics are asthetically pleasing and suit this game well.
The only things bad that I would like to point out about Tales From The Borderlands is there are a couple of choices that go too quickly for you to choose.  There may be an option to slow it down, I haven't checked, however there were a couple of times that it went by way too quickly and the option wouldn't have made a difference.  Also, there were a few times that I got black transparent squares popping up on the screen.  From what I could tell, this only happened during the racing scenes.  So maybe there's an adjustment to be made on the developers end, however it wasn't that big of a deal.
The content is a decent amount for what you get.  I still feel like they could of done more as far as bringing a special bonus mode, or choices that totally went off in another direction.  This would be easy to do considering the way the story is being played out.
All of the animations were nicely done.  The cut-scenes were enjoyable to watch and there were even sometimes when they were unexpected.
I enjoyed the graphical work in Tales From The Borderlands.  When you start a new chapter, there is a narration of the previous chapter with illustrations showing what had happened.  I really enjoyed that.  Also you don't see the title flash with the opening credits right off the bat, instead they implement it somewhere in the beginning of the chapter, but you don't know when until you play it.
While the gameplay is solid, I feel like it could use a little more direciton in the exploration field.  I understand it has to be linear to come to the conclusion of the story, however there needs to be more places the characters can explore with their LB and RB skills / items.  This was a big opportunity I think they sort of fluffed up on.
The controls are good and for the most part, it detected what I did, however, there were a couple of times when I did the action correctly, but it did not capture it right.  I know it was not user error either, so thats the only reason I want to point it out.
I had no issues running Tales From The Borderlands.  I think it's a reliable game and you shouldn't have any problems as long as you're meeting the minimum system requirements.
The user interface was easy to follow and you could figure things out fairly simple.  I do wish they highlighted interactive items much better than they did though, as sometimes I could see how it would be easy to miss certain things.
As I've stated already, they did an excellent job on the soundtrack.  It is pleasant.  The sounds were very good also, I didn't find any flaws there.  The sounds were timed well and rolled perfectly in sync with the game.
The story is amazing.  I really enjoyed seeing what the outcome would be.  Sometimes it made you laugh, sometimes cry, and at other points, you'd be mad at someone.  There are a few twists and turns that were unexpected, but all of them were enjoyable.
The community on Steam really likes Tales From The Borderlands, and rightfully so.  It's a great work of art, and I can see why others would recommend it to others.
Tales From The Borderlands is a great experience, and I'd recommend it to anybody.  From beginning to the end it was fun and entertaining.  The humor will have you laughing at times, the drama may have you sad or mad at times, and the story with it's twists and turns will keep you interested to see what happens next.
I do believe the price point is slightly high for the amount of game you get here, however for all the fun you'll have playing along, I think it's safe to say that it'd be worth a purchase when it goes on sale for sure.
They left the ending open to a sequel, and a lot of people are clamoring about that on their Discussion Boards.  I'd really like to see a sequel myself.  However, I do hope that they learn from their mistakes on this one, so that they can improve upon them in the next.  It'd be nice to have an aspect of freedom.  Like being able to shoot skags or just simply exploring further to find some useful items and actually being able to use them for other things.

February, 1991 - USS Saratoga - Persian Gulf
Iraqi forces continue to launch Scud missiles into Israel in the hopes of provoking an Isreali military response, and Israel's patience is wearing thin.  If the Israelis counter-attack, multiple Arab states are expected to withdraw from the Coalition, or even align themselves with Saddam rather than be perceived as allied with Israel.  The stakes are high, and the situation dire.
As the pilot of an F/A-18 Hornet, your job is to evade Iraqi air defenses, locate and eliminate Saddam's mobile Scud launching vehicles, and help bring the Gulf War to a close.  Strap in tight, because you will face the most harrowing experience of your life when you realize that, thanks to one small typographical error, you are instead playing the most pathetic match-3 game on Steam.
is a game custom-made for those of us who've played
or one of its many, many imitators, and said "If only this experience could somehow be made even
tedious and mind-numbing!"  If you wanted to see what
would be like if stripped of every feature that made it remotely interesting,
is here for you.
The game features a "Relax Mode" where you play until you realize how horribly you're wasting your life and quit, a "Rush Mode" where a countdown timer mercifully ends things for you if you just play slowly enough, and "Classic Mode" which features some rudimentary puzzle elements.  While Classic Mode is certainly the most entertaining form of "Dessert Storm," in the same way that reading a telephone book is still more entertaining than watching paint dry, it is also the most objectionable, as it features an anthropomorphized ice-cream cone whose only job is to shrilly scream "Ice Cream" at you when you complete a level, as though you needed additional punishment for the mistake of having played this bargain-bin reject of a game.
There are no powerups, no special combo effects beyond some extra points, nothing at all to detract from the tedium of the most basic and limited form of match-3 gaming there is.
Match-3 games are everywhere.  Many of them are free-to-play.  All of them are better than this.  Choose one.

I finished Lost World in around 7 hours and I didn't find it terribly enjoyable. First you'll notice that Sonic feels slower, you'll have to hold the run button in most scenarios when you want to run, which just seems silly for a Sonic game. Eventually, you'll find that you'll need to use the kick/bash/stomp button, I started the game and then dropped it and came back later, I don't remember going through a tutorial telling me how to utilize the kick button, I incidentally found out through frustration of mashing various buttons when trying to figure out how to knock down an enemy that I was required to destroy. Finally, you'll figure out that there's charge attack that is required to time just right, you'll wait for three, four, or five circles to click onto the enemy and you'll then have to quickly do a homing attack for the attack immediately after to be effective. It would really have been nice if a brief manual was attached to this game. Perhaps I should have looked in the community guides. Aside from those mechanics, homing sometimes seems flaky if you're on a sphere and the camera angle isn't quite right.
As for the level design, some of them are fun and others are boring or frustrating. I think I maybe would enjoy the levels more on a second playthrough, but I shouldn't have to play through a game once to get used to the mechanics so I can properly enjoy it a second time through. It really kinda felt more like a current Mario-style game, much more platforming and avoiding obstacles than running and speeding around. By the final zone, I was just wanting it to be over with.
As far as the audio goes, I enjoyed the music in the 16bit games and especially the Sega CD version (both US and international), but the music just keeps going downhill as far as originality goes; the music in Lost World is basically elevator music compared to past soundtracks and it's too loud (too much dynamic range compression). I just wish they would get back to the more edgy sound instead of this soft orchestral crap.
The last Sonic platformer game I played was Generations and it was much better than Lost World. If you read this review then you should now be somewhat familiar with the mechanics and could probably go in less frustrated than myself so at least you'd have that going for you.
In short, I feel like this was a Mario game repurposed as a Sonic game.

Sang-froid is a great game, in concept! The translation of the idea into a videogame is also done well, mechanics-wise.
The big problem, for me, is how unpolished and frustrating the execution has been, especially for a 15€ game.
The game feels dated in almost every respect. Graphics, story-telling, how the combat and guns work, transitions, item system, etc. etc. Everything is very imperfect and takes way more time than it should.
I don't want to make a full blown review, so I'll try to very briefly state the most glaring problems.
I've played the game twice. Once on Easy Mode, once on Hard Mode. Easy Mode was very uninteresting. Combat over strategy. Hard Mode was infuriating, since, while strategy was the focus, the combat was still very much required to a great degree, while your character was clearly very underpowered. As a result, almost every mission required multiple tries, even
I had the strategy laid and should have worked. I completely ignored the story and all of the other aspects aside from mechanics in the second playthrough.
Why? Because it's terrible. Honestly. The story is fairly cool, especially since I do like fairy-tale and folk stories, in general. The problem is how the story is delivered. It's... mind boggling to me. The story is told exclusively through "cutscenes" that are merely characters talking to one another. Nothing fancy. The problems are: the writing isn't good, coupled with horrible voice-acting. I don't think the actors were in the same room at all. Each line feels completely disconnected from the situation at hand, and the tone is completely off. It just doesn't deliver.
Then, there's the fact that, visually, they use some pretty bad 3D models, just because. The animations aren't all that great either. Nothing justifies the choice for these "cutscenes". A simple 2D conversation, with little animation and no voice-acting could have been much more polished without half of the work.
Not to mention that this had nothing to do with the game. Yet, it's one of the main elements of the product, and it sticks out like a sore thumb.
It's really, really, bad. I don't understand this choice at all. I could understand a sub-par execution, if it was a new idea, or something. This brings nothing new, nothing impressive. On the contrary, it's glaringly bad...
The game itself, for those of you not aware, is like Orcs Must Die, although the tower and combat phases are completely separated. First, you place the traps you can. Then, you fight each wave successively, with combat. That's fine, although it can be kind of annoying when you don't know exactly what will come at you (they tell you which enemies and where, but there are nuances...) and you have no chance to fix mistakes without restarting.
You'll get a plethora of different traps that you can later upgrade, but some of them are mostly useless or situational.
Still, they fit the setting, and some combinations were fun to use.
You can also buy potions and weapons in the town. Potions are useless, except from the health ones. The others are burnt money, unless you're on the last missions. Why? Because you barely get any money to upgrade. So, why waste it on consumables?
You gain so little money that you'll take until the last few missions to be able to get a decent combination of weapons. Espcially on hard mode.
Far too long.
The upgrade system is cool, although you can completely lock yourself if you use your points in the wrong place. You can "undo", but only when you choose where to put them. If you "confirm",you're stuck with them.
Ok, what's next?
Graphically, it's a PS2 era game. If that. You can't see 7 meters in front of you, and I'm not sure if it's a design decision, or a performance choice. Then, the game suffers from fps problems when there are too many enemies active. And I have a 3.4Gz quad-core. There's no justification that I can think of, really.
The combat is extremely clunky. That could be fine, since you're not supposed to use it a lot. Except... that you need to, since traps are very limited. So except lots of restarts. The game has a lock-on system that will often change targets when you least want to. There are some enemies that will go underground to heal when they're low on HP. So, you want to kill them asap.  The problem is: when there are several characters, the game may very well choose to target someone else. Well, crap...
The gun suffers a similar problem with the auto-aim. It "snaps" to the closest target... sometimes. Sometimes it also seems to lag, and suddenly aims completely off, leading to a failed shot.
You also take a loooong time to reload, which is cool. Bullets are also fairly expensive, so the point is to hold on to them. Which is infuriating when the game throws your aim off!
Here's another thing: the game rewards you for using less traps. You can use Actions Points to cut trees, instead of placing traps. This further encourages combat, rather than strategy. Encourages the clunkiest system... And unbalances the game has a result, a bit. On Hard Mode, where you want to maximize traps, you end up getting way less money, making it even harder to upgrade, thus making the future missions even harder.
There's a bit of a snowball effect, here... and not a good one.
Then, there are various other problems. The interface is big and full of boxes, and still manages to miss several very important aspects... You take far too long to navigate from the stores to the village and your home. It's the clicking, but there are way too many. There's also a lot of information missing, leading to even more time wasted...
There's no plain restart button that starts you exactly at the level you were in. You always have to go to the strategy screen, and then click like 3 or 4 times to confirm textboxes before you go into the level. It doesn't help that there's always a load screen between transitions. So, except 2 loading screens every time you make a mistake and want to restart. Or simply die...
I realize this review is a bit toxic. I apologize for that. The game isn't terrible. The game itself, if I ignore everything else, can be fun and challenging, at times. The problem is that the game has way too many issues in too many different places, and it results in a very frustrating experience, overall.
It tries to do a lot more than the game itself, but it doesn't know how. Seems like a lot of wasted work. I just can't understand the people claiming it to be a "masterpiece".
In concept, it's great. Execution... not really.
Orcs Must Die is a far more enjoyable game (both of them, in my opinion) and they provide more content than this, for a lower or equal price. And undoubtedly more finely tuned and polished.

A Tower Defense/Third-Person Action hybrid in the style of "Orcs Must Die!" based on Canadian lore. The game's structure is broken into pre-mission cutscene, pre-mission preparations, the actual defense of your structures on foot, and a post-mission cutscene, with no deviation in this structure. Of the twenty missions available, the first few are thinly veiled tutorials which quickly ramp up in difficulty once supernatural enemies are introduced. Unlike most games, the difficulty doesn't budge; for the most part it was a non-stop train ride through a frustratingly difficult game. I was finding myself quickly frustrated and had to restart missions many times because of accidentally hitting myself with a lethal trap, getting sidetracked defending one objective while another was being destroyed, or just dying from being overwhelmed by enemies I was unprepared to face at full health because they "dodged" a trap I set for them.
While the story is good enough to push you forward and explain character actions and interactions, it really feels like it was stretched thin and simply made to build a game around. There are no sidequests, no mini-games or diversions, no non-main story character to chat with, or even any non-story or non-shops to visit while in towns. I loved the game's atmosphere and environments but much of the game feels rushed and lazy, as if the devs said "this is good enough, ship it!" The story also seemed to end abruptly and un-satisfyingly, as if the devs couldn't decide to lead into a sequel or not.
I would love to see a sequel that wasn't such a barebones narrow corridor of gameplay. Simple touches, like actually being able to walk around in towns, would have added much to the atmosphere of the game. This could have been a cozy, atmospheric game with a unique spin on tower defense, but instead it feels like a quick in-betweener for a dev looking to make money for his next big project.

I just finished playing Gunpoint, a really great game from a first-time developer. This came out over a year ago, but the Mac version didn't get released until recently…
This game is fun. This game is funny. This game is self-aware, has great music, great pixel art, interesting mechanics, a decent story, and most surprisingly, choice that actually feels "meaningful"…
…More meaningful then many AAA, big-budget titles that I've played, where choice basically comes down to binary decisions that amount to little more then either a) rescue the orphans from a cartoon villain, or b) burn the orphanage down yourself (thus becoming the cartoon villain). In Gunpoint, you have choice about who to work for, how to achieve your objectives, and how much to cooperate with your clients.
In terms of game mechanics, there may be multiple ways to approach any given mission, and various levels of success in completing your objectives (were you a "ghost", never being detected, or did you have to knock a couple of guards out, or worse?)—this game certainly has replay value (I'll probably replay it at least once).
At the end of a play-through, you get to sum up your feelings in a "blog post" that generates an actual web page—a pretty cool way to contextuilze your experience, as well as promoting it to your friends. Congratulations to the developer for actually USING the term "ludonarrative dissonance" inside the actual game!

Years ago, I had the original version from a non-legit source, and the graphics is what kept me from playing it through. I bought the Definitive version on steam a while back and I could tell a big difference in the graphics. It was much better looking, ran smoother, and had less artifacts (no V-Sync required this time around.)
I was extremely lucky I guess, as I had no major issues with this version of the game. There were some minor bugs, like a few cars disappearing after I went inside of a building (which would suck if I had supplies in the bed of a truck.) But other than that, the game played like Aces for me.
I really enjoyed the gameplay and customizing melee weapons. I love the slow-down effect when you slice an infected's head off in one clean blow. The durability system (while annoying) is probably less harsh than it could be. Considering how thick some of the infected bodies are, your machete would really dull quite quickly.
I do think that the inventory space is a little too limited for all characters, considering how much junk is found EVERYWHERE. And if you return to an area you've already been to, or just do a Quick Save and then Quick Load, the items are back in the suitcases... not very realistic, but I guess it works.
I do wish there was a better mapping system when it comes to Quests and Objectives. Some quests require you to go pick up an item from the other side of the island and then return it back to this person, only to end up getting a quest from someone else who requires you to return to that same area on the other side of the island. There's a quick travel feature, but the maps required aren't as abundant as it should be considering how big both of the islands are.
The story line wasn't too bad either, although I feel like there's some plot holes they could have filled. There's also some areas that seem like they would lead to a secret cache or something, but are really just there to waste your time, or draw infected out of hiding.
The most annoying thing in the game is collecting the special Skulls to get the Legendary Developer weapons, as they require some very specific things to be accomplished in a very specific order, otherwise you will cut off access to that skull until later in the game, or possibly just lose access completely. Also, guns seems much a bit underpowered once you either get the developer melee weapons, or just learn the right blueprints. Elementals Melee weapons are tïts!!!
It is also good that the infected level up as you do, so that you are always getting a semi-decent amout of experience. This is also helped by the fact that they will re-spawn once you're out of an area long enough. At first, this was also annoying, but considering how much experience you need to get to level 50 (or beyond), it makes sense.
Overrall, I thoroughly enjoyed this game and would play through it again. I recommend it, but be wary of the bugs that others are reporting. You may luck out like me, though, and have no issues at all.

This is a great game in the style of classic NES-era platformers.  Like most games in the genre, the difficulty comes from a combination of reflesxes / timing and level memorization.  It's a lot of fun!
I found it easy to get into the game and was excited when I would find hidden coins, or relieved when I found the coveted and rare bean soup.  There are some levels where you have to be really cautious, and others that you can dash through.
You die easily and frequently, but on the casual mode the checkbpoints are frequent so that most players will be able to beat it, with a little perseverance.  The playthrough here is more like the early games in the genre, and less like the extremes of more recent 'hardcore' games like Super Meat Boy, etc.  Of course, for a decent challenge there is the Old School mode, where you only get 3 lives for the entire game.  There are also some short Challenge time trial levels, which are separate from the regular game.
The graphics and audio are simple, but they have a natural charm to them.  There are lots of details in the background and sprites, and it all seems to blend together well into a coherent aesthetic, with a cute story.  The enemies are unique and there is some variety both in enemy appearance within the same AI pattern, and different attack patterns.  The bosses are relatively easy, and there aren't many tricks to them.
The hidden coin collectibles and recipes add a little depth to the game, and I haven't gone through and found them all yet.  There are 100 coins per world, and 5 worlds, so 500 coins total.  The regularity of the per world coin amounts help you keep track of where you're missing coins.
I like the idea of recipes to go with the goblin chef protagonist character.  They are actual recipes that you could try to cook in real life, although I haven't tried any yet.
There are some shortcomings; I do think the hitboxes for some enemies like the bats (flying nopes, ravens) are a little confusing or not quite right.
In the end, it's really a fun game, especially for fans of old school platformers.  Playthrough is around a couple hours to get through casual with the bare minimum, and probably a lot longer to try to make it through old school and find all of the coins.  Great, simple, traditional game!

My main complaint is that it's not integrated with / using Steam's licensing system, and so you have to manually copy the key into the app using the enter key in lower left corner of the main UI.  Because it doesn't follow Steam's usual licensing, there's a separate limit on number of machines, etc.
That having been said, the program is a lot nicer than most programs of this sort.  It tends to not false positive a lot, it usually can automatically install the right driver or drivers, and it generally doesn't recommend wrong drivers as some do.  It lags behind some of the auto updaters bundled with hardware devices, however it also doesn't result in a million separate update processes running continuously in the tray.
The big thing is because licensing is not integrated, you're going to potentially run into issues if you are using Steam on multiple devices, and then you're also going to have to manually copy the CD code from your library and use the "enter code" button at the bottom of the UI (it's the humorously small button underneath the huge "send us cash" button) to enter the CD key to activate the product.  Using Steamworks to tie to the Steam account would likely be nicer.
To be clear on that point -- one of the reasons that I buy games through Steam, GOG and the other download sites is that when I get a new computer or replace an existing computer, those games can follow me without having to fish for install media, registration codes, and who knows what else.  I just deactivate Steam on the old machine and activate it on the new, and my software is all there and ready to go.  No digging through email for codes, no manually deactivating the over 400 programs I have through Steam's platform.  And if I need to, I can just download the app(s) again.
When a given program drifts far from that model, it is annoying when hardware fails or when I have to move to a new machine.  In this specific case, since it is an extremely useful program after a mainboard or video swap, it is particularly noticable.
But I still recommend it over all, and the licensing is clearly marked when you make the purchase.

Operation Desert Storm, popularly known as the first Gulf War, was the successful U.S.-Allied response to Iraq's attempt to overwhelm neighboring Kuwait. Kuwait's liberation in 1991 brought to the battlefield a new era of military technology. Nearly all battles were aerial and ground combat within Iraq, Kuwait, and outlying areas of Saudi Arabia. Iraq inflicted little damage on the American coalition; however, they fired missiles on Israeli citizens.
At the request of the Kuwaitis, Kuwait had become a British Protectorate in 1889. British forces protected the area until 1961. Kuwait was a part of Iraq until 1923, when borders were drawn. On June 19, 1961, British protection ended and Kuwait joined the Arab League. Iraq objected strongly and claimed that Kuwait was part of their territory. Kuwait formed its own constitution on January 1963. Accordingly, the emir held the executive power, organized with a group of ministers. By January 23, a national assembly was elected. By October, 1963, Iraq gave up its claim on Kuwait. Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein wanted to regain that lost land for Iraq, and so he invaded.
On August 2, 1990, Iraqi forces invaded Kuwait. Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein had been making threats against Kuwait for some time, but his actual invasion caught most of the world by surprise. The magnitude of the invasion also was a surprise. Those who had expected an attack, such as the commander of U.S. Central Command, Norman Schwarzkopf, expected a limited attack to seize Kuwaiti oil fields. Instead, within a number of hours, Iraqi forces had seized downtown Kuwait City and were headed south toward the Saudi Arabia border.
Word of the Iraqi attack reached Washington, D.C., as Iraqi forces assembled at the Saudi border. The Pentagon had plans in place to aid the Saudis, and U.S. forces went on standby for the Saudis' request. Secretary of Defense♥♥♥♥♥♥Cheney and General Schwarzkopf met with King Fahd of Saudi Arabia to brief him on the plans, which he approved. Within minutes of the meeting, orders were issued, and thus began the largest buildup of American forces since the Vietnam War. Within a short period, members of the 82nd Airborne Division, as well as 300 combat aircraft, were headed for Saudi Arabia.
President Bush (with Saudi approval) ordered an additional 140,000 soldiers, including the Third Armored Division with its Abrams M1A tanks. During that period, reinforcements from numerous other nations arrived, including British, French, Egyptian and even Syrian forces. On November 29, the UN Security Council passed a resolution authorizing the use of force if Iraq did not withdraw from Kuwait by January 15.
On the morning of January 16, 1991, Allied forces began the first phase of Desert Storm, also known as Desert Shield. American forces first destroyed Iraqi border radar stations, then other key elements of the Iraqi anti-aircraft network; lastly, they began to bomb key targets in downtown Iraq, including the presidential palace, communication centers, and power stations. The Allied forces lost only two aircraft during the attacks. The assault continued day and night.
Those initial air attacks constituted the first time the American military witnessed how their new arsenal performed in combat conditions. With such ground systems as the M1A1 Abrams missile and the MIM-104 Patriot missile, the Iraq military had little opportunity to defend themselves. Also, such other groundbreaking technology as the Global Positioning System (GPS), helped to pinpoint hits by the Tomahawk missile and other weapons.
The damage done by U.S. air attacks was devastating to Saddam's vaunted Republican Guard. The following U.S. aircraft left "a big hurt" on the enemy during the war: AH-64 Apache helicopters, B-52 Stratofortress bombers, E-3 AWACS surveillance aircraft, F-117A Stealth fighters, E-8C JSTARS radar command posts, and the RPVs (drones).
Overall, the coalition air campaign (consisting mostly of U.S. pilots) accumulated a total of 109,876 sorties over the 43-day air war — averaging 2,555 sorties per day. Of those, more than 27,000 sorties struck enemy Scuds, airfields, air defenses, electrical power, biological and chemical weapons caches, headquarters, intelligence assets, communications, the Iraqi army, and oil refineries.
Scuds fired at Israel and the attack on Al Khafji
At 3 a.m on January 17, the Iraqis fired seven Scud missiles at Israel. Israelis were awaiting the Scuds with gas masks on, thanks to Saddam's previous threats to burn half of Israel with chemical weapons. As it turned out, the Scuds bore only conventional warheads, but their terror value was high. To avoid a wider war, U.S. officials pleaded with Israeli officials to not respond to the Scud attacks. The Israelis agreed because the Americans promised to target all Scud missile sites and knock them out.
On January 29, following two weeks of punishing coalition air assaults, the Iraqis mounted their one and only attack subsequent to the invasion at the Battle of Khafji. The Iraqi Fifth Mechanized Division attacked south, capturing the Saudi town of Al Khafji eight miles south of the Kuwaiti border. The Iraqis overran the first Saudi force that attempted a counterattack and, despite massive American air attacks, they held on to the town through the day and night. The next day was a different story, however, when Saudis recaptured the town, forcing the remaining Iraqis to flee to the Kuwaiti border.
After a 38-day air campaign, Operation Desert Sabre, a massive ground attack, was launched by Americans and the coalition into both Iraq and Kuwait.
Day One ground attack. On February 24th at 4 a.m., Allied troops led by U.S. Marines crossed the border into Iraq. During the days before the attack, Iraqi troops had been subjected to merciless air attacks; every imaginable target was destroyed with accuracy.
The Allied offensive targeted three major offensive venues: the first aimed at Kuwait City, the second to the west aimed at the Iraqi flank, and the final one far to the west, beyond the major Iraqi lines that would totally outflank Iraqi lines. In the first day of the war the marines advanced halfway to Kuwait City and the western advances proceeded without difficulty — while capturing thousands of Iraqi deserters. The first day of ground fighting resulted in minimal American casualties.
Day Two ground attack. As Day Two approached, an Iraqi Scud missile destroyed the U.S. barracks in Dhahran, killing 28 U.S. soldiers. With morale nevertheless high, American troops advanced on all fronts. The marines approached Kuwait City, while the western flank began to cut off the Iraqi Army's retreat route. Coalition casualties for Day Two were, once again, light.
Day Three ground attack Day Three dawned on the largest tank battle in history. The American armored forces engaged the tank forces of the Iraqi Republican guard. Like shooting fish in a barrel, the American tanks destroyed the Iraqi heavy armor without losing a single tank.
On February 26th, Iraqi troops began to retreat from Kuwait while setting fire to an estimated 700 Kuwaiti oil wells. A long convoy of Iraqi troops, as well as Iraqi and Palestinian civilians, formed along the main Iraq-Kuwait highway. That convoy was bombed so relentlessly by the Allies that it came to be known as the "Highway of Death." One hundred hours after the ground campaign began, President Bush declared a cease-fire — declaring the liberation of Kuwait on February 27, 1991...

3D Sonic games can be a guilty pleasure. They have never reached the heights of 3D Mario games, even though they have tried - many times - to revitalize the excitement of the original Sonic Adventure. The original SA was a technical marvel back in the day, and also a pretty good game. But it also had terrible story, horrible side characters, and a lousy overworld. Many Sonic games have come and gone, ranging from terrible to pretty good. The newest game is a typical example of 3D Sonic games, in many ways: quite awesome at parts, and quite terrible at others.
Sonic Lost World, inexplicably, chooses to heavily invest in story, which has never been a strong suit for the series. But this shouldn't surprise us. Sega has always made bad decisions regarding Sonic. After realizing you can skip the cut scenes, you can start to enjoy the actual game. The visual aspects of the game - including the world design of the different areas of the game - are perhaps its best parts. (I said world design, not level design, quite consciously.) The game is pretty long, and luckily it doesn't have unskippable adventure portions or sections with Big The Cat, or Amy.
The game is "pure" Sonic. The Mario Galaxy-inspired gameplay feels derivative and never quite reaches the heights of its source of inspiration. There are still too many sudden deaths and camera angle frustrations. But once you get the hang of the controls, there is incredible fun to be had with SOME of the levels. The levels are colourful and speedy, and they range from 2.5D to 3D sections, just like Sonic Generations. Unfortunately the level design is a mixed bag. There are some truly wonderful levels, but there are also more than a few totally unfair, and frankly pointless, levels. Luckily, if you can't get past a particular checkpoint, you can eventually skip the part, although only after dying enough times (5 or so). This is a good design choice. Without the ability to skip some of the most unfair sections, it is doubtful I would have ever seen the end of the game. But I'm glad I played through to the end, since there are some good boss fights and awesome sequences to be experienced. The middle part of the game drags on and increases the frustration of the player, but the overall content of the game is positive. In addition to unfair and frustration levels, which obviously have no right to exist, there are some truly challenging (in a good way) levels, that utilize the game mechanics to wonderful effect.
I doubt we'll ever get a flawless masterpiece of a Sonic 3D game. This game is not even close. But it plays differently enough from the other Sonic games (because it mimicks Mario Galaxy pretty well) that it is an interesting experience.
I would recommend to game, at a discount price, for anybody who has two characteristics: 1) They are willing to excuse a lot of bad design choices. 2) They appreciate fast and fun 3D platforming. This game is a flawed, but quite a fun, platformer, which doesn't do anything to make the 3D Sonic games advance to A class. They are still not worthy of being called Mario rivals. But they are damn fun games.

Not too sure what to write here so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings

Sonic Lost World is yet another 3D and 2D Sonic platformer from Sega, which changes from Boost gameplay basic into new Parkour one. It was made to be Nintendo platforms exclusive in 2013 only to come out onto Steam in 2015. Made by Sonic Team. Get ready to face the sissy six!
It also came out for WiiU, as said, as well as 3DS. 3DS version is quite different, you know, same title, tried to do same theme but made from scratch, by Dimps.
Let's talk about differences between this release and original WiiU version that it's based on. First, each copy of game on Steam has Nightmare DLC, which was available only to bonus prepurchase edition of WiiU games, from what I read. Sadly,  Steam version it doesn't have two different DLCs, that are Zelda and Yoshi themed ones. No wonders, they are Nintendo licensed ones, so not blaming Sega.
WiiU also supported 2-player play, mostly races. One player has TV screen, another player has gamepad one. There is no multiplayer on PC.
That, and PC version doesn't use any other WiiU feature. Like, you can control Wisp powers normally, no fancy. Or there is no Wiiverse implention, so you can't exchange powerups with other players. Also, bomb powerup that you could get only through exchange is now part of mission rewards or Nightmare zone one.
So, WiiU might be the version that you want to get, but PC isn't bad either.
As for technical problems, yea, there are some with this release. Most importanly, this game is locked in 60 fps. I don't mind 30+ fps limits, but in this case it also means that if your computer can't handle 60 fps then gameplay itself will slow down, not daring to skip the frames. Thus, slooooooooooooooooooowwwwww Soooooooniiiiiiiiiiic!
Another bad glitch is that if the game detects while running that you have a controller that isn't xinput, then it's going to glitch up when you enter any cannon. Gameplay will just stop, nothing will happen. Pinball section in game also becomes unfinishable. So make sure that you play it with xinput gamepad. Keyboard is also possible, but please no, it's a platformer game.
And yea, Deadly Six. They are main antagonist of this game, and they are supposed to be Deadly. Maybe. The plot is actually not good. Wasted. All the silly soap opera happens in cutscenes and seems to have no meaning in the end, Tails sub-plot just going past without any special gameplay related to it, ending just comes. Yea, could be good. I recommend to just watch "Sonic Lost World in minutes" from Roger parody after beating this one.
And since it's Sonic game, it requires a separate mention of music. As usual, it's awesomesauce. No dissapointment. It actually has a different, less Sonic-like style to it. But by now, variety is a good thing. And look, it still has final boss music that is awesome, so there. Graphics are also simple, yet colorful and awesome.
And when you start the game the most obvious thing about this one you will notice is that it's actually a shameless ripoff of infamous Knuckler's Chaotix special stages and the cancelled Sonic Xtreme. Which means that actually developers try out something new, to use various geometry shapes and gravity to give players more interesting choices of movement and environment, with tubes, mini-planets and such. It's still a linear game though.
And most importantly, they changed Boost gameplay core into what they call Parkour. What it means is that while Sonic is much slower, you do much more of actual platforming, carefully positioning and having fun. As a gamer who's childhood was spent on the first Sonic The Hedgehog, I really enjoy this aspect. I sure missed. The feature of this gameplay is that Sonic now learned how to parkour, which in this case means that he learned to run over the side of wall or right onto it, which is a very excellent idea. Closer to what I wanted 3D Sonic to be like.
Oh yea, and it has missions system. You can have three at the same time, but sadly they get to the point where instead of helping you to motivate to do something during main walkthrough, you have to go out of your way, possible into previous stages, and grind them out.
Sadly, one of game's fault is that it explains how it works really badly. Or, rather, not at all. Thus I highly recommend to read the Steam community guide that does exactly that, which is better than having pain due to, say, not knowing that you can kick enemies. Or how wall-running works. Or to learn that you can go fast because the spin dash is actually limitless and you can keep speeding and spinning.
Another thing is that game is quite hard. It's one of the harder Sonic games around, ignoring the 8-bit ones. You lose a lot of lives during stages. But you also gain more of lives. And I like it, an actual hard platforming. It does sadly have some gimmick stages that people don't enjoy, mostly snowball one, where you keep trial and erroring through, being hard to control. But oh well.
Sadly, this game has a huge flaw. The bosses suck. Badly. It actually is more like the usual sad rule of 3D platformers "hard stages, easy bosses", main innovation of Mario 64. The thing is, though, is that Sonic is a game with linear stage progression and the difference in difficulty between stages and bosses is way too huge. As a result every boss is anticlimatic and even final boss makes the game feel empty. Which is worsened by the fact that the plot itself holds on Deadly Six being Deadly. But while the boss battles are varied, they die in pretty much one or two hits, being empty air, making plot empty air as well.
But in the end, it's a good 3D platformer. I would recommend it, for gameplay and that stages are fun, while having awesome graphics and music. Just a shame that plot and bosses are almost not exist. I wish Sonic Team will keep moving in this direction, as I surely prefer this over the Boost mechanic.

A familiar and welcome addition to the Borderlands franchise with a new and unfamiliar take on gameplay within that universe.
Seeing the Borderlands world from a different perspective was quite fun. It takes the story based combat-heavy FPS RPG and expands the story-telling part of it into an almost movie-like graphic adventure. Not everyone is a fan of the Tell-tale style type of games but I think if you are at all invested into the Borderlands story then you will really enjoy this.
The game takes place after the events of Borderlands 2 and expands on a few details between. Not only is it a good story on it’s own, that introduces new characters and continues Pandora’s story, but it sets up a pretty interesting place for Borderlands 3 to pick up from once that is out.
I’m glad to be able to say that this game gets into the spirit of the humour that we have grown to expect from these games. Light-hearted and very amusing but can also tuck on your heart strings in the right moments. I have actually played this through twice now and I can actually say that the second time around was just as fun, if not more. The first time around I found this slightly more ridiculous in humour than it’s predecessors, one moment it is totally serious and you’re nearly in tears and the next you’re genuinely wondering what the hell is going on with a mixture of laughter and utter confusion. I’m looking at you Chapter 4.
All in all I really enjoyed this game. I’m a fan of Tell-tale but an even bigger fan of Borderlands and I would say this is by far my favourite Tell-tale game to date.
In terms of achievements this is an easy 100%, all you have to do is complete the game.
TL;DR : If you are a fan of Borderlands definitely try it. It’s different but it’s a great addition to the franchise.

I just finished playing Gunpoint, a really great game from a first-time developer. This came out over a year ago, but the Mac version didn't get released until recently…
This game is fun. This game is funny. This game is self-aware, has great music, great pixel art, interesting mechanics, a decent story, and most surprisingly, choice that actually feels "meaningful"…
…More meaningful then many AAA, big-budget titles that I've played, where choice basically comes down to binary decisions that amount to little more then either a) rescue the orphans from a cartoon villain, or b) burn the orphanage down yourself (thus becoming the cartoon villain). In Gunpoint, you have choice about who to work for, how to achieve your objectives, and how much to cooperate with your clients.
In terms of game mechanics, there may be multiple ways to approach any given mission, and various levels of success in completing your objectives (were you a "ghost", never being detected, or did you have to knock a couple of guards out, or worse?)—this game certainly has replay value (I'll probably replay it at least once).
At the end of a play-through, you get to sum up your feelings in a "blog post" that generates an actual web page—a pretty cool way to contextuilze your experience, as well as promoting it to your friends. Congratulations to the developer for actually USING the term "ludonarrative dissonance" inside the actual game!

At the height of Alpha level, you are very restricted in what skills and ships you can have. A handful of destroyers, the very first tier of mining ships, and skills that will not give you a chance to survive in firefights against subscription players that have been playing for a while. Even weapons and drones are limited, so you can only equip weaker weapons and can't even use mining drones. You'll be hard pressed to make a million credits in a reasonable amount of time, when buying PLEX with in game money costs upwards of a billion credits. Doing so as an Alpha-level is not feasable. It pains me to say it, but I recommend you do NOT buy this DLC. It's fan-made and unfortunately, it shows.
There is a strange 'sliding' effect where you continue moving for a second after you stop input. For precision platforming, that's a big no-no. Enhancing the problem is poor level design where a lack of precise measurement will drop you to your death very frequently. (Compare that to the original games where so long as you jumped from roughly Point A to roughly Point B, you could be sure of landing safely 99% of the time.)
Trial and error is required to work out which screens will kill you or fizzle the cube and which won't (and which will allow you to shoot through them/which won't). There is at least one section where it seems that the level was designed for movement A but due to gel not adhereing as it should, only movement B is possible. There is at least one section where the voice-over repeats itself. Often, the voice will talk to you at the very end of levels with nothing to do or look at but the exit and no way of knowing if this is a 'scenic' exit that will let you listen to them as you travel the piped or a 'loading now' exit.
It probably would have been a good idea to give the gel gun a third mode - water - so you can erase mistakes or annoyingly large sections of blue without having to kill yourself. Also, relying on the physics engine to get the occasional cube onto a button is never a good idea unless it reliably works almost every time. It does not.
The opening had potential but the credits were too long and too intrusive. Spoiled the illusion.
Not worth the money, even the relatively little they ask.

Bleh...
So I invested about 90 hours into this game. 89 of which was being afk docked in a station, reading forums or watching videos on how to actually play it. /s...but not /s at the same time...
Overall, EVE Online shows its age in a number of ways that make it just kind of "meh." I'm presenting my opinion here, my overall thought is its ok to check it out for curiosity sake, but don't waste your money.
The bottom line is, the internet community in general can be toxic. Now, imagine if every chat troll had guns, and were in the same room as you. That's EVE in a nutshell.
Pros:
-It has spaceships. If the people killing you leave your escape capsule alive long enough, you can get to see some that you'll never be able to afford.
Cons:
-Its not as massive as it makes itself out to be.
This is an age issue. Today's open-world MMOs are huge. Alot of that has to do with the art design and scale. EVE has a space background, but it feels more like going through an underground pipe system. It is divided into series of small "rooms" in each space system, that you can only travel to through gates, or by warping within a system. So its less like flying around, more just hopping room to room. This is also how most PVP happens, with factions setting up ambushes on the other side of a gate, so when you come in you are met with a volley of missiles before you can escape. If you scroll out all the way, you can see how small the room actually is. Eve would have been amazing back when it first came out, but its not that impressive compared to nowadays standards.
-PVP.
This game advertises and prides itself on a continuous PVP environment. However, you have to remember how old this game is. Every slice of space has been claimed, and the large Corps (corporations are EVE's version of guilds) keep themselves alive by forming giant alliances. The actual PVP in this game is based on ambushing/ganking, primarily outside of gates or trade hubs. The large Corps accomplish this by "blanket wardecs." Wardecs, or war declarations, is one Corp declaring war on another. Blanket decs are done by literally sitting outside a trade hub and declaring war on everyone that is not part of their alliance. This allows their members to kill and steal everyone's stuff at will.
The primary target for PVP is new players, or small Corps that can't fight back. This itself is not a bad thing...remember some people have spent years of their lives and thousands of RL dollars getting the best ships, skills, and equipment. But as a new player you are totally at their mercy.  The wars you see on the videos are staged events primarily, PVP is 99% raids and ambushes outside of gates or trade hubs.
-Corps (corporations)
So you want to avoid being a victim? Good luck getting into a established Corp. The reason is the game is divided between Alpha (free players) and Omega (subscribing players). As a new player you are an Alpha, however so are the spy alts of all the older players. Paranoia is rampant in this game, so most Corps won't take new or Alpha players because they don't trust you. The ones that will are smaller Corps that just get brutalized so are always trying to find more people. Literally if you look up the "war logs" in game, most involve massive slaughter on one side, and no ship losses on the other side.
-Paywall
This game is P2W. That's ok, think of being an Alpha player like a trial account. However, a free account is locked out of all the good stuff. If you want to be relevant, you have to drop serious money. There is a subscription fee, but since skills are trained by timers in queues, if you don't want to wait you can drop $20 a PLEX, which will give you 30 days of Omega time, or 1 skill injector (500k skill points). Keep in mind established Corps won't take you unless you have like 2 million skill points or even more in some cases.
Skill doesn't matter. Only fitting (ship equipment) matters. Combat is by mouse clicks (you don't manually fly your ship), victory is just numbers. If your DPS and armor is higher than your opponent's DPS and armor you win. Alphas are limited to a low tier of gear.
I list this as a con because in alot of games like ESO the sub benefits are mostly cosmetic or convenience. In EVE, if your sub runs out you can't fly your ship or use any equipment that is Omega tier. An Alpha ship won't even be able to complete some of the PVE missions, and in PVP are just used as "suicide gankers" because its understood you won't survive any battle you're in.
-Clunky
The UI is bad. Everything is basically point and click. The tutorials are so bad that there are volunteer moderators in the "rookie help" chat channel, and Corps like Eve University to try and help people understand the game. For example, the "exploration" tutorial mission doesn't tell you how to use your scan probes, and the entire career path is based on using your scan probes...its just really wierd. Nothing is intuitive Fanbois write it off as "it doesn't hold your hand" or "git gud noob," but the reality is the gameplay aspect is totally outdated.
-Community
People play MMOs for lots of reasons. I play them to interact with people. The best way I can desribe EVE is imagine you move to a new neighborhood, then go to a party where everyone else already knows each other. You try to mingle, but you're an outsider, and everyone thinks you're there to steal things from the house. Some of them seem friendly, but you realize its because the rent on the house is due, and they want you to donate money for it. They tolerate you as long as you have an interest in paying. Then they randomly punch you in the mouth. If you don't run away screaming, they offer you a job mowing their lawn. That is the rest of your lfie, because  the truth is the house is crumbling, and you're 15 years too late to ever be one of the family.
TL;DR: there's way too many games out there to spend money on this. If you want to play on a free account, it might be worth it just to be part of the experience while it lasts. EVE does have things like the record for the largest ever PVP battle and some fun history. But for a older game it seems to be selling itself based on things long past, and its way more expensive than newer and more polished things you could be playing.

This is basically the same game as Solitaire Christmas: Match 2 Cards but with different music and new card layouts.  As such, I'm copying with small changes, the same review below.
Personally, I enjoyed it.  It's a simple relaxing solitaire game.  The music is soothing and catchy.  Quite a lot of levels which lends itself to the one-more-turn syndrome.  And these levels add just enough variety not to make it too repetitive.  Different levels, based on the different card locations and number of shuffles lends a bit of strategy to where in the layout to focus one's matches.
It's not without it's flaws though.  Card clicking can be frustratingly non-responsive and takes a bit of getting used to.  And the most annoying thing for me was the "Earn 1,000,000 coins" achievement which actually means you need to gather a total of 1,000,000 coins at the same time.  I mistakenly spent a lot of coins on upgrades and had to grind 100,000s of coins just to finish the final achievement.  If one is conservative with upgrades, you'll hit 1 million coins well before the finish at which point you can start spending like crazy to finish the last levels and get the "Use XXX Upgrades" achievements.  And this game has the additional problem that the stack of cards leans too close to the play piles making it very easy to click it by accident when you don't want to.  I don't recall having that issue with Solitaire Chrismas: Match 2 Cards.
Overall, despite it's flaws and simplicity, there is quite a bit of game time to it which made it worth it's asking price for me.  Not going to say it's a "must buy" or anything like that.  It could be more polished (see flaws above), but I enjoyed it as a nice casual game.  At $1 more than Solitaire Christmas and an additional flaw, it's less of a recommendation, but given it sucked 40 hours of my time, it's worth the price.

A nice time-waster type of game that I find strangely addicting.   I wil keep playing the same level over and over until I get the lucky break where the cards are in a good random order and I'm able to get a perfect score.  But I might end up playing 10 times before that with crappy scores.   It reminds me of old-fashioned solitaire (the one that used to come free with Windows) that I would play every day even though I lost 75% of the time!  There's just that thrill when finally everything goes right.  Must be some endorphin release in my brain or something like that and I get addicted to the feeling.
Anyway, basically you click on two cards of the same number (or King, Queen, etc) to clear them from the board.  There are a certain number of gold cards per level (anywhere from 5-7) and you have to clear all the gold cards to get a perfect score.     The levels are arranged in sections, 10 each, and you can't go on to the next section until you get a certain number of gold cards cleared in the entire section.  It counts by the max you have ever gotten, not cumulative when you replay a level.
There are cheats you can use to help you out: Shuffle, Mulligan (go back one step), and Wild Card.  Occasionally you will get them through play or you can buy them from the in-game store with money earned from matching cards.  Note to achievement hunters, though, DO NOT buy anything until you have earned 1,000,000 coins because there is an achievement for that.  Just keep playing and earning coins until you've gotten that million, then you can buy all the bonus cheat things you want because there are achievements for buying a certain number of them and using them.  It will take a looooooong time to get all the achievements (this ain't no Zup game!)
Theme is tropical, each area has a different background (sorry no chicks in bikinis) and you can choose from several different patterns of card backs also.  Music is soothing boring background music.  I turn it off and play my own but I keep the sound affects on for that Zing! sound.
tldr:
Addicting time waster
Achievements are all doable but will take a looooong time
2 difficulty levels: Tourist (easy) and Traveller (hard)

I'm confused by the Sonic franchise; everytime a game comes out it's apparently the worst game ever. I remember this title coming out for the WiiU and getting destroyed, and I also remember Sonic Colors coming out for the Wii and receiving the same treatment.
I played Sonic Colors; it was actually a fantastic game with a great soundtrack. And I've played this title, and it's NOT a bad game. So it's either one of two things: either the Sonic franchise is legendarily good and the games never live up to the Half-Life esque levels of expectations, or a segment of people blindly hate the series.
Whatever the case, Sonic Lost World is the previously WiiU exclusive Sonic title which was created with some collaboration by Nintendo. It shows; Unlike Colors or Generations (the last two 'mainline' Sonic games), Lost World is a slower, more platform oriented game in the vein of Mario titles. Not all levels are speed affairs whereby you have to make quick jumps and precise moves to get onto the faster path down the course. Granted, Colors had less of this than Generations, but Lost World is even slower than that.
This isn't to say the game isn't fast. It's still a Sonic title and there are plenty of levels and segments that are speed affairs requiring quick reflexes, but for a Sonic game there's an unusually higher amount of 'slower' segments than these games typically contain. The experience isn't a constant, though. By which I mean: some levels are pure speed, others are entirely on-rails with you needing to jump from rail to rail, whilst a few are entirely 2D platforming levels. Overall it's a thoroughly mixed experience that feels 'experimental', with the developers trying out a bunch of different ideas. In many ways this feels more like Mario Galaxy 2 in how the levels can vary wildly in both length and design.
In general, that variety maintains the game fresh and adds to the title. But some levels, like the slower, mario galaxy-esque 3D platforming levels I could do without. It's not that they were bad, it's that I don't wanna play Mario; I wanna play Sonic. Thankfully they're kept to a minimum and there are, like, less than 5 of those levels. But there's also some of the 2D levels which are also a little slow, and the on-rails levels which are pretty meh and linear to a fault. Granted, these aren't really critiques as the levels aren't bad, they're just not to my particular liking and wants in a Sonic title; you may disagree.
Overall it's nothing amazing or groundbreaking like the levels in Sonic Unleashed and Generations; like I've said, the game feels somewhat experimental in how much variety it has. One of the downsides to that is that you may not always hit the mark, but this game generally stays close to it (or close enough to it) for me to have enjoyed my purchase. I'd say it's a forgettable Sonic title that doesn't do anything wrong, tries variety in its levels to varying results, and as a whole is a game to play and spend your free time with. In other words, not one of those ''must-play'' games that you MAKE time for, but more of a game that you SPEND time you have.
Don't get the wrong impression; it's a good game. Just nothing astounding or worth noting; I'd give it a mild recommendation. If you have better games to play go for it, but since I'm somewhat of a fan of the series I'd say it was alright. It's certainly not a bad entry into the franchise, but it's also not noteworthy. It's just....another entry...into the franchise. If you like Sonic games you'll like this one, but you won't love it like Generations.
It's worth noting that 3D platformers are somewhat rare nowadays, so it helps the title stand out. Unlike Colors or Generations, which I'd tell you to play, I'd say you can skip over this one. Not because its bad, but because it's whatever.

Oh Sega, where did you go so wrong? I can pretty much sum up the main reasoning that Sega has lost touch with Sonic in one sentance: There is a sprint button. If you're not constantly holding down the trigger on your controller, Sonic walks at a dreadfully slow pace. What happened to the always "Gotta go fast!" mentality? This leads to a whole other issue in the game's ice level, in which if you barely move left or right while holding sprint, you slide incredibly fast in that direction, making it awfully difficult to dodge obstacles correctly.
A lot of the reviews here are mentioning Super Mario Galaxy, and that's definitely true. 3D worlds and jumping between random planets, but the charm of Galaxy is missing. All you need to do is pratically run from one end of each "planet" to the next. The level design in Frozen Factory is probably some of the most frustrating, as a whole chunks of the level are placed on a single planet, resulting in a long amount of backtracking to where you were if you fail a jump. I believe the most fun I had was in a (literally) on-rails grinding section. There was a fun little rolling snowball section, but the final boss was incredibly frustating, with it being hit-or-miss as to whether you'd actually damage your targets.
The tutorial is lackluster, never telling you what you want to hear, but appearing frequently for the most annoying reasons. The color aliens from Sonic Colours are back, but we've never had Sonic Colours on PC, meaning you won't know what most of them do until you use them. And on the other side of the spectrum, every single time a power runs out the game feels the need to pop up a "This colour's power has been depleted", which was already fairly obvious. The game has some kind of item system, but it never explains anything about it at any point. Thus I've played through the game without using it once, and still don't have a clue now.
In all, I'd say you want to get this cheap in a sale, and go in with low expectations. C'mon Sega, Sonic 4 Episode 2 was a good move forward, don't mess it up now!

I have mixed feelings about it. It could be absolutely great if not for some not most important but still annoying things.
First of all - the most important part - platforming - is great! Both in 2D and 3D parts it's responsive, levels are imaginative, like always in Sonic games give you choice between many routes, encourage exploration, replaying, have score attacks and time runs - a lot of fun. Only nitpick I have is that there are very few really fast parts, I'd expect more of them from a game about extra-fast hedgehog ;)
Graphics are mediocre. It can be easily seen it's a WiiU port and that WiiU is not a powerful machine. In some parts it looks worse than older Sonic Generations.
Now to actual problems.
First off story and enemy characters. Sonic games were never known for great stories and you don't really need epic tales in a colorful platformer, but this game takes the crown for the most stupid, boring and unimaginative plot ever presented in any Sonic game. Top it with the worst enemies ever (they are the most cliche baddies you could ever think of, have nothing to them except for one attribute that 'defines' them aka this guy is a glutton and only wants to eat, this guy is an emo, hates the world and want to die, this chick is totally self involved and wants to polish her nails all day long) and it becomes really hard to get invested into the story at all.
Another big problem is total lack of any tutorial, in-game explanation, actual tooltips, important UI elements etc. For example - you do missions and collect items which you can use later on. But game only show you an icon of an item without any explanation what it does. You have to either memorize all the icons or alt-tab to check items in the internet all the time. Another example - game introduces new mechanics and expect you to use them without even informing you you can do anything new. Like you don't learn anywhere what is Sonic Kick, how is it any different from Homing Attack (their animations are very similar btw, so you can go for most of the game not even aware you have two kind of attacks), or you are never informed that you can charge your homing attack and do it up to 5 times. Then you are simply presented with a boss that wil require first breaking his defense with Kick, then moving him through platform with charged attacks, then kicked again, then charged up to 5 then attacking. And you never even had to use any of these mechanics before, you don't even know you have such attacks. Again you are forced to look for guides and manuals on the internet, because without them you are simply wasting your time on unbeatable part of the game. It's one thing to learning boss patterns, it's another trying to beat a boss which requires you to use special attack you don't even know you have because the game never informed you about it.
That being said it's still a good platformer. It could be great, it could be SEGA's version of Mario Galaxy, but as it is it's only good but I don't think it will become a cult classic. Still if you can look past it's problems you can have a lot of fun with it.
