Hi there and welcome to a long review about 'Tales from the Borderlands.'
First, I'm a huge fan of Borderlands franchise. I bought all the games, all the DLCs (except the costumes DLCs), and ready to play 'em anytime if someone asks me to. Literally my first game that I bought on Steam is Borderlands 2. And from that purchase, I'm beginning to turn into an addict person who just loves Borderlands so much. Trust my words, IT IS A
Plot (10/10) :
The story takes place after the events from Borderlands 2 & Borderlands The Pre-Sequel. You play as Rhys, a salary man at Hyperion and a fanboy of Handsome Jack. Rhys has a best friend called Vaughn. Together, you'll do your first mission to steal a deal from Vasquez, which is a guy that you really hate in Hyperion. Stole 10 million dollars and buy a vault key from August. But, later in the game, your mission gets bigger and bigger. You will play from a different perspective here. Yeah, you will play as another character with another objective. You will play as another character called Fiona, a con artist who teamed up with Sasha, her sister, which is also a con artist. Fiona and Sasha set a deal with August to sell a vault key to a guy named Vasquez, but it turns out to be Rhys. The deal went off, just saying. Your mission, which is to buy a vault key, turns into a mission to opening a vault. And remember, this is one of the Borderlands franchise, so prepare to get mind blown with the damn plot twist.
Art (9/10) :
The art still suits the Borderlands franchise with a touch from Telltale Series, but seriously, the art feels like a completely Borderlands franchise and it feels like Telltale didn't even touch the art style. The Borderlands franchise has its own unique art style that I found myself fell in love with.
Sounds (8/10) :
Why an 8? Because sometimes when the character says a line, the intonation just doesn't fit in for me. Despite that, the music in this game is good with the sound effects that fits into the scene. The jokes in this game are unbearable. It is so good that you suddenly forgot that you've cried a few minutes ago. Yes, I did not expect to cry when I played this game, but boy I cried.
Gameplay (10/10) :
It's the usual Telltale Series, so obviously it's a choice maker and your choices will definitely do something about the next events in the game. I made some wrong decisions in this game, but do I regret it? No, not even a single one. This game has 5 episodes to play with an average of 2 hours per episode. I recommend when you play this game, do a one episode session. I'm saying this because I didn't enjoy the time when I was really tired and I have to go to sleep and ended up closing the game. It's so frustrating to wait until the next morning to play this game again.
OVERALL (9,8/10) :
This game is too good for me. I just love the way how they started an intro of an episode. which is pretty epic and I love how they do it. You want some sneak peek? Go to my screenshots and see it for yourself.
This game is RECOMMENDED for you who loves story-based and choice-maker kind of games. But if you want to play this game, I suggest you to play the Borderlands 2 & the Borderlands The Pre-Sequel to completely understand where is this story began. But if you don't wanna do that, that's completely fine. I'm just saying that if you play those 2 games first, you'll be able to enjoy this game at its finest.
What are you waiting for? Go get some money and buy this game!

EvE is for:
My Pros;
- A strong community that is less toxic, and more mature. (Usually) Average age here is much, much higher than most games, and most of the time the reviews I see online and in person are from a) people who want instant gratification in their games, which usually leans towards the younger spectrum of players who don't end up enjoying EvE. (I didn't until I was older and tried several times.)
- A sense of danger at all times.
- Not pay to win. (Not sure how some people think this.)
- Alpha is free to play, but there are limits due to how fragile the game is as it is a free market. CCP employes five full-time Economists on its staff.
- Something no other game has been able to do well, and has been around for well over a decade to boot.
- Space and how beautiful it is.
- Every person can make an impact. Grouping up feels amazing when you acomplish something.
- Real politics and war.
- One server. That's it. No "Hey, what server do you play on?"
My cons;
- First starting, this can be pretty daunting. Join up with a newbie corp. Or do what I did; read the wiki everytime you're in the bathroom sitting on the toilet. That's how I learned fast.
- First starting, you have to train a lot of skills needed, and you can't do a whole lot right away. You have, HAVE to specilize in something early to start making isk.  While it seems tempting to try and crosstrain four careers or more at once, it can feel hectic. In a month, you can get really good at one thing, then focus on the other. It'll take you that long just to sorta learn that career.
Overall;
This is the most unique experiences. The emotions that run from this are unlike any other and bleed into your personal feelings in an amazing way. The people you meet, the stories that you are a part of, they're all there.
It's not for everyone, and it's hard to get into for some (took me four times before I found a corp/alliance that I never wanted to leave), the feeling you get from EvE is unlike anything else, and I have tried to find anything close to it, and nothing ever comes close.

This game is one that I have enjoyed since I was very young. It is basically a Star Wars Age of Empires II, but with some added and changed features too add to the Star Wars feel (Shields, Blasters, Aircraft, Lightsabers,Robots, etc,). This game has alot of things going for it, The campaign is ok and allow you to experience Star Wars from multiple perspectives not captured in the films (Trade Federation, Empire, CIS, etc). In addition to the campaigns there is a skirmish mode which allows you to play as any faction in the game and to face any faction in game.
The strategy layer can be as simple as "shoot that building till it explodes" or as in depth as directing your siege weapons to attack structures and fortified positions while directing your other ground forces to engage the enemy's. Despite the negetive reception that this game has gotten I think that for a mod of a game this is good content! Because my parents didnt really let me play video games when I was a kid, I only recently discovered the awesomeness of Valve and the gaming world. Needless to say, after I finished Portal 2 back in February/March of this year I felt I needed more! So when I saw the preview for this game on youtube I was estatic.
Things that were great:
1. The Soundtrack. I loved the Portal 2 soundtrack so much, and this is a very good addition to my music library. It had its own style, while still sticking to the same themes as Portal. Its clear to me that a lot of work was put into this.
2. The 'recycled' levels: I enjoyed how this game took us back to some of the levels from Portal 2 and how we (at the beginning) saw old Aperture. To me that was really cool. I saw some people complaining about that, but I believe that it actually improved the game because it gave us a time frame. We were clearly there a long time after Chell escaped. It also contained one of my personal favorite levels and songs, Test Chamber 18. That really put a smile on my face.
3. Multiple Solutions: Many of these levels has multiple solutions and I think that's a great idea, because I find that when you play a puzzle game like Portal, unless you missed an easter egg, it has little replay value. (Though I still replay Portal 2 all the time anyway). So it's nice to have to think other ways.
4. Multiple Endings: I think games with multiple endings are as cool as levels with many solutions. For those who havent found the other ending, keep looking :)
Now onto critisms:
1. Voice acting: I think that the voice acting was okay, a little rough at points, but with some hard work he could make a career out of it! Also, I think a good idea for the voice of Nigel would have been to alter his voice to sound more electronic like GLADOS. Just a thought though.
2. Difficulty: The puzzles were either extremely easy, or a little bit tempermental. Though it does add a challenge, the orange gel mechanic does need work.
3. Dialog: Going back to the voice acting for a minute, some of the humor in it was rather forced, and in my opinion, a little too childish for Aperture Science. Like sure, I still laugh at poo/pee jokes, but I still think there would be a better way of implementing a little humor in to the game.
Oh and one more thing, people are allowed to charge money for things they spent a long time on. If I had a lemonade stand and asked for money would you blame me for charging, just because someone else invented the idea of a lemonade stand? Probably not.
In conclusion, this game is worth your money and your time, as long as you arent expecting an acutal Portal 3 with professional actors, design etc.
Thanks for reading~

To be honest, I don't know whether to recommend this or not.  I love the concept, but there's just something.... lacking.... in the execution.
I'll start with a disclaimer: I'm horrible at the "classic platformer".  You know the type, jump at the exact second, not a millisecond to soon or too late, or you're in a pit.  Me, I end up living in those pits.  With Portal and Portal 2, it's different.  So long as you place your portals more or less correctly, you're generally good to go.  You don't need the twitchy reflexes and perfect positioning so much.
That being said, I found myself missing the jumps a LOT in this, and getting put back to the beginning of the level again again again and again.  I'm not saying I never fell in Portal 2, but in this, oh my god.  There was a level with a light bridge you hop onto and I must've over or under jumped it at least a dozen times.  The level design isn't nearly as intuitive and you end up trying the same jump over and over and over because it *has* to be the right way to go, but it is just out of reach somehow.
Gels are fun in Portal 2, but this becomes an exercise in frustration and I find myself having to walk away from it after only half an hour of play (if even) to keep from losing it.
I'm not totally against paying for mods.  I get that it takes a lot of time to make good ones.  I can't blame folks for trying to recoup something for all the hours put into developing it.  That being said, I just don't think this is quite there yet.  There will be folks that will enjoy this, but I'm not one of them.  I just find it too frustrating and unpolished.
I'll keep an eye on it, and give it another try should there be any significant updates, but until then, I think it'll be collecting dust on my virtual shelf.  A sad end for a great conceptual add-on to a game I love so much,

I just finished this game last night, and overall, I though it was decent. It had it's flaws, but I don't regret spending $5 on it.
The Good:
I will never, EVER get enough of seeing Aperture Science. The level design was fun, and none of the puzzles were counter intuitive or anything. Some were pretty fiendish, but once I'd solved them, I was like "It took me that long to figure out THAT?" Nigel, your guide through the test chambers, was fun to listen to, and I was surprised to find that I didn't miss GlaDOS at all. I had been expecting to miss her snarky humor, so it was pleasant to find that things move along just fine without her. Nigel is also pleasantly, well, pleasant. He seems to genuinely care about you and your safetly, which is quite the change for Aperture. His voice acting was superb. It was also a nice touch to have two different endings.
The Bad:
The game suffers from a few issues. The controls can be a bit wonky at times, and your directional control whilst in midair seems to come and go. There will be times you'll press spacebar to jump on the repulsion gel, and the game will cheerfully ignore your, often causing a death by falling into toxic waste. This issue also comes up sometimes when running down propulsion gel. You're supposed to jump automatically when hitting repulsion after running down propulsion, but sometimes the game just won't do it. There will also be times when you'll lose your forward momentum for no apparent reason, which reduces that epic leap into a feeble hop.
The Ugly:
The above issues are, at most, minor annoyances during the regular test chambers, but in the final area for Chapter 3, all of them combine to form the most hair pulling, screaming in fury, ragequitting experience I've had in a while. A timed race to the end that I was never able to get past because the game stubbornly refused to cooperate with me. Jumps would fail, forward speed would be lost, sliding off platforms could happen at random, culminating in a final jump that I was NEVER able to make, despite trying for two hours. The only saving grace was that I was able to skip it and jump to Chapter 4 via the Main Menu.
The Conclusion:
If you want to see more of Aperture and solve some good puzzles while playing with the gels, this is the game for you. If you're looking for tight controls and perfect physics, this is not the place to look. It's very good for a community made project, and I have to give props to the crew for turning out something this well done. Further tweaks were needed however, which sucked some of the fun out of it for me. Overall, I do recomend this game, just don't expect things to be perfect.

This is easily the greatest X-COM/Jagged Alliance alike you've never played. I am going to tell you why, with a bit history on the side.
Long before Aperion was founded and way back in the 90s, Vladimir Ufnarovskiy finished his college degree and proceeded to make his first computer game - Remember Tomorrow (or Pomni Budushcheye), a 4X title with a few unique spins. Sadly, that game didn't really take off anywhere, superseded in popularity by games like Master of Orion and the Russian multi-genre, cult classic Parkan: Imperial Chronicles. A modern reimaging of Remember Tomorrow was released on Steam months ago: Polaris Sector. That game is absolutely worth checking out if you want to scratch your 4X itch.
Apeiron came to frution in 1999 under Ufnarovskiy's direction, and in 2002, a free to play prototype of their first game E5 was released. It gained a lot of positive attention, and 1C offered support and funds to help turn it into a full retail title. The proof of concept version of E5 had the foundations of all of Aperion's games: intricate control of squadmates and insanely detailed bullet ballistics. It was a mild success in its native country, but hardly made a dent outside of it. Regardless, E5 has earned a place in the hearts of those who wanted to see what 7.62's precursor is like and stuck with it until the end.
7.62 was released as a direct sequel to E5 in late 2007, and improved upon its flaws in various ways. I'm not going to beat around the bush - the UI in E5 is horrid, but 7.62 improved interaction with the game and made it more easy to swallow for newcomers. 7.62 is Aperion's most well known title, and for a lot of good reasons. Have you ever wanted to take upon the role of an mercenary operator in the middle of some sweaty and hot fictional South American country undergoing a civil war? This is what makes 7.62 great, even if it does suffer from bugs. You can obsess over every little piece of equipment you can carry and see how it can serve you best. Combat feels confusing, weighty and incredibly satisfying all at once. Not a whole lot compares after seeing a hostile flop over dead when you shoot him with your hunting shotgun, or tagging mulitple hostiles at once with said weapon. Just about all of the missions in 7.62 in are 'go there and do this', but it's impossible to predict if you'll get there safely because of how frantic the combat is.
Sadly, there is a fly in the ointment for just about all of Aperion's games: the meele combat feels like an afterthought, but that's something to expected for an game engine that puts so much thought into how firearms affect everything. Along with this, all of their games are very ambitious and are riddled with bugs from development oversights. Still, if you have the patience and don't mind some bumps on the ride, you owe it to yourself to check out 7.62. A small, but incredibly dedicated community has worked to iron out the most offensive bugs, so make sure you take the time to see what fixes are out there.
Another thing to note is that Apeiron provided development and historical counselling when Battlefront was making Combat Mission: Afganistan. There's an extra little tidbit for you if you like the Combat Mission games.

Hi there and welcome to a long review about 'Tales from the Borderlands.'
First, I'm a huge fan of Borderlands franchise. I bought all the games, all the DLCs (except the costumes DLCs), and ready to play 'em anytime if someone asks me to. Literally my first game that I bought on Steam is Borderlands 2. And from that purchase, I'm beginning to turn into an addict person who just loves Borderlands so much. Trust my words, IT IS A
Plot (10/10) :
The story takes place after the events from Borderlands 2 & Borderlands The Pre-Sequel. You play as Rhys, a salary man at Hyperion and a fanboy of Handsome Jack. Rhys has a best friend called Vaughn. Together, you'll do your first mission to steal a deal from Vasquez, which is a guy that you really hate in Hyperion. Stole 10 million dollars and buy a vault key from August. But, later in the game, your mission gets bigger and bigger. You will play from a different perspective here. Yeah, you will play as another character with another objective. You will play as another character called Fiona, a con artist who teamed up with Sasha, her sister, which is also a con artist. Fiona and Sasha set a deal with August to sell a vault key to a guy named Vasquez, but it turns out to be Rhys. The deal went off, just saying. Your mission, which is to buy a vault key, turns into a mission to opening a vault. And remember, this is one of the Borderlands franchise, so prepare to get mind blown with the damn plot twist.
Art (9/10) :
The art still suits the Borderlands franchise with a touch from Telltale Series, but seriously, the art feels like a completely Borderlands franchise and it feels like Telltale didn't even touch the art style. The Borderlands franchise has its own unique art style that I found myself fell in love with.
Sounds (8/10) :
Why an 8? Because sometimes when the character says a line, the intonation just doesn't fit in for me. Despite that, the music in this game is good with the sound effects that fits into the scene. The jokes in this game are unbearable. It is so good that you suddenly forgot that you've cried a few minutes ago. Yes, I did not expect to cry when I played this game, but boy I cried.
Gameplay (10/10) :
It's the usual Telltale Series, so obviously it's a choice maker and your choices will definitely do something about the next events in the game. I made some wrong decisions in this game, but do I regret it? No, not even a single one. This game has 5 episodes to play with an average of 2 hours per episode. I recommend when you play this game, do a one episode session. I'm saying this because I didn't enjoy the time when I was really tired and I have to go to sleep and ended up closing the game. It's so frustrating to wait until the next morning to play this game again.
OVERALL (9,8/10) :
This game is too good for me. I just love the way how they started an intro of an episode. which is pretty epic and I love how they do it. You want some sneak peek? Go to my screenshots and see it for yourself.
This game is RECOMMENDED for you who loves story-based and choice-maker kind of games. But if you want to play this game, I suggest you to play the Borderlands 2 & the Borderlands The Pre-Sequel to completely understand where is this story began. But if you don't wanna do that, that's completely fine. I'm just saying that if you play those 2 games first, you'll be able to enjoy this game at its finest.
What are you waiting for? Go get some money and buy this game!

Are you tired of playing One Piece fighter games and want to play as your favorite One Piece character while battling hordes of enemies? Then choose this game. Per map you play you have thousands of enemies waiting for you, and sometimes some bigger dudes which want to stop you.
There are 3 different modes: Story mode, "Free log", and "Dream log"
In Story mode you can play selected episodes of the one piece timeline, up until the famous dress rosa arc. There are different additional goals for each episode which challenge you and add replay value.
In free log you basicly play the same story missions, but you can freely choose from all unlocked characters. Want to help usopp beating captain kuro while playing smoker? Do you want to fight at marinefort with enel? This is the mode which allows that.
the dream log has a lot of ilands with different themes and missions. You pick your character, travel to an island and choose, which party you want to support. There are also random enemies with bountys, traveling around the see and which you can hunt.
You can level your character and additionaly increase his strength with coins from beaten opponents or characters which helped you. At some situations its wiser to repeat a mission to farm some coins and boost your power instead of trying to beat the next mission for the 100th time.
If you are familar with "warriors" games, then you get what you expect. The only small downside for me is the locked levelcap at 50, which can be increased to 100 later on. But you are unable to level the characters beyond 50 with berries.
Besides that I had a lot of fun playing this game so far. I still haven't unlocked everything so I jump back every now and then to sail accross the see and fight tough enemies.
At a last note: I highly recommend using a controler.

Nice indie tower defence game. Took around 20-30hrs of playtime to 100%. Much of the playtime is used in formulating a strategy for the upcoming night; determining which traps to use, where to place them, and how to create and use chokepoints on the map. The map is basically the same each night, but expands into a different area every few days. The variability from one level to the next therefore comes from differences in which enemies will attack, how many waves you'll face, and where on the map they'll all spawn. During the fight, you play in 3rd person perspective, luring enemies into your traps but also fighting them with your axe and rifle.

Essentially, they took the updated engine from Dying Light, ported over some resources, and gave the game "high definition" graphics and improved post-processing effects. Due to the updated engine, no one really knows the metric for adjusting the converted numbers in its configuration files, and I fear little interest will be placed in such. It's been over a year now, and I'm as disappointed now as I was then. I would say, if you have interests like mine, get the original, as well as its "sequel", Dead Island: Riptide, and enjoy the plethora of mod support and texture overhauls that make the game come close to this reskin.

This game use to be super cool. It was basically War Thunder/ World of Tanks but you built your machine. It revolved around you protecting your pilot seat, the core block to your ship, in your mech while trying to destroy the enemies. You only had one life so it was your goal to make a mech that could take some hits and still be able to make it through the fight. If you died, you just left the game and queued into a new game. They even added some medical guns later on so other people could repair your damage. Progression was in teirs and each block had a weight that would add up to place you in a rank.
So a hacking problem started to break out that had to be linked to bad programming because you just edited some text file and you could do things like 0 reload times. So freejam forced everyone to install some anti-cheat that was super invasive and would literally screenshot your computer and upload it a server to see if you were cheating. I was a beta tester for this program, and I've got to say, it is pretty good. However, I wont hesitate to point out what needs to be fixed :)
First of all, DBM can make a pretty decent bot, in the time I've used it, I have made a fairly average bot. DBM can make advanced bot mechanics as well, like leveling system and image manipulation. Looking through its pre-existing features, I do believe that you can make a fairly advanced bot if you put the time into it.
I have seen many people talk about the pricing of DBM. I can understand why many people aren't too happy about it. The developer did make the mistake of giving a pricing estimate too early and he has acknowledged that. However, DBM is actually well worth it. The developer has put a lot of time into making this, and he has had a lot of struggles as well as sometimes having to remake entire sections of the program again. I think he is deserving of the price, and DBM can currently do a good amount of bot making so I think it is worth it.
Despite it having a lot of features, for beginners, it isn't actually all that easy to understand at first. It can look fairly hard to understand, but once you know how to use it, I think you can create some pretty good bots. Fortunately the developer has said that he will post tutorials, hopefully this along with the Discord Server for DBM will help people who find it difficult to use.
The developer has also been very professional and calm when responding to people and criticism. He takes in suggestions and feedback. I have no doubt that he will make it even better in the future to come.
As well as the already existing features, for advanced programmers, it is easily possible to add your own actions into the program to fit your own needs.
I will say that there are a few features that I'd like to see:
-Changing prefix
-Reading and writing data to files.
-Obtaining information from the internet (from sites like YouTube etc)
-A kill command to turn off the bot
-Role requirements for commands (instead of just permission requirements)
-Voice channel support (joining VC etc)
-Dragging/moving around commands for organisation purposes
Some features that were originally planned weren't added due to time constraints, which I can understand. The developer has said that he will continue to update DBM so I hope these features will come eventually.
Overall, I think DBM is a very good program. It can make fairly advanced bots (although it's not the easiest thing to do). It does lack voice support, but that will come soon and it can look complex for someone who has no knowledge in coding and/or bots. The program will be updated in the future and there will be tutorials made on the program so I hope to see it become a top tier bot maker.

+ Visually the game looks absolutely amazing. It's hard to believe, but they did an amazing job recreating DBZ in a 3D space with beautifully crafted models and environments. While watching some of the cutscenes it almost felt like an improved version of the Anime.
+ Story-wise Dragon Ball fans can rejoice. This game includes all of the most memorable scenes from Dragon Ball Z, some from GT, and some new content with new characters to fight against.
+ Voice-actors directly from the show for essentially every character. I love it!
+ The combat system is fantastic. It's fast paced and action packed without having to remember long button combos like in other fighting games. (Last DBZ game I played was Budokai 3, I felt this game's combat was very similar)
+ Tons of skills and abilities to learn. You can choose to be a close-ranged brawler or a long ranged ki blastor. It's actually pretty fun to try out every new skill you come across and find the best setup to your liking.
+ The game is quite challenging but can be very rewarding once you learn the mechanics.
+ Lots of content, 20hours+
+ Plenty of extra content, including a hidden Saga where you fight Broly
- Personally, I did not like the whole "time travel" story line. Time is being distorted, and you must go back in time to various era's to "correct the timeline" by helping defeat various memorable foes.
- I found that creating your own hero felt a bit out of place... I would have much rather enjoyed playing as Goku or the actual characters that fought in the time line events instead. You sort of just appear out of nowhere, and everyone is just like "who the heck is that guy?"
- The Difficulty and Grind.  This is my biggest issue with the game.  Basically the story-missions are reletively short, so they decided to severely up the difficulty as you progress to the point where you won't be able to win. You are supposed to stop every so often and do side-quests called "Parallel Quests" repetitively in order to level up your character and unlock new skills. Unfortunetely, these side-quests mainly consist of refighting the same exact enemies you fight in the story.
- RNG Drop Chance....skills and items are basically connected to Parallel Quests, and you have a random "chance" of earning a reward from doing a mission. The chance is very low and mixed in with other items. The problem with this is that skills that every DBZ fan wants, like Kaioken, Super Saiyan, etc. have a completely random chance of dropping during a particular mission. This means you can literally spend over an hour replaying the same mission over and over just to get a skill. (You CAN NOT buy these skills from the shop until far later in the game)
- I came across this by accident, but there seems to be an overpowered glitch involving the Blue Hurricane skill, the game somehow slows down and enemies get hit for an incredible amount of damage. (Spoiler: Super Saiyan + Blue Hurricane = Win)
- The "Resurrection 'F' Pack is a bit overpowered for new players. I bought the Bundle Edition, and the game literally gives you some of the best gear in the game, and lets you play as God Goku, Vegeta, and Golden Frieza straight from the start making Parallel Quests extremely easy.

First off: I can see why people don't like this game. If you like it, congratulations. I like it too. The story is simple, and so is the gameplay. Controls are good, etc. Level design is also good, and balanced between speed and platforming.
While there's no breaking any sound or light barrier in this game, gameplay is still relatively fast.
Parkour is a new mechanic, and is the only thing I both love and hate in this game. It's difficult to learn, but when you do, it feels so satisfying to parkour across the level.
Story is surprisingly simple this time around. Won't be Adventure 2 or Unleashed level of story, more like Generations.
Dialouge is... okay. Some jokes were just stupid, some made me chuckle, and some made me laugh.
The main enemies were.... okay, I can see why we haven't seen them since.
If you're worrying about glitches, because of the franchise's reputation with glitches, you won't find many here. Some minor, some normal, few game-breaking. You won't be dying every four seconds by clipping through the floor. This ain't '06 or Rise of Lyric.
Overall, I recommend this game to both Sonic fans and Newcomers, but if you're expecting speed like Unleashed and Generations, look somewhere else.

A very fun and lighthearted murder mystery puzzle platformer. You're a megajumping gumshoe on the case, trying to solve the murder of one of your prospective clients. You do this by jumping, climbing, and hacking objects all while trying to not get shot by the numerous guards patrolling the secured facilities you are infiltrating. The gameplay is snappy and has multiple options for reverting to a time checkpoint when you're killed, allowing for rapid iteration. The writing is well done and genuinely funny, and the music suits the narrative.

For those a fan of meticulous strategy, this game is for you. If you are a fan of RTS, you'll likely be bored. 7,62 plays at a slow pace. In my current 89 hours of gameplay, I've experienced a couple of firefights that sucked up two hours of time. Due to the player-controlled pausing system in which you can stop time to give directions to your mercinaries, an hour-long realtime firefight can be composed of only three or four minutes of action.
That's part of what makes this game great though. This system allows for complex and detailed micro-management of your squad of mercs in ways not achievable with other titles. Not to mention the attention to detail of the engine's weapons and ammo system. An incredibly diverse and large in-game arsenal compete with weapons attachments makes this game very enjoyable for the kit or gear-♥♥♥♥♥. Red-dot sight not cutting it for you? No problem, slap on an ACOG. Need a higher round count or faster reload time? Here's a 100-round Beta C-Mag and a roll of duct tape to tape two magazines together. Just to highlight how deep the game goes, most FPS or shooter-type games use an ammo-pool system where the ammo is reloaded from a pool of round. Detailed shooter games use a magazine by magazine system, where the ammo is counted by magazine (i.e. Red Orchestra). 7,62 uses a round-by-round system. The engine counts every individual bullet in the magazine. This leads to some interesting situations where you can top off your shotgun's tube or a partially filled rifle magazine with a different type or quality of ammo.
7,62 is not without its faults however. The game in its vanilla form is unplayable due to the glitches. You have to play this game with mods or you simply won't play at all. Fortunately, the Steam copy comes with the community patch and Blue Sun mod standard. Blue Sun is not without its glitches as well, but it does make the game playable while greatly expanding the arsenal and features as well as adding an entirely new questline seperate from the main questline.
7,62 also suffers from a unique "memory drain/leak" issue that I'm not entirely sure how to explain. This presents an issue for lower-end machines that should have no issue running it. With low-end and mid-end machines more than a few years old, expect CTDs up the wazoo once you put some hours into the game. Unfortunately, there isn't a fix for this short of deleting all local content and reinstalling fresh and it can only get worse. Heed my warning, hard save frequently.
This is an enjoyable and realism-based title that I really wish was more polished. If you're a fan of detailed military strategy, for the couple bucks you'll pay for 7,62 High Calibre on a Steam sale its absolutely worth it.

Galactic Battlegrounds is one of the few real-time strategy games set in the Star Wars universe. Simply put, you build a base, gather resources and build an army to defeat your enemies using one of eight factions from the prequel and classic trilogies.
The game runs on Ensemble's Genie engine, famous for powering Age of Empries II. For all intents and purposes, SWGB can be considered a total conversion of AoE2. In my opinion, this leads to a few shortcomings. For instance, the factions are all very similar to one another. This wasn't such a big deal in AoE2 given the game's "historical" setting, but in a Star Wars game it feels downright strange to have Gungans with mech units that essentially mirror the Empire's. Factions do come with a few unique bonuses, but it doesn't quite cut it.
SWGB still has some advantages over AoE2. The factions all have unique visuals for their units and buildings, which still hold up nicely. They also added air units which give an extra layer of depth to the gameplay. John Williams' score is used masterfully throughout the game.
The campaigns are serviceable but vary in quality. The missions are usually about building a base and destroying the enemy's, just like in a standard game. Also included is a scenario editor, which people have used to create some pretty cool custom maps.
The main long-term attraction of the game should be the multiplayer component, but in this day and age you will likely not find many people online even using replacement services. Unless you have some friends to play it with you, I wouldn't expect to get a lot of reliable multiplayer gameplay out of it.
Overall SWGB is a solid game and definitely worth the price for curious Star Wars fans. Its use of AoE2's engine can be seen as either a blessing or a curse depending on your mileage with it. I'm personally a fan of more unique factions in RTS games, which led me to be a bit disappointed with SWGB, but it's an enjoyable game for a Star Wars fit.

One of the three Apeiron games, famous with their game engine, made exactly for squad-based tactical wargames simulations. Recently it was updated with Hard Life community mod, which optimised some of game's features and edged to maximum its strong and weak sides.
In short, I can suggest and propose that game only to quite small cohort of true fans of tactical squad-based games a-la "Jagged Alliance". In fact, community-upgraded versions of 7.62 and Brigade E5, another Apeiron game, are probably the most capable successors and inheritors of Jagged Alliance good fortune (along with just a few more titles, like Silent Storm and some more).
So. You take the command over small group of mercenaries, merged into another domestic war in small 3rd-world country. You manage guns , tons of them, equip vests, scopes and other tacticool little things which make you a bit more ready-for-anything... And you constantly engaging in some fierce shootouts, where you need to use all your tactical skills and the best of luck, to stay alive for another day. Fight, collect trophies, rest, find a new quest for your squad, get to the new location, goto 10 - the golden formula from Jagged Alliance. If you're still reading, guess you already know all that drill.
Now, what's the special about Apeiron engine and game in general?
First, it is NOT turn-based, it is using smart-pause real-time pattern instead. You could have seen that in the recent "remake" Jagged Alliance: Back in Action, but trust me, it was only spoiled there. Apeiron created, up to the moment, the most complicated and advanced engine to perform a gunfight between small squads. Ballistics, lines of sights, variable reliefs and layouts, combat interferences, contusions - just name it - it is there.
Second, if we don't speak about engine, but overall game's features instead - sadly, it is weak, at best. Lame scenario, questionable and obscure quests and so on. If you're coming to the game not just for refined tactical simulation, that's not the right project. I can suggest to look for the next Apeiron game, Marauder, as there will be at least some of plot, narrative motivation and other things we're usually expecting from the complete game, as of the any piece of art.
As of conclusion, 7.62 is a niche product, connoisseurs of the tactical combats only. The gameplay is about tune your gear, shoot some folks, rince and repeat. Guns-adorers would find many satysfaction there, with all charts, graphs for hundreds of various tools of death. Normal players, who are not ready to shift all those irons hours after hours and then perform one battle, about 2-3 minutes of "clear" time, in another dozen of hours, with every second micromanagement fixes, saves and reloads... Normal players will be either bored from the first look, or drained and exhausted, when with all time needed to finish another Call-of-Duty project, they only (probably) manage to clear the first village there...
As of my mark, usually I'm not high about projects where so many gameplay parts are obviously ill-performed. But, with 7.62, with all community support... It is worth my 8/10 mark, as I'm really like squad-based tactics and guns, and this is one the best on given patterns.

Summary of the game (no spoilers). At first, my review was positive, but then I changed my mind. Here is why -
Story 3/5  -> Original, somewhat engaging, but a bit shallow
Graphics 4/5 -> for an action/tower defence game pretty decent
Voice acting/ cinematics 1/5 -> terrible voice acting, but that is not such a big deal. Cinematics are a nusiance.
Gameplay 2/5 -> You want to play. You want to think about the layout of your traps and strategy. But the game will not let you. It is very easy to place the traps, and melee combat is mostly about going near enemy, hitting MB1 (your character will target and hit enemy automatically, even if they are behind you) and sometimes dodging or running away. Shooting would be more fun, but you need to reload every shot which takes way too long for practical purposes and is impossible in melee combat. You can not place traps exactly where you want them, (I am not talking about terrain restriction now), so they happen to be too much to sides for maximizing their potential - and that is just irritating. You also keep XP even from nights you fail, so you are rewarded for failing. It also makes the game less chalenging, which sux.
In-game mechanics and options 5/5 -> there is everything that fits the atmosphere and nothing more that could disturb or overhype it. It is detailed, but not overdone, they put a lot of time into it and they did a good job. It also works quite well, I only saw one or two minor bugs. + they explain the mechanics very well.
Saves and loads mechanics 0/5 -> Daytime starts by cinematics, after that you tend to plant traps for waves of enemies that come at night. There may be 1-6 waves each night. If you screw up even the last wave, you need to start from daytime again (you can relocate the traps) and go again through all the waves. If, however, you decide to turn the game off, it will start with the beginning cinematics of the day the next time you play it, and your traps will be deleted, so you need to place them again. The game loads extremely slowly for such a small game, but the loading song makes up for it.
Fun 3/5 -> This game had great potential. It could have been so much better, perhaps the most complete tower defence / action game hybrid ever made. After a few rounds (when my review was positive) I had great expectations and was looking forward to playing this game. But as I played, it was becoming somehow irritating because of the factors mention above. Still, it was a decent game.
Shoul you buy it? No. It is definitely not worth the price.
However, If you see it on a sale like -80% or so, then YES, you will not regret it.

Having avoided Telltale Games from my own misguided attempt at TWD - and an apparently inaccurate impression that these types of games just weren't for me - I can admit that I am rather late to the raining-stars-review party of Tales from the Borderlands... luckily. Luckily because on a dreary Sunday I binge played all six episodes - something I didn't bother to look to see if other reviewers had done - and was delightfully sucked in to the well-known and slightly unhinged universe of Borderlands.
You play as one of two main protagonists: Rhys, a Hyperion employee who may have a slight fandom obsession with Handsome Jack; and Fiona, a quick-witted hustler who should really reconsider her hat choices. There is a full line-up of well-rounded, yet sometimes archetypal characters and a few fan-favs from the series making their own memorable appearances.
As with all Telltale Games, choices matter and decisions have consequences. Yet during your sometimes rather eyebrow-raising adventure, it is impossible not to feel connected with the characters. They're all so well written. In fact, this is the greatest strength of the game: the writing. Each character just fits: their scripts fit, their delivery is spot on and the voice acting is top-notch – also, I have to mention Kronk is unmistakably there (If you don't know Kronk, I'm sorry.). I laughed real laughs - not just half-amused nostril flaring - and I was deeply somber at times. This is a true testament to the richness of the writing. Being able to stay true not only to the off-the-wall world of Borderlands, but also to allow the audience to become engrossed emotionally in the storytelling.  Some people may complain - oddly enough - about the lack of action in an episodic game but I can say at times I had to be reminded that I was actually supposed to be playing rather than only watching and enjoying - I can also admit that I may have died a few times from my delayed response time.
How to end such a rave review? Perhaps with a TL;DR: The art, the wit, the charm... real lols from arguably superb banter, and a fantastic soundtrack - it's all there in spades. Telltale Games has successfully adapted one of the most beloved worlds, keeping all of the facets that have made Borderlands such an amazing series, and have combined it with their own unique brand of storytelling. All the stars for this one.

Overall, Prototype 2 is a more polished but more streamlined version of the first Prototype. If the Prototypes were computers, Prototype would be a Windows- more features, but more complicated and less polished- while Prototype 2 would be a Mac- slightly less features and slightly less depth, but much more fun to use and play, although it holds your hands a bit too much sometimes.
Compared to the original Prototype, Prototype 2 improves upon the areas in which the first Prototype failed. Graphics are very pretty to look at, especially at night. Gameplay is smoother and less chaotic. And each power has a more distinct style and strength to it, although you may argue that this is worse than Prototype's combo-based combat. I never really got into it, so I prefer Prototype 2's more linear combat more. Also, dodging is easier now, and you can actually combine abilities to create new attacks in the sequel. Its story, although not very good, is more organized than Prototype's, and I felt it had an overall structure to it, rather than Prototype's "I hate everyone let's go kill them". Stealth is also better in Prototype 2, and stealth consumes are much easier to perform with the all-new "hunt" feature.
However, Prototype 2 also got rid of statistics and the nice "military expenditure" screen that popped up at the end of every fight, which sort of annoyed me, as I always wanted to know how much damage I was causing the military and Blackwatch (especially with those new vehicle finishers- those are fun!). Prototype 2 uses a very linear and cliche leveling-up system, and I prefered the original's more open upgrade system, where you could allocate points in very specific areas that you wanted to improve upon, rather than just a more general area.
What I missed the most, however, was Prototype's progression. As the story progressed, you saw NYC turn into a more military-run place, with infection slowly destroying the city throughout. Police are replaced by squads of soldiers, and overall there is a real sense of progression as you play through the game. You feel like you are really living in a viral outbreak. Prototype 2 had none of that. It had the zones instead, which overall fall flat (the Green and Yellow zones are basically stepping-stones for you to progress through to the Red zone). They do have a very distinct quality between each, but they don't give the sense of progression and decay that the original Prototype had.
So- should you buy this game? Yes. And if you haven't played Prototype 1- buy and play it. Both have their own little merits that are worth experiencing, and I would happily recommend them both.

I really enjoy Sonic Lost World.
It was my first game I got for my Wii U, I have probably close to 100 hours logged on it there. This game has a bunch of weird ideas, but that isn't necessarily bad. Some of these ideas are executed well, some need improvement. This games story isn't exactly amazing, but for a platformer, I think its pretty good, even if it has some silly moments. I love the way Sonic controls in this game, the problems I had in Generations are nonexistent here. Sonic is even more mobile than before, having the ability to run up, along, and hop between walls. Wisps also make a comeback. I don't like their inclusion as much as I did in Colors, but they're much better than they were in the Planet Wisp level of Sonic Generations. This games art style, in my opinion, looks nice. Sure, its simplistic, but it was trying to achieve 60 FPS on Wii U, so don't expect Generations like graphics, even though in my opinion they're pretty close, but its hard to tell with the different art style. Some parts of the level design are frusturating, and will probably make you rage quit. Last world/zone has a huge difficulty spike, and it'll throw some cheap deaths at you any chance it gets. Soundtrack is great, but this is Sonic, so that's expected. I think the modding community for Generations could do some interesting things with this game, but we'll just have to wait and see if anything big scale (like the Unleashed Project) is made. I would grab this on sale personally. 8 hours ish for me to beat on PC, but I know the mechanics, controls, and level design well, so it'll take longer for someone on their first playthrough. $15 is a great price, I think. Hope to see Sonic Colors on Steam next, never expected Lost World to come on Steam.

The puzzles are unique though very difficult and often rely on mechanics you would not actually think you need to utilize in order to pull off a few segments. The voice acting is rather disappointing and has little to no life to it other than the vibe of an over-proud teenager that can't actually emote anything with his lines, regardless of their obvious tone in the words.
There is a serious issue with professional polishing. While all the puzzles function from what I found in my playthrough, I was stuck multiple times (as to be expected from any decent puzzle game) and thought perhaps I was supposed to try and go places that were actually just for scenery. The unfortunate part was, I was ALLOWED to access these scenery-exclusive areas, meaning I was literally stuck outside the map and had to reload the game to free myself. There are multiple issues with level design where the developers did not anticipate what the player would try, and only solidifed what the player was supposed to do. In fact, some of the things you WERE supposed to do were rather irritating to get working even though you knew exactly what you were supposed to do. It wasn't an issue of skill or understanding of mechanic, it was really just poor level design. No player likes to fail at doing something they already understand completely, but are only delayed because the level design is oddly difficult to get functioning. Being a mapper myself, it made me scream "PLAYER CLIP BRUSH IS YOUR FRIEND" - as well as a good few other things - in rage whenever I thought I figured out the route, but it turns out I glitched the map instead or just
suffered an unfair death or difficulty due to poor geometry or calculation with said level design.
Over all, the work put in to this is certainly worth AROUND the price it wants, however the QUALITY of said work doesn't quite cut it. Everything is aesthetically appealing, but unfortunately the real complaints come straight out of gameplay alone. I even glitched the ending because the level design was SO lazy as to not guarantee someone can't get to a certain area before the ending occurs and completely dodge the triggering intended to start the credits.
If you love Portal 2, buy it and play it. If you're looking for a brand new experience well fleshed out and intricately delivered that can actually get you invested in more ways than just puzzle solving (like the original portal games did) this is not for you.
It's creative, and looks professionally made, but most certainly isn't in a good few places.
Just know what you're going in to. It's a MOD. a MODIFICATION, made by players and individual developers potentially not even out of high school yet at the youngest. That doesn't mean what they made is♥♥♥♥♥♥ far from it in fact, but it's obvious the decision-making that took place during the development of this game is far from competent or wholly sound.
Buy it only if you really like Portal 2 (because unfortunately it recycles a few levels from Portal 2 with hardly any changes, a sign of potential lazy development disguised as creativity) and if you have a decent to significant tolerance for imperfection splattered throughout your experience ranging from map glitches, mechanic optimization issues, petty/annoying voice acting, and dying. Lots and lots and lots of dying, because in later levels, the mechanics don't function the way the game taught you they do sometimes. It can be infuriating using said mechanics going back and forth to figure out your surroundings and complete the puzzle itself.
For example, running across speed gel gets you going fast, and putting blue gel at the end will make you jump off it automatically when under the effects of the speed gel. However, if you don't go fast enough, but still faster than you can actually walk, you will NOT jump automatically, and often kill yourself by putting too much trust into the game mechanic to keep you safe. Other than the paint gun itself (which has a serious problem with having infinite ammo, allowing players to flood tractor beams with paint, and lag the hell out of their game as well as have their paint flicker in and out of existence) they didn't actually put any work into the mechanic of gel itself. In fact the most disappointing aspect of the game is that they did NOT complete and utilize the fabled purple gel, allowing you to walk on walls and ceilings. Apparently they had no coders on the team, just a butt load of modelers, texture artists, and what feels like a small handful of actual animators and level designers.
Final say: Not worth the money it asks for, but only just barely. It has plenty of those lovely puzzle game "Ah hah!" moments, and surrounds you in a well-detailed atmosphere (for the most part). Buy it when it's on sale if you value your money more than most.

Okay, new game/mod, so figured I'd write this to help buyers and the programmers alike:
First of all, if you enjoyed the gel-related tests in Portal 2, I'd definitely would recommend this mod for that reason alone. Most of the tests are just downright fun, plus you get to paint where you want! Sadly, that does lead to a bit of a weakness, where painting where you want can sometimes lead to a little too open-ness, making it a bit difficult at times to figure out where you're supposed to go and what to do. Other than that, this mod is pretty fun and a nice add-on to Portal 2, most of the time.
Some weaknesses to note, however:
1) Weak acting/story. I've noticed this mentioned a lot in other reviews, and I'd kinda have to agree with them. Still, this IS fan-made, so can't complain about that too much. Nigel (the core) seems a bit too flat at times, though, plus a bit of a randomly bi-polar personality that doesn't really make much sense, even in the bi-polar sense. Best I can recommend here is just to try and play the game for the levels and kinda ignore the lack of background.
2) Some of the levels are FREAKIN' HARD! One that stood out to me was the speed course at the end of Chapter 3. Now, there is an option to skip it, but it's not the course itself that's really a problem. The issue I had was with the paint gun and the gels just not working right. It was basically a crap shoot as to whether or not the sprayed gel had any effect whatsoever on the ground/walls you put it on. Oftentimes, it seemed that the gel was there visually, but the physics that they applied were missing. Still, I do have to give props to the wall surfing parts, I'm absolutely awful at that particular skill, but didn't have too much trouble with it here in Aperture TAG.
3) Part 4, Chamber 7. Dear god, this one nearly ruined it for me. (WARNING: SLIGHT MAP SOLVING SPOILERS AHEAD) I spent at least 30 to 45 minutes stuck at the very end, trying to figure out how to fling myself out of the portal. I saw what I needed to do, but couldn't figure out to gain the momentum needed. Even worse, if you fall out of the orange side of the portal without doing the fling correctly, it is painstakingly awful to get back to the blue portal, making death the best option to reset your position. Thankfully, somebody on Youtube figured out this chamber, so I was able to progress, but I definitely think this chamber could use a bit of work. At least put an easier way back to the blue portal, please! (END SPOILERS)
4) Not sure how I feel about the ending... but okay. Enough said here buyers, I'm not giving anymore spoilers.
Anyways, this game is fun, though the difficulty gets absolutely insane towards the end. All I can say is try to be patient, and if all else fails, go to Youtube and search "Aperture TAG Walkthrough". Not bad for a fan-made mod, though it could use a bit of work in a few areas. Also, if you don't know how to surf walls and curves, this isn't a bad place to learn, though the 180 turn in the surfing chamber can be a bit tricky.

Aperture Tag is a delightful mod for Portal 2 that abandons the series' signature portal gun and replaces it with a device that shoots Portal 2's gels, previously only a testing element activated by switches.  With the ability to shoot either a 'bouncy' or 'speed' gel, there are a surprising number of ways that the two can be combined to create interesting puzzle combinations.  Each new element or technique is appropriately introduced, and this balanced pacing serves Aperture Tag well.
The difficulty generally ranges from easy to medium, but even the easier puzzles were rewarding to solve when put into motion, as your character zips and jumps across each level with increasing complexity. A few puzzles relied on timing and reflexes more than puzzles in Portal seemed to do.  I had no problem with it, and in fact I liked the acrobatics, but it may turn off some players who aren't accustomed to it.  A final consequence of the mechanics of the two gels is that you may often find yourself accidentally bouncing or sliding into a pit of death.  Frequent autosaves meant that I never lost more than a few seconds, but, again, this might be frustrating for some.
Aperture Tag is generally strong visually, taking you through the gritty inner workings of aperture science, and frequently zipping you around through labrynthine tubes, allowing you to see the massive, intricate construciton of the facility.  Original music also adds to the experience.
The mod maintains Portal 2's distinct sense of humor, supported by frequently sharp writing and clever surprises. Unfortunately, the voice acting delivering those lines is definitely amateur.  While it certainly wasn't bad, I feel that a professional voice actor would have greatly elevated the experience.  GLaDOS, after all, was an enormous component of Portal 2's success, and without Ellen McLain's performance, I think I would not have nearly as strong an emotional connection with that game.
The elephant in the room, which I'll address, is that Aperture Tag was originally going to be free.  With the mod suddenly having a price tag on it, gamers have responded angrily, to say the least.  However, I don't think that criticism really addresses the mod on its own merits.  Were Aperture Tag free, I suspect it would be hailed as a must-play mod for any fan of the series.  I was engaged and entertained for the entirety of Aperture Tag's 2-3 hour playtime. For the comparatively low price that I paid, I would absolutely recommend it to any fan of Portal 2.

I was excited to see this game out on Steam, since I'd enjoyed Colors so much on the Wii. I was looking forward to playing the game now that it was no longer exclusive...
However, it ended up being very disappointing.
The stage designs aren't bad. The villains are poorly acted but no worse than some others I've seen. The graphics are nice (though the colors are a bit gray at times). The music is the high point of the game, aside from the boss theme it's quite good.
The main problem with this game is how Sonic moves. The new double jump/target jump combo handles poorly, often causing accidental damage and even death. The colors handle far worse than they did in Colors, and pop up an immersion-killing message every time they wear off. The brake is poor and never useful. But the biggest issue is...
Sonic moves SO SLOWLY.
I wouldn't mind if it tried to handle itself more like a slower game. Mario games are slower and play well. But this game tries to combine Sonic mechanics with the low speed, resulting in something that always feels painfully slow. Your maximum speed is reached very quickly, since Sonic accelerates like he always did; making it feel like he's TRYING to hold back. And the occasional speed machines (don't know their official name, the things you've always run into to go faster in Sonic) propel you forward at a more classical speed (though that is slower as well), they lose their boost rapidly, killing off any rush you might've gotten from it.
Overall? Sonic Generations is on this store, as well as 2, CD and Adventures 1 and 2. Any of them would make a better choice. This was a nice attempt with one fatal flaw...
But that flaw kills it.

I can't do it, I just can't do it. I wanted to like this game, it had a few okay levels at first, I even got myself to laugh at some of the dialogue for a while. But it just can't last. The story just makes less and less sense as it goes along, and the characters feel alienating, when there is a clear, external antagonist and instead they just focus on bickering between each other, and having Tails turn into a sarcastic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (more so than Sonic, I mean) part-way through the story just feels weird for me, especially when it just comes out of nowhere. But honestly the story and writing is the least of my problems with this one.
The score is lighthearted but utterly feels uninspired, as do the world designs. The zones can get pretty inconsistent, especially the second 'desert' zone that contains two desert levels, one level set in a beehive, and another level set in an alternate universe that is literally made of sweets and cake and that kind of thing. I really don't know where they came from, honestly. Lots and lots of cheap deaths because of the cumbersome movement controls, that's what killed it for me. It all feels kind of weird: they try to use the old 2D sonic physics (with Sonic having a lot of weight and taking time to get up to speed) without providing anything in the 3D space to increase momentum in most levels. It's considerably slower than the Sonic Adventure games, or at least it feels that way because of how sprawling a lot of levels tend to be, though at least eschews the darker pallet and more 'realistic' textures for a bright and smooth look. Except the gloves. The gloves are unusually textured, and I can't not notice it. Fighting enemies will kill your momentum in an instant though, and speaking of which, they slowly introduce enemies that require extra steps to beat without any clear rules of how to accomplish those steps. I hope I'm not the only one who didn't know there was a kick mechanic because it only activates when you're in the air and locked onto an enemy, and on the ground it just makes you do slow rolls, which I believe are literally useless, I have not determined a single use of them thus far.
There are some cartoony demons that comprise the boss fights of the game and their basically just some character tropes. Spastic redneck, fat idiot, old mustached karate master, materialistic beauty queen, and of course the red one who is the leader because he is red. Oh, and one more--the depressed one. Honestly it was just strange, interracting with this enemy. His design is kind of still bright, just using muted shades of blue and grey, and looks very much in-line with the game's aesthetic, but his dialogue is just very ... unique. He just, talks about having depression and waiting for death without a hint of irony or hesitation. Not caring about anything, not wanting to do anything, even get out of bed, telling sonic that "nothing matters" and "in the end we all die anyway", or "In the end, the Reaper is the only one who wins." Honestly just look him up because it feels so out of place. I don't think a game clearly intended for young audiences SHOULDN'T be allowed to have characters who are clearly and openly depressed, even suicidal, and they definitely don't make it over dramatic here, but it's hard to tell if all of this is just a joke like literally every other boss character, or if they are genuinely trying to be serious about it, in which case, it feels kind of pointless, for at least as much of the game as I played, nothing really happens with those character traits at all. It feels silly to go on about that character as much as I did but I legitemately suffered through the most wretched and painful to play zone, the Silent Forest, just because he was talking in it the whole time. Saying that now I have to wonder if that was meant to be like the suicide forest, though I may be stretching it there. But hey, the frustrating levels made me want to kill myself, so there's that.
The game has a couple talking points in it, if only to see how Sonic games have changed over the years, but at the end of the day, this felt empty, poorly designed, with cumbersome and awkward controls and characters that felt disconnected honestly. I wanted it to be good, but I don't think I can easily recommend the game to anyone when it's just not really that fun.

While I recommend Gunpoint I would also like to clarify that there isn't a whole lot of game there and that you might find your time better spent elsewhere.  That said, I think playing it is worth the experience so I do recommend checking it out.
After playing the demo a year or two ago I was under the impression that this was some sort of stealth or action game but that is certainly not the case.  Rather, Gunpoint is a puzzle game which largely revolves around adjusting activators to accomlish your goal (get further into the stage by opening doors/killing guards).  There aren't a whole lot of sensor types -- guard activated panels, sound activated devices, elevator switches, normal on/off switches and motion detectors -- and that kind of drags the game down a touch.  While the different combinations could have possibly been explored more within the story the game also felt somewhat lacking, like you spent too much time/too many stages figuring out the same or similar tricks.
There is a level editor for what it's worth and while that's cool I think I would have liked to see an additional story arc or two within the main game, possibly centering around different events or characters.
I very much enjoyed the sound track but there are only a few different tracks.  Still, the haunting melody suits the noire atmosphere well.
Oh, and there's a story but it feels like an after thought.  The plot is alright-ish but the writing itself isn't strong.  At several points I caught some small grammatical errors.  Beyond that the dialogue tree felt largely unnecessary and at times it didn't seem like my choices made a difference in what the other character responded with.  I don't mind the writing so much but the game felt like it was relying on the story for it's missions.
On the other hand end-game moral choices can ♥♥♥♥ off.  If you intend to 100% this game then back up your save before you make the final moral choice so that you don't have to replay the whole thing to do it.  Having said that, I have 4.2 hours logged and could almost certainly clear the game again in about two hours.  It's very, very short.
Check it out though.  It's cute, short and original.

Whether you're (brand) new to One Piece (And generally overwhelmed at the thought of having to watch several hundreds (no exaggeration) of episodes, to catch up with the latest episodes released), or catching up on past episodes before you binge again (fortunately, some story arcs are mercifully, and entertainingly abdridged (I'm talking a good 50+ episodes condensed into an hour tops of gameplay)), or just want to beat the crap out of literally thousands of pirates after another (to blow off some steam), or even missed out on some minor details of the Pirate World as you've been watching/playing through (See: Glossary, and unlockable story as you play; and heck, enjoy some of the soundtrack, while at it. Helps explain to those who haven't gotten their sea legs quite yet.); this is actually a pretty good game.
Now granted, it's a bit Dynasty Warriors-esque, but given the world of One Piece, it's kinda an appropriate theme for it, and makes a good medium to condense arcs from being watched/played from a few/many/tons of hours of binging, to maybe half an hour or less (depending on skill) per-arc, for a single playthrough. While at it, some episodes/scenes get quite an upgrade aesthetically (and sometimes, in-game battling, can give you a better perspective of how justifiably scary some characters are), compared to the original episodes. Although, if you're a fan of filler, you won't get much of it here, unless you're a fan of unlocking Treasure Events, which, if anything, will tell more of the main story, and less about the townsfolk and such; or playing through the Dream Log for some quick non-canon battles. Of course, there may be some minor inconsistencies between game and manga/anime (limitations between media).
Each Legend Chapter works well enough to sum up every Saga the series has to offer (Granted, I still have quite a distance to go, myself. I may need to delay playing/beating the final chapter; out of fear of coming across some spoilers too early. I'm still quite a distance behind, myself, by a good 100+ episodes or so) but not too much for any really recent spoilers), giving you the mostly fun parts of the series (all the fighting (as most of the characters capable of fighting), and a pretty good rendering of the environments per-Arc), while the unlcokable glossary/gallery helps explain the series for anyone new to it, or otherwise, missing details about tidbits of the story here and there (I actually got a much clearer idea of some things, and I'm already through a good couple hundred episodes, and didn't know about others things that made it past me before, or I forgot since the last time I binge-watched an Arc).
Of course, if you want to take a break from the story, or want to check out other characters, level them up a bit more, or explore more of the unknown parts of the game/story, or want to mess around with different battle conditions and unorthodox/non-canon alliances (or again, just beat the crap out of even more pirates/marines), then check out the Dream Log, and apparently, Nightmare Log (unlocked late-game, probably post-Dream Mode; basically Dream Mode -- Hard Mode), and explore the Grand Line again.
For best gameplay, I recommend using a gamepad.

It seems like it wasn’t far too long ago that the idea of an fps that you could play for 100’s of hours as you grind for more epic guns to combat enemies equally as epic would put a giant smile upon the faces of boys and girls around the world. Finally, they’d exclaim as they wait the two or three hours it’d take to download and install, a game that marries the freedom of open worlds, frantic fun of fps, and longevity of RPG’s. But while the concept, on paper, sounds like something that’d get envious glares from Blizzard in terms of perfected time-sinks, it seems as though something was lost in the shuffle as the game mutated into the emptiness of open worlds, simplicity of fps, and mundanity of RPG’s.
Don’t be mistaken, those 12 hours may seem like a disqualifier that any fan of the game may find an excuse to dismiss my writing as trivial slander from a man with more time on his hands than reasons to live, but this is coming from a man who used to gleefully throw away every night playing Borderlands on ps3 before becoming bored enough to stop playing but repurchase the game again on steam out of sheer stupidity. And what greater stupidity awaited me when I saw the mess of pc port they had for this game. Yeah, so just on the merits of the game having an fov of about 75 degrees, frame rate dips, mouse acceleration, and what I can only suspect to be absolute hatred for my computer as it crashed into a blue screen, I’d already recommend against it. That would’ve been enough, but Borderlands is ambitious enough to be disappointing even after slogging through .ini files to make the game playable.
Its ambitions, although welcoming at a time where the world was ready for new IP to shake up the gaming scene, resulted in something that nobody took time to check and see if the game actually gelled together with its concepts in a way that wasn’t agonizingly boring. Yes, the greater sin upon the earth that this game commits isn’t is subpar port but rather the repetitive grind of going to a muck colored junkyard to shoot a bunch of masked maniacs and sift through the abundance of dropped guns to see which would most effectively aid in the job of killing more anger-fueled maniacs in other junkyards so that I may find more guns to OH GOD, WHAT AM I DOING!? WHY IS THERE NO END IN SIGHT?!
Well, there is an ending to it, but the ending lies somewhere in the dead end alley of a problematic town. That problem bit being the damn, seemingly absent story. It starts as a simple story of a character that you pick among the four playable ones being spoken to by a mysterious voice in their head that wants you to go on a quest for treasure through the method of committing genocide and grave robbing in order to find some sort of vault key that only appears every two-hundred years. So far, so simply sadistic. So simply sadistic, yet mundane whenever I try to think back on why the game had me journey through every location it did but can’t due to the fact that most of it melded together in a mush of screaming maniacs and RPG stat comparing. This was to the point where every time I felt compelled to recall any segment of the game that stood out, the only part that shoots to mind is a segment where you take a break from killing shirtless, surprisingly buff despite the drought ridden local, crazed maniacs to instead fights some diverse militia group called the “Crimson Lance”. I say diverse, they have four types, each somewhat representing each of the four playable characters. But at this point, I’d gladly take the change up of a challenge, even if it’s only for the three hours I spent there before the story moved on from there; returning to the volatile part of my memory that would immediately be emptied the moment the game ended with a sputter.
The ending, to its credit, did reignite some of my interest. The ignition being a quick and angry passion towards the sudden twist. This was right about when some corporation revealed to be following along in your adventure and beat you to the punch of getting to the vault of treasure. Of course, if they’d been paying attention to the actions of our protagonist, then maybe they’d reconsider the idea of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥on the parade of a person that would sooner burn their parade and pick through every gun to compare stats before moving on and consuming the flesh of the survivors. Well, I guess it doesn’t matter seeing as how they end up regretting in in time to realize that the treasure all along was friendship. Nice, monstrous, man destroying, friendship in the form of sci-fi Shub-Niggurath. So, instead of looking at this and leaving on account of the abundant lack of treasure, you kill the monster. With victory accomplished, that voice returns to explain that it was all part of her plan to get you to kill the monster in order to save the world. The credit roll, and our heroes walk away knowing that they no longer have to sift through the bodies of hockey masked, gymnastic maniacs and dull as♥♥♥♥♥♥guns.
Well, that’s assuming they did. For all I cared, the ending should’ve just been the main character angrily willing themself into existence and viscously beating every writer for this game while exclaiming “Are you ♥♥♥♥ing serious? You can’t just drop an angry, world destroying octopus on me and expect me to be satisfied with the challenge of the fight when I WAS PROMISED TREASURE!” I’d be this riled up, but all my enthusiasm was killed by stick wielding, moronic, computer breaking bandits. So do I recommend it? Meh, if you’re playing on console and like simplistic FPS shooting and level grinding, this will tide you over until killer squids emerge from vaults. Otherwise, there’s always the very handsome sequel to look towards instead.

Having avoided Telltale Games from my own misguided attempt at TWD - and an apparently inaccurate impression that these types of games just weren't for me - I can admit that I am rather late to the raining-stars-review party of Tales from the Borderlands... luckily. Luckily because on a dreary Sunday I binge played all six episodes - something I didn't bother to look to see if other reviewers had done - and was delightfully sucked in to the well-known and slightly unhinged universe of Borderlands.
You play as one of two main protagonists: Rhys, a Hyperion employee who may have a slight fandom obsession with Handsome Jack; and Fiona, a quick-witted hustler who should really reconsider her hat choices. There is a full line-up of well-rounded, yet sometimes archetypal characters and a few fan-favs from the series making their own memorable appearances.
As with all Telltale Games, choices matter and decisions have consequences. Yet during your sometimes rather eyebrow-raising adventure, it is impossible not to feel connected with the characters. They're all so well written. In fact, this is the greatest strength of the game: the writing. Each character just fits: their scripts fit, their delivery is spot on and the voice acting is top-notch – also, I have to mention Kronk is unmistakably there (If you don't know Kronk, I'm sorry.). I laughed real laughs - not just half-amused nostril flaring - and I was deeply somber at times. This is a true testament to the richness of the writing. Being able to stay true not only to the off-the-wall world of Borderlands, but also to allow the audience to become engrossed emotionally in the storytelling.  Some people may complain - oddly enough - about the lack of action in an episodic game but I can say at times I had to be reminded that I was actually supposed to be playing rather than only watching and enjoying - I can also admit that I may have died a few times from my delayed response time.
How to end such a rave review? Perhaps with a TL;DR: The art, the wit, the charm... real lols from arguably superb banter, and a fantastic soundtrack - it's all there in spades. Telltale Games has successfully adapted one of the most beloved worlds, keeping all of the facets that have made Borderlands such an amazing series, and have combined it with their own unique brand of storytelling. All the stars for this one.
