I was encouraged by my cousin to buy this game, and whilst my initial purchase was reluctant, I found a rather enjoyable game, if not a flawed one.
Let me start by stating that my first Telltale game was TWD, so I will make a lot of comparisons here.
Firstly, let's start with the Pro's:
1. Enjoyable story - I suppose
Set after the events of Borderlands 2, we pick up two new main characters, in which throughout the game you will switch between them for their takes on the story. The story was in most senses, predictable, a few little surprises here and there, but don't expect it to blow you away.
2. Entertainment factor - some genuinely comedic moments
I found myself laughing out loud at some parts, to note, but not spoil the corporate warfare scene, the face peel, the 'bro' scene and other various parts I legitimately enjoyed. Other times I found my eyes rolling at some pretty forced and flat jokes. A solid 50/50, I'd be generous to say 60/40. Some good laughs to be had, but expect some cringe content.
3. Gameplay - plenty of what we know, scarcely what we don't.
TftB adds some new mechanics over their other entires, such as the eye-scan for increased environment information, and a perhaps more fleshed out inventory, even if it is as 'unnecessary' as ever. The same old, classic, Telltale illusion of choice and on your feet response-based conversation system are ever present too. Expect yourself to have to pay a bit more attention in this one however; it is unwise to have your hands dawdle away from your keyboard and mouse.
I'm pretty sure I've listed most of the pro's here, now let me inform you of the cons:
1. Technical and system - no step forward, but 3 steps back
The game, frankly, runs like crap. A lot of shortcuts and poor animations are present in this game. Dialogue cuts out, and subtitles fail to properly synch to what the characters are actually saying, synch as in, they don't exactly say what the subtitles have you think they say. As much as I like Telltale's games, their engine clearly lacks polish and finesse, and the game suffers with its limitations. In particular, you will notice that the main characters and those in your immediate line of sight function 'satisfactorily' whilst everyone else is either static or sometimes glitching about the place. Compared to TWD, this game was a bit of a visual mess. Most character animations are extremely jarring and jagged, a right mess to witness. This was my experience at least.
2. Soundtrack - Jared Emerson-Johnson returns, only to miss the mark?
The soundtrack was a complete miss here, entirely lackluster and totally off point. I can agree that every composer/artist has their own flare, but I wasn't captivated, motivated, or stirred by any pieces in this game, and the nods back to the FPS games, with pieces done by Jesper Kyd, only further agitated me in realising the score was so off. The main menu theme alone precisely and accurately reflects my message here, the vibes are in an entirely different field.
3. Pacing - an ending that drags out indefinitely
Unlike TWD, this had to be one of the most dragged out endings I've witnessed in recent memory. To the point where I fidgeted in my seat in anticipation of it finally being over. I can respect and appreciate closure, but when the ending purposely drags on just to fit in one last joke, you really get a sense of wanting to get to the end as quickly as you can. For the actual ending, I enjoyed, it was a more serious note as opposed to the light-hearted jolly fest that the rest of the game was, but the ending definitely was a strange pace, fast in some places, slow in others.
4. Characters - love em', hate em', both extreme, but certainly not the former
I didn't feel much of a connection to any character outside of the main two. We do get character development sure, but most characters aren't fleshed out, or even, flesh-outable(?) The fact that towards the end of the game I was supposed to feel sad/happy/whatever have you towards some of the characters was a revalation in itself. At the end of the game, I felt a severe disconnect to most NPC's, this is only compounded when during the idle moments in the game, discussion with the NPC's is kept to an absolute minimum, as opposed to TWD, where, you know, we actually find out things about them, as there are plenty of opportunities to do so. Shame.
OVERALL VERDICT:

The game is a mix between tower defence and third person action, pretty similar to Orcs Must Die, Dungeon Defenders and Sanctum. If you enjoyed any of these games you'll probably love Sang-Froid.
Every night your house is attacked by waves of wolves and werewolves and you must set traps during the day to protect yourself when the night falls.
The first few levels are meh, but as the game progress you'll be dying quite a lot of times each night until you can find the appropriate strategy for each level (especially if you're autistic like me and started the game on hard mode).
The gameplay is divided in two parts, the planning mode during the day where you can buy stuff at stores, equip and level your character and spend money/time setting up traps on a overview map of the forest near your house, and the action part during the night, when you actually control your character around so you can ambush wolves with your axe and traps.
Although the graphics are "dated" the game still looks fine. Simplistic, but better than most indie games out there.
The OST is great, I mean, listen to the first video on the Steam store page. The background music always sets the perfect mood for whatever is happening. It's one of the strong points of the game.
To sum it up, it's an amazing tower defense and action game, challenging as hell if you play on hard mode, great atmosphere and excellent game mechanics. Definitely worth the full price.

762 High Calibre is a top-down RTS game with RPG elements. You play as a mercenary hired to find and assassinate a man hiding somewhere in the war-torn region of Algiera, where a corrupt government faces off against an equally corrupt organization of rebels. Bandits, smugglers, mercenaries, and drug cartels run amok-taking advantage of the civil war to turn a profit at the expense of innocent people. You will have to choose your battles wisely and your friends carefully.
The gameplay is good, with a focus on a large amount of weapon variation and the ability for players to choose how they want to apporach a given tactical scenario or situation. Either way, the player will almost always be vastly outnumbered by enemies, and combat is brutal (though in a good, challenging way.) and rarely felt frustrating to me personally. The player is given the option of choosing which side to support (The government or the rebels), which of course affects the story.
The game does have a number of issues-there are some translation problems here and there or stilted dialogue, and the camera is uncooperative, especially when trying to rotate when you are near the edge of a map. There are some very occasional crashes.
All of these things, however, are certainly worth dealing with, at least for me personally.
The game comes with the hard life addon, which adds a significant amount of content to the game, though personally, I would recommend the blue sun mod, which also comes standard with every purchase (and can be activated by going to your properties-->betas tab, and clicking "Community_patch_and_bsm" from the dropdown menu. It has much of the content from te hard life addon, plus much more.)
All in all, I'd say this game was an enjoyable experience for me.

Visceral, action filled and full of the satisfying dismemberment of the poor sods who get in the way of of a virtually indomitable superhuman consumed by a biological virus. It's an open world game in the spirit of the classic 'Incredible Hulk Ultimate Destruction' on the original Xbox. Set in the aftermath of the first game, yet again NYC becomes the victim of a biological apocalpyse set off by Alex Mercer dragging in Gentek and Blackwatch. Mercer infects a soldier, Heller, who develops the powers of his protege as he goes on a rampage killing anything and everything from both sides of the conflict in a quest for revenge for his daughter.
The free roam mechanics in this game are without question the best out of any game I've played. It is simply satisfying to run at superhuman through the war torn streets of New York, leaping up the sides of skycrapers and cruising along them then jumping and gliding high above the conflict. The sense of weight and power you carry without feeling cumbersome or bulky is just nailed, you look and feel like a lithe, dealdly human predator. Story and side missions along with the usual collectilbes are scattered around the map, which is split into 3 seperate parts. While I lost the sense of a large city I got from the first, it let all the elements of the map have personality, which is a tradeoff I'm willing to take.
The weapons and upgrades are disappointedly almost the same as number one with only a few differences. They are all still visually impressive and satisfying, but I held expectations for a more substantial roster of weapon options. The combat and movements mechanics are likewise similar with a familiar set of enemies, with just enough changes to justify its existence as a new game. The Evolved are quite cool though, plus it provides an enemy that plays and operates similar to yourself. The difficulty level is quite easy once you have a few upgrades, the tools at your disposal allow you to ignore or avoid almost all incoming damage sources. My first playthough on hard was very straightforward.

It seems like it wasn’t far too long ago that the idea of an fps that you could play for 100’s of hours as you grind for more epic guns to combat enemies equally as epic would put a giant smile upon the faces of boys and girls around the world. Finally, they’d exclaim as they wait the two or three hours it’d take to download and install, a game that marries the freedom of open worlds, frantic fun of fps, and longevity of RPG’s. But while the concept, on paper, sounds like something that’d get envious glares from Blizzard in terms of perfected time-sinks, it seems as though something was lost in the shuffle as the game mutated into the emptiness of open worlds, simplicity of fps, and mundanity of RPG’s.
Don’t be mistaken, those 12 hours may seem like a disqualifier that any fan of the game may find an excuse to dismiss my writing as trivial slander from a man with more time on his hands than reasons to live, but this is coming from a man who used to gleefully throw away every night playing Borderlands on ps3 before becoming bored enough to stop playing but repurchase the game again on steam out of sheer stupidity. And what greater stupidity awaited me when I saw the mess of pc port they had for this game. Yeah, so just on the merits of the game having an fov of about 75 degrees, frame rate dips, mouse acceleration, and what I can only suspect to be absolute hatred for my computer as it crashed into a blue screen, I’d already recommend against it. That would’ve been enough, but Borderlands is ambitious enough to be disappointing even after slogging through .ini files to make the game playable.
Its ambitions, although welcoming at a time where the world was ready for new IP to shake up the gaming scene, resulted in something that nobody took time to check and see if the game actually gelled together with its concepts in a way that wasn’t agonizingly boring. Yes, the greater sin upon the earth that this game commits isn’t is subpar port but rather the repetitive grind of going to a muck colored junkyard to shoot a bunch of masked maniacs and sift through the abundance of dropped guns to see which would most effectively aid in the job of killing more anger-fueled maniacs in other junkyards so that I may find more guns to OH GOD, WHAT AM I DOING!? WHY IS THERE NO END IN SIGHT?!
Well, there is an ending to it, but the ending lies somewhere in the dead end alley of a problematic town. That problem bit being the damn, seemingly absent story. It starts as a simple story of a character that you pick among the four playable ones being spoken to by a mysterious voice in their head that wants you to go on a quest for treasure through the method of committing genocide and grave robbing in order to find some sort of vault key that only appears every two-hundred years. So far, so simply sadistic. So simply sadistic, yet mundane whenever I try to think back on why the game had me journey through every location it did but can’t due to the fact that most of it melded together in a mush of screaming maniacs and RPG stat comparing. This was to the point where every time I felt compelled to recall any segment of the game that stood out, the only part that shoots to mind is a segment where you take a break from killing shirtless, surprisingly buff despite the drought ridden local, crazed maniacs to instead fights some diverse militia group called the “Crimson Lance”. I say diverse, they have four types, each somewhat representing each of the four playable characters. But at this point, I’d gladly take the change up of a challenge, even if it’s only for the three hours I spent there before the story moved on from there; returning to the volatile part of my memory that would immediately be emptied the moment the game ended with a sputter.
The ending, to its credit, did reignite some of my interest. The ignition being a quick and angry passion towards the sudden twist. This was right about when some corporation revealed to be following along in your adventure and beat you to the punch of getting to the vault of treasure. Of course, if they’d been paying attention to the actions of our protagonist, then maybe they’d reconsider the idea of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥on the parade of a person that would sooner burn their parade and pick through every gun to compare stats before moving on and consuming the flesh of the survivors. Well, I guess it doesn’t matter seeing as how they end up regretting in in time to realize that the treasure all along was friendship. Nice, monstrous, man destroying, friendship in the form of sci-fi Shub-Niggurath. So, instead of looking at this and leaving on account of the abundant lack of treasure, you kill the monster. With victory accomplished, that voice returns to explain that it was all part of her plan to get you to kill the monster in order to save the world. The credit roll, and our heroes walk away knowing that they no longer have to sift through the bodies of hockey masked, gymnastic maniacs and dull as♥♥♥♥♥♥guns.
Well, that’s assuming they did. For all I cared, the ending should’ve just been the main character angrily willing themself into existence and viscously beating every writer for this game while exclaiming “Are you ♥♥♥♥ing serious? You can’t just drop an angry, world destroying octopus on me and expect me to be satisfied with the challenge of the fight when I WAS PROMISED TREASURE!” I’d be this riled up, but all my enthusiasm was killed by stick wielding, moronic, computer breaking bandits. So do I recommend it? Meh, if you’re playing on console and like simplistic FPS shooting and level grinding, this will tide you over until killer squids emerge from vaults. Otherwise, there’s always the very handsome sequel to look towards instead.

Too many people hate on this game. They say "0mg 1t'5 ju5t m4r0 g4l4x3 0/10!!!!!!!!!!!!1!!!111", or "CANT LOWER FRAMES 0/10". They never give this game love and enjoyment. I mean seriously, if everyone were critical, the world would be boring. Boring isn't fun. I'm here to give it the love it deserves. But first, a lil history lesson!
Back in good ol' 1993, E3 revealed a game called "Sonic X-treme" for the Saturn. Everyone was talking about it. SEGA forced it into all of our favorite magazines, E3 booths, and even our librarys. It was brilliant. The game was GOING to be released in Christmas of 1996, but due to technical and staff (One suffered severe medical issues) issues, the game was silently scrapped.
Now, here's where that's related. Look at some X-treme gameplay (Search up "Sonic X-treme Gameplay" on the YouTubes). Now look at SLW gameplay. Pretty similar, aren't they? In fact, there's a bunch of X-treme textures that were leaked online. One of whch included a red, spherical flower with white in the middle. In SLW, look closely in Windy Hill. Boom. Same flowers, texture and all! Also, "running up walls"? That's in X-treme! Also, I'm aware one of SEGAs devs for the game confirmed X-treme was not the basis, as no other devs knew about the game. I disagree based on these facts.
Also, Frame problems. Yeeaaaa-no. You can fix these easily, SEGA made a tool to limit frames. I can't link since I don't have it, but it's X-perimental (HAHAHAHAHAHA!...Anyone? Well?...*sniff*...*runs off the stage crying*), so BE WARNED!
Now, gameplay. It's X-treme--and I mean the game. That's an insta-+ in my book!
Story, it's good. Not really rememorable, and pretty cheesy at X-tremely (Now do you guys like it?...At...at all?...*sniff*...*runs off the stage crying again*) rare times. All in all, a +.
Levels. As far as I know, they're not too fair. I don't see why, but this is coming from someone who just got it.
Replayability, eh. Unless it's a mod.
Oh right, MODS!!! Mods can be model swaps, camera changes, reanimations, all that. There's a ton of 'em on a guide, so I reccomend you look at it. (One makes it look more like X-treme by making Sonics model Sonic from Sonic R, then combine that with the clean up HUD thing, and remove lines from going fast/homing attack path, and you get X-tremely Lost World!)
So all in all, 9.9/10. It's almost perfect, but a not-huge lack of replayability. And, X-TREEEEEEEEEEEEEEME!
TL;DR:9.9/10 for a bit of a lack of replayability

Tales from the Borderlands is one of the best adventure games I've ever played.
It has a really, really good voice acting, which gives the characters life and charm (especially the main characters, Rhys and Fiona)
The storyline is splendid, it hooks you in your seat and never slows down from start to finish.
And the music... oh, the music! When you hear the opening/ending song of each Episode, you'll never stop singing them ( Episode 4's To the Top is the best!) The rest of the music is very good too, even some battle themes from Borderlands 2 and the Pre-Sequel come back.
The gameplay is very simple, it's just some walking, point-and-clicking and quick-timing but it fits the overall calm atmosphere of the game (compared to other Borderlands games) and the story, since Rhys and Fiona aren't badass Vault Hunters, they can't enter into some place guns blazing, it just wouldn't make sense.
Graphics are the same as the other Borderlands game, cel-shading with not very high textures and it's very cool.
Replayability is also a thing, with a ton of choices to make, you're bound to give the game another try in order to see the different outcomes (just don't expect plot changing decisions, most of them are medium to small changes)
Overall the game is one of the best experiences you'll get from a modern story-driven videogame with a rich story and memorable characters. I give it a 10/10
PS: The only con that I can find is that you can't ship Rhys and Fiona! The game only allows you to ship Rhys and Sasha, which sucks! Sasha should be with August and Fiona with Rhys!! Sorry for my rant... :)

I'll admit I was very wary of this game when I took my first glimpse in it's direction. While othing seemed mechanicly wrong with the game from the get go, nothing really stood out to me either as anything worthwhile. However with a recent sale, and a good friend of mine recomending it every chance he got, I decided to pick the game of and give it an honest chance
The first thing I'll mention aout the game is that while the combat has a clunky feel to it, it's surprisingly enjoyable and really fits the theme of the game, if theirs any time I found myself frustrated with an outcome in combat it was because I hadn't managed properly and felt the weight of it come crashing down on me. You play one of two lumberjacks fighting the Devil and his werewolf, spirit army. Pretty badass concept but it's up to you to be the badass of the story, the game won't do it for you.
Resource management is key to winning this game, and the trap and resource system is set up harsh but fairly. You really need to pay atention to what your actually able to spend on upgrading your personal gear like weapons, protective clothing and consumables, because while a good axe or rifle may come in handy, they only help you against one or two enemies before your overwhelmed, however a proper trap could take out four enemies in one go, nothing beats a properly executed trap.
The game also has a fear system, allowing you to scare off certain enemies , and help even the odds against the packs of wolves that often surround you. Alot of enjoyment is to be found making your enemies hesitate to atack you and start having to size you up before their confident enough to strike again.
Lastly but cerainly not least is the soundtrack to this game. This game has one of the best soundracks I've ever heard. It definitely has music you can stomp your foot to (I speak from experience on this.) The music of this game brings everything to another lvel, it makes combat even more enoyable, it gives you a goo sense of the world, and it's just plain fun to listen too.
In short Sang-Froid is a challenging but rewarding game that offers fun gameplay, a badass story, and some of the best music you'll ever hear in a video game, if not just in general. I'd recomend this game to anyone who likes a nice challenge and is a fan of strategy. I'd give Sang-Froid an 8/10. It's not the highest budjet game, but you most certainly et your dollars worth for it, most of that with the soundtrack alone.

The game itself has rather unique mechanics, being real-time with pause and all. Instead of other turn-based tacticool games like Jagged Alliance, 7,62 has everyone take their actions simultaneously, with all actions measured in seconds, with hip-fire shots taking less time and shots-through-optics taking much more. There are downsides to having this much slav magic packed into one game, though. Enjoy having your magazines labelled "clips" half of the time and "magazines" the other half. You may also run into terrible framerate lags, especially in towns, and I don't know of any fix. In fact, even the devs don't know how to fix some of the problems, but they sure try.

7,62 High Calibre tries to mix the genres of tactical top view shooter and RPG.
Keyword being "tries" here. Because it fails. It's not all bad but definitely a bad game:
PROS
* Character equipment customization
* Wandering around the streets gathering intel on objectives, playing in a undercover operative kind of way
* Active pause to give orders and evaluate situations before moving
CONS
* Terribly confusing. Knowing what to do, where to go or even what your objective is or why you're even here is a challenge in itself
* Terrible AI that makes the enemies either dumb as hell or incredibly overpowered
* Luck based combat: Sometimes a character can tank a few bullet like it's nothing more than mosquito bites, sometimes a single bullet will knock them down and they will take forever to get back up, while still being shot at (so it pretty much means death). This applies for the payer or the enemies.

Obscure, Buggy, quirky, funky UI, no tutorial, steep learning curve...but, wow, I havent had this much fun since discovering mount and blade : warband....similar game but in a modern setting...open world....picked up this game on a whim for $5...best $5 I have spent in a long time....a mix of an RPG adventure game, tactical battle sim and sandbox strategy game....micro manage your battles down to the 1/100th of second....fiddle with your equipment and loadout to your hearts desire...make sure you start with the Blue Sun Mod and Merc 1.2 mod installed...watch some Ninja2dan's Lets Play Vids....read some of the walkthrus posted and you will be good to go....takes some time to learn the game....virtually no instructions or help available except for the few diehards posting here....
Pros:
·       Perfect Combination of RPG/Sandbox/Tactical Battle Sim/Squad Building & Progression
o   RPG: Loose yourself in a Fictional Modern S. America setting. Character & squad stat progression, interesting text based quest/story line missions.
o   Sandbox: Establish a base of operations whereby you can send out militia to take control of towns, freedom of action to do quests, raids, random encounters, etc.. Light strategy and economy, options. Maybe you are cut out to be your own faction leader and establish regional control over the nearby towns and villages...
o   Tactical Battle Sim: This is the meat of the game. Engage in a thrilling firefight with various factions. Stop and go, pauseable RTS action that is a good compromise between real time and turn based tactical management. The detail is absolutely amazing: Reaction times, visibility, ammo, burst rates, mobility, positioning, line of sight and field of fire, aim/fire options, morale, wound care, weapons, weapons and more weapons. Save often, because you will be replaying game saves when you die…
o   Squad Building: Manage your team, equipment, progression, etc..
·       Detailed: Everything is represented: 100’s of weapons, combat, tactics, actions, ammunition types, loads of variety.
·       Immersive
·       A great many options and a variety of things to do
·       Compelling, addictive game play…hard to put down.
·       Semi destructible environment. Watch things explode or accumulate damage.

Cons:
o   Frequent crashes and game freezes. Save often. Some have found this a deal killer, but once you come to expect it, I don’t think it a huge issue…minor annoyance.
o   Unintuitive gameplay. The game is not polished and the quests are a bit buggy or finicky. You may have to do watch Ninja2dan’s youtube videos or read Ssanders walkthru’s to get an idea how to play.
o   Obscure company and game: Translation from Russian to English is rough. The base game is somewhat broken. Adding the fanbased Blue Sun Mod and Mercpocalypse 1.2 add ons are a must.
o   Dated Graphics.
o   Camera is clunky. You have to work around some camera angles. Manageable but annoying.

Update: I now have over 50 hours in this game...loving it....I dont know how i missed this game when it first came out...perfect blend of an RPG Sandbox and a Tactical Battle Sim....the detail is amazing....
Advice to folks who want to get started:
Watch Ninja2dan's 2nd and 14th 7.62 video in his series on youtube.
Read over ssander's chapter 6 pdf walkthru on Bennie and Clive. Look for link under the thread about walkthur's.
***Ninja2dan's 2nd video and the walkthru on Bennie and Clive will get you Paquito and Bennie as free team members.

I remember when I played Sonic Unleashed on the Wii and hated the fact that there were too many tutorials, some of them "teaching" stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥like jumping. But when you have a game like Sonic Lost World, in which the controls deviated a lot in comparison to the other 3D installments in the series, you need one of two things: level design that can teach the player the basic of movement and how to properly interact with the stages or a just a tutorial stage - or stages.
Since this game doesn't give you a chance to experiment with certain mechanics (like the parkour and unnecessary Wisps) before putting you to test with do-or-die situtations, a proper tutorial would certainly be helpful. This is probably the main reason SLW got a lot of hate on its Wii U release, by doing a bad job teaching the player.
If you endure some frustration (especially with some red rings and questionable checkpoints), you may be able to enjoy a fairly good platformer with great music, graphics and performance. I have a lot of fun replaying the stages, be it for the sake of exploration or just for speed running. I really wish the next 3D Sonic game gives us something similar in terms of controls, but with more clever level design and less gimmicks.

I find this game to be very immersive and complicated and the Tutorial does a very bad job at keeping new players interested, but once you get past the initial stages of the game its a very rewarding experience.
Eve Online and Texas Hold Em poker are the only 2 games that give me an adrenaline rush, and this is because of the risk involved. If you die in Eve you lose everything you were carrying with you especially if you have implants (in game item that are every expensive and increase how fast you gain skills) it can be very expensive. Some people might think this is a bad thing why spend 100 hours playing a game if you can lose everything, but if you ask me thats what makes it fun.
I tend not to pick on other players and try and be helpful whenever I can but in Eve hardly anyone is like this, expect to be ganked and attacked everywhere you go. (They say if you stay in high security space your safe, but in my experience if you carrying over 100 mil worth of stuff people will attack you even there.)
Another part of what makes the game unique and different to me is that this game is like the real world. The universe is a big place and a lot of people are already established and powerful, and just like in real life you are a nobody, getting dumped into a world full of billionaires and cut-throat competition with hardly any resources or help and expected to make your own way to the top. This is a breath of fresh air over most games out there where everyones a hero in an even level battlefield where skill matters more than time invested. Yes its going to seem unfair that 10 year old veterans with all of their skills are going to beat you, but what makes it most satisfying to me is that feeling of always having to watch your back, and that adrenaline rush you get when trying to escape from someone or battling away in space or the marketplace.
I have spent many years in Eve, I have many more hours than Steam displays since this game was released years before the Steam Store even included Eve, I can tell you this. Eve will seem boring at first to most people, but there is no other game similar to Eve out there, with a persistent world economy thats actually good, and a shared universe with so many people on the same server. Sometimes I feel most MMO's don't deserve that label, they all have heavily instanced maps and they are more like small group party games rather than real MMO.
Might aswell give Eve a try, theres an option to play it for free with restrictions to try the game out, to be honest, its a very good idea to play using the free account anyway until you have maxed your skills, thats more than enough time to decide for yourself wether this game is worth the subscription fee.

One of the great little gems to shine out of the cacaphony overload of indie games on Steam. I grew up in minnesota, so when I saw werewolves, and canadian foklore, and RTS AND action...I hit the purchase button faster than a Wendigo sneezes ice. It has a great folky soundtrack, and great hand-drawn visuals, especially the menu and town interfaces.
Being that it is indeed an indie game, the game budgets and amount of people working on this  title would be laughable to a mega-corp like Ubisoft or the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly EA. So there are a few expected rough areas, but they don't detract from the overall game. Mainly, the voice acting was terrible, I felt like random people off the street were pulled in to read children’s books to 1rst graders. If they every make a TOME II, it would be great if they addressed this. Conversely, the sounds while playing the game and the music are very well done. It really sends a shiver up your spine playing this in your room at night, the sounds of the wind rushing through trees, the crack of branches and snarls and howls of the beasts just over the hill expertly done to always create the feeling you will be attacked at any moment.
Mechanically the game works pretty smooth, and is challenging to say the least. It creates tense and relentless action when you hit the go button; it actually is scary in a way. There is a sense of dread and nervousness as you hover your mouse over the ‘begin’ button…setting in motion the nights terrors upon you.  You hope things will work out and you will survive, but it always feels as if the odds are stacked against you. My one complaint is the pacing...the skill tree becoming unlocked only started to open up toward the end, and by the time I could really afford some better weapons, there were only a couple missions left. I wish there was a patch to adjust this a bit. I love a challenge, but I hate seeing cool things that I can't afford and can't have fun using, then it’s over. When it was over though, I can say it was definitely a sense of accomplishment! This makes me want to go back now, play with the harder brother and see if I can get those last few achievements, which are not just filler achievements.
Overall, for a couple bucks, this game is well worth it, is unique, and hope to see their next game...though it looks vastly different in theme. A great 'first' game for this small team in Canada!

Ported from the Wii U, Sonic: Lost World lands on Steam! Let's take a look and see how well this port holds up!.
Let's start by taking a look at the game itself.
Eggman's up to something again and he has some backup on this one! A group known as the Deadly Six, formed by lifeforms known as the Zeti, a race of creatures native to the Lost Hex, a mysterious and unexplored continent floating in the sky and the main setting for our adventure. It's up to Sonic to foil Eggman's  plan once again!.
Counting with 32 levels, Sonic: Lost World features a more traditional platformer style with some of the speed Sonic is known for.
It mixes 2D and 3D sections. The former being more reminiscent of something out from a 2D Mario game, with a slower pace with lots of jumping and less running around. The later containing mostly cylindrical levels, places that allow Sonic to run on a cylinder shaped level that lets you move forward while running around the walls/floor and sections that are pretty similar to levels from Mario Galaxy, a spherical chunk of land with it's own gravity field. For the most part the level design is pretty good, most of the 3D levels allowing you to keep some momentum and speed around in classic Sonic fashion, however the 2D sections, while good, interesting and well designed for the most part, go against the sense of speed that one expects from a game of this franchise.
The game tries to keep it fresh by adding a few levels with different sections such as grinding, flying, ice skating, rolling around as a snowball and sliding down in sand, while the grinding and flying sections are okay, the rest feel a little bit gimmicky, adding some weird momentum and restricting movement, making the levels annoying and harder than they should. Fortunately enough, the game spawns a power up capsule with a wing inside that will allow you to skip a section of the level once you failed several times in a row. sometimes it can be annoying as you might not want to grab it, but it will spawn on a pretty awkward spot that will make it hard to miss it.
The Wisps from Sonic Colors also make a comeback on this game allowing you to take alternate routes on the levels but ultimately  adding nothing to the game. The game adds the ability to parkour. Sonic can run, climb and jump along walls with this new mechanic, Even though these individual movements have been previously showcased, the parkour mechanic allows you to use any wall in the environment rather than just specific parts. It's really neat and has its moments but could be better implemented.
The bosses, they're uninteresting, the battles are nothing special and Instead of having a dedicated stage for the boss battle, you have to fight them on the final part of the second and fourth stage of each zone, meaning you'll be stuck in a boss battle when you only wanted to play a level as fast as you can.
Rather than aiming for realism in the visual style, Lost world presents a cartoony look with really vibrant colors, round edges and lots of basic shapes making most of the scenery. However, accompanied by the level design, it really makes up for an interesting experience and some really nice and beautiful visuals.
The music, it has to be the best part of this game, I've fallen asleep listening to some of the music on this game, it's just
It has a slower pace when compared to most Sonic games but it's very fitting when paired with the levels, it's because of both that each zone has a really distinct feel to it. Forming a great atmosphere and making the levels really enjoyable to play.
But what about the porting itself? Well, here things start to get a little worse.
For starters, the game is locked at 60FPS, which might be bad news for all those power-PC users and a horrible thing for people with low-end specs, since the game suffers from a terrible slowdown that makes everything run REALLY bad. SEGA released a PBT version for the game, which can change the frame lock on the game, but it can break the physics making the game unplayable.
The port is also missing the multiplayer component of the game, so no multiplayer races for the PC users.
The controls with keyboard are simple and really good. They can be remapped in any way you like, I only had a small problem where the game would change the Sprint key from Left Shift to Right Control every time I start up the game, I have no idea what's causing it, but it's just a minor issue.
So, in short
Sure! I recommend this title to players that love platformers. Even better if you can snatch it with a discount. Just make sure you can run it at a steady 60FPS or your experience will be really hindered by the slowdown.

Where to start with this one. First of all, this is not a terrible mod. But when you put a price tag on it, it's no longer a mod. It's a game. And as a game, it's a pretty odd bag.
The biggest problem I can tell you is it's pacing. Portal and Portal 2 are both good at slowly introducing new concepts with it's mechanics, increasing difficulty. This game is good at neither. Some things you can do are straight forward if you played Portal 2. But if you never played Portal 2, you'd probably be lost from the start. The first few real puzzles have solutions so obtuse and ridiculous that I'm surprised I figured them out. Then there will be a level that's easy, followed by another level with an insane solution. It's really all over the map and incredibly frustrating. I would almost go as far to say that the levels are out of order.
It also likes to make references to Portal without really understanding what made those games funny. Or fun. It's really just a frustration fest as you fail a test that is about 90% luck and have to reapply your paint for the fifteenth-millionth time. Or get stuck on the terrain, or the visuals bug out, or you decide you want to alt-tab and the game freezes.
As a mod, I would say "that was interesting, but it needs some work", but as a game you have to pay for, I'd say "I want my money back".
EDIT: Music is pretty good though. Hardly enough to save it.

If you enjoy hack and slash games, love One Piece, or are a fan of the Warriors series, One Piece Pirate Warriors 3(OPPW3) is a great game to pick up. It's a highly addicting hack and slash, has a lot of content, and it just feels amazing to play as characters from the One Piece anime. (Just a heads up: for dub fans the voice acting is all Japanese. I loved it, being a fan of the sub!)
Something I noticed while playing this Warriors game vs a few others in the series(most notably the recent Fire Emblem Warriors) is that every character feels truly unique. There are a TON of playable characters in OPPW3 and each of them has a varied playstyle that fits well with their anime counterparts. Each playable character has the potential to reach level 50, and through a level break system eventually climb to 100 in the Dream Log (aka endgame content). There are also quite a few charaters that you can summon as allies who are not playable as well.
The plot of the game covers everything from the first season all the way through Dressrosa. Side Note: this game was created when Dressrosa was not finished so the plot for that arc is game exclusive. Each story level covers the key parts of an arc and really gives you a nostalgic feeling for your favorite moments in the series. There are a few noticeably missing characters from various arcs (ie: most of Blackbeard's crew and various other side characters from several arcs) but this is a small oversight in comparison to the large pool of people you do see.
The controls are where the game suffers a bit. The pc controls are pretty klunky and i gave up on them almost immediately. However, if you download XInput and use a controller, this game is infinitely more fun. I highly recommend just doing that from the start. There is a great guide on Steam in the guides section for this game called "True Solution for all XInput Controller Problems" that gives you ideal button mappings that worked perfectly for the 140+ hours I played OPPW3. Also the game does not really give you clear direction on how to use certain moves at some points, and it can be easy to miss how to do something important (ie: kizuna rush). The combo/button menu is your friend.
Overall the OPPW3 experience is a great deal of fun, and I would definitely recommend it. Have fun punching your way through pirates, marines, and anyone else that gets in your way. Kaizoku-o ni ore wa naru!

Firstly, let's forget the theme. You're going to be mowing down digital humans for fun, it's hardly important what clothes they're wearing so chill your triggers.
Secondly, it's a puddle deep turret shooter with some progressive persistent unlocks. So enter only those who want a violent alternative to minesweeper.
That said lets get onto some observations.
The persistent unlocks offer something to strive for, of course that also means once you've unlocked some of the juicier items you're left chasing scores and leaderboard positions. These do highlight your friends which is kind of neat but you can only see this while playing, can't see an option to do it from the menu which is a bit odd.
As the developer of Hatred I did expect a bit more gore but alas you'll need to settle for some nice explosion effects. Reality is you'll rarely see or have time to appreciate any of the human/bullet relationship detail.
Grind. Each map unlocks after achieving a cumulative enemy and vehicle kill target. This means you'll be playing the same map many times before you can move onto similar gameplay over a new canvas. The lack of variety therefore is a bit of a negative, the positive being you're not going to see all the maps in less than 4 hours and well you'll be earning xp to unlock those persistent skill upgrades.
As noted by other reviewers, some of those upgrades remove a lot of the hinderances the game starts off with such as needing to reload or operate the rotation of the turret via keys. Judge yourself whether you feel this sucks although it should be said you don't have to upgrade those skills (but you can't deactivate one you've purchased!).
Levels play out randomly which can impact your run and I question to some degree how leaderboards would be totally reflective of people's skill when RNG could influence the result but bah, it's a silly game so why worry about that.
An annoyance I found most impacting of my fun was the attacks from the sides. While it's neat you are forced to change your focus to a new area of the maps it's also often done while you're also being attacked from the front. There are some support powers you could call in at this time but it again leaves you somewhat open to RNG on how much damage you'll be unable to avoid.
On the whole. I'd reccommend this if you want some dumb brainless fun with some challenge (and a sprinkle of RNG). Workshop support is in there (although I see only two entries as of writing) so there may be some additional longevity or at least eye candy in the future. Get it cheap and I think this is a good one for a quick blast now and again.

Possibly the only game marketed as "Finally the game where you kill can kill Gungans with AT-AT Walkers", to paraphrase the PC Gamer review, Galactic Battlegrounds was the second RTS game set in the Star Wars universe, with the first (Force Commander) only being remembered for it's nifty main menu music and average review scores. Releasing Force Commander around the same time as the highly anticipated RTS Dark Reign 2 didn't help either so Lucasarts decided to play it safe and release a more bog standard real time strategy game the following year which could also cash in on the sweet sweet Clone Wars lucre.
Galactic Battlegrounds would be that game and you couldn't get much safer than being an Age of Empires 2 clone even down to the using the same game engine, called the Genie Engine, as well as the same company Ensemble Studios which is both it's major strength and it's major weakness.
If you've played any Age of Empire game or general RTS in general you know the drill. Collect stuff with dudes to build dudes and research badder dudes before making bad (or good) dudes suffer a critical existence failure via applied use of dudes.
Said resources this time are Carbon (Wood), Ore (Stone... kinda), Nova Crystals (Gold... also kinda) and Food (Food) collected by worker units and deposited in a main base structure with other structures providing troop production, research and trade. It even has houses to support population cap which feels a tad wonky with the military base aesthetic but if it ain't broke...
A new build mechanic introduced in GB however is the use of power structures that provide a zone of power which are vitally important to the production speed of your buildings and your defensive structures defending you. While fairly common in modern RTS games (insert additional Pylon joke here) it was fairly novel for the time and made for some interesting tactical choices especially in the early game where resources are tight.
The main issue with this is that it is just more of the same, there was a degree of fatigue for this style of RTS back then with the engine being rather old and 3D games being the in thing which detracted from the appeal of the setting.
The actual factions however are where this game shines with each being distinctive and recognisable enough to warm the heart of any Star Wars fans provided they aren't the five or so who like Ewoks or something. The choices are a mixed selection from both the Original Trilogy and the Prequel stuff which was one of the main draws back in the day.
While generally following the cookie cutter principle of the AOE games with slight variants depending on the faction chosen they tend to more greatly reflect how they were portrayed in the films. A basic overview of these are...
Galactic Empire: Good at ground wars but crap at anything vaguely air or sea orientated.
Alliance to Restore the Republic (Rebels): Go to guys for air superiority (fear their A-Wings).
Wookies: Pulling arms out of sockets with big burly infantry natch.
Trade Federation: Mass production of crap units but lots of trade tech for max monies to buy said units.
Royal Naboo: Expensive but look really fancy to make up for it.
Gungans: Game breaking on any map with a drop of water, death incarnate with unstoppable overpowered everything.
The expansion released later in 2002 added:
Grand Army of the Republic (Clones): Can pump out infantry fast but still fairly costly. Sound kinda samey.
Confederacy of Independent Systems (Seps): Have battle droids that are actually threatening.
There might have been more planned going by a rather obvious space for a second expansion on the original CD start up screen but sadly the idea was put on ice. Rather ironic really considering the only new faction added in Revenge of the Sith was the Wookies.
With the gritty grey of the Imperial buildings and walkers to the organic wooden yet high tech structures of the Wookies everything feels so very Star Wars. Even the naval ships which while a staple of AOE are kinda weird for a Star Wars game, though at least they create a plausible reason why everyone has a navy (it's to get destroyed by the Gungan Bongos). To cement the Star Wars feel aircraft are also added and naturally for a game engine designed for historical warfare are kinda clunky basically being hovering ground vehicles that only AA units can shoot. The expansion even added what basically amounts to a flying battering ram.
While there is a fairly decent campaign split over both the original and prequel movies that provides some very nice expanded universe fluff (now sadly not canon) to the setting, always nice to see General Dodonna get captured and Veers having a barney on Hoth, it was kind of rushed (including re-using some Age of Empires 2 scenarios) and overshadowed by the main draws of the game, namely throwing everything together in a massive fan fiction toy box in the custom game mode or multiplayer and the rather impressive construction set that comes very close to being able to do anything you can imagine.
Custom games allow for a large amount of players and faction mash ups which was the reason I brought it. Having the might of the Empire supported by Rebels and Wookies showing who is the better movie trilogy is always fun and one of the reasons I reinstall the game every year or so.
While I didn't fiddle to much with mods and custom scenarios there were some amazing ones including a more rpg/adventure game style remake of Episode 1 as well as tweaks and rebalances some of which are still being worked on today such as the Expanding Fronts mod. Heck that even adds in the Zann Consortium from Empire at War.

Overall it is a very solid game that's only really great if you are a Star Wars fan otherwise Age of Empires 2 would probably be more preferable. It plays it too safe to be really memorable which is probably why Empire At War has overshadowed it but what it does it does well and I'm a sucker for any game that has Rebel fleet troopers and Tauntauns in it.

Alright.
I completed Prototype 2 less than 5 minutes ago, and Prototype 1, I've played probably more than 200 hours in total.
Are they the same experience? NO. With a change of protagonist and a complete revamp of the abilities, upgrade system, and fighting mechanics, Prototype 1 and PRototype 2 are two very different (and both incredible) experiences.
The Abilities.
Instead of one ability equipped at a time, with a multitide of combos and attacks, P2 features 2 abilities assigned to Mouse Button 1 and 2. This makes combat simpler than P1, but not nessecarily better. P1 contains thousands of combinations to simply desecrate your enemies. P2 has much gorier attacks, special moves, and kill sequences, but P1 simply goes more in depth. If you wanna know more, play the goddamn game.
Upgrade System.
Prototype 1 had a currency based upgrade system in which you would collect EP (Evolution Points) in ludicrous amounts and spend them on upgrades, of which there were, I believe, over 100. Prototype 2 features a leveling system, in which the EP (still present) acts as experience points. Upon leveling, the player chooses a single upgrade. Whether either one is better, I can't say, because I didn't have a problem with either of them. They were acceptable mechanics that did what they were meant to. Can you really ask for more?
Fighting Mechanics.
Incredible. Please just play it. It's Incredible.
Story.
In my opinion, P2's story was FAR better than P1. The original Prototype has more of a focus on the hack and slash, kill everything, be a total badass through ACTIONS. P2, on the other hand, has more of an emotional story, in which the character (still badass, still ♥♥♥♥s♥♥♥♥♥♥up) is less cold, and is more emotional. I felt more immersed with Heller than with Mercer.
Final Thoughts
If you can spare the funds, ♥♥♥♥ING BUY IT. If you can't, you better start a damn trust fund, because both Prototype 1 and Prototype 2 are excellent, amazing games that give 2 amazing experiences.

I'm gonna write just a small review here 'cos I have already reviewd this awesome developers' other game in this series (namely "My Coloring Book - Animals") and this one follows very similar patterns :)
For just 0,99$/€ (and of course way less on sale and with coupons) you'll have here almost 50 different and beautiful cartoony images of any kind of transport vehicle, from planes and cars to trains, motorbikes and so on; all of them are unlocked from the beginning, so if you like these games or even better if you have kids around (this is a game designed for kids primarily, but it's still lots of fun if you're in a casual/relaxing mood XD) you/they can choose your favourite vehicle and also you'll see it already colored in a miniature, so you'll know how it will have to become!
In-game, this one unfortunately still takes on the same bucket painting pattern of the other games in this series: on the right side you'll have 20 different colors (some of them are quite similar to each other but you'll get accustomed quite early if you keep on playing it!) and with your bucket (which as I said unfortunately is too big and positioned on the left side, like if the screen was inverted and it can "cover" a little bit your white image) you'll have to fill it with colors according to the miniature example on the upper right part of the screen and well, keep on coloring your vehicle :)
The upper right template features a big magnifying glass and when you'll click on it, instead of enlarging the image it will superimpose the correct, full-colored image to the one you're coloring and this is extremely helpful, since you'll see directly if you have put some wrong colors or which colors you'll need to use.
Since the game has lots of details, it's highly recommended to play it full-screen, otherwise even on a big monitor you'll have problems to see everything right; before starting the game you'll have the opportunity to choose different graphics settings so keep it at the maximum ratio: if not played on full screen and with high details you'll find it harder to fill the smallest spots, trust me xD
Unfortunately, as with many other Steam games, the game hub store is machine-translated and completely unreadable in Italian so I'd suggest you to get right into the game, you won't need any kind of tutorial or explanation :)
I just say this thing every time since I found it a little bit misleading, when a game says that there are full subtitles and interface while actually only the game hub store page is in the language your client's running and more than this, it's machine-translated and unreadable, with lots of childish errors.
At this point, in my opinion as an adult player who was forced to learn English in the '90s in order to play the NES and SNES games, it's way better to leave everything in English - it's simple English, you won't make such horrors like these translations and maybe you'll help younger players to learn the ever-useful English if they wanna stay on the Internet and live in the contemporary world xD
Which I'm opposed to of course, but we must accept reality :P
Anyways, of course, as I said the game features no text and only coloring so except for the bucket issue and the fact that some colors (mainly the blue ones) are quite similar to each other (but when you start to make a smart use of the hint/magnifying lens system you'll find it way easier to fit) well, for its price and its longevity, and also the fun ratio for kids I think that this game is completely recommended to anyone who likes the stuff I tried to analyze!
Plus kids usually love sport cars, planes and so on so I found this one easier, but also funnier than the animals coloring book ;)
Have fun with it and keep it into your library section for kids ;)

Each branching path goes in a totally different direction in a way that makes no sense and changes everything about the characters, even their backstory. It's hard to care about what happens to the characters when they aren't consistent characters to begin with. For example:
- There's the story of a murderer who hunts down an idol.
- There's the story of childhood friends finding each other again.
- There's the story of two amnesic people waking up on a random street.
So you'll be playing episodes with flat characters that aren't the same as the last game. You might think these sound like interesting stories. Well, there's nothing else to them. The game is just a series of pitchlines with nothing else. Each story takes a minute to read. The whole "script" would fit in a leaflet. It's not a story, it's a summary. A bad joke of a game. The store page did say that was the gimmick behind the game, but I at least expected it to be parodic or humorous in its ridiculous plot... but no. I couldn't endure it more than five minutes and I have a quarter of the game done.
I feel bad for writing this negative review because I've been following the game's creator for a while on twitter and I know they care about this. It doesn't feel like a bad hoax to get money, but an actual passion project. But that doesn't erase the fact that this game isn't worth any money, and I doubt it's worth your time either.

7.62 High Calibre is a Strategy Game developed by Apeiron and is the sequel to the game Brigade E5. It almost feels like a spirtual successor to the old Jagged Alliance games, which have influenced many games in their time. This game does not fail to impress, and emulate all the key elements of Jagged Alliance which made it such a good series, while bringing new features to the table.
Based in the fictional nation of Algeira, a country just north of Brigade E5's previous warzone, you are a mercenary who has been hired to hunt down a Russian man who screwed over a bank and was never apprehended. He has fled to Algeira to avoid prosecution, and you'll have to hunt him down by any means necessary, and bring him back dead or alive. Of course, you'll start the game with rather ♥♥♥♥♥♥ equipment which means you have to spend some time doing jobs on the side, but that's one of the big advantages of the game in a way, as it is a strategy game, yet you get to carve out your own destiny and plan prior to getting stuck in and finishing the main quest before you've even done the cool parts. If you go try to go ahead with the main plot and speedrun it, you'll most likely get curb-stomped unless you know what you're doing, but you're always free to roam the jungle and cities of Algeira, finding quests and new mercs to hire on your way, up to a 6-man squad.
A big plus in my opinion is the HUGE variety of weapons you can get. Literally tons, from Glock 22's and P220's to Remington 870 Magnums and AKS-74U's, all the way up to FN Minimi's and M14 SOCOM rifles. You'll never go more than an hour without finding at least a few new weapons to play with, and they all come in many flavours of calibre, allowing you to mix and match your ammo with Armour Piercing Rounds, FMJ Rounds, and many more variants. Many weapons can also be custom rigged with scopes and lasers to allow you to get the most out of them in a firefight too. Even better is that the game can be installed with the Blue Sun Mod which adds a massive amount of content & weapons to a game which already has plenty to play with. I will mention how to install this mod at the end!
The game's key feature is Real-Time Pausing, which allows for a mix between turn-based and real-time gameplay, allowing you to experience the best of both worlds. The game can be paused at any time to allow you to command your merry band of mercenaries, and then unpaused to let them carry out their actions. Alternatively you don't need to pause the game once (The game does it automatically VERY often but it can easily be disabled), and instead command your team on the fly, allowing for fast-paced combat and tactical planning to overcome the enemy.
Sound Effects - 7.62 has a lot of good sound effects, mostly for the weapons you can get your hands on. Turn bass up on your computer and expect to hear some ear-shattering explosions and gunshots loud enough to kill a blue whale.
Graphics - The game is a little dated now, and the graphics aren't really up to competition with the likes of XCOM - Enemy Unknown, but it's still a beautiful game. Watching the sun set over Algeira as you mow down squads of bandits with unending bullets is truly a wonderous sight. Some of the textures of the game aren't the greatest, but again, it's not a new game.
AI - The AI is what makes the game so challenging. They're bloody smart, and will routinely change tactics just to get the drop on you. Snipers on your squad can be expected to be flanked while they shoot at other bad guys, and you'll have grenades thrown at you purely to force you to retreat, giving the enemy more ground to corner you into. They'll even retreat themselves if they know they're in trouble, and will regroup with their buddies so they can have another pop at you. If it seems too difficult however, you do have an option to dumb down the AI so they aren't performing counter-attacks that would see Delta Force hang their heads in shame.
Playability - The game is very playable and enjoyable, albeit being a bit confusing at first. Tossed into some Latin country with nothing but a TT-33 and ammo can obviously be a little uninformative, so you'll have to do most of the snooping around yourself. The controls are relatively simple, but do get a little getting used to. One of the good (or bad, depending how you know guns) things about the game is that guns must be cleaned, have their magazines filled individually, and then loaded into the firearm that uses them, as it obviously doesn't help trying to fire empty mags at someone trying to take your head off. So bear in mind to use a firearm effectively -
1. Make sure you have the right mags for the gun.
2. Make sure you have the right calibre of ammunition for the gun.
3. Make sure you have the gun loaded with a mag of ammo.
It may seem a little condescending, but it's painfully easy to run into battle and forget that you never loaded your mags up, leaving you one full magazine to fight many enemies, unless you want to waste ages loading up each mag as you get shot at.
~The game also gives you a lot of leeway too, you aren't in a rush to complete the main quest, and you never really have to. If you just want to shoot cops in a 3rd World Dictatorship then the game won't stop you. But the Army might. On the other hand, if you want to hire your own private army and run a revolution of your own, then you can quite easily do that.
~The developers of the game are very supportive and helpful to their community, who you can find on the discussions of this game frequently assisting players with technical issues and other options. They are very polite and can definitely be relied on, which is always a good thing.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The bad things worth mentioning
~ The game does have a tendency to crash. Make sure you save often and keep more than one save. The game auto-saves quite often, but even losing one save can set you back a little.
~Sometimes enemies will get stuck on ladders for whatever reason, so if you've killed all the enemies you see but are still technically in 'combat mode', check the ladders.
~Whether this is good or bad depends on how you like your game, (I like this but not everyone might) but the game is ridiculously difficult. You can add as many modifiers to make the game as easy as possible as you wish, but even then, enemies are very accurate and can shoot you in the head, (Near blinding you) shooting you in the chest (Crippling you), leg shots and even arm shots which will send your current weapon flying on the floor, stunning you in the process. Sometimes you'll end up in shock if you encounter many enemies at once, get shot at, or whatever else. It can be frustrating, but the enemy is also prone to all of this, so make your shots count. (The game is rather punishing but very satisfying to play)
~The game is rather cheesy and I wouldn't blame you for forgetting you aren't fighting in the Congo in the 80's, especially with some of the silly dialogue options. The only thing that convinced me otherwise was the fact you can find things like Kriss Super V's and XM8's if you're lucky.
~Like most RPG's, you can screw some missions up, and not even realise until you get to them. What I mean is that last guy you blasted in that town? Oh yeah, he's part of a quest later. So try not to be too trigger happy, even if it is just so you can kill them and take their weapons.
[All in all however, this game is definitely worth buying. It's a steal too, for only $5, or £4. The Blue Sun Mod is recommended, as it adds a lot to this great game, as well as having patches. You can install it by right clicking on the game, going to propeties, beta (I think it's the last tab) and clicking the community patch.] One of my personal favourites, and I hope it'll be one of yours too. 9/10.

Don't Undock in something you can't afford to lose.

So I ended up trying this as a result of the yogscast jingle jam bundle. After a single game I was hooked harder than I had been on any game in a long time. Showed it to my roommate. He played a single game. He built a crappy little car thing, killed one person and died 20 times, and instantly purchased the lifetime premium because it was _THAT_ good.
People can whine about meta, or how it used to be better, or whatever, but so far, up to gold MMR, ranked is genuinely balanced and fun. Everything has a counter, and sometimes, skill can get you out of the way of that counter. For instance: after tinkering around and getting some parts, I built a bomber - heavy attacks to hit the ground, some really light anti-air for dealing with tiny drone planes, and some homing missles for emergency dogfights. As you'd expect: I kill the crap out of ground targets, but a dedicated fighter plane will ruin me - just like in real life.
There's a few 'meta' archetypes that exist, but honestly, it's refreshing, because they're archetypes, and not actual models. Everyone has different bots, and everyone has different variations on a theme. Some work well, some... don't. Really don't. The experimentation is what makes it that much more fun. And the best part? You can't 'solve' it. There isn't an 'answer' - lots and lots of things are viable, and that's what makes this so awesome.
One additional note - you may think my hours played count is pretty low, if you're seeing this review just after it's been written. Note that I've owned the game for 2 days, and my 19 hours are from just those two days. I've been doing basically nothing else but this. Yep. That good.
Play it. It's free. And the premium is A) not obnoxius - it's absolutely not pay to win - and B) worth it. If you get hooked after the first game like I did, it's definitely worth picking it up for the acceleration. The best part is experimentation, and more parts faster means more possibilities.

At the time of it's release, the gaming world was oversaturated from too many WWII shooters (Call of Duty, Medal of Honor, etc etc) and Day of Defeat didn't have much to separate it from the pile of historical shooters already out there at the time.

Counter-Strike, Team Fortress, Left 4 Dead, even Half-Life Deathmatch are all massively addictive, appealing games that satisfy as only the best games out there can do. But Day of Defeat: Source doesn't stand out like those games.
Ultimately it comes across feeling like a watered-down version of Battlefield. There's objectives and classes, but the maps are small and there are no vehicles to drive.
So, if you're going to buy a multiplayer shooter, I highly recommend you buy something else. There's nothing actually wrong with Day of Defeat: Source, but for 10 dollars or less you could do way better.

Ok, I feel I have to make this review, difficult though it is.
Aperture Tag is a feld of contradictions, and I really am not sure whether to reccomend it or not, and whether or not to review it as a mod, or as a paid-for game, whether I should compare it to Portal or view it as a standalone. And furthermore, I'm not sure if I should review this as the big Portal fan I am, or just as a general gamer.
As gameplay goes, it is fun, that much is easy to say, the makers obviously have a lot of experience with Portal on the workshop most likely, and each chamber is fairly well finished. The puzzles are challenging to an extent, which is as it should be, and only being able to use gels does give an interesting element to gameplay.
As many have said before me, it does fall down a bit in areas like cohesive-ness. The general storyline is 'Here are some tests, solve them' which isnt bad in and of itself, but the problem is this is based off Portal, something well known for its good story, and was one of the main things that made the two games memorable. Additionally, there isn't that much of the gameplay, it's about the same size as the first Portal game. When compared to its big brother, it doesnt stand up because it simply can't, this is a mod, made by a few fans, and it shows through in places like the story, and how the core that shows you around is fairly badly recorded, and basically has a one dimensional personality. The references to Portal 2, even putting you in a few chambers from the game, and how 'Nigel' is a bad mirror of Wheatley show how it is straining to live up to the original in ways it never can.
But I'm nit-picking this in ways that some of you may think is unfair, I shouldn't compare it to the game because it is just a mod etc. But the problem is this isn't just a mod, if it were I would say A+++, and be done with it. No, the thing is you have to pay for this, which makes it a product, which means you have the right to have your say because you're paying for it.
At the end of the day however I just need to review this, so here it is: I enjoyed it, it was fun, challenging tests, new gameplay idea, great soundtrack courtesy of the ever brilliant Harry Callaghan, and for me as a big Portal fan I don't really regret buying it.
Yes, at times it has the slightly unpolished feel of something that belongs on the steam workshop rather than the store, and yes the story falls down a lot, but it's fun, which is what a game should be.
So, if you are a fan of Portal, and you're willing to pay this much, I would reccomend you do. If you are looking for a cheap puzzle game to spend a few hours on (only a few mind), then again, reccomend it. But if you are hesitant, or not that big a fan of Portal, or not that prepared to spend money on a mod, I wouldn't, go spend it on something you're sure of.
TL;DR Fun, challenging puzzles, bad story, short play-time: If you're a portal/puzzling fan, reccomend buying, if you're not, wouldn't reccomend buying.

Yes, Aperture Tag: The Paint Gun Testing Initiative is a mod. Yes, it's not very well polished, and the voice acting with Nigel changes in quality every now and then. Yes, some of the puzzles kinda bug out in the weirdest ways. Yes, even I'm sorta iffy on the fact that I paid money for this.
Do I dislike it? No. In fact, this is actually a pretty fun romp with the gel mechanics of Portal 2, and I legitimately enjoyed what I played. There's some interesting puzzles here, along with some nifty rooms that require quick thinking to zoom through with combinations of Blue and Orange gel. Plus Nigel (despite that his voice kinda got annoying after a while, what with the quality changes every few rooms) has some interesting quips to dish out.
The game does has it's flaws though. As I said before, it's a bit unpolished. Though considering that it was a mod and I doubt the guys behind it had the funds to truly bug test and work out some of the worse parts, I'd give them a little bit of leeway. Bugs and polish aside though, the main thing I disliked about my experience was the reactor section. It wasn't the time limit or the fact that it's difficult, but rather the button that lets you skip the entire section. On my first try, when I saw the prompt for a  time limit on the top of my screen, and the fact that I saw the button's panel beforehand, had me rushing for it because I didn't exactly know what it was-- till I pressed it. It then whisked me away throughout the course for me, and then plopped me down into the next chapter. Sorta my fault, since I didn't pay too much attention. I'm not saying remove it completely, but maybe offer a choice after the end of the short movie asking if you'd actually like to try the course again or something. Like maybe you got stuck on a specific part of the course and didn't understand what's being expected, and after seeing the short movie the button shows you, you wanted to try for yourself again.
But anyways, Aperture Tag is pretty entertaining, with some old mechanics blended together with a new one. If you can look past it's faults, you'll probably enjoy what this game has to offer. If you're wanting a AAA experience with the same quality as Valve puts out though, you'd best stay away.

Fun game for VR. It's a horror themed Half-Life 2 mod. That's not really a bad thing though. I've been playing it on the Oculus Rift DK2 and it's been entertaining. It's got a nice atmosphere and a pretty standard remote small town horror story.
Decoupling aim from look for the Oculus is always welcome. Some native Razer Hydra/STEM controls would be a nice addition, but things work very well as is.
It's also not really a shooter. Ammo is very limited and resources need to be managed. You're not going to blast through hordes of enemies in this. Physics puzzles are present, but nothing to brain wracking, mostly involving building a ladder or steps to get over a tall obstical. It fits the gameplay though and doesn't bog things down.
There are a few things about it that could use some work. One of the enemies is wearing a yellow shirt and looks like an undead Star Trek extra which kind of threw me off a bit. The "creepy music" is a bit overused. It plays throughout acting like every moment is tense and scary. That may be what they were going for, but overusing that kind of musical cue lessens the effect.
The flashlight has a limited charge, but it's not really a necessity. One could easily play through the entire game without it, and I only flicked it on to get a quick peek into a darkened area on occasion to make sure I wasn't missing any items and mostly ignored it. Most of the areas are very well lit and I don't recall any moments where an enemy jumped out of the darkness at me. Most were clearly visible beforehand or hiding behind objects and not in darkness.
Another thing is that losing the firearm and giving the player a melee weapon actually made the game less scary. Previous to this event I found myself worrying about conserving ammo and that helped with the tension. After I got the hammer I could simply run up and bludgeon any enemy I came across. There was no worrying about running out of ammo or resources after that point.
Obviously Half-Life 2 physics rules are in effect here and that may be why I didn't find it all that scary. I'm used to how things work and never found myself in any real trouble outside of cutscene induced setbacks to my progress such as being captured or having a floor drop out from under me or something similar. It also has a case of "I'm just an innocent dead body that in no way will come after you" syndrome. Many enemies can be bludgeoned or otherwise dealt with before they are 'triggered' to wake up and come after you.
Despite it's flaws, I recommend it. Especially if you've got an Oculus Rift. The VR really adds something to the game. All and all it's an entertaining title. There are a couple of mild jump scares and a few moments where flight is better than fight, but it's a moody atmospheric survival horror jaunt. It's more PG-13 horror than anything really graphic, gore is present, but you won't find yourself drowning in blood or hacking off limbs.
You can't beat the price and it's worth an evening of play.
