Naruto Shippuden: Ultimate Ninja Storm 3 Full Burst is basically the 'Ultimate Edition' of Ultimate Ninja Storm 3. It includes revamped graphics, all the costumes released as DLC, new character and a new Story chapter and Challenge mode. It is a fighting game developed by CyberConnect2.
Story: The story of UNS 3 closely follows the Naruto Shippuden anime and takes place during the Fourth Great Ninja War. I don't wanna give too much away so I'll leave it at that. Having said that, the story is told really well using in-game cutscenes. Each chapter is presented in such a way that closely resembles the anime and while watching the cutscenes, you are even fooled to think that you are actually watching an episode of Naruto. Each cutscene has high production values with great graphics, voice acting and dynamic and over-the-top camera angles.
Graphics: The game employs cell-shaded graphics for its characters and environments. I think this is a good choice as the visuals depict the anime fantastically, with characters and special attacks (jutsus) rendered at a very high quality. The game looks stunning at the highest graphical settings and no jagged edges are present anywhere.
Sound: Each scream, attack and catchphrase delivered by the original Japanese voice actors sound great. They give performances worthy of an anime episode and each cutscene just feels like you are watching the TV show. When the voice actors convey anger, you feel that anger. When they convey sadness, you also feel that sadness. Those are the signs of experienced and talented artists.
Gameplay: The gameplay of Naruto is fast, frantic and alot of fun. It is easy to pick up and play by anyone, as you can immediately mash the B button for a combo or press Y and B together to do a jutsu attack. The controls are laid out well on the controller and they feel intuitive to reach for and press. The LT button (on the Xbox 360 controller) has been cleverly used for performing Substitutions while LB is used to block. The easy to memorise layout of the controls add to the fun of the gameplay.
Overall, Naruto Shippuden: Ultimate Ninja Storm 3 Full Burst is a faithful rendition of the anime it is inspired by. The characters look, act and sound like their anime counterparts and the gameplay is addictive.

I have to admit, I wasn't expecting much of this game when I first saw it. Not even because it looked good or bad, but just because I never bothered to look much into it, despite the fact that it has a big manly lumberjack on its main Steam picture (lumberjacks are awesome!).
In terms of graphics, I'll admit the game doesn't look that amazing, but that's understandable considering this is the studio's first game and the game's price. However, the atmosphere that's presented completely balances this off, by making you forget about the simple and sometimes clunky models with its pure Canadian charm. I'm Canadian, I live in Quebec, I love snow, I love the night, and I can absolutely guarantee that this game feels very authentic. This mood is even backed up by Canadian folk music.
Even the story feels very Canadian, using myths and legends that are very historical, which also includes native folklore. At some points I'd play the game and think to myself "this reminds me of that one folk tale I read in high school..."
While the voice acting is somewhat bland, I was pleasantly surprised when I tried playing the game in french. Except for one character, I feel there's a lot more emotion put into the dialogue, and the characters even speak with the regional accent!
As for the gameplay, it's really unique and thoughtful. Not only are you up against creatures much stronger than your character, you have a limited amount of ways to survive each night. The planning feels very difficult, but if you do it right, it will really pay off. The combat is also very strategic, since you use an old timey musket (5 or so second reload time), and your stamina rarely allows you to get more than a few hits off at once. Luckily, there's a fear mechanic for the enemies, which you can manipulate to help you survive a bit longer.
Overall, I'd definitely recommend this game! Especially for the price!

I am loving the music and sound effects. The gameplay is enjoyable. Overall, I like the story.
I think a level editor would be nice (editing what enemies spawn where to create custom challenges).
The loading time to start the game is fairly long for me, but once it's loaded, things move fairly smoothly.
I got the game at a discount and have found it to be worth it.
The idea of a "fear factor" is a nice idea, but I feel there aren't enough things that influence it. It's often a case of the enemies being afraid of you most of the time, or never being afraid of you (at least until the final levels). There's no way to scare any of the wolves into temporarily running away or scattering, for instance - the most you can do is light a fire, causing most enemies to stay back for a minute.
Nonetheless, the game presents a good challenge with a variety of ways to solve any one level (in addition to one's playthrough strategy -- does one focus on trap upgrades, or character health?)
I disagree with calling this game a "tower defense" - the traps/buildings you can construct are generally reset each day, and you need to operate most of them manually. It makes it very important to plan out how you will tackle each enemy from each wave. If they didn't tell you where the enemies were coming from, exactly what path they're following, and exactly how many there are, the game would be very different (and possibly better, though it would require a major redesign of how the traps work/how expensive they are). The major downside to the current system is that it seems less like strategy and more like "Which is the cheapest trap [or trap combination] that I can use to kill these enemies?"

Descent 2. Where to begin. In my humble opinion, it is the greatest shooter of all time. The story is eerie and compelling, the enemies intelligent and cunning, the gameplay thrilling and dynamic. Each world feels totally different than the last, with twisting labyrinths full of enemies, power-ups, hostages, secret passages, complex door/forcefield/wall locking/unlocking systems, incredibly fun boss battles, and the infamous guidebot. With six degrees of freedom, barrel rolls, afterburner, and brakes, the skill cap of Descent 2 is sky-high. There's a certain complexity to movement and dodging that only flight games seem to require.
On top of that, this isn't an open sky game like War Thunder, there's plenty of barriers to hide behind, doors you can ope n/close and traps you can set for enemies to run into. You can trick the enemies into hurting each other, combine different tactics such as activating a forcefield and using it as a barrier with guided missiles, you can even use robots as robo-shields to protect yourself against its comrades' attacks. By having elements of flight combat sims and traditional fast-paced shooters, Descent 2 is one of the most challenging, exciting games out there. The modern competitive scene is extremely skilled and you have to have reflexes as sharp as a fighter pilot to succeed.
The art, animation, and robot design is beautiful and intriguing. The variety of robots you face have a wide plethora of behaviors, acting individually, sometimes as a swarm, and sneaking up on you with near-human level combat comprehension. While this game may be very old, there are plenty of mods available that create taxing high-def textures and very realistic particle animations. Your $1000 graphics card won't be able to keep up when fully modded.
An enormous single player campaign, limitless potential with multiplayer, an active competitive scene, incredibly beautiful mods, and the most innovative FPS gameplay ever, makes Descent 2 a game worth far far more than a traditional $40 or $60. Oh wait, it's only $5? ONLY $5?!? If you don't buy this, you're a complete fool missing out on PC gaming's pinnacle game. 5000/10 is my rating for Descent 2.

Let me start by saying that 'Portal' 1 & 2 are among my most favorite games. I also really enjoyed 'Tag: The Power of Paint'. The fact that this mod isn't free led me to expect a certain degree of quality, but sadly, I've been very disappointed. I feel that the product page SHOULD CLEARLY STATE THAT THIS WAS NOT MADE BY VALVE OR TAG TEAM, since I was left with the incorrect impression that it was.
The puzzles are poorly designed. Whereas Portal's puzzles always gave you a very clear indication your goal and clues as to your methods, this mod fails to make it clear just what you're supposed to be doing. The quality of the levels built around the bad puzzles is mediocre at best, buggy at worst. I couldn't even tell how this game tied into Portal 2 (before? After?). The few custom models and textures that were added tend to be of amateur quality.
And then there's the voice-acting, as mentioned in many other reviews. In a word, it's bad. Whereas Glados, Wheatley, and the other Cores had synthetic-sounding voices, this mod does not. I initially thought it was a supposed to be a confused human employee reading off a computer screen. It turns out to be a new Core, for no good reason, somehow sitting itself on a chair. The character comes off as dumb as Wheatley, EXCEPT NOT FUNNY.
I feel a pressing need to highlight this fact: This mod LACKS PORTAL'S HUMOR. So, lacking good puzzles, story, and humor, I simply must recommend against getting this mod. If you want more 'Portal', you can get better mods than this for free.

It's one of the better DBZ games I have played in recent times. I was a huge fan of the Budokai series on PS2 way back and I played some others like Budokai Tenkaichi 2 and 3 which were okay games but I perfered the classic fighting camera and the QTE's in the original Budokai games made it feel like the show when Tenkaichi did not.
The reason say this is because when I bought Xenoverse I wanted that Budokai feeling I had when I was a kid. A game where it felt like I was apart of the show or getting to see some dream fights I had as a kid. Budokai captured that for me but Xenoverse did not sadly.
I didn't like Xenoverse that much because of the pacing. Yeah, we've all seen the show in a million times in other games where Goku goes Super Sayian for the first time and you're like "What the hell is happening" and when you realize its one of the best moments ever of DBZ. Suddenly, this just became your favorite show.
This game didn't capture that. It wasn't as epic as it should have been. Any of the big scenes in Xenoverse weren't even close to captured as the main show and it made the single player feel rushed. I would perfer if they just brought another games version of it over and recycle the voices lines instead of this.
Next is that I don't like they tried to make it like a MMO, without the tools that make a MMO. Its like they went half way. Oh you can see other players but you can't really interact with them. Maybe they did this because there might be kids purchasing the game and they don't want to have to deal with someone spamming the N word or something.
Lastly, the combat for this game is actually... pretty good. It felt polished so the gameplay was there and that is the only thing that made this game enjoyable and got me a good 25 hours of it before I stopped playing it. Only bad thing about the gameplay is online PvP is sometimes laggy and pot spamming and that makes the game unbalanced. Who thought that was a good idea?
Overall the game is okay. I'm mixed about it. If you're a DBZ fan I recommend it and if you've never heard of DBZ skip it. This game won't convince you to like the 90's show or get into that much at all because of how they tell the story of this game. If I wasn't a fan of DBZ I would of hated this game but it was fun for a little bit because I wanted to recapture my childhood again.
6.5/10

I really, really enjoyed this game. Way more than I expected too.
It's got a very well set noir-y atmosphere that heavily contradicts with the main characters more-or-less frivolous/whimsical attitude both in game and in dialogue. The game features a well-written story that removes itself from simple binary notions of good and evil and makes you make hard decisions that often leave you feeling like neither one was a good choice but knowing that you HAD to pick one lessens the impact. The story is very much themed around being in a position you don't want to be in and having to do things you don't want to do to get out of it. This is reflected in both the narrative dialogue-segments AND in the gameplay, where you are constantly making risky decisions and choosing between what appears to be the less dangerous of two fatal choices.
The gameplay struck me was "What Watch_Dogs wanted to be" in terms of the hacking mechanic unlocked a few levels in. You can rewire electronics in any room so that flicking a light switch in one room will open a door on another floor, and any combination therein. The satisfaction of creating a rube-goldberg chain reaction to trick the guards into running around while you sneakily drop in and out without being seen is beyond rewarding. You'll want to keep playing the levels again, and again, and again. It helps when the clients are able to give you certain optional objectives that effect your end rank (and I think your pay but I'm not certain), and so the game finds a way to keep itself fresh without actually chaining you to it's idea of freshness. This client wants you to leave nobody alive, so if you've been playing super stealthily this is a nice change of pace, BUT nothing is FORCING you to play the game like this. It's merely a suggestion from the employer that could lead to better review.
This games length isn't incredible BUT it will leave you wanting more which is where the fan community and level design kit come in handy as people on the steam workshop are keeping this game alive with new levels on a daily basis.
Overall I'd say this game is definitely worth checking out. Maybe wait until it's on sale if you don't like the idea of a 3 hour campaign but I think it's important to emphasize the replayability of not just the campaign but the game in general with it's level design kit.
This game gets a strong recommendation from me.

Like the first Prototype, this game allows the player to kill everyone in a multitude of very satisfying ways. It's too bad some features from the original aren't there this time around- air strikes, patsy, armor, and hanging onto walls like Spider-Man, to name a few. Unfortunately, it's impossible to get all upgrades in one playthrough so if you're looking to fully upgrade Heller, be prepared to play the story twice. Boss fights start out hard encounters but after acquiring many upgrades, Heller can go to town on them like nobody's business. There are even upgrades that let you destroy tanks and helicopters with one button after hijacking them. In the rare case you get overwhelmed in a fight, just summon your pack of Brawler Hunters and you win. The only real challenges are the Goliaths and the last boss fight. Prototype 2 is still a very fun game though.

Turn off your brain and start shooting like a mad-man.
It is your classic sentry gun shooter, enemies everywhere, explosions and death as your crossheir like some mark of doom straves over the slime of humanity, daesh.
You can hear them scream, just shoot them, or if you are the more refined killer, aim on their heads and shoot it off, burn them alive with your unlockable icendiary missiles, or just blow them up yourself or have them blow up by artillery, missile wielding choppers or just the good ol' napalm airstrike.
You'll start off a little weak, but no fear, you'll rise up to the level of almighty god soon enough... by far greater than whatever imaginary deity is leading these poor, hapless daesh fellows to you.
The good:
+++ Brain off, start shooting.  It starts up quickly, runs smoothly, no quests or thinking required, just chill and shoot
+++ You have to play to get the unlocks... it's a cheap trick to make you play, and it works.  You are always eager to get yet another upgrade. It takes some effort, but not much
++ the graphics are pretty good. Not AAA, but decent
+ the sound is sufficient.  Some attention was made to have the first few moments bring a moment of peace and quite... hearing the birds or a gentle flare being fired
+ flank attacks are nice
The bad:
- feels to have a wrong scope.  I don't know why, but I don't feel sentry guns should turn 360*.  The flank attacks are nice, as said but idk, it seemed better to have the rest my back is covered.  Also, it would have liked to see the enemies requiring more time to actuallly run to you... make them storm you if needed, but.... you know.. have you ever played medal of honor, the beach level, where you could be the gunner in one of the towers in multiplayer?  That specific kick is not received here.
---- Some epic encounters could be implemented... Maybe some boss, like Al Baghdadi showing up and when you kill him, he rises up as a monster to take out.  Now it's always the same 5 enemies (2 soldier, 3 vehicles) and that is it.
But, overall, this is thumbs up.  I'll probably play it from time to time, when I don't have that much time but still want some casual gaming

This game could have been good if it didn't fall into the same trap as the old Dreamcast/GameCube/PS3/360 trap of adding all kinds of gimmicks that stop you from enjoying playing normally as Sonic and instead make you do annoying stages with no explanation about the new mechanics.  It results in a lot of frustrating trial and error as you die from rule changes you had no idea were in effect until you encounter them.
It ranges from boring but otherwise inoffensive gimmicks like sticking you into a snowball which limits your movement ability, to auto-scrolling stages where Sonic drifts to the top of the screen and you have to press and hold the jump button to move towards the bottom of the screen (which isn't explained at all and you only figure out after smashing into a wall and dying a few times as you try all the buttons to figure out how to move up and down), to incredibly dull stages that are nothing but grinding on a rail the entire time,  to stages that change the rules and mechanics from screen to screen.
There's an incredibly frustrating stage near the end of the game where you start off on a section that totally changes the rules.  Instead of traditional left to right 2D gameplay that Sonic is known for, you're in a section where you can walk off the right side of the screen and appear on the left (and vice versa). The screen also scrolls up as you go up, and should you fall, instead of the screen scrolling back down with Sonic until you land on lower ground like it normally does, you die.  And this is yet again not explained at all, you only find out the first time you fall and unexpectedly die.  After this you transition into a sliding "half-pipe" section that is actually fairly typical of the game, aside from the fact that you can't jump this time.  Then you transition into another 2D section where this time you are allowed to fall and the screen scrolls down with you instead of killing you.  Then you go to another half-pipe section, but this time Sonic is moving towards the screen instead of away from it. This creates more frustration as you come to a section where it looks like you can stay on your current path or follow a pipe Sonic catches over to a second path, and it's only if you choose to stay on your current path that you find out you actually have no choice at all and staying where you are leads to instant death. After you get past this section, you go to another 2D section where once again, you can walk off one side of the screen and end up on the other, and falling kills you instead of scrolling the screen back down.  Then you come to a boss fight in 2D where you'll think at this point that you can still go from the left side of the screen and appear on the right, only to find out when you try it that you can't anymore.   And then to top it off, to deal the final blow to this boss and win the fight, you have to get the homing attack to "lock on" 5 times before you hit him, which you wouldn't possibly know because up until this very point, the most the homing attack would lock on is 3 times.
All this constant changing of rules and mechanics and play styles within single stages and without any warning or explanation just serves to frustrate rather than entertain.  The game is actually pretty great when it remembers what it was trying to be and lets you just play the Super Mario Galaxy inspired stages.  You run, you jump, you bounce off springs, you smash some robots, you have a good time.  But there's just too many stages in here where instead of having fun playing the game you wanted to play, you instead have to deal with frustrating trial and error to figure out how to proceed.  Variety can sometimes be a good thing in games to stop it from feeling repetitive, but this much variety is too much.  It feels like it's trying to be too many games at once, and that just isn't fun.

Lets be real. Day of Defeat: Source is a old game. (2006 to be exact) It was built on Source, the engine Valve engineered for Half-Life 2, Day of Defeat: Source features amazing graphics and physical gameplay for its time back in 2006. The main object of the game is to cap all the flags and then the round is over. Most servers that you play on unless its a 24 hour server of the same map will then change after one team caps all the flags 5 times. Day of Defeat: Source is kind of like a WW2 game of Counter Strike but with this game you can respown after you die before the round is over. There has always been cool mods for this game that make you crawing back for more and more. Game mods like Left 4 Dead (DoD:S) stile, realism mod and gun game just to name a few. The game is smooth and movement at times can feel like your just floating while in movement. What keeps me interested is the fact that the game is easy to learn but hard to master. You have to learn how to compensate for recoil of every firing weapon in the game. If you are not happy with the sights that are the defalt sights you can always change them to your liking to diffrent cross hairs and diffrent colors. There are not that many set backs to the game besides that all the models are the same. However you can go on Gamebanana and download any skin you may like and change it up a bit even change the weapon skin. At times you might feel like your team is at a disadvantage because of your map postion but thats again is what keeps you into the game. The number one thing that will keep you into the game is the community. This community is very helpful with any questions you may have about the game. Just know that if you have never played Day of Defeat: Source dont expect it to be like a Call of Duty game that is easy to play. Like said before this game is easy to learn but hard to master. Before you start to play just know your going to die and die a lot but, with time and good practice you will start to become better. Dont expect it to be like a Call of Duty game that is all about how many kills you get per round but more so about just having fun with other players. Most if not all hard core Day of Defeat: Source players HATE Call of Duty and do not appreciate when little kids talk all about how Call of Duty is so much better. The game is very cheep for what you get and you will not be let down.

I was extremely hyped when Sega announced this game was getting ported to PC - this was the only major Sonic game besides Sonic 06 that I had not played at least one version of, and since I didn't have enough money to spare for a Wii U, I thought I'd never be able to play it. This, of course, changed when Sega announced this port. I waited for the Steam sales when this game was 50% off and purchased it. How was it in the end?
Well, it's pretty good.
The level design is generally interesting and open, the boss fights are fun (if quite easy), the soundtrack is SUBLIME, and the graphical quality is pretty sweet. While I'm not crazy about the wisps, I approve of the improvements made to Lazer, Drill and Rocket over their original controls in Sonic Colours. Getting extra lives also becomes increasingly easier with this game, as clusters of them can be found at reglar intervals like at Honeycomb Highway.
I can't really say if there are improvements over the Wii U version (as stated above, I've never played it), however I approve of the ability to use the mouse in-game to open hints and the item briefcase. Also, if you're like me and you're not a fan of Lost World's storyline, you can skip the cutscenes, which I'm grateful for.
I do have a couple of problems with the game itself though:
- While using the run button isn't too much of an issue, I'd much prefer Sonic to just have a naturally fast momentum as he usually does. Also turning while using the run button cuts down his momentum noticably.
- While i praised Lazer, Drill and Rocket earlier, some of the wisp controls are odd - for example, you have to hold down the run button in order for Hover to float wheras in Sonic Colours it was the jump button, wheras Eagle appears to decend if you press either of those.
- There are times when I'm running along a wall and try jumping to the one opposite, only to fall off and (usually) die. Perhaps I'm doing something wrong, but it confusingly works well with some walls and terribly with others.
- The red star rings. Whilst most are easy to get, others will really test your patience (case and point, the third one in Frozen Factory Act 3)
- Finally, Frozen Factory Act 2... The entire level. You play as a snowball. Enough said.
Overall though, this is still a very good game. I'd recommend Sonic Generations more, but this game certainly wouldn't be far behind it.
So, as a final request... Colours and Unleashed on PC?

Pros :
+ This game is Age of Empires II, and Age of Empires II is great.
+ Star Wars universe
+ Every civilization has its own skins for units (as well as special units as in AoE II)
+ Interesting campaign which is not a retelling of the movies
+ A few interesting additions
Cons:
- This game is Age of Empires II, only that the nouns have been slightly disguised (There is no wood, there is carbon. This is the new Jedi Code.). So much for immersion.
- Old and slow.
-Not as much civilizations as one could have dreamed of.
Verdict:
If you like Age of Empires II, and if you don't mind too much about replacing Huns with Trade Federation droids, this game is much cheaper than AoE II HD on sale on Steam, and works on junkier machines. If you are a fan of Star Wars, and profess a slight taste for RTS, then if you don't have Galactic Battlegrounds, you are missing something huge.
Long version:
This review could be a review of Age of Empires II, as there is no significant difference between Star Wars: Galactic Battlegrounds and the undisputed king of RTS. Same graphics, same UI, same buildings, same units, same resources, same costs... When you are building a farm, and you need reseed it once the harvest has been collected, you start to wonder if you really are in such a far, far away galaxy, after all. Fortresses has replaced castles. Long-range cannons have replaced trebuchets. There a few changes though which are worth mentioning:
-Priests are now Jedi warriors, which mean they can fight quite efficiently as well as convert. However they don't heal anymore: you have physicians now, as soon as the First Age. Holocrons (read "relics") can still be gathered at the temple to generate gold income.
-Aerial units. They can be devastative if you don't have anti-air units. In some maps their use is mandatory.
-Invisibility. Some units have the ability to remain concealed while they are not attacking. They can be detected with the proper units.
-Energy. You can build energy generators to fasten the speed of production of your buildings.
-Shields. You can build a shield generator to protect you base. Shield is different from armor so that shielded buildings have two bars, life and shield. Shield bar regenerates quite fast ; and as long has it is not emptied, buildings take almost no damage. Some units and buildings (e.g. destroyer droids and walls) have their own incorporated shields.
Otherwise it's pretty much all the same!

We've all played RPG's where you choose a class, and then put together the available abilities for that class in a way that suits you. But why not choose what those powers are in the first place? That's what Magicmaker advertises and, good gracious, it delivers.
Want to play as a bootleg Naruto who throws suns at people? Or how about a slime wizard who opens portals that armies of slime allies fall out of? Boulder-throwing half-dragon? Time-warping cultist? Ghost queen who causes mass hystaria? You can do all of it and more in Magicmaker.
The way this game works is with a modular spell system. You can combine up to four (at first three) different spell essences into your wand, spell slot, or robe. Each module gives a different attribute to your abilities. Wand abilities are mana-free, but weaker. Spells cost mana, but are a lot stronger. And robes grant passive abilities.
For example: A fire module causes a spell to set its target on fire. A brick module causes a spell to arc when thrown, but makes it a lot stronger. And then a vampire tooth causes lifesteal. Combining those three modules together would make a spell that allows you to throw a flaming mortar that heals you when it hits. Drop by the artist to decide whether it looks like fire, bricks, or teeth, and you're set to slaughter monsters at your leisure.
The game also comes with a system that randomly generates the dungeons you go through, meaning you can do the same quest twenty times and have a different experience each time. Meaning even after you've complete all the quests, you can go through again like it's brand new! Infinite replayability for loadouts and worlds.
Still not sold on it? Download the demo. It gives you access to everything that comes from the first zone and the hub. It will give you a couple of hours of gameplay and three-thousand seventy-five spells to taste test. From there, you're only ten bucks away for more than five times as much content.
So far, my only real want is more missions. While the randomized dungeons do give the individual missions some replay value, it would be nice to continue to go above and beyond. But I hear that the studio is still adding stuff to the game, so that's pretty freaking awesome!
Overall, a game with ludicrous amounts of customization, with more on the way. Adventure, magic, and massive explosions await!

I actually own a physical copy of this game, lost it, purchased this  on Steam, then refound my copy. Happens.
So, Descent 2 is a classic example of how to make a sequel. Why? It did what Arkham Asylum and Arkham City did: Use the same formula and add a ton of stuff. Funny how games in the 90s were better at making sequels than ones decades later. There are double the weapons, a lot more robots to kill, more bosses, and more complex levels. Pretty the Descent 1 with a ton more stuff to play with.
So what about the game? It's a true 360 degree FPS--you need to roll, elevate, lower, strafe side to side... You're a space craft can go in any direction. This means the enemy robots can do the same. Speaking of enemy robots, they all make their own sound effects and tend to have their own form of attack, like using certain rockets, planting mines, or charging the player to melee attack. Unlike today's games where it's just another dude in a different shirt, the robots are varied.
In most levels you destroy a reactor and make for the exit; others you kill a boss robot and make for the exit. This may sound tedious, but there's a thrill when, after destroying the previously mentioned things, there is only 45 seconds to fly to said exit. The ship shakes around and it can be difficult to find the exit sometimes. This makes exploring the levels really important. There is key hunting, just like Doom or Duke Nukem, but the change in style--360 degree space craft--makes up for it.
Graphics are really, really dated. Even if you get DXrebirth, which really improves everything, all the games enemy's still look like polygons. Level textures are as about as detailed as the stuff you'd see in Quake 1. Still, like Quake 1, the gameplay holds up.
Story is... um... The robots are infected with a virus and you're a mercenary who is supposed to stop them, or something.  The story acts out like any shooter made in the 90s: Find the key and kill the badies.
All in all, I'd highly recommend this game.

Knight Squad is simple to understand, it's fun, and doesn't require much skill to play.
Some people hate on it for that reason : it's too random and not skill-based enough. Maybe. I would tend to believe those people simply have trouble seeing where in Knight Squad is skill required (ie. moving so that your sword ends at the right place while your character doesn't end impaled), but let's admit they're right. Is this game made for huge esports tournaments where skill is everything and randomness has no place because of the money at stake? Nope, it's just a family-friendly party game for everyone...
But let's forget about that and focus on the game itself. When I booted it, what greeted me? A nice interface that automatically chose the correct resolution (2560*1440, which isn't properly detected or even supported by way too many games), and an options menu that let me remap controls.
Of course, I remapped the keyboard first, since it's not QWERTY. Then, I plugged in an xbox controller, which obviously didn't need remapping. Then I plugged in an old usb1 controller that's some kind of chinese knockoff of a ps1 controller. It worked and I remapped it so the game was playable with it. Then I plugged in a Gamecube controller adapter I got on Aliexpress for 8€ a while ago, and plugged two gamecube gamepads on that adapter. Each Gamecube gamepad was tied to a player and remapped.
The result? I got 5 characters that could be played properly, with literally zero investment because I already had several old controllers. And I could get 8 players like this if I moved my butt downstairs to get the other old controllers.
My point is, it's really well made on the technical side of things, and that's a big plus. Contrary to Clusterpuck 99 that disappointed me a lot on that matter (doesn't allow remapping so anything non-xbox is useless), Knight Squad truly has a solid technical foundation.
Now, for the gameplay, I can't say that I've played a lot, but it does look fun. Several game modes, tight controls (it's not twin stick but that's a gameplay choice, not a missing feature, for anyone that would think otherwise), nice graphics (nothing pixelated because of stretched textures)... Looks like the family reunion will be fun this year.
I'll try to think of updating that review as soon as I've spent some time playing it in December, but for now I really want to make it clear that 80% of the negative reviews have been written by disingenuous and/or stupid people.

I really, really enjoyed this game. Way more than I expected too.
It's got a very well set noir-y atmosphere that heavily contradicts with the main characters more-or-less frivolous/whimsical attitude both in game and in dialogue. The game features a well-written story that removes itself from simple binary notions of good and evil and makes you make hard decisions that often leave you feeling like neither one was a good choice but knowing that you HAD to pick one lessens the impact. The story is very much themed around being in a position you don't want to be in and having to do things you don't want to do to get out of it. This is reflected in both the narrative dialogue-segments AND in the gameplay, where you are constantly making risky decisions and choosing between what appears to be the less dangerous of two fatal choices.
The gameplay struck me was "What Watch_Dogs wanted to be" in terms of the hacking mechanic unlocked a few levels in. You can rewire electronics in any room so that flicking a light switch in one room will open a door on another floor, and any combination therein. The satisfaction of creating a rube-goldberg chain reaction to trick the guards into running around while you sneakily drop in and out without being seen is beyond rewarding. You'll want to keep playing the levels again, and again, and again. It helps when the clients are able to give you certain optional objectives that effect your end rank (and I think your pay but I'm not certain), and so the game finds a way to keep itself fresh without actually chaining you to it's idea of freshness. This client wants you to leave nobody alive, so if you've been playing super stealthily this is a nice change of pace, BUT nothing is FORCING you to play the game like this. It's merely a suggestion from the employer that could lead to better review.
This games length isn't incredible BUT it will leave you wanting more which is where the fan community and level design kit come in handy as people on the steam workshop are keeping this game alive with new levels on a daily basis.
Overall I'd say this game is definitely worth checking out. Maybe wait until it's on sale if you don't like the idea of a 3 hour campaign but I think it's important to emphasize the replayability of not just the campaign but the game in general with it's level design kit.
This game gets a strong recommendation from me.

The game's villain was apparent right from the start and was all but moustache-twirlingly evil. Blackwatch appears to have become an organization of deathly stupid dog-kicking nazis who (minor spoiler) release infected into "test areas" apparently just for the fun of it.
The open-world gameplay didn't work for me either; I found the city area cluttered and overly full. The new look works and it makes sense to have people sleeping rough etc., but I missed the clear lines of the first game. The control change for gliding and airdash REALLY annoyed me as well, especially as I had replayed the entire first game and scored platinum on all movement events for the fun of it just before starting the second. I loved the way movement flowed in the first game and it just seemed completely unnecessary to change it in the second.
Some of the mechanics seemed promising (consuming specific evolved to gain certain powers, etc.), but all in all, the cartoonish "villains" and idiot unsympathetic protagonist killed this game for me very quickly. What a shame.

If you wanted to see how Mario Galaxy would have been made by a lesser development team, this is your game.
Starts off strong, utilizing the mario galaxy gimmick of small planetoids lets sonic team design 3d areas without relying on boxing the player in with bottomless pits. However later in the game the levels revert back to mostly bottomless pits, so the galaxy gimmick is wasted.
In addition the later stages (ice world onward) abandon building up the difficulty of stages and replaces it with new gameplay entirely in the form of the gimmick levels. These have different gameplay concepts that don't transfer to or from the normal game, and are full of instant deaths.
This game is one of the worst at trying to convey information and mechanics to the player.
There are new parkour platforming techniques, but the game never gives you the space to try them out and get used to them. Then later in the game when they are required to progress, the penalty for failure is a bottomless pit.
The new mechanics seem imprecise or strange to use.
Here are some examples:
The lock on mechanic is really frustrating when it fails to lock on in a logical way.
There are multiple types of homing attack, different enemies and bosses sometimes require a specific type of attack but don't give any indication about which, so you have to use trial and error.
Jumping once lets you hurt enemies when you land on them. Using a double jump to correct your aim results in you getting hurt.
Spindash is a thing but doesn't work consitently. Seems to travel faster up walls than along the ground.
Wall jumping while wall running in 3d mode rarely seems to work.
Also, the new characters are really bad. But that is standard for Sonic games.
On the upside, the zones before the ice world are fun. Everything after that is a terrible mess of poorly implemented gimmicks.

“The Agency: Chapter 1” is the first installment in what probably will be an episodic game series (like how TellTale games do it e.g. Game of Thrones by TellTale Games, The Walking Dead by TellTale Games etc.) Unlike TellTale Games your decisions don’t bear any weight towards the ending and storyline. The decisions are more “aesthetic” than anything else and are more a means to get more information and immerse oneself better in the world of this game. This is what they call a “kinetic novel” where the story is linear. There is gameplay though, in the form of an image puzzle game. The story revolves around a young man named Jack Beckwith, who joins a detective agency in the capital of the fictional nation he lives in.

Ok, so the facts are done, on to the review.
Story
When you’re doing this type of game, your story better be damn awesome. In that respect the game passes with flying colors! The writing is solid and the dialogue is very stylistic towards Victorian speech that really helps towards immersion. There is a whole and fully fleshed out fictional world that one can believe the characters live in. The characters themselves feel rounded and real and the mystery plotline that caries the game is intriguing.
Art
The sprites aren’t very good, perhaps the greatest failing of this game. The backgrounds on the other hand, are excellent and very stylistic. The general steampunk style behind the UI is very satisfying and should please even the most hardcore steampunk fan.
Music
The music was very appropriate towards the feel and the style of the novel.  The melodies were nice and complemented the storyline and general emotions behind the piece.
Minigame
The VN has a minigame where you put a scrambled image together. It can get a bit tedious and repetitive at times but were in themselves generally harmless.  Some of the images chosen were (perhaps purposefully chosen to be ) quite difficult due to the strangeness of the images (you’ll see when you play it yourself).
Duration
The game isn’t what they call long and given you’re not someone who does a lot of these image jigsaw puzzle things in their free time they may take a bit of time. The game has these nice little cutscenes, which also add to the duration, but all in all I’d say the game should take the average player around 2 hours. It ends with a cliffhanger, unsurprisingly
Overall
I liked it. It’s not the best Visual Novel in the world but it’s certainly not the worst. I enjoyed the 2 hours entertainment it gave me and am looking forward to seeing chapter 2.

I purchased a bundle just to get this game, and I would have just as quickly bought this by itself.
If you like strategy and tower defense games, you will really love Sang-Froid - the execution is fantastic.
The aesthetics are very good and the music flows well with the theme and atmosphere.
The controls are not too difficult to master, the tutorial videos are given quickly and right before each new mechanic (like new traps) is introduced. Recommend you do not skip these, as they are very helpful. The learning curve is not too bad, however, preplanning and strategy is critical to this game, and the game has a nice feature where you can restart at dawn or dusk (allowing you to restart with or without all your traps still on the field).
The story is pretty decent, however, I must admit that the theme does not appeal to me very much (devil + his minions) - I've started skipping the cutscenes.
Each "night" or level adds a layer of complexity, adding new traps, enemies, and areas of the map (the logging company will clear new areas every few levels).
The upgrading tree offers a lot of different areas to select from to best match your preferred play style, and there are 2 characters to select from (one specializing in combat and the other in trap-laying and strategy).
You can go to town to buy new weapons, bless your weapons/buy blessed bullets (to do extra damage to "evil" enemies), and later you have the option of buying silver weapons (to use against the Maikans {wolf humanoids; distinct from werewolves}).
In the preplanning screen, you can select traps to use. These all cost action points, however, the ones that also cost money are permanent and will persist through the nights so long as they are not used. You can also click on the wave tabs to see which enemies you will be encountering. A very useful feature is your sister's precognition, which will show you where your enemies will travel if you click their tab - this is essential for planning where to place your traps. As you progress, you will unlock more buildings that provide more AP to your pool, however, they also provide more targets for your enemies. You lose if any building is destroyed.
There are many cool mechanics during gameplay, one being wind and shouting. Wind affects where your scent can be detected, and shouting also pulls all enemies from a large radius. You unlock a talisman later in the game that allows you to manipulate where the wind is blowing - very useful for pulling enemies from an even larger radius than shout. A red icon shows where enemies will look for you, and you can use this to lure them to your traps (like spike traps or hanging nets {with rocks}).
Fear factor is a very interesting concept, and enemies will attack you when their fear factor matches yours. This allows you to control the flow of combat - so long as your fear factor is higher (like when you are near a fire) than your enemy's, they will be less likely to attack you right away. Werewolves have a bloodlust ability that gives them infinite fear factor (aka aggro). Attacking and defeating enemies will lower their fear factor, and there are items that further increase your own (like necklaces and potions/drinks).
The game runs incredibly well, and it is extremely fun to plan out how to best deal with your enemies - especially in the later nights when different groups and waves will target different buildings. Investing in zip line towers is critical to increasing your mobility. There are also fire walls, and these are integral to survival because they will force enemies to reroute (to potentially longer routes), buying you more time to deal with your priorities. Blocking enemies off completely will cause them to take the shortest route (and the damage).
Any leftover AP you have can be used to cut wood, providing you much needed money. Maximizing your trap efficiency and wood cutting will ensure that you have a of money to spend on weapon upgrades and other equipment.

Faithfully tells the story of the anime from after the end of the Pain arc through the Great Ninja War.  The plot part of the game can be nailed in less than ten hours; then the game goes into "free roaming" mode, which is essentially RPG-lite.
For fans of the anime who don't mind revisiting the plot (or who stopped watching at the end of Pain arc), it's amusing enough.  The combat is largely satisfying, if nothing too original or ground-breaking.
There's at least one boss-fight that is a terrible exception though - where the combat design seems to have taken a jump back 16 years:  Instead of a fun fight, instead you're stuck repeating the same ultimate move again and again and again to chip down an enemy's ridiculously over-large health bar - while your attacks are inexplicably♥♥♥♥♥♥weak for the first time in the game.  The game instantly stops being fun at that point and becomes a massive chore where you've got to memorise attack patterns and slowly grind away like it's a game out of the late 90s.
The RPG elements aren't great - it's cool walking around the Hidden Leaf, etc, but the world's pretty small and most of the quests involve wandering around the same areas blindly until you stumble over such-and-such an item.  Some of the quests are unclear about what you're supposed to do - which makes it feel even more aimless.
Also refuses to give you quests all at the same time - literally forcing you to retrace your steps for absolutely no reason other than to pad the game's play-time by a tedious extra 10 hours.
The gameplay is pretty fun on the whole, and it's cool to revist the anime; but there's questionable depth to it, and the franchise seems to be rendering older entries obsolete with each sequel, making it of questionable value to spend time exploring every odd corner of the game, etc.
For people completely new to the anime, this isn't the best place to start.  You'd be better off streaming Naruto anime online; then move on to streaming Naruto Shippuden before moving onwards.  It's not that the plot is hard to follow, or anything, just that there's hundreds and hundreds of episodes of the anime that cover plot before this game is set - and a lot of the backstory simply isn't covered in this game.
On the other hand, if you just want a quick silly anime-themed 3D fighter to mess around with - then you might find you like the setting enough to go back and check out the anime instead.
Generally, I'd say steer clear of this game unless it's ridiculously cheap and you literally have nothing better to do.  And be ready to drop it as soon as it becomes a drag, as there's a lot of content that is even more boring than the time wasted unlocking it.
I'd suggest using a gamepad to play this game (I use a generic gamepad with X360CE and it works flawlessly); as a 3D fighter it uses both thumb-sticks as well as a D-pad simultaneously, so a fight-stick won't be optimal.  I gather that players using the keyboard are enjoying the game fine though, so YMMV.

This is not your typical Tower Defense game.
The action involves both placing traps, then some 3rd person melee fighting.  Your axe is your primary method of taking out the beasts.  You do get a musket to use and can load it with blessed (costs extra) slugs, but with the slowness of loading and getting the gun ready, it is by no means a "Primary Weapn".  The gun is there to be used as a mobile trap and only while the mobs are still afraid of you.
This game is not "Action Packed", there are a ton of speed bumps here.  While the cut scenes provide a dialog and story that isn't found in other TD games and I apprecaite that, it does feel "slowing" to me.  Much of the game is spent going to town to spend your pennies (wisely), setting up your traps, working out a strat or wrapped up in dialog.  The battle-time where you're running around swinging your axe winds up being cut down to maybe 10% of the overall game time.
(Note: I didn't time it out to verifiy "10%" but it feels like very little time, goes by quickly.)
If you try to go back and replay a map, you lose all of your progress.   So you can't replay "Day 3" with "Day 7" gear.  Again, this is "Forced Story-Line" gameplay.  You can't muck that up with better weapons/traps.  It would be nice to be able to do that though, since you could gain XP and Cash to make moving forward easier.
This is a good Stategic Thinking trainer though.  You really do have to plan out your night, where you're going to run and when.   You have unlimited time to sit there planning out your trap placement and sequence of movements.   (Stay at farm for wave 1, move to the chicken coop for wave 2... etc.)  The Zip Line is an excellent addition for movement though, you will greatly appreciate that tower!  Walking is slow and running burns your stamina too quickly.
Overall, I give it a Thumbs Up, but for the reasons listed above I'm going to say "buyer be aware".

Super Game Jam is an episodic documentary—in each of the five (30-minute-ish) episodes, two people get together and spend 48 hours making a game. Because each episode features different people, the entertainment value depends on ten individuals and the chemistry of five pairings. That's why episode one is, by far, my favorite. And why I could
finish episodes two and four.
As others have mentioned, the technical quality varies dramatically throughout the documentary. The camera work in episode five is especially awful. You will also see the cameramen sometimes, which is just poor editing.
Each episode starts by showing you some things the jammers have made in the past, or are currently making. Then you get a game prompt (episode one's prompt, for example, is "breakup"), and a discussion of what the game will be. Then they start programming the game, making the music, making the art, and recording the sound, depending on the episode. There are points during each episode when they play the game. Mostly it's just the jammers discussing the game, with over-the-shoulder shots of their screens. The episodes finish with a quick play of the game, a short pub/house party segment of other people playing the game, and mini-interviews with the jammers talking about the experience/game.
SGJ isn't just five video files and five games. It's a surprisingly buggy, fullscreen-only application with absolutely no settings, which comes in the form of an 11.5 GB download. The video player has three features: pause, volume control, and seek. Thankfully, you can avoid the application altogether and view the videos in your preferred video player by browsing through the SGJ's files. (Which you should do if you have blurry video in SGJ's built-in video player.)
These are jam games. While some of them are cute, you probably won't play any of them for more than five minutes.
SGJ comes with "uncut discussions" and/or deleted scenes for each episode. Some are quite short (1 minute), others relatively long (18 minutes). And you probably won't watch them.
It also lets you listen to the music. I didn't like the music.
Is too high.
I really did enjoy episodes one and five. Some people enjoy all five episodes. If you think the entertainment you'll get is worth the price tag, then you should buy it. But maybe only when it's on sale.

I have to admit this game took me by surprise. I got it in a bundle and while it looked interesting, I put off playing it for several months. In fact the only reason I started playing in June was because of a promotion to earn credit on GMG for getting achievements, but I got drawn into the game and played the campaign to completion. And just about every aspect of it was great.
The game has a very unique setting, in fact as far as I know it is the only video game ever made that takes place in 1858 French Canada. As someone with an interest in history, this was really cool to me. Considering how many games these days reuse the same tired settings over and over (genric scifi/fantasy, generic urban setting, modern war, WWII, etc.) it’s nice to see more games like this that finally start to tap the vaults of history for unique settings that have never been done before.
Some people might consider the story a bit simplistic, but it’s still really good and somewhat unique. It centers around two lumberjack brothers, and their struggle to defend their sister, their home, and the surrounding area and people from creatures controlled by the Devil and other malicious forces. The story is told through cinematics and in-game cutscenes. The cinematics appear somewhat sparsely throughout the game, but they feature nice high quality artwork. Some may be disappointed that these cinematics are pretty low on actual animation, but considering this is an Indie game I can forgive that, and they still get the job done. The in-game cinematics, which feature the character models from the game, are also decent. I cringed a little bit at the voice acting at first, but as I kept playing I got used to it. It varies between the characters, some aren't that great and some are really quite good and fit the game very well. It's an Indie game so don’t expect AAA voice acting. In terms of dialogue, Jos can be a bit cringe-worthy at times with his simple meat-headed approach to everything, but most of the dialogue isn't bad once you get into the game. Obviously the story is a bit silly with the werewolves and magic and everything, so you have to have the right mindset coming into the game. At the same time, though, I think it is a good story that can be taken seriously with the right approach.
Now, for the gameplay. Basically, at the start of the game, you choose which brother you want to play as. One acts as the “normal difficulty” mode, while the other acts as the “hard mode”. I only played through the campaign once so far, with the “normal” character. Basically, during the day you have a map of the woods around your cabin. Each day (the game takes place over a few weeks in December 1858 and each day is like a level) the map changes a bit, as new paths are revealed and there are new buildings you must defend. Looking at the map, you can see the paths the enemies will take in each wave (augured by the sister with mystical powers), and place a variety of different traps accordingly. Each trap takes a certain number of “action points” (which represent time for the characters) to set, and some also cost money. There are a variety of different cool traps that are unlocked as you progress, like wolf traps, exploding barrels, ballistae, and mortars, and other helpful things like watchtowers and bonfires. There is a lot of strategy involved in where you place your traps, and it’s awesome to see the plan you worked hard on play out perfectly during the night. During the day, you can also visit the nearby village, and later the Amerindian tribe, to stock up on supplies and buy new weapons. The game also features a pretty big skill tree, allowing you to upgrade a lot of different aspects of your character and traps. It’s simple to use and it really adds a lot of depth to the gamplay deciding which skills you want to upgrade and when for best strategy. During the night, the game becomes a third person action game. Many traps require some action on your part to be used, and most of the time you will also have to engage in fights against the enemies that the traps didn’t kill. You have an axe for a melee weapon and a musket or rifle for longer ranged attacks. The combat is a bit a basic, but it does have a really unique feature called “fear factor”. Basically there is a meter showing how frightened your enemies are of you. Over time they muster up for an attack as the meter reaches a certain point, and sometimes they become enraged and are no longer affected by the meter. You can do a number of things to bring the meter down before an enemy becomes enraged, such as shouting or standing near a bonfire. Keeping your enemies afraid of you offers more depth to the combat, and gives you time to reload your musket or regain some stamina. Overall it works well and makes the combat really great. Being surrounded by a pack of hungry wolves, watching as they slowly circle you, waiting for the perfect moment to strike, is a thrilling experience, and I’ve never seen anything quite like it in a video game before.
The music in the game is fantastic. Every track is great and fits the game well, and I never got tired of hearing it. I should mention that this game can be surprisingly immersive, and the music really helps with that. The game also features interesting descriptions of the items, characters, and their backstories, so there is a lot of lore outside the cutscenes. For example, each axe and musket and some other items have a description detailing things like the year it was made, and what it was used for, etc. History buffs will probably enjoy this. There is also a lot of lore surrounding the enemies which relates to diabolism/demonology and/or pagan mysticism, which will probably be cool if you’re into stuff like that. A lot of it actually turns the traditional Werewolf lore on its head, and it brings in some elements from Amerindian culture for certain other enemies, so there’s definitely a lot of unique and original ideas going on here. With the great music and the attention to detail in the sound, text, and visuals, I found myself getting very immersed in the setting, even while just visiting the different shops and buying supplies.
In terms of longevity, I got about 16 hours out of my first playthrough of the campaign, and enjoyed just about every minute of it. Of course your mileage may vary, but I’d say that’s pretty damn good for a campaign mode in this day and age. Of course it also has replayability, as you can play through the whole game again as the other brother, and have a slightly different experience.
The graphics are nothing to write home about. It’s got a nice cartoony style that works well, but it’s nothing particularly impressive. I don’t have any complaints about it, I’m just saying you shouldn’t expect AAA graphics. However, the artwork featured throughout the game is really nice for the most part.
There isn’t much to complain about. The game does lack a bit of polish in some places. The text is a bit sloppy sometimes, there’s a few noticeable bugs and glitches, and as I stated earlier the voice acting and dialogue isn't perfect. The game also seems to have some framerate issues for me sometimes, though it doesn’t detract from the game too much (I have a very capable desktop though so there’s no reason this game should have issues).
Overall, this game is absolutely fantastic. Sure there are a few small issues, but they barely detract from everything that is great about this game. I highly recommend this game at any price you find it at. I got it in a really cheap bundle, but I almost wish I paid more now. Considering how great this games is, I think the devs deserve some compensation. So don’t delay, if you are even remotely interested in action, strategy, or tower defense, or just want a unique and immersive game, you will probably love this. If you want a number rating I would give it a 9.5/10.

There's a lot of people that've left negative reviews because they're frustrated about the delayed release of episodes. I held off buying Super Game Jam until all the episodes were released (partly because I was most interested in the final episode) and for the sale price of £7.49 I don't at all feel duped or scammed.
If you're interested in documentaries - and in game development - then this is a fun little collection of short films that shed light on how indie developers operate. Though it doesn't represent everyday game development, the conceit of a 48h 'jam' makes for some interesting tension over the course of each episode. The strength of the documentary itself is probably the cinematography - it's filmed beautifully with a very intimate feel (especially since the setting is always the home of one of the developers); the score is also spot-on. As a designer I can really appreciate the way the content is presented through the Steam client in a very clean, simple interface. A similar attention is paid to the graphics in the documentary itself. And if you don't want to watch it in the Steam client the files are available as HD .mp4 files in the local files - so you can just pick them up and move them about DRM-free.
If you're only interested in the games...then I wouldn't bother. The price you pay is not worth the five rushed prototypes - but that's because at its core, this project was about the documentary. It's about the process of making the games, the people who make them and how they cope in a high-pressure environment. The games included in the purchase are not the focus - they're almost like special features. Speaking of special features - the 'posters' aren't all that great (in terms of resolution/quality), but you also get some nice bonus cut content and an EP-sized bundle of music from Doseone and Kozilek.
For £15, this is a tougher sell but you have to realize that not only is this a unique venture, it's an independent film. You'll pay something like £10 for a DVD in the high street, so consider the extra 33% the price you pay for supporting independent artists (the filmmakers and developers). If you don't feel like paying £15, wait for it to go on sale - anything below is a steal if you like quality, interesting documentaries made with a clear love for the subject.

The game is all about the labyrinthine level design, and navigating extended levels. You're given a map, but challenge yourself to not use it. OPPW3 is the kind of game that isn't very difficult to complete, but is insane to 100%. The main game can be completed in about 7-8 hours, but if you want to 100% this game you're going to need to pour 100+ hours and play several hundred battles if you know what you are doing.
OPPW3 includes all the major arcs up until the Dressrosa, and are adapted decently well. I don't expect them to be exactly how they were in the anime, but I do wish they were a little more like that, as they had to cut out certain charcters and simplify them into stages. Most of the stages were good though, expect Thriller Bark, that one sucked.
The Dream Log is another major part of the game, and the palce you're going to spend most of your time. You play individual battles on islands as you make your way across an expansive map. I had fun with the Dream Log until I had to replay the whole thing again [I had to end up completing it 4 different times].
Pros;
Stages are decently long and fun
All of the major arcs are present
Large number of playable characters
The game has decent graphics
Insane number of collectables and objectives
Lots of things to do after completing main story
Character progression
Feels like One Piece
Cons;
Gets repetitive
Occasionally crashes [might just be me though]
In conclusion I would say that OPPW3 is a great game that you will really enjoy if you like destroying hordes of enemies. You will have fun during the main story, but if you aren't planning on a 100%, you won't really have an incentive to play the Dream Log. OPPW3 is a completionists nightmare, as you need to collect all events, music, objectives, coins, rare coins, and level up all 80+ characters [Playable and Support], although that isn't a bad thing. I had fun getting a 100%, although it felt repetitive after a while, it was also rewarding.

Being able to move with six degrees of freedom is finicky, but super rewarding once you get used to the movement scheme. It's hard to imagine a space shooter take place inside narrow corridors, but it really works in this game.
On the surface, weaponry is pretty spectacular; ten different primaries and 10 unique secondary special weapons you can collect and horde and never f*cking use because you might need it later. Really 8 of the ten primaries are "laser" altered in purely cosmetic ways; some can bounce, some can charge, but it's all lasers at the core. Lack of interesting weapon choices is the only thing holding this game back. The levels are amazingly well designed, though there's nothing really to compare them to. It's incredibly easy to get lost in the true three-dimensional maps, so there is the optional guide-bot to help you through, a small drone that leads you to all key locations. The drone is to descent what CL4P-TP is to borderlands, which is to say unbearably annoying, but it is entirely optional, which I appreciate.
Lifespan is long, there are sooo many levels, with challenging boss fights at the end of every chapter, cutscenes are chock-full of true nineties charm and of course, there are plenty of secrets and hidden levels for replay value.
It's not perfect, but its a fantastic game with unique gameplay, well  worth trying out if it slipped by you a decade ago.

At first I was surprised by it's size, as it's not all that different from Descent 1. I found out that the Redbook audio CD is included in this one! Too bad the Vertigo expansion is not included.
As for the game itself, 1st Descent remains the best imho. Here you get the most overpowered weapon on lvl 3 (Gauss) and never switch to anything else, unless you run out of ammo (you don't, not even on higher difficulties), shich kind of ruins the nice variety in weapons that D1 had. In D1 every weapon had it's use, which was nice.
Secret doors are trickier in D2 than in D1. You have these switches which you can destroy. They sometimes open secret doors permanently or for a limited amount of time. So if you miss the oportunity, you are screwed. I hate these new kind of secrets.
The new secret levels are nothing like the ones in Descent 1. Most of them are like armories. You load up on lives, health, energy, powerups in them. Most have some tricks to getting through them. You can always return to the same secret levels until you destroy the Boss robot of that planet, or the secret level's reactor (which usually opens up new secrets within the secret level). It's usually a good idea to visit them only when you are about to fight a Boss, so you can grab all the invulnerability/invisibility powerups in there.
Since I talk about Bosses, I want to mention that they are a lot tougher in D2. You don't always get invulnerability/invis powerups to fight them. E.g. the Ice boss has double omega cannons and homing flash missiles. You only get 1 invisibility to fight him. On higher difficulties you get zapped with the omegas in less than a second.
8.5/10 The last good Descent game.

It's more of an interactive movie than a game. I say this because most of the so called choices in this game have little or no consequence to the plot. I would enjoy this game more if choosing different actions can change the plot more significantly and the story can branch to, like, 5 different endings (I don't mind even if 3 of the endings are quite similar). But
Sure, the music and the graphics and such are quite pleasing, but I feel cheated because the store page says "Your choices matter, changing the story around you, and making the tale yours." Yes. You forgot to mention they don't matter much.
I've played RPGs (where the main selling point isn't the plot branches) that has more plot flexibility than this. And I'd rather watch some of my favourite movies again if I knew that this game doesn't give what I want - plot branches. The top 3 helpful reviews being 2 sentences long at the time doesn't help.
TL;DR Misleads people into believing plot branches as one of the main selling points of the game. If you can enjoy an interactive movie where most of the gameplay is picking choices but doesn't actually branch the story out, good for you. I won't buy anything from Telltale anytime soon though.

This review is coming from someone who's 100%ed this game on Wii U and bought the PC version for the mods (and to support Sonic Team).
Here is the MAJOR ISSUE with it: this port is done by Sega Europe. What that means is, the controls are sluggist and delayed as hell compared to the Wii U version. This game emphasizes precision fairly heavily, so the sluggish controls are honestly a dealbreaker when maneuvers that were easy to pull off on Wii U are nearly impossible here.
Something funny to note is that the 360 control map is literally a graphic the devs lifted from a deviantart page. They stole art. Wow.
Get this only if you've already experienced the game in its best form on Wii U and were desperately craving another Sonic mod experience since Generations.

More than enough game for $10.
Yes, the game ran out of money, yes there is only 1 developer left.
But. The game is really good. Most games in this situation would shamelessly 'release' with half the polish and content and ask for $30.
So, what does the game have?
Very polished mechanics (gunplay, stealth). And they feel very good and natural.
Multiple game modes: single, co-op, multiplayer, wargames, missions, challenges, multiple difficulty modes. Plenty for some ~15 hours of single player, much more multiplayer.
What does it still lack? There are some bugs left, and more content (esp. maps) would also be good. There is also a lack of visual variety - a single kind of environment, and a single look for enemies.

This game is pretty great. They did a good job at making the game feel real, for being a videogame at least, and I'd reccomend it to people who want a fun FPS game down the road. Right now, the game severely lacks content, with nothing but a few training missions versus robots, and a larger scale training mission with players and robots, and some challenges available to play. Right now, there isn't much replay value aside from a couple hours of interesting gameplay before things get repetitive. The game has stagnated for a very long time, because of multiple reasons on the developers end, but recently the head honcho came forward and announced that he is not in fact dead, and is still working on this game. It's shaping up to be a fantastic FPS game, and what I would like to see is more missions and less Wargames. The Starcrown & Neurogen missions were fantastic to play, and id personally like to see more of that, maybe less training robots and more real-steel missions.
4/5 from me, despite the stagnation and incomplete-ness. I want to give it the benefit of the doubt

James Heller is hell-bent on avenging his family's death, but Alex Mercer has plans for James that will change everything.
James' has a better character background that players can sympathize or relate to.
The same, straight forward HUD with an improved menu interface for navigation.

The revamped levelling system rewards completion rather than farming Evolution Points.
Same fun combat with faster skill mapping to pick the right tool for the job.
Hunting mode was extremely fun, though it could have used more implementation outside events.
The map has been extended and allows simplified searching for collectibles.
Cinematics have had great improvements in quality, style, and purpose.
The NYZ has had a graphical boost and no longer feels console-restrained.
Fewer, new challenge modes require completion rather than perfection to earn fun upgrades.
The soundtrack is as dull as it was in the original game.
Compared to most, the difficulty was very low even on Hard.

For those of us who participate and enjoy game jams, this series is an absolute must-watch.   For those of you who are aspiring game designers,  here's your introduction into the industry. In each episode,  two game developers (you might recognize a few of them)  are given a theme and are given 45 hours to make a game based on that theme.   In every case so far,  the two members seem to have very different backgrounds and talents.   You'll watch them struggle as they come up with basic game mechanics,  visual / audio effects , and work around various bugs that come up along the way.
It is unfortunate to me that most of the episodes have failed to meet their respected release dates.   However,  I'll let this slide, since every episode so far has been well put-together and properly polished into a professional looking product.

This mod is greatly disappointing. I should have looked at the reviews before I bought this. I thought that because it was a portal mod that, like the games that precede this, it would be gold. Oh, how wrong I was. The voice acting is mediocre, and the gameplay needs serious refinement. For a game to be successful, it either needs an attention grabbing story, or it needs solid gameplay, portal has always been about the gameplay. That’s not to say that the story is in anyway bad, they had some very creative writing in the 2 portal games that were made, and an excellent voice cast to bring that writing to life. This mod has neither of those things.
The gameplay is a serious issue in this mod. The concept up having a gel gun, is at first thought a very fun idea. I have played a couple portal 2 mods, that have puzzle race tracks using different types of gel, to make you fly through obstacles and through the air at breakneck speeds, so it is proven to work. When you add a gel gun to that mix, it should make the experience even more compelling, but it unfortunately doesn’t. This game has some interesting level designs, but there are a lot of levels that get recycled. The gameplay is imprecise, especially when the blue gel is involved. More times than not, you will bounce off the blue gel, trying to go in one direction, and end up going in the opposite direction, only to fall to your death. The orange gel is less troublesome, but when you have to use both gels together, the blue will end up screwing you over again.
There was never a point in the portal games where I rage quit because of broken game mechanics, but I have done so, multiple time in this mod. There is one level in particular that I found to be a game breaker. It involves flinging a cube into a tractor beam so you can drop it through the portal underneath. The concept is that once the cube falls through the portal it will fly out the other portal and land on a switch behind a glass wall, but the stupid thing never lands on the switch. You just have to hope that the cube will make it. I have never played a puzzle game where you had to rely on chance in order to complete a puzzle.
Now I may be too judgemental of this mod, but I have seen some truly fantastic mods come out for games like skyrim, that, in terms of quality, blow this mod out of the water, and they don’t even charge for those. So the developer who produced this portal mod, really doesn’t have an excuse.
In the end what it really comes down to, is lazy voice acting, poorly designed gameplay, and inconsistent levels. This game has no heart, something that was clearly visible in the portal games. The biggest offence, is that they have the nerve to charge for this. I understand that this was greenlit, but valve should have been paying more attention to the quality of something that is going to use the portal name. The only thing that could save this game is the modding community on the steam workshop. I have seen some fantastic content come out of the modding community, and will check back to see what they have to offer once this game has a little time under its belt.
Worth every penny spent.
