This mod was a nice taste of the Portal universe again after having not played for ages.  The puzzles were fairly fun and some of the later ones challenging.  Though I prefer playing with a portal gun compared to a gel gun it was a fresh change having to approach puzzles in a way that didn't (usually) have you thinking with portals.  The story was decent enough and I had no issue with the voice acting.  It was nice to have a personality core be somewhat funny at times but not be over the top like Wheatley or someone like Claptrap.  The reused set pieces during travel segments mainly in the earlier part of the game were really cool to see showing from a different perspective some of the areas you covered in the Cave Johnson areas of the previous game.  The very few Portal 2 rooms that are reused are still not the same rooms as without portals they must be solved in totally different ways.
My complaints about this game are relatively minor.  There is one music piece/joke used at a point in the game that went on a bit longer than it should have before the core shuts it off.  Sometimes you'll set up a speed jump and the blue gel area at the end of your jump isn't big enough to trigger a jump (though it certainly looks like it's big enough to work) leading you to usually charge right off the edge of a platform.  The "skip escape sequence" button during a point in the game should have been better understood not to be a sort of joke button but an actual thing that skips the sequence.  A few of the puzzles where you have to jump at an angle off of the blue gel can be very picky on how precise your position needs to be.  There is one puzzle near the end of the game where to reach the exit you have to perform a very precise jump into a portal, back into a wall to bounce forward, kill your forward momentum just enough to land on another gel spot and not overshoot it, and finally keeping at a straight angle that whole time so you go straight and not sail right by the platform you're aiming for.  That puzzle was not fun, it was frustrating.  The game does have something to help mitigate a lot of this at least.  The autosave function is pretty good most of the time and you won't lose much progress when you accidentally go swimming in the acid water.  Barring that you can manually save pretty much anywhere, such as right before a really tricky jump, and if you happen to die you'll be right back where you saved at.  Very handy on the aforementioned very frustrating puzzle.
Bottom line is for the money that it costs, especially with it on sale, this was a fun mod to play through and definitely worth paying for.

Dead Island Definitive Edition is a "Remastered" version of the original game.
Review of the Remaster:
It seems to have "tweaked" a couple of the weapon and crafting mechanics as well, adding new stuff to craft and tweaking the durability slightly for example, but not by much.
The main difference is the texture, lighting and sound upgrades they have done and though it is not the best remastering I have seen it is a decent attempt.
Now to Review the game itself:
PRO: The game is a fun Survival Horror/Action Horror/!st Person/Horror RPG Hybrid that I enjoyed no end when it first came out.
CON: The game does suffer from a minor "repetive" flaw, but as most 1st person action games suffer from this as well, it is not a huge problem. Most of the game is kill Zombie, find weaapon, find crafting materials, repair/upgrade/craft weapons and repeat.
PRO: The game is more like an MMO than a game that was first released on console. Main Story quests and sub quests are the actual plot of this game with some minor Cutscenes linking everything together. Good for short solo or co-operative play.
CON:  This way of doing the game can get boring for some people who want a more "story driven" Zombie game and the game can get boring in longer sittings.
PRO: There are tons of weapons to find, craft and upgrade in this game and they are dotted everywhere.
CON: The Durability of the weapons is realy bad as they break after a few hits (Higher grade/level weapons don't break as often as the lower grade ones but it is still anoying)
Notes:
There are a enough people in the "Online community" playing this game in Co-op that intentionally mess with people, when you play in the "Public Online" option, for fun. This can ruin playing the game in Co-op when an idiot does this to you. I recomend you only play with a friend to avoid this.
Some people have made mods for this game that address some of the cons I have stated, but there is a huge risk of you getting banned for "cheating" in using them, as some people have been for using the mods in online play. So IF you want to use the mods turn off online play.
I do have fun playing this game, but it is not the sort of game to play for several hours in one sitting.
Verdict: It is a fun distraction to play for an hour or so, alone or with a friend.
Score: 7/10

In its' current state, this game is not very good at all. Originally it was to be a very ambitious tactical sci-fi shooter; with dynamic VoIP acoustics, customisable weapons, and different character classes. Currently, there is none of that, unless you count attaching a silencer as customisation.
There is currently a short threadbare campaign available that consists of three missions on three different maps, not counting the tutorial. These all feel very similar and do not help demonstrate the game's "tactical" gameplay, as it is very simple to run-and-gun as the enemies are not very bright and infinite ammo is available.
The saddest part is that it could have been better, had it had more funding. In promotional material, and partially in the game, characters are able to remove their helmet to talk clearer and to see easier. When your visor is down, it is almost similar to Metroid Prime or Star Wars: Republic Commando, with raindrops and sunlight glare obscuring your vision when it is down. In promotional material, this was also shown to change the sound of your voice, with your voice being more muffled when the visor is down, and clearer when the visor is up. Unfortunately, this feature is not available in the game and probably never will be.
To sum it up, let me recount an experience whilst poking around the game. If you clip inside the player character's helmet, you will find a fully modelled, but untextured face. It looks ready to be used, but unfortunately never is. This sums up the game, potential is there, but the game itself is incomplete.

This review is hard to articulate, so take from this whatever you can.
(30 hours of in-game experience)
(23/24 Achivements)
(Huge fan of the books)
(Lover of tabletop and card games, as well as video games)
(Received the digital expansions for free due to backing the original via crowdfunding)
(...I don't think any reviewers here are paid? But I'm not being paid for this, for whatever it's worth.)
+The game is a faithful recreation of the physical card game, and save for a few minor UI issues that I was informed they're going to patch, the game for what it is, succeeds quite well in doing that.
+As with the physical game, I like the artwork (for the most part) of the cards and character depictions, and the card designs themselves aren't overly flashy or obnoxious with their layout or designation. Simple, straightforward, and clear.
+The game is challenging (but this is also part of my biggest issue), and I do think that the on-sale price of around 16.00 USD is a fair pricepoint vs amount of time I have played so far.
+The game is very stable; never had any crashes or freezing occur. In fact, the only issue I had with that was a necessity for an online connection every time I wanted to use the expansion decks (which when asked about, the Devs were VERY prompt with their response of their working on it, and it seems to have been successfully patched).
~The game's aesthetic is alright; card artwork aside, the lack of animations and flair is a little underwhelming. But this isn't supposed to be a Yu-Gi-Oh! card game or similar style of games, so it doesn't really hurt the game. (And I'm kind of torn; would I prefer really ugly or low-quality "effects" or not have any at all? I kind of am inclined to the latter.)
~The music/sound effects are a mixed bag: the music is supposed to vary by each Book's deck, but save for one or two noticeable sounds, it all kind of sounds the same and is forgettable. But that doesn't mean I didn't enjoy it; they remind me a lot of those cheesy but fun Halloween ambience cd's. (I can easily see people groaning or facepalming in regards to this sort of direction.)
-The game is essentially a micromanagement/resource/numbers game. (See below)
-Level of skill of player is irrelevant towards gameplay.
(?) I can't attest to the online play, as I don't have much interest in that with the game, so I can't give any informed opinion on how good or bad that is.
So, you might be thinking "Why aren't you fully recommending this game when you seem to like more than dislike the game?"
Well, the simple fact is, I despise the game (but NOT this digital version of said game).
The whole "pitch" for this game was "What-if Harry had different allies in the various adventures, how would things play out?" as well as it being focused on co-operative gameplay. The latter is EXTREMELY important, but the former element goes by the wayside. This game comes down to resource strategy and management, and the only fun you're likely to have is with friends. You have Fate Points, which is the currency you use for the cards' costs that you play. Instead of having the experience of going "Aw man, how is Harry and ______ gonna deal with this?!" or shouting in triumph when you succeed in defeating an iconic villain from the series, you're just focused on MIN/MAX-ing every single play you make (which, don't get me wrong, not saying that A. that attitude is wrong or B. it can't be fun to do that) and it feels more like work than entertainment. Instead of being excited on having Dresden cast his trademark Fuego fire-spell, or Sanya wielding Esperachius, you're focused on which card's effectiveness best deals with the random organization of Foes, Cases, Obstacles, and Advantages on the game board. It makes the thematic elements of it being a Dresden Files-based game completely irrelevant. You don't care about the cards' meaning or context, just what it can do for you. (I'd compare this to the "Casual" vs "PRO" card game player mentality, and how in this game, it's very much the "PRO" mentality.)
The second huge issue that deals with the gameplay is how the random dispersal of cards can and will put you in situations that are literally impossible to win, regardless of how effective your plays are. This is caused by the inclusion of the FATE system dice rolls and FATE points to use as cost payment for your cards. I'm not going to lie: I really, really don't like the Fate system... at all... When it comes to losing a game? I'm fine with that; sure it sucks, but whatever, right? Just get back in there and try again. But NO game, be it a video game, card game, tabletop or RPG game that is impossible to win or overcome, and especially not by random chance. After a while, I was able to tell just by glancing at the board whether the setup was defeatable or not, and would just back out, and start the match up all over again, sometimes handful of times over and over until one came up that was viable. (And I'll gladly admit that resource management/number crunching ISN'T my strong suit, so maybe the game is harder for me than others, or I play ineffectively. Could very well be.) If this was a collectible/competitive card game where you build your own decks for play, THEN the failure is 100% on the players; you might pick the wrong cards or less effective ones than your opponent, etc. But when the game's randomizer just gives you an unbeatable match, all that happens is you get some frustration and practice.
So do I recommend this game to the general public? No, I don't; but NOT because of this game's digital recreation: Developers, if you see this, and I hope you do, I TRULY think you did a great job recreating this game in this format, and will be checking out other games you've done/other games you'll be doing. Excellent, prompt, and courteous communication, etc.
But the game itself, not the video game recreation of it, is frustrating and not fun or entertaining for me. I backed the crowdfunding for the game, hopeful for it to be fun and it wasn't, but I was still supporting the series I love. I bought this game for the same reason, and played as much of it as I have for that reason as well, and to support the developers.
If you're a fan of the Dresden Files and want to support everything related to it, you already have/love the card game, or enjoy resource management/number crunching card games, then you'll probably love this game.
Otherwise, I strongly suggest watching videos about the game before purchasing, as well as taking a look at what others have said about the game (seriously, don't just listen to me, get a broader view than mine) before buying; but DEFINITELY consider picking the books up if you like Fantasy/Urban fantasy, as well as keeping HiddenAchievement on your radar.

The core of the game as described above is towerdefense meets action rpg. You set up traps at the start of the night and then run around with your choice of brother trying to take out the wolves before the destroy your vital buildings. What makes this hard is that the money you gain from winning a map has to be used to upgrade your character and to buy equipment. This in combination with introductions of new elements keeps the set up fresh and makes you having to rethink your set strategies on the fly. This keeps every night frantic where you try to make sure that you keep everything in one piece and try not to die in the process. This is of course helped along by the amazing soundtrack, which suits the timeframe but gives the entire game a frantic upbeat feel.
I'm honestly suprised by the amount of fun I'm having with the game, so yeah I'd give it a try if I were you.

A faithful recreation of the original, worth it for fans of the board game, although the price feels a bit high.
For those who are unfamiliar with the board game, its a game of strategy with just the right amount of dice based risk taking.
A team of 3 or 4 characters from the Dresden Files universe work together to solve cases and defeat foes. Each character has their own special stunt, talent, and deck which will help you complete various adventures based off the books.
Each turn consists of players paying fate (from a shared pool) to play cards to interact with the board, using their unique stunt, or discarding a card to recharge the team's fate.
Eventually the players advance to the "showdown" by running out of cards, overspending the team's fate due to bad luck, or just deciding they want to test their luck by rolling lots of dice. Victory is determined by whether more cases were solved or more foes remain on the board at the end of the game.
If you are unsure about the game itself, I recommend learning more about the game play before purchasing. You can view my getting started guide
or you can view the official youtube tutorial for the board game

But every map looks different, you have to account for enemy attacks, bug spawns, hostile animals, aliens and that is only the outside influence, Think you have the best colony ever? Too bad one of your colonists got drunk and now you need at least one replacement eye... which you can get from prisoners or just build a cybereye instead. Or just restart in the frozen tundra or hostile desert and see how good you really are.

I was rather excited for this mod pre-release. It had a cool looking mechanic and the assumption was that it would be free. When the developers announced that it would be sold for a price, I was ok with that, developers have the right to be compensated for their work, but I also assumed it would be a higher quality product. I played the game to completion and while it is not bad, it still feels very much like a free mod.
I was kind of hoping the voice work present in the trailers was just temporary and would be replaced in the final release, but no, the voice actor has a very noticable accent and his voice sounds out of place in the portal universe. The character he voices is also uninteresting and very poorly written. The story is overall not very compelling and feels extremely derivative of Portal 1 and 2. The ending in particular was extremely disapointing. But the story is not the main attraction to the Portal 2 mod, so how is the gameplay?
The level design and gameplay fares a little better. Most levels in the first 3 chapters of the game were interesting, and there were fun throwbacks to Portal 1 and 2 where you solve similar levels with different tools. Levels are designed intuitively and the visual language of the game is relatively clear, helping point you in the right direction most of the time, but not making things too simple. However, I felt that in the 4th chapter, some of the levels have an extreme spike in difficulty. One level in particular, the second to last map of the game, was incredibly frustrating and unintuitive. The developers admit in the in-game dev commentary nodes that under half of playtesters used the intended solution, many finding exploits to get past the level. That seems to me like a red flag that your level is not well designed. When I finally got past the chamber, it was not so much a satisfying "a-ha!" moment of clarity as much as a "seriously? THATS the solution?" type of bummer.
I feel that most of the criticisms with the game could have likely been prevented by hiring a better voice actor and giving the later levels more playtesting. I honestly believe the developers could still fix many of the issues, especially with level design in a post-release patch (another indie game, Hydrophobia, did something very similar to that) and I would be happy to change my review if that were to happen. Until then, I'm sad to say that this mod is probably not worth your money.

I played both the original robocraft and the one currently available on steam.
The original one had and Experience progress system where you unlock different weapons and lbocks with exp you earn, after which you could buy these blocks with creddits you would earn or with money. During the building of your bot your tier level would increase, which would influance which opponents would roughly be searched for to go up against. Battle were fought somewhere between 10 v 10 or 12 vs 12, but could be randomized (like 6 vs 9) depending on how strong the bots were. Battle was fought world of tanks style. One life, one enemy base, one friendly base, and go.
New version has different battle modes, of which the main mode is a conquest based map with 3 different points to capture, and respawn enabled. There is no Exp system, and no tier system. you have a maximum of 2000 points to use, that's it. Blocks can be bought, with points (slowly earned or recycled for with parts you own.. don't know the numbers but seems like 20% or so of it's original worth) or with money. they can also be earned with... our all time favorite ..... lootboxes.
Now, the reason i came back to the new steam version was because i remember Really enjoying the old verison. And to be fair, although i would rather battle multiple enemies at once and retry next round, the new battle mode is still fun, going around with bots. Building is still the same (appart from the tiering stuf), and it's fun to build. However, what put me off was the ridiculous amount off ..... I would describe it as "Rubbing it in" that you are not currently a paying customer.
Some examples:
When recycling your unwanted parts for dust points it blinks on screen that you would get 4 times as much dust if you were premium.
When opening lootboxes, which you do get at a fair rate (1-2-3 a match), you open 8 blocks, weapons, etc. off those, you receive the bottom 4, the top four are closed off with a neat sign saying Unlock with premium.
I would say i am resistent in buying these things and only spend money when i am certain the developers deserve it, more as a donation then actually buying the stuff presented. But this game forces me to evaluate if i should not spend my money on there every 10 minutes.
In short, Fun game, went in the wrong direction, still fun but not worth the trouble if you don't intend to get premmium.

After completing this game, I am happy with my purchase, I don't understand why I see reveiws like "The game took a majority of it's levels from portal and portal 2." The majority of the levels were made by the developers it seems, and the only map they took from portal was the chamber portal 2 also took and re-used. The maps they took from portal 2 (and from portal for that matter) still used the paint gun which made you have to experiment if you played the portal series. Gameplay is smooth but can be frustrating at times with little things that don't really need to be there, such as using the orange gel to launch yourself off a ramp and if you were looking even a tiny bit off it seemed like you would miss your platform. This game would be GREAT to speed-run if they added a tiny thing, leaderboards. The game really isn't that fun to speed-run currently because of the missing of leaderboards. Voice acting was undone in my honest opinion, the script was ok, but the voice of Nigel just did not fit the role of a robotic voice, voice editing would have solved half of this, since there also was missing emotions in his voice that just did not get me immersed like the voice of Glados did. The soundtrack was iffy it was relaxing but good, but after 3 hours of play you start to notice a general rythm, but it was good nonetheless. If you play a game for a story or expecting a prequel maybe sidestory of portal DO NOT buy this game, you will be very dissapointed in both regards, the game takes you through aperture labs, you can even see the lower levels of the labs when going through the tubes that get you from chamber to chamber, but their was hardly any connection from the portal series to this game, besides maybe a couple goofy little refrences. If you're expecting a story all in it's own, don't be sad when it turns out to be bad. POTENTIAL SPOILERS AHEAD!!! The game itself was not immersive fun yes, but the story could not please me, there was no reward to beating it hardly any reaction with you and Nigel, in fact they had an escape section in the middle of the game (very fun) but at the end of the game nothing, no boss, no escape, nothing. The developers just thought it be good you shoot 3 turrets with gel gun then you get tossed into fire, picture playing portal and the glados fight at the end didn't happen and the whole inner aperture levels left out, that's what you'll feel in this game. Even when Nigel is giving you his parting words, I had no emotions, I didn't feel hatred, sorrow, or felt like I was backstabbed, the reason why is that you didn't develop any feelings through the actual game. As a whole the game is extremely fun to play and brings a new amount of fun for speed-runs and just a casual game, so in those regards, I reccomend purchasing it. However, if you are planning on buying the game to have a quality story, you should not buy this game.

Picture this.
A 3D flappy bird. The goal is to get past 300 pipes.
The problem is this goal is next to impossible. Also, there is a HUGE lack of autosaves.
That is this game.
This game is well made. This game has a good story. This game has good art, and autosaves and physics screw-ups aside, has good maps. Spectacular at times.
The problem is, this game is not fun. It is infuriating.
this game will torment you by dangling a carrot far out of reach, and waiting for you to die hundreds of times before you decide "screw this bull" and noclip to get the carrot at the end of the game.
If you ever thought playing with gels would be fun, please, get this game. I dare you. It will crush any of those feelings to dust.
It is too punishing. It uses gel with far too many hazards, disregarding just why VALVe toned down its use. There were never any timed crushers and the like in Portal 2 for a reason. I spent a half hour on one of the earlier chambers, slept on it, and spent another half hour, just to find out my "solution" was to jump on to the darkened roof of the entrance, which was practically hidden by the bright orange indicator beam. Did I feel that euphoric "aha!" moment VALVe tried to add to their games? No. Not at all.
At times, this game shines brilliantly. If the developer commentary didn't spoil it, I'm sure I'd be much more amazed. But this game clearly was not play-tested with the difficulty vs payout options in mind. Even the last secret is hardly worth the hour and a half previous I spent trying to get to it, before I just didn't care about beating this game legitimately. Frankly, this game was fun, but it has left me utterly infuriated, with no "real" payoff. And the ending secret? A complete copout.
I can say with full confidence, next to no players will get the ending's secret. It cannot be done. I have tried covering every portal, do every jump, on top of pillars, platform and any other methods I could possibly see. 99.9% of players will never see it, unless they cheat. It is bewildering that their game dev commentary says they want people to see the ending, but make no attempt whatsoever to make that ending possible to reach.
All faults I see are of map design with professional speed runners or glich-portallers in mind. The kind who glitch through walls, do jumps in mid-air on flinging cubes and the like.
Then there is saving. The developers completely removed opening selected saves. Only someone who can navigate the developer console can save and load where they please. This is particularly frustrating when facing a tough level. You can autosave, sure. But does the game tell you? No. Only those who know the Source Engine will know how to. (F6 = QuickSave, F7 = QuickLoad)
Saved in a bad place? Too bad. You cannot select any other save, as the developers disallow that.
Believe me, if there were no policies on politeness, this review would be twice as long. I spent a total of two-three hours just trying to navigate the ridiculous random physics-based screw-ups. One "surf" may not be the same as the other. One bounce can be wildly different than others too. There is no consistency.
Right now, unless there is more autosaves and hints on how to get to  the end's secret, as well as several in-between chambers having similar issues with showing the path forward, I cannot recommend this rage-game.

I bought this game because I sought more Portal action. I loved Portal 1 & 2. This game obviously revolves around the gels incorporated in Portal 2. The game feels like a mod, or maybe should've been offered as DLC for Portal. However, it doesn't have Portal's character. Without GLaDOS it just doesn't feel right. The voice acting for the Personality Sphere is awful. It feels dry, lacks character, doesn't fit in with the portal universe. Rather than contribute something new to the portal Universe, it feels like the jokes in this game were just recycled from the first and second ones. A significant portion in this game revolves around entropy it feels. Also, they force you to watch yourself travel through the tubes, and it feels like they incorporated that in order to make the playtime longer. The Levels don't have the polish that I had come to expect from Portal. And well this game looked like portal, it certainly did not play like it, or feel like it one bit. I understand making a mod takes time, and there was only a small team of developers but this does not do Portal justice. If you're looking for more portal fix, I suggest simply sticking with additional custom test chambers for Portal 2, and not buying this game. However, if you're looking to waste money on a measley 3 hour game, this is your chance. Overall, as a person who finds themself loving portal, I have to say this game had me wanting more, and probably expecting a bit too much. Also the ending feels like rubbish, absolute rubbish.

Interstellar Marines is bland. Like plain runny oatmeal, with no seasoning, bland. It probably has the most gray I have ever seen in a game. Everything is gray: the floor, the walls, the crates, the sky... even the enemies are gray. Even sunny jungle areas somehow feel bleak, empty, and uninspired. The game has been in development for over 10 years (it is still in Early Access) and that's exactly what it feels like - a game made in the early 2000's, with large empty rooms and hallways. There are only 3 weapons in the game, 1 enemy type, and a handful of missions, all of which are training missions against humanoid androids. There is some kind of stealth system, but it feels broken as enemies are still alerted by silenced gunfire and seem to spot the player from across the map, instantly delivering a killing headshot on Realistic difficulty and forcing a mission restart. The multiplayer is dead and doesn't offer anything that hasn't already been done better elsewhere. It is a barren husk of a game, kept on life support with no hope of recovery.

Ultimately this game is a solid beat-em-up, with some sandbox elements; don't expect a lot of variety in terms of alternative things to do. It can be a little samey and drag as you approach the end, but you want to forgive it because the core gameplay usually feels good, and gives you so many options when trying to figure out how to smash through a set of enemies with as much health remaining as possible. I can't recommend it at $40 but if you can get it heavily discounted then it's definitely worth your time.

I haven't played many hours of this game yet (it's a platformer, you can get through a lot of levels fairly rapidly), so take my positivity with a grain of salt, but I was so taken with the following thought that I felt compelled to write an early positive review:
Do you remember how people always wondered why Sonic didn't translate well to 3D?  Play Lost World and you'll realize why: the previous approaches weren't correct.  THIS feels like a 3D Sonic game.  The importance of momentum returns; but more importantly, the classic Sonic design of multi-leveled stages returns!!  Who'd have thought modeling the game after Mario Galaxy would finally nail the classic Sonic feeling?  Having planetoid-styled stages lets you choose the direction you want to take through the stage.  Feel like the ground-level, spikey route?  Take passage A.  Feel like flying high, springing and bouncing from place to place?  Take platform B.  Feel like a combination of the two?  Try C.  In my opinion, the two hallmarks of the original Sonic trilogy were route choice and momentum, both of which return in grand form in Sonic Lost World.
The controls take a little getting used to (you now have to hold a trigger to run, which actually works wonderfully in the design of this game), mainly because you'll be expecting the Sonic controls you've grown accustomed to over the past decade.  They've changed.  They're more complex.  But, it really adds depth to a series that was lacking it.  The new controls give you more command of the hedgehog, plus a bit more variety in the way you want to tackle obstacles.
Another plus, for me, is the fact that the aesthetic is reminiscent of classic Sonic as well as the old Sonic cartoons that I enjoyed as a child in the 90's.  I love it when developers are as nostalgic as the players.

This game is delicious!
Waves of wolves try to get a good taste of fresh human flesh V´´V.  At night... every night they attack a small farm owned by two nasty lumberjacks and their sister. Those filthy lumberjacks put up a huge variety of dirty wolf traps, towers and even shoot at everything that approaches their farm using either ordinary, blessed or silver bullets. Those cowards seek protection near lit fire places and assault all those poor hungry wolves with axes.
Luckily there are enough different types of wolves and werewolves that vary in strenght, speed and ability to keep the game fair for the wolves. So sometimes the game can be challenging for the lumberjacks, Jos and Jack, too, (I think this is how this food is called) and if they didn't try hard enough a pack wolves can finally feast on their well-deserved succulent midnight snack inside those small cabins. At most times those foolish lumberjacks seem to have huge problems with their conrols, that leave them vulnerable to attacks. Their moves and attacks are quite unreliable, laggy and look unpolished to me. In general I think this game is an average tower defense game, which definitely is more than worth its money (90% steam sale in my case). Aside from suprisingly long loading screens the game is well paced and doesn't get boring too soon. You might end up spending more time planning your stategy for the next night on the overworld map than actually surviving the night. I also think that this game doesn't have a great replay value and I don't really know why (maybe I'm already tired of seeing wolves being murdered).
If you are one of those players who insist in pin-point accurate gameplay or blockbuster action, you should stay away from this game! But if you are easily affected by a mysterious and dark atmosphere, neat soundtrack and interesting ideas you should definitely give it a try.

Full review:
When I picked up this game, I was expecting something else than what I got. Are there over 2 million possible spell combinations? Yes! Is it fun? To some extent, yes! Is the gameplay diverse? Yes, and no.
Commenting on all of the questions and answers above, the game delivers its purpose quite well: you get what you're promised. However, questions like "Are all the 2 million spells so different from each other?" or "How difficult is the game?" or "Is the game long?" are the downfall of this game (in addition to the horrible story).
From the 2 million spells you can have, you'll most probably settle with the one or two easily most overpowered ones. The other 1,999,998 spells are not even worth it to check out when you realise that the game is super boring to play if you don't have your OP laser beam with you. Or maybe you'll feel happy with that weak and useless charming spell that just slows down your gameplay and makes you underpowered.
The game doesn't get repetitive mainly because it's so short. All the different missions, ultimately, dumb down to the category of "go there and kill stuff" with an addition of "find something", with the random occasion of something a bit different. Most of the time I have in this game are from customizing my character (the character customization sucks pretty much though) and spells as well as AFKing. I'd say the game took me about 3h to beat, the only difficult part being mission where I had to kill a boss without killing 20 Fairies, which are probably the weakest enemies in the game. Never did I feel like the enemies were strong or challenging at all.
Now that the bad sides have been covered, what's left? The game has many good sides to it, too. The grammar is fine, with only few mistakes. The humour got me a few times, which is pretty uncommon. The game plays well with its tight controls, and only once did I end up in a dead end despite the maps being randomly generated. The music reminded me of Maplestory for some reason, which is a game I played a lot in my childhood (also Maplestory 2 is coming soon!), so props for the nostalgia (although the BGM plays a bit awkwardly; you can hear the music replaying itself, which annoyed me a lot)! The game didn't lag for me, although I've read comments of people raging about their fps rate, just thought I'd say this.
The game is okay, but not worth the 9,99€ it asks for. I'd buy it during a sale. Still recommending it despite its minor flaws (and the major flaw of horrible balancing) 'cause it's a solid game.

A simplified match-3 puzzle game, with nice artwork (backgrounds, mainly) and not-so-nice in-game art.
If you play this in its easy mode, there's no challenge at all; and actually it's not purely match-3: you just need to click on the "more than 3" gems in order to pop them. Fortunately, every level can also be timed and so, made more challenging.
The story mode anyways is quite short, playable in three hours I think (60 total levels). And it doesn't need that much strategy.
And you have the well-known features of every match-3 or similar puzzle game: boosters, unpoppable blocks, coins to collect and so on.
Story-wise, of course, it's worth nothing or little more. There's a small plot but it's weak even compared to pure smartphone games.
Nevertheless, it still manages to be a nice way to spend some minutes in your day.
If you're into these kind of simple puzzle games and you've been playing them for years, I think this isn't a waste of time. Just get this on sale - 4€ of course is insanely high, but for instance now it comes for 0,50€ and it's the right price for a game like this.
Can't review this negatively - the premises are matched, you get what you are shown in the game's Steam page and I kinda liked it. Music is also quite nice, and it's not that common in minimalistic puzzle games.
Quite simple, that's it. And it has also cards and achievements!

Just about an hr and a half into the tower defense game, Sang Froid Tales of Werewolves, and for $1.50 or 90% off asking price, this was a steal!! I kept my expectations very low. I thought, why would a $15 game be discounted more than 50%? I had to find out.
It's about hunting werewolves! That alone had me interested. The story is about 2 brothers Jack and Jos, at odds with each other but have to work together to help save their sister Josephine, who is possessed by some evil spirit. You have to choose one of the brothers to control. Jack is the more strategic character that lays traps (according to the game difficulty, it's hard). Jos is the stronger of the two, an effective melee attacker (game difficulty, it's easy) to which I'm assuming that he has a bigger health bar. I chose Jack to play.
What I was surprised about SF was how much you can do. From basic combat with wolves and werewolves, to planning out strategies to take on waves of enemies (mostly wolves and werewolves). Each successful night, gives you XP to improve your character, weapons, and traps. You can go up to level 15. Very well designed maps, menus, tutorials, and screens. The art direction follows more of the comic cut out look during the cutscenes. And it's nicely done. The controls are not the best, but very manageable. You can use a melee weapon from up close and ranged weapons from a distance. The best part about the combat is that you can use both types without overusing one or the other.
I haven't played much strategy/base defense games before. The closest that I can think of is Assassin's Creed Revelation's tower defense (which was a bad addition to the franchise). Sang Froid Tales of Werewolves is a very good tower defense game. Get this game before the deal while on sale.

Great game with interesting teasing facts and varying gameplay.
Gameplay is skill based, includes velocity and associated applied physics like mass influence. Depending on the planet you set a starting velocity, have a targetable speed boost, or shoot (further planets feature different skills still) each providing a very unique touch to gameplay in the same environment. You influence an asteroid to gain mass and dodge obstacles in space.
Each level starts with a narrator/moderator text box with interesting facts or hints to the level.
When playing we travel our solar system, visiting each planet with a unique ability and multiple (always 15?) levels. Progression is fair, you are unlikely getting stuck as next planets unlock after completing /some/ levels. Each level has 3 golden asteroids to pick up as an additional challenge.
Note that the Store page promises a full editor and online level sharing, which is unlikely to happen at this point. It’s been over a hear, and forum does not get a response.

Even though I do not recommend playing this game, it does have it's moments of fun gameplay. But here's why I do not recommend playing this:
-Endless cycle of the Approach, Lock on, and Orbit commands

-VERY slow tutorial due to the talking speed of the A.I. in your ship mixed with the difficult controls
-You create an entire character just to be used as a profile picture in game, and never actually explore as your character out of your ship
I really wanted to like this game, and it is an amazing concept, but I feel like the devs made things a teeny bit more complicated and tedious than originally planned. If I have to repeat the same actions over and over again each time I want to go towards and destroy a ship, i.e. "Approach, Lock on, Orbit", just to circle that ship and fire at it while it fires at me, and can take my hands off of the keyboard and mouse while shooting said ship, that is a very clear and serious game design flaw if you ask me. It just didn't keep me engaged nearly enough for me to be able to enjoy the game.
EDIT: The game itself is fun to play. I was talking about the mechanics of the game above this edit, as they were a little to complicated for a casual gamer like myself. Also, the graphics of the game are top notch, and the game looks AMAZING.

Ignore my play time on Steam because I have played the game on an non-Steam client. I have been playing the game on and off since 2008.
Now that's out of the way I'll keep it short. There are 3 main things you have to do to play Eve and have fun:
- You will have to invest time. This game has a tremendous learning curve. It is much much MUCH higher than most other MMOs. It is a completely player driven world with its own rules, own history, own professions, own market, own culture, own geography and own community. You will need to learn lots of new♥♥♥♥♥♥ You will have to commit time.
-You will have to invest money. Eve do not have microtransactions but you will need to sub. Alpha state (free to play state) is ridiculously restrictive and only good for introducing people to the game. You can't stay in alpha and have fun forever. You may be able to pay your sub with in-game money someday but it will not happen soon. You will have to sub to play it properly.
-You will have to interact with people. Eve is a sanbox game, completely different from theme park MMOs where someone is always telling you what to do and where to go next. It is player-driven world, military alliances, commercial corporations, production, market, exploration, building/destroying; everything is handled by players. You will have to interact with people, join corporations, participate in market pvp, avoid scams, join organizations etc. to have fun. Playing Eve solo is usually not rewarding and gets boring fast. You will have to communicate with people.
If you acknowledge these three points and still want to experience the biggest player-driven virtual world the gaming has ever seen, you should give it a chance. There is no game near the scale of Eve online out there. No game offers such strategy, organization and cooperation where thousands of players get together for common goals and shape the game world. Take into account the points above so that you can keep your insults to the game for yourself in case you don't like it and move on to other games more suitable for you.
Also, don't fly what you can't afford to lose.
Peace out.

Sonic Lost World, originally a Wii U exclusive, has made it's way to Steam.
I was tempted to get a Wii U at one point, and this game was on my list of games to consider getting. I ended up not getting one, and I saw this crop up on the new additions to the Steam Store.
Naturally I'm a sucker for Sonic games, but there's quite a few I'm not keen on.
This isn't one of them, I love this game, and I feel the presentation, writing, gameplay and voice acting is top notch with this entry to the Sonic The Hedgehog series.
Note, play with a gamepad, whether with an Xbox 360 controller or a PS3 controller (which I use), of course I assume they support Xbox One or PS4, but I can't test that...
This game was recieved with mixed response at launch, it seems relatively positive on here, and it's a solid port! It can run on many systems which is nice to have flexibility, it's only £19.99 over here in England and that's not a bad price in all honesty.
You're probably thinking, so, is it worth me forking out money for this game? Well I ask, do you like a game with experimentation? Because this game does just that, it has different kinds of gameplay methods, some of which can be painful, but only last a stage or two, which is good, but makes you wonder just that purpose they had.
The stages are very well crafted too, and with the new addition of a run and dash button (seperate, not binded to the same button), Sonic has never felt better to control. The only gripe with control for me is Sonic's double jump, which feels a little sluggish at worst, but it's nothing to lose sleep over.
Again, play with a controller, the game even tells you this when you boot it up everytime. Hope I helped in one way or another ^_^

The dialogue oozes with the maturity of teenage focus group testing and is the kind of thing I may have thought was amazing when I was in middle school. Everything about Prototype 2's story is a vast step backward from Prototype.
Despite all of that, I still had a blast, because the mechanics of the game feel good. They make you feel powerful. Thankfully, there is no pretense of heroism throughout most of Prototype 2, so  you never feel guilty about using and abusing every bipedal meat buffet in your vicinity. It wants you to wreck everything around you, and makes it feel good to do so.
It's better than the original Prototype because many design concessions have been made for the sake of playability. Rockets are now telegraphed by a laser and a beeping sound you will hear long after you stop playing the game. Upgrades are handled differently and the majority of them are awards for completing side objectives that are surprisingly fun to complete. This means that the collectible component in most free roaming games is actually meaningful in this game.
All in all, a fantastic experience.

Essentially building on the gameplay of the first, Prototype 2 succeeds and fails on roughly the same merits. Fancier black and white cutscenes can't disguise a poor story that trods on the character development of the first, while many of the new methods of unlocking all your slimy, spike-covered evolutions are now tied to list-checking side-missions. The air of requirement on these side missions turns them from a fun diversion in the first to a tedious chore in the second.
However, the gameplay itself is, in its way, improved. The list of mutations lost Muscle-Mass but gained the Tendrils, and underachievers like Whip-Fists and Hammerhands gained noticable improvements. Graphical fidelity is improved (but of course, it's the PC port that does it), but it's still roughly more of the same. The change in environments is nice, but in some ways a sour note. In the first game, the ownership of various districts shifted back and forth between military, civilian, and infected ground. Now, the game simply divides into three islands, an infected hellhole, a military lockdown, and a civilian slum. While this does mean that they can sculpt the three types into a much more varied experience, it requires tedious travel between them through abusing either the accidental fast-travel of playing the side-missions from the menu, or running to the few places one can hitch a helicopter from island to island.
A game I'd only recommend on sale, but would still recommend.

Luna's Wandering Stars is a wonderful, wonderful puzzle game.
The basic game play is easily explained: You control one or more moons with gravity and rockets, all the while trying to collect enough materials to finish the level. If you manage to collect the three gold clumps while you're already at it you'll get a 'perfect' on the level.
The level design is really diverse and the challenges range from accidentally perfected on the first try to a dozen resets and still no luck. The only thing that never changes is the map border made up of text that you really shouldn't cross... I warned you!
The graphics are first class and the controls fluid and intuitive. Well, as fluid as trying to steer a moon using rockets can be anyway.
The written narration is quite witty and the comments when you crash may sometimes tickle a laugh out of you.
Bascically this is a really fun game that I can recommend to pretty much anyone who likes to crash celestial bodies into one another.

There are a number of effects that one can use when making spells or enchantments.  However, The results are hardly unique.  For a game having "literally 2 milliion spells" I thought that there would be more to them than a bunch of effects bound to different sprites.
There are multiple tiers of runes you can use to craft spells and enchantments.  Each tier up provides a rune with slightly better effects (not by changing the effect of the spell or enchantment, but by increasing the modifiers of the rune).  I think the developers included all five tiers of runes when calculating all the spell combinations.  It is stated that there are 40 different materials.  The triangular number of 40 (Which calculates the combinations of two slots), multiplied by 40 (for the third slot), is 32,800.
32,800 combinations, average gameplay, and sub-par artwork.  I was drawn to this game because of my love of procedurally generated levels, and decided to buy because it promised near infinite spell possibility.  I recommend buying one of the many other games that feature level generation such as Binding of Isaac: Rebirth or Crypt of the Necrodancer.

It's 4 am and I just beat this game. It was worth every moment of my time. Before anything else, you should know that this hasn't got all that much hack 'n slash in it. That doesn't mean it's not fun though. The moments before you spring a deadly trap are as tense as the combat that comes after the trap thins the pack (or fumbles miserably). Speaking of traps, there's a pretty good variety of them as well as a fair variety of enemies that are quite distinct from one another. The game has a number of interesting mechanics that set it apart, such as the fear factor and the ability to manipulate your foes via noise and scent. Unfortunately the voice acting and cutscene animations are kind of terrible. The story isn't that great (let's hope it's a set up for a better one in the sequel). Please don't let that put you off, though. This game absolutely deserves your time and the devs your money.

This game is frustrating in so many ways.
-At times, the clicking doesn't register.
-You have to wait a few seconds for the gems to fall after you destroy them, as the registration time is janky.
-In the easier levels, you can just click randomly around the screen to win.
-In later levels, getting to gems that are trapped in the corner, or in hard to reach areas is increasingly frustrating, because you can't predict which gems will drop down onto the next segment, due to the fact that gems drop and shuffle randomly.
-Also, when trying to get harder gems, in addition to the frustration of trying to combat the random shifting of gems, you'll have gems manifest themselves from illogical spots, like the sides of walls, right on top of where you're trying to clear out a spot, making getting to a certain spot nothing but an rng crapshoot, where you'll spend 10 minutes trying to hit one spot, and when you finally get it, then you have to do it two more times, because it's a thicker block that you have to hit multiple times.
-When you finally finish getting the tricky gems, amid much irritation, you're forced to collect hundreds more of the colored gems, which means more random clicking around the screen.
-Power-ups are basically useless, except for the dagger.
-Many levels start you out with a tiny, tiny play area, where you're sure to have only one move, two if you're lucky, and many times you'll run out of moves almost immediately.
-In addition, frequently you will run out of moves on one side of the screen, which is segmented, and are forced to utilize power-ups just to clear gems so that you can have moves again.
-The story is quite mediocre and dull.
-When you power through your frustration and finish the game, you discover that the arcade mode is 100 levels of the same nonsense. Just no.
Give this game a pass, as there are many better games of this type on Steam. It's just way too frustrating to be worth your time and money.

Gosh, what a bad game...
If anybody needs proof that a match-3 puzzle game isn't the kind of thing where you can afford to be a lazy programmer, then here it is.
PROS:
- None. Quite rare for me, as I'm easy to please when it comes to gaming.
CONS:
- The gameplay is a mix between 'Clickomania' (a very old match-3 game, and certainly not the most exciting kind) and 'modern' match-3's with powerups and other silly things. But Clickomania's main interest was based on whether you could remove all of the tiles from a board without any lockups. You know, an actual puzzle... There's no such thing here, and lockups most likely happen at the beginning of a stage when very few blocks are available to click on. Then the level just reshuffles, very slowly. And it's not even our fault...
- Sometimes when a level ends, nothing happens. You actually have to click the Menu button, then Resume, for the game to find its way again. And if it shows you an achievement, then you have to do it twice.
- Story is ridiculous. It's only told through a simple block of text at the beginning of each season (series of levels). I didn't get any story panel for Autumn, which is either a solid bug, or even more laziness on their side.
- The first season is mostly dedicated to tutorials, but you get rainbow blocks in a few levels before they're properly introduced.
- Clicks don't always register. A mortal sin for a match-3. In fact, there is no feeling of pleasure when you click stuff.
- The music is bland and generic, the graphics are passable in general but blocks themselves vary from okay to very ugly. And since you'll be spending most of your time watching them, hmm...
- Power-ups are incorrectly explained. Seriously, did the game bug and forget to tell me something?
- Some levels are hard and annoying (requiring you to wait for animations to complete so you can actually reach a single tile), and are followed by a very easy level. Where's the difficulty curve?
- Levels require you to click a certain amount of blocks of every color, but they also ask you to finish something that wasn't explained everywhere and that was expressed in percentage values... Okay... Except you have to get that value to zero, rather than 100. At that point, the game designer may very well be a misunderstood genius.
- When you complete a level, the game says it was level '2-1' (first episode, season 2) when the bottom of the screen gives you a sequential number (16). Quality check, anyone?!
- Level time limits are so short (even in relaxed mode, where running out of time doesn't end the level), that you can't help but think that they expect you to click mindlessly everywhere.

Given that zombies is a very cliched premise, Dead Island had a very big advantage over other zombie titles in their time. Their hype was MASSIVE. Looking back at it now, their voice over casting wasn't bad either, they were definitely in character for the most part and their "acting" is pretty much believable. Then you get Dead Island's story that is loosely threaded by the endless fetch quests advancing the plot from point A to B, B to C, C to D and so forth. Everything felt so rushed, no real background is given on the story just that the "survivors" wanted to GTFO off Banoi. Plot and Story make or break an RPG game,
, but this is not one of those.
6/10
It has the fundamentals of your generic RPG, which are decent overall.
+ Crafting
+ Levelling (HP Gain + Skill point) - superficial, with baddies scaling in level with you the only thing it does is make you last longer given the bigger health bar.
+ Character Customization
- Endless Fetch Quests:
Let me get this straight, this not exclusive to Dead Island, even Triple A RPG titles like Witcher, Skyrim ME has had their share of endless fetch quest and Kill this Enemy quests; BUT you see less people complaining about this in their games. Why exactly is that? Their Storyline is solid, their fetch quests incorporate additional lore and enrich the actual plot. What about Dead Island? You're basically being treated as everyone's b@#%$... during the f@#$*^! apocalypse. These fetch quest do very little to give insight to the story, just another barrier to progress into the game and another Thug/RAM/Butcher guarding that objective. That is the fine line between Repetitive and Amazing.
- Weapon Durability:
This is not a new concept. Only problem is that the durability runs out TOO DAMN fast. SInce the enemies scale with you, your gonna need a lot more hits to dispatch baddies, but the durability of the weapons don't seem to scale with your level as well, just the damage. And that means more trips to the work bench + points to tedious.
- Glitches and Exploits Galore:
Dupe & Level Glitch still active 5 years later and still appears in the remake... Really??!! While I did profit from during my achievement run of the game, doesn't mean I can't call it out. This is just pure laziness.
A fairly decent RPG title with some major flaws in gameplay and plot. If you are game for some mindless zombie bashing, feel free to give the game a try. However, if you are looking for a game with an engaging story better look for it elsewhere.

I have nearly 300 games on Steam, and while I've bought some bad ones, AND even though I picked it up for what would some consider a measley 4.89 (myself included), this is the first game I genuinely feel I'd want a refund for.
Here's my standout issues with this game:
THE VOICE ACTING:
Really? I'm sorry, but he sounds like every teen youtuber narrating (via a built-in mic) a self-made video on how to find the Windows control panel. For the life of me I don't know why they didn't at least conceal his voice with some sort of digital processing (e.g. SW Ep1 style droid vocalizations, etc.)
THE SCRIPT:
What were they thinking?! Portal 2 has some of the best, most nuanced humor in any game. In stark contrast, this game's writing, paired with the aforementioned voice acting, has to be the worst attempt of humor I've ever witnessed, professional or amateur. I can't even begin to describe how flat it falls. The game would have been far better without any dialog whatsoever.
THE GUN MODEL:
Not only is it the only thing you're staring at the entire game, but it is also the game's only real original asset. This would be fine if the gun model's geometric detail didn't look like it was ripped directly from a 1998 shooter.
REHASHED PORTAL 2 TEST CHAMBERS:
Again, really? I realize they wanted to tie this game into the Portal universe and provide some familiarity, but none of the Portal 2 maps that they used lend themselves to the new mechanics. I basically feel like I'm hacking these maps to get to the exit.
THE DIFFICULTY:
It's all over the place. To make things worse, many of the original test chambers for this game are designed with a large amount of needless decoy structures that makes you waste time and paint. Pair this design issue with the freedom of the paint, and it's far too easy to complete the map in an unintended way, or worse, break it. And don't even get me started on Chapter 4, Test 7.
And you know what's sad? None of these issues would be a big deal if the game were FREE. You wouldn't even be hearing from me. I would have simply installed it like any other free mod, tried it out, saw that it was bad, uninstalled it, and, at worst, lost a couple hours of my life.
That said, I really do feel for the game's developers, and I'm sure they did their best, but in its current state, it just isn't up there enough in quality to justify a price of any kind, period.

Pros:
Some puzzles are very creative.
If you're a speedrunner you'll likely enjoy this game because it's very sequence-breakable. Most puzzles have at least one solution that the devs probably didn't think of.
It feels great just running through the levels while painting.
One of the few portal mods that isn't just more puzzles with portals. Think of it not as a Portal mod, but as an extension to Tag and the Power of Paint, and you will enjoy it and get your money's worth.
You can make your own paint gun levels. This is important to note because it's very different to make levels for a paint gun compared to a portal gun.
The recycled test chambers from Portal and Portal 2 are actually pretty interesting just because of the Paint Gun.
Pretty good amount of content from a mod.
Cons:
The voice acting isn't the greatest and sometimes it takes a long time to paint an area that needs painted. However, both of these can be easily fixed using one of my favorite console commands- host_timescale. Set it to 1.5 and you'll still be able to hear the voice acting but it will sound more like the voice of a core, and the paint will travel at 1.5 times speed, but it won't affect you at all.
Didn't have anything that could erase your paint- the fizzlers don't erase it, you just can't shoot through them, and there's no water to clear it up. This would have made it possible to make some great puzzles.
The default ending (yes there's another ending) doesn't work as well as it could have. If it would have been the same as the first Portal ending- you finally fight back against the overwatcher- it would have been great, because a paint gun is even more fun with no artificial restrictions than a portal gun. I won't spoil how it does end by default, but I will say I was disappointed. If you are too, play the alternate ending.
Some "puzzles" are legitimately just tedious. There aren't *too* many of these, but it's annoying when you know exactly how to do something but have to do 4 other things first.
How the Devs could fix it in an update (I think every review should include these, because some devs actually care):
-Increase the speed the paint travels.
-Synthesize the voice in some way or other. It just didn't feel robotic.
-Lengthen the ending with the player fighting back and (maybe) a boss battle.
-Replace the tedious puzzles (I'm sure others can tell you which are the most tedious) with new puzzles that rely on "true fizzlers" that reset all paint. It would be really interesting to see what they could do with this, especially Mevious. It seems to be his favorite testing element in Portal 2.
-Better jokes. I'm sure they can find somebody to come up with some. There were a few that were funny, but they could have been improved upon just by better timing.
-Possibly *more* recycled tests? I enjoyed them, personally, because it made me think about the differences between the portal gun and paint gun. However, I request that if this happens, all the fizzlers in these recycled tests are replaced with *true* fizzlers.
-Seriously, make the fizzlers fizzle all the paint you've placed so far, and add new pseudo-fizzlers that don't, or vice versa, and some puzzles using the new ones. This would make the game so much better, I cannot stress this enough. As it is you can essentially paint any area of the game as much as you want as long as you have the right device. Parts you can't paint would be fantastic for puzzles. Please do this.
As it stands, the game is very entertaining while it lasts, but it is very different from Portal 2. I would say it is more akin to the *first* Portal in that it doesn't restrict what you can do with your device very much, instead having the environment restrict you. I would say that if you enjoyed Tag and the Power of Paint or using the gels in Portal, and don't mind unprofessional voice acting, this is a must-buy. For a traditional rating, I would say 7/10. If they add normal fizzlers and puzzles revolving around them, or a section of the game where you fight back against Nigel, it would be *at least* 8.5 out of 10.
The trailer is pretty accurate as far as what you do in the game, so the best judge is whether you enjoy the trailer. I bought it before there were bad reviews covering the front page and I do NOT regret my purchase. At any rate, it's actual gameplay that *is* enjoyable while it lasts, so don't believe that bad reviews. If it interests you at all, give it a try.

Generally, I'm interested to see how the story unfolds. I was also pleased with the length of the mod, all things considered--I put in about 1.5 hours, but was expecting much shorter. Overall, I feel this mod has a little bit of everything that makes for a satisfying playthrough, and would highly recommend it. What have you got to lose?

Sonic Lost World is a frustratingly difficult mess of a Mario Galaxy rip-off.
At first.
When playing through the game on the Wii U I found that I was so frustrated with how Sonic controlled around the tube-like structure, which is very similar to that of Mario Galaxy. Seeing as I don't even like how the structure of Mario Galaxy's levels, I don't like it here either. It's not that I don't think it's good design, and it is for the most part. However taking controls from Mario Sunshine or Sonic Adventure and putting gravity physics into the mix, doesn't always end well. You'll notice both Mario and Sonic had to incorporate some form of a double jump into the control scheme because the gravity physics can screw up the jump arc you might need. When taking that into consideration, you really can't be formulaic when making a gravity based game like this.
Now that's not saying that it's a bad game. I did have my fair share of fun with this game and I played it twice. Once on the Wii U (bought it day one) and once on Steam (pre-ordered it this time for the DLC). While both experiences were enjoyable, the Steam version was the most enjoyable. But why. First off, it's not because it's "1080p at 60fps!" No. This is a pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ port that only allows for windowed fullscreen mode. Meaning no anti-aliasing and no lower resolutions for people whose computers can't handle this game at full 1080p. The technical aspects of the game themselves don't make this the best version, what makes this the best version is because it's not on the goddamn Wii U. You don't need a heavy brick to play this game. You have any controller you want at your disposal, even the Wii U Pro controller, which you can't use to play this game with on the Wii U! Plus there's no Miiverse crap or other stuff, and I notice the hints and item bag a lot more because it's on the screen I'm looking at.
The next reason is because I have played the Wii U version 2 years ago. Was it that long already?♥♥♥♥♥♥ Anyways, back when I first played this game on the Wii U I had no idea how to control Sonic and navigate the levels with parkour and crappy gravity physics. Now that I know how to handle it better, I actually had a much more enjoyable experience. With a bad experience under my belt (and the fact that I impulsively bought it like a little kid on a sugar rush), I thought that I made a mistake purchasing this game for PC, but I was wrong. Playing the levels with some more practice and skill than when I first did made me notice that this game is much better the second time around, and after Sonic Boom, I appreciate this game a lot more now.
Bottom line is this game is better the second time around. I can say that I enjoy this game a lot more than I first did two years ago, but that doesn't change the fact that I had a frustrating time trying to get used to the game's unusual control and level design, even if it does look good on paper.
Sonic Lost World get's a 7/10
And a reccomendation to play it twice. Not 'cause it's great, but you won't notice it's good until you start another new game.

This is one of those moments where I wish Steam had a Neutral button when it came to recommending games.
Here's the deal: Lost World is, in one word (two, technically, but whatever), half-baked.
On one hand, the "core" of the game is pretty solid; on the other hand, it's in desparate need of refinement.
On one hand, there are some quite solid ideas in the game itself (the parkour system, for instance); on the other hand, the execution is pretty flawed at times (the parkour system will activate so long as you're holding the run button, which can cause you to run up walls when you don't want to, and triggering a wall-run is an imprecise science at best).
On one hand, the game can be a great deal of fun; on the other hand, some of the later levels are borderline infuriating.
Would I recommend Lost World? I honestly don't know how to answer that. If the price dropped a bit, then I'd say sure, go for it. It's a competent game. Maybe not the best PC port ever, but it's not awful either.
For now, though, I'd say wait until either A) the price drops, or B) modding the game has really taken off, making some of the more annoying stuff... well, less annoying. (shout-out to sonic retro)

Our childhood blue hero is off an adventure again… with new gameplay mechanics, entirely new level designs, a straight-foward story… SEGA! Cut this out. I’ve been playing Sonic my whole life, and I’m sick and tired of seeing our loving hedgehog go through so many changes. You don’t see Mario change in every game they release. They slowly add mechanics to him. I wish Sonic Team would stick with a mechanic, and improve on it. They had it right on Sonic Adventure 2, Sonic Generations, and other games.
Regardless, I will admit that Sonic Lost World gameplay took a while to get used to. From beginning, you may either hate or love it. If you played Sonic Generations for thousand hours like I have, it will take some time to get used to it in order to achieve Sonic’s max speed and blast thru maps. Unfortunately, Sonic doesn’t exactly go as fast as Sonic Generations, and it’s not as rewarding either.
There so much positives and negatives about this game. Depending on how you play and like about sonic games will determine your purchase.
Right from the beginning, the type of graphics and enemy designs are quite charming and nostalgic. I hope they continue with these type of designs as I rather see more toonish badnicks than GUN robots or realistic monsters. However, the environment feels so empty and lackluster. Nothing feels so lifelike and most of the planets end up looking the same. Not to mention, lot of these levels have too many hazards that prevent you from going fast. I almost feel punished going fast, and lot of level designs prevent you from doing it. Side scrolling levels are the worst type of level design and other level designs felt outdated or stuff you would see on a Nintendo Gamecube. Nothing was unique or stood out. Not to mention, there were some awful enemy placement you have to destroy by a timed homing attacks. Why can’t I destroy them with spindash or bounce over their heads? Sonic Generations had better enemy designs because they weren’t so annoying, and they were mostly there to help you reach shortcuts you couldn’t before. It maded Sonic look and feel like the badass we loved since the Genesis.
Sonic’s movement is absolutely terrible in this game.  Well, his controls have always been negligibly bad, but it didn’t matter since maps were straight and linear.  However, when levels require precise platforming, this becomes a problem. There were so many times when I died because I was struggling to get a Red Ring. Sometimes, I’d have to side track back, but I couldn’t tell what was behind. Being able to control the camera is a must! I hate that I kept getting killed only because of an unfair sneak attack. Also, whose bright idea was it to remove the front trigger turns from Sonic Generations? Lot of the levels that require moving down a straight line became much more difficult because I couldn’t get Sonic run on the narrow path in time. I liked having the ability to turn left and right quickly. I will admit that after a while, I started to like the ability to walk, spin dash, and jump instead of homing attack. However, it was quickly ruined by the game’s terrible physics. Seriously, Sonic’s speed drains very quickly and returns to his max run. Sometime I really love to do in Sonic Generations was launch myself using the boost to reach other platforms. I can’t necessarily do that in Sonic Lost World as the spin dash doesn’t launch that far. I have to magically jump twice in order to double my speed in order to launch myself, but then I immediately fall down with no horizontal speed. I could go forever on the physics of this game… But I won’t. Oh, and the parkour system. Best way to describe it: It’s exactly like how I feel about Assassin Creed's parkour. When it works, it’s great. When it doesn’t, you will hate it.
I will say that I absolutely loved Sonic’s animations. They’re the best I’ve seen in a Sonic 3D game. I love how he runs, walks, jumps, acts, etc. I hope the next Sonic game has animations as detailed as now. It brought such good smiles just like the original 2D sprites. However, the Deadly Six are the most cliché Villains I’ve ever seen. I can’t stand any of them. None of them stand out at all. When you fight and hear their dialogue, you’ll understand what I mean, especially Zeena.
There so much this game does right that I hope SEGA uses in the next Sonic Game, but there so much that brings this game down. Some of my complains can be avoided, but your first playthrough may not be so memorable. I recommend this game when it’s on sale. It’s not worth at full price especially when you can beat it under 5 – 7 hours.

In the rugged, frontier days days of the Internet 1.0 waaaaaay back in the late 90s, one game was widely recognized in middle school computer labs across the country: Space Pengine. It was a quaint, plucky game with the simple goal of launching a penguin via slingshot into a black hole, assisted by planetary gravity along the way.  My nostalgai had me thirst for a new Space Penguine for the modern age, and that's when I found Luna's Wandering Stars.
While the first world, Mercury, gave me the Space Penguin slingshotting I missed, I then learned with Venus that LWS is actually 9 games in one. Each planet (Yes, including Pluto) brings a new mechanic that manipulates you (the moon) in different ways. From Saturn's power to shrik and grow your mass at will, or Mars letting you shoot at obsticles, players are bound to find a favorite section of the game that will win them over. Come for the inadvertant planetary descrution, stay for the addicting quest to collect all the golden asteroids.
It's a strategy/tower defense game for those who usually hate these genres.
