It just feels as though the developers kinda.. well... dumbed it down for example the progression system in the origional was that you would earn EP (Evolutionary Points) through the main story and through doing side missions and then you could freely choose how you would evolve your character with a few story limitations (which made sence) and could unlock new abilities and combo moves.
In Prototype 2 however the EP that you earn are directly channeled into a liniear level up bar where once it is filled simply gives you a level up point that you can choose to place in either:
Health
Regen
Movement
Mass
Finishers
and Disguise (which in almost completly pointless I might add)
Once the point has been placed it simply gives you a straight up boost to the thing that you choose.... and thats it....how boring. Now before people go off at me YES you can do side missions to aquire "mutations" (selectable passives) but again that is quite boring and not worth going after as the game can quite easily be completed without aquireing more then a single passive...
Another problem is that many of the enemies you will encounter are just re-skins. There are some new enemies but most if not all will instantly be recognisable which is a shame.
most of these things I could deal with but what really put the nail in the coffin for me was
*not really a spoiler*
The final boss fight, Obviously you fight the protagonist from the first game (Alex Mercer) and I have to say it was one of the worst if not THE worst boss fight I've ever had to force my way through, because I refused to give up on the game after making it so far, but my GOD it was terrible.
I like many of you I'm sure remember building up Alex to be the ultimate badass killing machine. Yet once you reach him, to destroy your maker.... it's just pathedic. The fight is a spam fest of dodging and back stabbing with scripted movements, camera angles and area restricting nonsence.
First off. The spam. my GOD the spam. Yourself and Alex literally jump around each other constantly because many of Alexes attacks are unblockable and auto hit unless you are spamming the hell out of dodge. Then once you land behind him you back stab him a few times, then rinse and repeat.
The camera angles kind of lead into the area restriction problem. you confront alex on top of a building and after having the whole game free roam, you are now restricted to this one roof top for the duration of this fight and in doing so the camera has to use funky angles just to try and keep up with all the stuff flying around the screen causing many, MANY problems and it is just stupid. Yes the origional did the same with its boss fight but at least it had a semi decent reason of being on an aircraft carrier and at the very LEAST that boss had minimal scripting and the fight was still "free roam"
In all honesty it would have been better if they had just made Alex like the (minor spoiler) Evolved where they fought you around the city in free roam. It would have made the fight so much better.
All in all I am dissapointed which makes me very depressed as I absolutly loved the first game and played the hell out of it, this sequal.... just makes me sad.
If you are new to this universe go buy the origional and have a blast. If you are a fan like me? then just avoid this and go have fun with the origional again.
%99 of the time you'll be smacking your head to the table till the back of your face becomes the front of your face.

Day of Defeat Source is an official sequel to Day of Defeat mod for Half-Life. It's a WW2 based multiplayer competive team-based FPS with classes. And aiming and headshots and dieing as you are peaking the corner from one bullet.
Multiplayer community is still alive. You will find at least few full servers that play same popular maps 24/7.
If to say about it short, then imagine Counter-Strike, but more balanced, with classes, more fun and without having to wait until the end of a round. In WW2 setting.
And amazingly enough, it has interesting non-symmetrical maps, which is quite a rarity. Not sure if it's as balanced for both sides, but it makes it much more interesting to play with both teams. More team games should do this.
And yea, it has system where you lose energy if you sprint of jump, so if you plan on getting somewhere far away as fast as you can, just walk there, losing energy gives a huge temporary penalty on your speed.
You also can run, walk, crouch or go prone, all will decide what kind of accuaricy you will have. Actually camping is a legit tactic there. But watch out, shootign gives you away, with all the muzzle fire effect and big light they give off, so don't expect to camp for too long, relocate. Or push. With teammates.
And it has two modes: 5 control points and detonation. Not much should be told about control points, though the last ones tend to be won by a sneaky person, tend to be too close to the enemy spawnpoint to really push with whole force. And I never got to play detonation maps, not popular enough, sorry.
So, what Source improved over original? Well, you guessed it, the most important change is the inclusion of ragdolls! Well, fine, not important, still nice. Graphics look more clean, less muddy.
They did some good work on class system, streamlining them and making them all more or less unique. In original, each side had 9 classes with seemingly random equipment, and there could be big difference between each side. In Source there are only 6 classes now, balanced and each made to have something that others don't have. Even better is that you can tell away what you are fighting against.
Anyway, let's get to it:
- Rifleman are made for fighting at medium and far ranges. And short ranges. Can kill with a single bullet, but they don't shoot fast and their accuaricy is too lacking on the move. They are support to the main force, as well as sniping. Not going to do good at the very front of a force. They can now aim down iron sight, but seeing how they are accurate when standing and aiming down iron sight makes you crawl like turret, it's kinda useless. Can also shoot grenade out onto quite far distances.
- Assault classes are good only at close range and only if you are moving, otherwise you may use Support instead. Recoil and accuaricy losses on his main gun is minimal, it's just that it's not accurate to begin with. Has grenades. And importanly, has smoke grenades, that he can either use for himself, to get into smoke and use his close-range gun at advantage. Or he can use it to team, for tactics, like covering place which is dominated by enemy machine gunners.
- Support class is actually the main class around there. His automatic gun is kinda average, for medium ranges. Have to learn to aim with this one. Can shoot one bullet at a time in alternative mode. Also has grenades. Has pistol.
- Snipers are like rifleman but with sniping scope that makes them accurate. But without grenade-shooting. No, you still don't camp, machine gunners do better job than you. And rifleman do better job at you. You should be at far away but still moving and starfing a lot. Switching to scope mode is instant and accurate fully even when you are standing, so use it to full advantage.
- Machine gunners are the people who defend and clean streets and open spaces until there is nothing left inside. Can defend rooms too, but that asks for a nade. And can do better job than camping snipers. They really kill anything at any range, you have to know where they are and to come out from unexpected angle. Good thing there is a limit on them. You have to go prone to set up machine gun, but you can use any ledge you find as well. At least they can't shoot much while undeployed at least, the recoil and accuaricy loss are gigantic. There are however some players who use while travelling through small rooms, when you can just "shotgun" anybody, having learnt to compensate recoil. But at least there arent many of such players. Also have pistols.
- Rocket class has rocket launcher and autoatic little weapons. In original they were just there to have "random" selection to troll you, being useless, only there to blow some objectives in very few maps, I heard. In Source, the explosion of bazooka was buffed up, having bigger radius. It's actually good at taking out machine gunner spots. Some of them. the thing is, you have to put them over shoulder to shoot and that makes you crawl, so it's still kinda weird support class. But hey, at least they have automatic gun as backup weapon, not pistol. Those are actually good. So yay source!
So yea. Still addictive, still campish. Still good. Or better. It's more streamlined and feels more sane in balance for sure.

Love this game to bits, not sure how you can not like it if you are into magic of many different kinds.
It is so fun to screw around trying to discover new spells, you might end up spending a lot of time customizing the appearance of yourself OR your spells (which is awesome).
There are 45 different materials and they all got 5 different tiers you will love to look around for more materials, heck you can even craft them yourself with other loot you find.
You use materials to design spells with and all these materials has a secondary effect if used on your robe as well.
An example material could be "Evercold Ice" and if it is used in a wand or spell and you attack them with it and hit, it will slow down enemies and their attacks, but if you use it on your robe it will instaid provide you with a rechargable shield that gets hit before your hp goes down. I think most materials are very viable as well so everything has a use :)
I have so much more positive i want to say about this game, its on par with games like magicka and path of exile in its own way.
Pro's ============================================
*Beautiful and charming 2d graphics.
*A lot of possible spell combinations and materials.
*Option to randomize a lot of things, including: wizard appearance, spells, spell names, or randomize it all by playing the randomize challenge! great fun awaits :D
New game+ which offers you more replayability after you complete the game.
Cons ============================================
*It doesn't have multiplayer/coop or ways of messing up your friends ( by mistake mind you  :P )
*Few spells you can actually use in combat, its: 1 basic spell from your wand, 2 from spells, 1 passive from robe and 1 pre-designed artifact that you cannot customize and once you go into combat you cannot change your spells and are required to exit to change.
*Difficulty drops significantly very quickly as you gain more materials and material slots.
===============================================
All that staid, even if i wreak everything easily its fun to play and the moderate at best difficulty is a good reason to start experimenting with other builds or ways of playing other than the "min/max" builds we are used to.
tl;dr.... I will strongly recommend this game if you like magic creativity and games like magicka or path of exile.

Naruto Shippuden: Ultimate Ninja Storm 3 Full Burst is perhaps the most extreme example yet of Namco Bandai's attempt to appeal to the converted and only to the converted. Here's a game not simply for any old Naruto fan, but for Naruto fans who are completely up to date with the story and characters as they currently exist in the anime/manga episodes and are seeking a new way of experiencing previously explored plotlines. If you're not up to date, then not only are you going to struggle enormously with the story as depicted in the game's early stages, but you're going to ruin what you've not yet seen of the TV series. Unfortunately, due to gameplay that is as unwieldy and bloated as its title, Full Burst is not an acceptable way to get yourself up to date with this franchise.
his may be a beat-'em-up, but the primary Ultimate Adventure mode features so little gameplay in comparison to cutscenes and dialogue-heavy exposition that you'd be forgiven for thinking you're sitting through a barely interactive (albeit combat-heavy) soap opera. It feels as though developer CyberConnect2's plan was to create a condensed edition of the anime in which fight scenes are playable, rather than create a game in its own right. This leads to an experience that features such haphazard and irregular pacing that your principal cause for intrigue rests in trying to work out just how long it's going to be before the game asks you to pick up the controller again--and even when you do, the core combat is a shallow, button mashing affair that requires little in the way of skill. While there's definite and worthwhile value in repackaging the events of a beloved series in a new format, there's also value in a game giving you something to do.
There may be a lack of interaction in story mode, but that doesn't hold true for the package as a whole. Including all of the downloadable content released for the original Naruto Shippuden Ultimate Ninja 3 release, the volume of content on offer is gargantuan. Chief among the additions is the extra Ultimate Adventure chapter, which sees Sasuke and Itachi Uchiha take on the nefarious Sage Kabuto, a segment that is so phenomenally difficult in comparison to the rest of the game that all previously learned tactics become essentially redundant. The same Sage Kabuto is unlockable as a playable character if you have the patience to jump through the numerous hoops to unlock him, and there are also some new costumes to swoon over.
he biggest, but certainly not most interesting, piece of extra content comes in the form of supplementary challenge missions. One hundred of these have you beating an opponent in a fight while handicapped in some way--removing your ability to jump, for example, or setting a limit on the number of attacks at your disposal. While these missions do add some welcome variety to the combat, they primarily serve to highlight just how shallow the core mechanics are. Without these externally shoehorned twists on battle, fighting suffers from an overwhelming shallowness that sees you engage autopilot once the basics become second nature. Only during set-piece boss battles are you asked to do something out of the ordinary.
To compound matters, the most members of the enormous character roster plays in the same way. You swap between characters regularly during Ultimate Adventure, but this is done predominantly to facilitate the narrative rather than to spice up gameplay through variety and diversity. Granted, significant and impressive visual flair is achieved by switching often between characters with attacks that are literally out of this world, but that aesthetic quality doesn't remain interesting long enough for the combat inadequacies to be forgiven. Clearly, this is not a game with the remotest desire to cement its place in the bastion of hardcore fighting game legacy, but that doesn't excuse the fact that there's so little meat to the gameplay that you're essentially feasting on elaborately painted bones.
Similar problems exist with Ultimate Adventure's role-playing-game-lite elements, which allow you to roam around a number of different environments with a view to collecting and buying items to use in combat (health potions, strength buffs, and so on) and optionally talking to loitering non-player characters. At times, these moments provide a welcome break from the cutscene/fight/cutscene pattern, but more often than not, they feel designed to artificially lengthen the game and trick you into thinking you're playing something with genuine genre-blending aspirations.
The closest comparison to this format is Asura's Wrath, another of CyberConnect2's offerings. However, where Asura's Wrath succeeds in this style of storytelling thanks to its short length and ferocious pace, Ultimate Ninja Storm 3 suffers from attempting to cover far too much ground for the core mechanics to handle. If you do classify yourself as a Naruto aficionado, then simply having another medium through which to consume the narrative is potentially going to be enough to satisfy you. Without a doubt, everyone else should look elsewhere.

Well... After all the good deals in steam, I guess it's fair to get one or two bad ones...
First of al, if you are interested in the concept, go play TAG: The Power of Paint instead. It's made by the same guys that implemented the gels in Portal 2, and it's
better than this. And it's actually free.
Free, just like this mod should have been. Just like all the game mods usually are.
But eh, this one costs money, so it should be better than all of them, right? I mean, if there's a budget, it'll be more professional...
NOPE!
First of all, the voice.
There's a reason The Stanley Parable paid for a narrator - to provide a voice suitable to the game. A teenager doesn't suit Aperture Science at all,
; and trying to imitate the humour used in the original game (failing, of course) is just secondhand embarrassment.
And worst part, it wasn't even needed. You could remove all the voice in the game and it would
not matter at all. Well, maybe it would make the mod better.
Second, the maps. You could've browsed a bit through the Workshop section, pick one or two surf map from CS:S/TF2, and you'd have the same thing. Anyways: They aren't clear about what you need to do at any moment. You'll never know if there is a platform below yours, if you will need that cube later, if that laser is actually needed there... And if you fail to pick up the non-existant hints, you gotta restart again. And again. And again. It's not funny or challenging, it's about throwing a dice and hoping for a 6. Or in this case, hoping that the jump you made will be just enough to reach the border of the platform.
Third, the story. Yes, yes, I know, the point is to play with a new concept. But come on, give me something to make me go to the end of the puzle other than "yay I made it". Thinking with Time Machines (
) did it and everything turned fine.
Fourth, music. The only good thing about the game. It fits the game, and I had a chuckle with the Aperture Beats logo. But a good soundtrack isn't worth this price.
I regret my purchase, which is why I took the time to write this review. Please, don't make the same mistake as me.

Out of my experience with Half Life 2 mods, this one really takes the cake as one of the best, if not the best mods I have played, with Miverva: Metastasis being the only one to come close to the level of work put into this (and that mod is entirely different in tone in comparison to this).
My favourite part of the game, by far is it's beginnings, where it is night and you're trecking through the suburbs, not really sure what to expect or when to expect it, despite there only being one kind of enemy the way they were placed put me on edge on quite a few occasions and with the amazing ambience, it just blew me away.
The later parts were more thought provoking than anything else, I started to ask myself, who are these guys, what is their goal and why the hell am I an enemy to them? I'm sure these questions will be answered in the acts to come but damn it was so interesting to try and find clues about these guys.
The ending was kind of abrupt and for lack of a better word anti-climactic, although maybe I am jumping the gun a bit on the events, as it wasn't really confirmed and to be fair it does open up to a number of different ways the second act can start.
Gameplay wise it is about as good as Half Life 2 mechanic wise, which is pretty damn good, nothing was notably bad or wrong, and all the added mechanics were really good too. However the combat was a tad lacking, as the zombie enemies were rather easy and the ai of both the zombie and human enemies weren't incredible, although I feel that the game is more built around it's story than it's action, so I feel I should give this a pass.
In conclusion, this mod is rather amazing and is well worth playing, in my personal opinion I wouldn't mind paying for this game it is that good, I shall be eagerly expecting the second act, which I am convinced will be just as good as the first.

Interesting fusion of strategy, tower defence and 3rd person action wrapped up with a quirky theme which is overall an enjoyable experience and worth a look if you want something different!
The game has you taking the role of one of two brothers defending initially their cabin, but eventually a number of buildings and locations throughout a forest from ever increasing waves of wolves, werewolves and other mythical  creatures. Gameplay is split into two phases:
Day Phase: This is basically the 'setup' you are presented with a map of the forest showing the spawn locations, number and targets of the various enemies you will face during the night. From here you can set traps, or place other structures to help you survive the night. You can visit shops to buy new equipment which the money you earn and spend skill points which are unlocked by levelling up your character to give you bonus abilities.
Night Phase: During the night you must take control of your character to enact you plan by running around the forest, springing the traps you have set and taking on the enemies in combat (both gun based and melee).
The game provides a good variety of enemies, each with different strengths and weaknesses to plan for, and a range of traps allowing you to pick your tactics. The 'Lumberjack' theme is nicely carried through the game in the art style of the menus and the soundtrack. The 3rd person combat is a little clunky, but is designed to keep you thinking tactically rather than just charging into a group with your axe.
The game certainly has negative points which might put some people off. The story is overly complicated, fairly non-nonsensical and unnecessary. The voice acting/dialogue in the cut-scenes isn't amazing and in general I didn't like the way it was told, mostly in dull dialogue between characters. Occasionally there would be a cut scene represented in a kind of hand-drawn animation style (completely different to everything else) which actually worked really well and I can't help but think the game designers should have had a simpler story, but stuck to this style.
The loading times are also quite long and although you can restart a mission at 'dusk' with all your traps in the same place, you still have to go back to the planning screen, start the night, go through the inventory screen, wait for the level to load  and click through any cut-scenes before you can make another attempt at a mission you failed, which gets annoying if you make a few mistakes early on in a mission.

This was a tough one. This game has lovely art, great controls, a fun combination of strategy and action, and an enchanting mythology set in old Canada. A plague of possessed wolves and werewolves begin attacking a small Canadian village and two estranged brothers, one a trapper and one a lumberjack, must unite to protect their beloved sister as the Devil seeks to claim her for his own. Almost everything about this game is outstanding.
--The music is very well done, and I enjoyed quite a lot to listen to it and take a small break from figuring out what to do next.
--The controls are smooth, and as the levels progressed I found myself diving and climbing through maps like a true spy would.
--The story, I found, was actually really interesting. It pulled me in and actually I cared so much about one of the characters that I just stared blanky at my screen for a minute or two trying to process what had happened to them.
--The levels are very well designed, and I never felt that the game was asking too much of me to complete a task.
--The upgrade system is neat. Not the best, or most detailed, but I appreciate having it there.
--The dialogue is interesting to read, and often pretty funny.  I laughed a couple of times.
A negative point, though, is how short the game is.  I have five hours on record, and in that time I've beaten it twice and gotten 100% of the achievements. (I did that in one sitting. That's how good I thought this game was.)
Is it worth $10? Yeah, I'd say it is.  Should you get it if it goes on sale? Most definitely.
Overall, I'd give this game an 8/10. Definite Recommendation.

An overall fantastic game that fans of spellcrafting, bullet hells, 2D platformers, and 2D shooters will love!
Story: You are an out-of-work wizard who gets hired by a temp agency to be a security guard. You then spend your time adventuring, collecting treasure, hoarding ancient artifacts, killing fairies, and basically doing everything except guarding the school you're supposed to be guarding.
Graphics: Everything is made out of paper, but the game really rocks that look. In addition, the 2D graphics make it suitible for lower-end machines as well as gaming beasts.
And the ALL IMPORTANT GAMEPLAY: Amazing. The spellcrafting system works wonderfully, and while there are some limits - such as a cap on the materials that can be used to make a spell - chances are, if you can imagine it, you can make it. The platforming controls are a bit odd, mostly with the hold-down jump mechanics and the relatively slow move speed, but you can enchant your robes to take care of that if need be!
Outstanding Feature: I especially enjoyed the multilayered shielding technique I used for my robe: A Lightning Rod to block projectiles, a Magic Boomerang to block melee attacks, and a cube of Evercold Ice to absorb any damage that got through. These all regenerate over time as well, and there are also spells that can regenerate health on a kill, so it's pretty forgiving.
Final Comments: Magicmaker is a wonderful game that really deserves a place of honor in anyone's game library.

The first Naruto game on Steam, Ultimate Ninja Storm 3 is a great addition to the saga. I've been a fan of the Ultimate Ninja games since they were on the PS2 (in fact, I have all the Ultimate Ninja games for the PS2), as they're excellent fighting games. However, this is my first game since Ultimate Ninja 5, as I could not afford the newer consoles. The combat system has changed since the old PS2 days, going from a traditional 2D fighting style to a more open 3D arena, and I'd say it's a great change (of course, I think this change occurred when the Ultimate Ninja Storm saga started).
The combat system, in itself, it's quite simple at first sight, with physical attacks alongside the traditional jutsus from the anime, and ranged attacks using different ninja weapons like shurikens or kunais. The traditional Ultimate Jutsus remain here, and they're bigger and better. The animations are pretty good, and the art style closely resembles the anime itself.
As for the story, it starts with a prologue set during the destruction of Konoha by the Kyuubi, and then jumps onto the Five Kage Summit, and ends during the Fourth Great Ninja War. The story mode features the already common open world featuring several landmarks of the ninja world, including some of the hidden villages. Besides the story itself, you can also take different special missions, including fighting some "historical" battles from the franchise (ie, battles that happened before the main story of the game).
The game includes a large roster of characters, each with their own skills, straight from the anime. Among them are the Hokages, the Jinchuriki, and the Akatsuki. The game also allows you to select up to two extra characters to help you along during battles, which can create some very interesting and dynamic teams.
If you're a Naruto fan, or fan of fighting games in general, then this will be a great addition to your library, I recommend it.

Right from the start, this game isn't for everyone.
The game is a huge time sink, Although it only shows me having 100ish hours, I'm probably closer to about 300, I've had the game since before it was on steam.
It is a great framework, the mods are what makes this game shine, the base game can be played by itself, but you really don't get the same experience. With the globe being implemented, allowing exploring, and showing other colonies, and expanding the view of you're not alone, the game is less complete than it was before the globe.
There was little need for it to be added, don't get me wrong, I love the idea of the globe, showing traders, giving more things to do, and achieve, hell you can wipe out entire colonies "just because". But overall, it wasn't needed, a game that has been essentially in beta for a long time now, shouldn't be adding additional mechanics. From a game design perspective, that just seems to be a good way to shoot yourself in the foot.
One of the largest complaints I have, is, it is a time sink, You can speed up game time. Which is needed, but you can't speed it up more, and I feel this is because the developer has opted for a slower time, to allow for larger levels to be generated (You do get warned, bigger levels = more chance for lag, makes sense), through developer menus or other, the option to speed the game up further should be allowed. Giving ample warnings that the game may slow down in such cases. I would love to play this game sometime at 5x, 10x speed, just to pass time in mostly idle moments, with the introduction of the globe, time passing is even worse, as if you decide you want to have a migrating backstory for what ever reason, you now speed a lot of your game, waiting.
Great game, good framework for mods, but overall, the developer needs to improve the already established features, instead of creating a ton of half-established mechanics and letting mods complete them. I love the game, but due to how long it takes to get anything done, I don't see myself continuing after to many more playthroughs, my main complaints aside, if you have free time, and enjoy a more backstory driven playstyle, definately for you, if you're more for action, strategy kind of gameplay, not so much, but you might be surprised by just how much you do actually enjoy it.

Now I'll be honest here: I liked this mod. I liked the idea of firing gel wherever I wanted and being able to bounce around and run like the wind at the press of a button. But almost immediately I was taken away from the experience by a plethora of issues. The lazy voice acting, horrible scripting, and general lack of what makes the Portal games amazing were a very quick turn off. More upsetting was the fact that there was no way to use water or erase any of your gels. The best you can do is cover them up with each other, but being able to clean surfaces would make the game far less frustrating. To top everything off, just a few levels from the ending, I find myself unable to progress in any way except to restart the chapter. There are visible saves but no way to access them, and being that the level design was done incorrectly and the player is able to reach autosave checkpoints far before they're supposed to, I am trapped on a platform with no way back to the beginning of the test chamber and no possible way to jump back. Try to reload from the begining of the test but the game will only allow you to start from the last save or from the start of a chapter.
In addition, at some points in the game you are expected to fire orange gel right in front of you as you run to keep your momentum. But half the time, the gel fails to land before you do and all of your momentum is lost, often resulting in death. One section in particular forces you to race against a clock while trying to use this broken mechanic, and more than half of the twenty or so times I attempted this, I was unable to clear small gaps because the gel failed to register in time.
Don't spend your money on this. You're better than that.

I feel cheated having paid money for this game. When you pay for something, you would expect it to at least have been playtested enough so that it functions like it should 99.999% of the time you play it.
This was not the case for Aperture Tag.
Not only did I come across several sections that required pinpoint accuracy early on in the game, but about 75% of the way in I struggled to complete a timed section of the game not because of my own actions, but because of the game's physics not responding correctly or getting stuck on objects.
Overall, it has such a lack of polish that I'm astonished it even got approved for sale. It's not terrible - there are certainly worse mods out there for any game, much less Portal/Portal 2. This mod, however, is nowhere near worth the asking price of $7 or even $5. Please, please, please save your money and buy something else. There are plenty of other games (and even free mods!) that play better than this for the same price. Hell, go download the original Tag and you'll get a better experience for free.

This is, in my opinion, Telltale's best one so far.
And no, I'm not just saying that because one of the main characters is literally me (or at least as close as I'm ever gonna get till I start making games myself lol).
This game is far closer to a typical adventure story as compared to something like The Walking Dead. Where The Walking Dead is filled with continual sadness, this game gives you that Hero's Journey-styled story that I know I've been wanting from Telltale.
It does a fantastic job of integrating previous Borderlands lore and characters with new ones. Many characters from previous entries in the series will appear, and yet the characters from Tales from the Borderlands fit right in with the wild universe that Gearbox has created.
If you're a fan of the Borderlands universe, grab this game for sure. If you're a fan of well-written adventure stories (which means pretty much everyone) then I'd still recommend looking into this one. Experience with the Borderlands universe makes this that much more special, but it should be just as enjoyable to a newcomer to the series as well.
And hey, if you ARE a newcomer, then that gives you the opportunity to go play through the otherBorderlands games yourself! Lucky you!

On a line-by-line basis, this may be the best visual novel I've read.  The author can write... sentences.  The story that develops is tragic and touching in many ways.
If the author hadn't included the AIs, if we'd been left to discover what had happened and ponder it ourselves, it might have been a passable story.  But you must let both AIs comment on every letter, which slows the game down TREMENDOUSLY, and mostly they just make heavy-handed commentary and force us to answer inane questions (is slavery of women good?  It's totally messed up to teach women to read, amiright? ... and more in that vein).  One of the AIs is an interesting character, essential to the story, but her persistent hammering on me to make sure I got the message that slavery of women is bad, 'mkay? made her more annoying than endearing.
Throughout history, there have been two opposing views of stories and of art.  One view, the older one, says that the purpose of stories is to answer questions and shut people up.  Creation myths.  Stories about Jesus.  Soviet Realism.  Mein Kampf and the sculptures of Arno Breker.
The other tradition says the purpose of stories is to ask questions.  Is history made by great men, or small actions (Tolstoy)?  Is civilization built by rational choices, or by mercy and grace (Dostoyevsky)?
The question that Analogue ultimately asks is: Is it okay to destroy society if it's hopelessly patriarchal?
Is that a genuine question that's socially relevant for today?  Yes, it is, if you're a paranoid schizophrenic living in a fantasy world in which the Handmaid's Tale is relevant to the US in the 21st century.
In fact this is one of the few questions that contemporary "literature" Is allowed to ask, which is the reason I'm reading visual novels on Steam instead of the post-modernist crap found in literary fiction today.  The entire point of modernism, Marxist critical theory, post-modernism, post-colonialism, and everything else found in "respectable" critical theory today is to convince people to destroy Western civilization.  It's the same trick the Nazis pulled with "Kultur", just in the interests of different people.
Analogue's agenda isn't really to get you to ask that question; it's to surreptitiously get you to accept the answer "yes" to the question, "Is Western society today hopelessly patriarchal?"  That puts Analogue in the tradition of propaganda stories.
It isn't that hard to destroy civilization.  Western civilizations have fallen many times: demographic collapse across the entire region circa 1187 BC, the destruction of native North African cultures at the end of the Greek Dark Age; Rome destroyed by Christianity after 300 AD; the total destruction of Arianist (no, I don't mean Aryan) Christian Europe by the Franks and Byzantines; the destruction of the Sassanid and Byzantine Empires by the Muslims; the devastation of Eastern Europe and Asia Minor by the Mongols in the 13th century; etc., etc.
News flash:  Destroying civilization has never worked out well for women.

Analogue: A Hate Story is one of the most "literary" games of recent history, in a recent history which includes a great deal of games with significant literary merit, from Night in the Woods and Gone Home to Undertale. There's been, to understate the issue vastly, "controversy" around literary games, or as a certain toxic subset of the gaming community terms them, "SJW" games - usually called such because they have the audacity to include a queer character or characters of color or to critique some trend in dominant gaming culture. I am an unabashed "SJW" or "social justice warrior." I have a full page dedicated to doxing me on a prominent alt-right website. I also think that while it absolutely deserves its place in the "canon" of video game history as a game which managed an impressive amount of storytelling with an incredibly small amount of art assets, and indeed made a fairly impressive effort at social critique, Christine Love's Analogue: A Hate Story ultimately fails as a game and as a social critique. Before elaborating, I do want to warn people who don't know what they're getting into that Analogue is more or less a space opera retelling of Margaret Atwood's The Handmaid's Tale, a harrowing novel about♥♥♥♥♥♥and misogyny. Both of those things exist throughout Analogue's narrative and intentionally discomfort the player. The game also has an undercurrent of fetishistic sexuality which is not something I find objectionable in itself, but which is handled in ways that seem quite hypocritical given the narrative the story is telling. At one point, for instance, one of the artificial intelligences who delivers the majority of the narrative in Analogue becomes angry with the player's character if the player chooses to dress the character in a particular outfit - an outfit which the game provides and which the character invites the player, in character, to dress her in. Full disclosure: my distaste for this game is absolutely driven by a personal dislike of the out-of-game politics of its creator. Christine Love has been a vocal spokesperson for transgender people and is perhaps the most visible openly transgender woman in gaming. She has also shamed a young transgender woman for having the audacity to praise Love for being a trans woman in games, because she has had "the surgery" and considers that part of her life over with. The games she writes are filled with transgender themes, but as the author she is downright condescending and insulting to anyone who wants to examine how these themes are dealt with. Do I recommend the game? Yes. Am I a fan? No. Analogue: A Hate Story is one of those terrible literary books you have to read in high school, and you should totally read/play it, but it's still not very good.

In the future, mankind discovers and harnesses the power of dark matter.  As they explore and colonize the galaxy, they come to realize that they are alone after a couple of centuries of failed communication attempts.  Then out of the blue, they are aggressively attacked by an alien race known as the Constituents of Nothing.  Since this alien race uses dark matter technology as well, mankind's weapons were useless against them.  That is until humans discovered anti-dark matter particles.  This blue-energy is humankind's last hope against this alien threat.
There are thirty-six story missions that span across nine planets.  Well, technically eight since Pluto isn't considered a planet anymore.  In fact, the Steam achievement for completing all of the Pluto missions is "Not a planet."  The story missions can be played solo or with up to four players locally.  Having people to play with is highly recommend since the missions get really tough towards the end.  Some of the missions will have an AI unit assist you, but most of them don't.  Most of the time you'll be protecting AI ships instead of working with them.
If you're not escorting or defending an ally's ship, chances are you're defending a generator or two instead.  The generators are crucial for converting scrap metal into usable resources.  The scrap metal can be used to upgrade various attributes of the four different ship classes.  I went with the balanced class ship, The Euphrates.  There is also the Rio speed class ship, the Volga assault class, and the Potomac support class. Most ships have a limited number of missiles and turrets, but some ships have mines and the ability to heal allies.
In total, there are nine upgradeable ship options.  Each additional upgrade costs more scrap than the previous tier.  You can upgrade the number of turrets, missiles, and increase other attributes including armor, top speed, maneuverability, acceleration, firing speed, and bullet power.  The upgrades help, but fighting the medium and heavy class enemy ships goes a lot smoother when you have a partner fighting alongside of you.
The controls are pretty straightforward and the PC version of the game supports keyboard and gamepads.  I used my Xbox 360 controller and it worked flawlessly.  The left analog stick moves the ship while the right analog stick fires the bullets in the direction its pointing.  Deploying turrets or mines is done by pressing the Y button and firing a missile is accomplished by using the B button.
Graphically SCHAR: Blue Shield Alliance is pretty basic.  The space ships all appear to be flat and the bullets, bombs, and missiles are all pretty simple with minimal special effects.  The characters in the game are cartoon like and the space atmosphere is pretty simplistic.

The audio is pretty barebones as well.  There is no voice acting, but the sound effects are passable. The dialogue can be a little colorful with a character  threatening to kick my *ss twice if I failed in protecting them.  The soundtrack is decent and available for purchase for $0.99 on Steam if you got the game by itself.  Alternatively, the soundtrack edition of the game sells for $5.99.
While SCHAR: Blue Shield Alliance is rough around the edges, there is some fun to be had in this title.  Especially if you have people to play with.  Xbox 360 owners may want to consider picking this title up for $0.99 while the Xbox Arcade is still around.  For Steam users, I recommend picking this game up if you see it on sale.

DoD:S is a plenty fun game, and has no major flaws. It's a lot slower-moving and less forgiving than a lot of modern FPS games, and it handles recoil pretty heavily - you can't W+M1 and expect to do well. You have to think about what you're doing and be pretty cautious. The community is kind of small, but weirdly they're the nicest, most courteous playerbase of any online game I've ever played. I feel like this is because most of them are mild-mannered suburban dads who like history. It also feels like most of them are pretty good, like they've been playing since the game came out.
Overall, it's a fun game, and while there's nothing really wrong with it, there's nothing especially great about it either - you probably won't hate the experience, but there's not much to keep you coming back either. Still, you probably won't regret picking it up, even if you just get it so you can use the textures and files for Garry's Mod. Pick it up while it's on sale.

If your game is constantly crashing due to a driver issue then it's most likely due to you having Nvidia Shadowplay turned on, simply switch it off and the game will play as one would expect.

Compared with other FPSes:
-Without server-side mods (like Gun Game), this game is always multiplayer and team-based.  Teamwork is key to success, but you don't have to be highly organized to succeed.
-Map design is highly detailed, with plenty of places to hide or take cover (very important in this game, but not required for everyone's play style).
-This game is class-based, and players who focus on their role will succeed the most.
-Aggressive, but not careless, offense usually wins.  Be where the enemy doesn't expect you to be.
-You have to hold down the recoil manually, and the recoil is more than in the average game, but varies greatly from one weapon to another.
-Weapons are most accurate when you stand still.  Weapon recoil is reduced when you crouch, and reduced further if you lie down ("go prone").  So there is a strong tactical element: You cannot effectively shoot your opponent and be a moving target at the same time, and there is some (small) advantage to waiting for an opponent to come to you instead of the other way around (but excessive camping ensures failure, so the game is still balanced).
There are still plenty of DOD:S players.  I'm pretty sure I have played this game more than any other.  I could never get into any of the CS games because CS is not clear about how recoil affects accuracy, whereas this game is very clear about it: The camera follows the recoil.

Robocraft is not as good as it was before the loot boxes, but it is still fun and worth giving a try.


Robocraft is a game that has its major flaw definitively displayed to the player the first time they log in each day (loot boxes) and the game has undeniably lost a large amount of the charm that made it what it was back in the good old days, when it was one of my favourites.
When the tech tree still existed and healers were worshipped, as well as the fastest to level up.
When there were pilot seats and megabot vs standard when there were heavy blocks and helium.
When blocks had tiers and electroplates were worth using, when radars still existed as a non-super item (really what the hell, nobody ever used the radar and the FJ went and made it a module and decreased its usefulness).
Nowdays, healers don't do jack, death isn't permanant and even in the modes were it is, self-healing is a thing, oh and did I mention loot box progression? It's incredibly frustrating to see this happen to a game I used to love so much, it's just not the same.
Having said all that, Robocraft is still moving forward in other areas (not that it redeems what they've done).
We now have sprinter legs, propellors, graphics changes, paints, an array of new weapons, whacky thruster-enabled wings, they reintroduced mega blocks, now light blocks and swapped the never used radar for a more expensive and more useless radar.
Recently they also added a community robot sharing store, as fun as it is to see people purchase what you made, I despise the store, as well as that friggin bodybuilder update. Now 80% of the game is just waiting on parts, once upon a time you actually had to build your robot and if you won, it was because you were the better shooter and builder. You got an immense feeling satisfaction whenever one of your original designs outperformed the opponents. Now it's just... the building aspect can be completely avoided
So after all that you're probably wondering, "why the hell is this guy recommending this game?"
My answer to that is: even with all the bad, and even though it's not as good as it was, it's still a fun, albeit grindy, game.

This mod is pretty good for what it is. I'm hearing some complaints about the price, voice acting, and unpolished nature of the mod. I know these people behind the mod, from
, and the reason for some of this is that this mod wasn't created in a studio, unlike Portal 2! I think the price tag of $5/$7 is reasonable considering my previous point about Portal 2, which is $20 as of this review's post date. These people were probably creating this mod in their very own homes with their own limited resources. They don't have access to established professional writers and voice actors! This mod is based on enthusiast-level experience with Hammer. They are most likely not trained by Valve employees. I'm actually shocked it looks, sounds, and plays as good as it does. It's not an easy task! I bet most if not all of the developers of this mod were doing this in their recreational time and have jobs unrelated to the game industry.
I know Mevious, Lpfreaky90, BenVlodgi, Motanum, and Miss Stabby (there are more developers but I don't know them very well). Mevious is known for outstanding Workshop items for Portal 2, "Portal Pro" mod, and "Rexaura"mod. Lpfreaky90 is an excellent Hammer user (she has some maps on the Portal 2 workshop) and is creating her own mod for Portal 2 called Portal Stories. BenVlodgi is creating Portal 2 Back-Stock and is responsible for BEEMOD of Portal 2. Motanum is the guy that started Aperture Tag with an early alpha map on the Portal 2 workshop called "A La Tag" which I remember playing as early as 2011. I had no idea that alpha map series would turn into Aperture Tag. This was a good collaboration.
The musical themes are awesome. They have a strange ambience resembling the game this was inspired from (Tag: The Power of Paint). Some of the custom themed rooms are pretty cool looking while still staying within the artificiality of Aperture Science. The tests did require some thought. I was afraid that the tests would be not very puzzling because no portal gun. I've played some really crappy Portal 2 workshop items that use a "hacked" portal gun (from BEEMOD) that behaves very similarly to the paint gun of this mod and they all suffer from being too generic and do the same thing. The tests in Aperture Tag are very inventive.
4 minor problems I came across:
1. This game seems to "clash" with my Portal 2 test chambers. My subscriptions from Portal 2 don't show but my "blueprints" from the "create chambers" mode of Portal 2 does.
2. The gel launches below the crosshair. I know the gel is affected by gravity but the initial launch position is set below the crosshair. It did interfere sometimes during my playthrough.
3. There is a part where you have 50 seconds to escape death as fast as possible. This part made #2 in my problems list very apparent. I kept dying despite knowing how to escape. The worst part about this is that they included a skip button! Why? Instead of fine-tuning the time-pressure part, they included a way to skip it.
4. I was able to exploit a couple of chambers. Bypassed some logic like jump on a cube, cover it in blue gel, and then jump again to the exit. I don't know if the developers are aware of my workshop map for Portal 2 but my map "Hop" does interesting things with orange gel. Potentially some more skips may exist.
Oh, and there are two possible endings; one good and one bad. I actually got the bad ending first because I solved the last chamber the wrong way. With a little more clever painting, you can find the good ending.
With recent innovations when it comes to video games, this mod can and may be easily updated to fix some of the problems that others and I have experienced so far. Cut the developers some slack! Enjoy it for what it is! If you think you can do better, then you create a mod! What I can conclude is that people like playing the rushed crap that gets released on the Portal 2 workshop claiming it is good (there are gems though but not many) and yet hate on Aperture Tag which has been Greenlit by those same people and had more effort put into it? What a bunch of jerks those people are! I suggest playing the game in commentary mode after you are done because maybe you will get an idea just how hard it is to create a game.

A stunningly beautiful, immersive, and boring spaceship management business simulator.
This is a not space flight simulator like Elite nor is it a starship simulator either.  It is best described a business simulator set in the future and focused primarily on owning, operating and managing spaceships and spaceship related equipment and accessories.
The first thing you will notice when you first start to play EVE is the graphics.  They are awesome and captivated me right off the bat.  The detail to the ships, the huge starbases you encounter, and the beautiful celestial bodies really make it candy for the eyes. Even space itself which is usually depicted as boring and black, is a lovely feast of colorful nebulas and backdrops.  Graphically EVE is what space games should aspire to look like.
As you start to interact and fly around the attention to detail with the immersion is well done.  From the automated computer voices announcing what you are doing like docking or warping, the billboard advertisements, the UI, sound effects, ambient music, and even the player portraits, it all makes it feel like you were transported to a living breathing space opera universe. The player driven events and economy only adds to this experience and makes you feel like a real person in New Eden.
Running a spaceship and spaceship related equipment and accessories business involves needing to get money and fight other ships.  Semi-nonviolent ways of getting ISK (the in-game currency) involves mining, doing missions, transporting, crafting/selling, and surveying relic sites.  When you first start the game they all seem to be rather novel activities which eventually become a bit repetitious.   Thankfully you can switch between them with different ship types and mix things up enough to keep this aspect of the game somewhat engaging.  Keep in the mind though no matter how rich you get or how powerful your ship is, everything seems to drive toward one main goal in EVE: ganking others (or preventing yourself from getting ganked).  There is really no other end-game than this.
If you were hoping for a more exciting combat intensive experience, then this is the weakest part of the game.  EVE online has the prettiest, boring fighting I have ever experienced in an MMO.  You don't fly your ship directly, nor do you really give it much in the way of ship commands.  You are more like the starship owner, who radios to the captain if he should fight or not, and then gives a few him a few basic orders.  You target and tell your ship what to fight, how far it should stay from the target, then tell it to shoot.  That is pretty much it in most battles.  You then sit there and watch the lovely non-engaging fight unfold.
You don’t choose what evasive maneuvers to use or where to aim your guns, you mainly just sit there and hope it goes your way.   It is somewhat like paper/rock/scissors, but with no rock.  Either you are the scissors in fights and win pretty easily, or you are the paper and get splattered.  There is very little in between, and there is very little you can really do in fights if things aren't going your way.  The outcome is usually predetermined based on your ship/equipment and numbers.
EVE online combat is a throwback to an earlier era.  Did you ever play early PC games like the Bard’s Tale or the goldbox Dungeons and Dragons?  Those games had more exciting, engaging and dynamic combat…  There are occasionally some items you activate (kind of like abilities) as part of ship combat but they are few and very situational.  Combat is what really did this game in for me and bored me to death and caused me to stop playing.  PvP is a big part of this game so refer back to my paper/scissors analogy.  Either your ship will be fitted better or you will have the numbers and will usually always win, or the opposite.  If there is any randomness involved it is simply in encountering or surprising someone in the first place.
There are some positives to EVE’s combat style.  It is the only MMO where I can eat with one hand, play with the other, and really be at no disadvantage compared to a player with both hands on the keyboard/mouse.  It is also the reason I started playing EVE in the first place. I had some hand injuries and it is one of the few MMOs where you can play if you are disabled since the whole game is slow paced can be played with one hand very easily.  I subsequently got bored of the game when I healed up and could play more interesting games but if this is a permanent issue for you then EVE online is a good MMO where disabled gamers can play quite well and competitively on par with everyone else.
Summary: If you want a beautiful and immersive spaceship management business simulator then EVE online is the game for you.  If you were hoping for something more akin to an “MMORPG in spaceships” then I do not recommend this game.  The weak and repetitive missions, dull combat, very lopsided fighting, and the lack of any real end-game except to try and gank people makes the game rather unsatisfying and boring..

Admittedly I should have read more carefully before picking up this game. I didn't realize this was a fan created workshop mod when I purchased it, I thought it was something Valve did, or allowed someone else to do.
That said, this is NOT a bad game. A lot of people are angry because of the mod-like feel of the game, and that is (to an extent) understandable, but the developers did a good job in creating something unique with Portal 2. It has it's own, if bit thin, storyline. It has it's own feel with using the gels. Some of the later puzzles can get difficult to wrap your head around (mileage may vary, I found it easier to get used to the portal gun than I did the "paint" gun). There are a lot of puzzles where you have to tinker and think your way through, while others are far more action oriented...
On the flip side, this is still a little buggy. it's a fan mod, and it shows in areas. The physics on the gels in game never felt as solid as that of the portal gun, and it shows even more here when you're firing it off all over the place like an 8-year old with a super-soaker. The voice they got for Nigel is good, but falls flat in many places, lacking that same "feel" as other characters did. Also a few of the action pieces are poorly paced and seem to come from nowhere. One major one I had to retry a few dozen times just to get the timings exactly right. It doesn't have the same organic flow to it as the puzzle portions do.
The music additions to the game are fantastic, easily the best part of this mod. Take from that statement what you may. All in all, it's a good mod, longer than some professional DLCs I've played. I am a bit leery about the idea of monetizing the Steam Workshop, but that ship has set sail. If you think five dollars is too expensive, hold off for a sale or price drop dsome months or years down the line. Otherwise, I'd recommend getting it.

After playing my fair share of Single- and Mutliplayer in
, I unfortunatly can't really recommend it. It's not extremly terrible of course, but the negative points are pretty overwhelming, once they start to actually occure. But here is a typical pros and cons list.
- The fighting system is pretty intuitive and easy to learn, yet hard to master. Zooming around in huge 3D areas and pounding enemies into the ground or mountains is super fun.
- All animations and sounds are as close to the anime as it can get. You get a little reaction shot for super moves, your character shouts it's name, etc.
- There is a universe of possibilities for character customisation. Most likely every costume, attack and super move that ever occured in the manga or anime, and probably more, are in this game. You can unlock those via the story missions or parallel quests.
- Hence, you can level up your character and invest points in stats to form him/her like you wish. You can be a melee powerhouse or a ki-blasting ranged fighter.
- You replay every important fight in the story mode with your custom character, from Raditz to Beerus, the whole Saga is there.
- You can gather the seven Dragon Balls to get Shenron to grant you a wish! Pretty cool!
- The voice acting is just like in the anime!
- The voice acting is just like in the anime!
- The music is repetative and more or less not even existent.
- NPCs never shut up in fights. They repeat the same lines over and over, its extremly annoying. You can mute the voices in the options, sure, but that also mutes fighting grunts which I would like to have.
- The story is nothing super exciting or original. Bad guys try to alter the time lines and destroy the universe or whatever, you're a time cop and have to stop them.
- The hub world was a terrible idea. It's slow and just annoying to get around in.
- Loading times are pretty long, worst is the simple connecting to the server.
- When you fail a story mission, you have to skip through all the cutscences again, instead of just starting over the fight.
- While the fighting is pretty fun, the experience gets pretty much drowned by some super annoying things:
- There are no ingame stats for items or skills what so ever. Wanna know how much damage this skill does in comparision to your other? Have to try it out first.
- The game is entirely based on RNG. You need a certain item or skill from a certain parallel quest? Well, good luck, for it is luck and luck alone that even the requirements are met for the item to drop.
- Most parallel quests are just recycled, you fight the same round up over and over again. Super boring.
- And probably the worst about the whole game:
Until I hit the point in the story mode in which I had to fight the two androids, it was pretty fine. Cell was ok to fight, but 17 and 18 pretty much insta killed me without any chance to react. Fine, I thought, doing more parallel quests, unlocking more stuff and so on, it's fun. But holy cow, the parallel quests get longer and longer, and you have to do like 3-4 of them get a level up and 3 points to increase your stats. (Wow) And it's aaaaalways the same!
This is the kind of game which lures you in with exciting gameplay and hooks you with unlocks and motivation, but the longer you play it, the more you realise it's unfortunatly riddled with flaws and bad design choices which makes the experience annoying and not fun anymore.
Edit: After I managed to unlock the Super Saiyan ability for my female Saiyan, I beat the whole story mode in one sitting around lvl 35. How? Because you can exploit the NPC's easily with an ability called "Vacation Delete." Super Saiyan let's you spam ki-skills with no limit, just draining the bars slowly. This ultimate attack has a big hitbox, does moderate to high damage and stuns the enemy for like 5 seconds. You do it over and over and over, and the enemy has no way to get away until they're knocked down. How did they not change this? I cant believe it's intentional. Completly broken.
Also to mention, if you're a die hard fan of the franchise you will get enjoyment out of this game, for a while at least. It's the holy grail of Dragon Ball fanservice, if you will. And if you like this kind of grind go for it, I guess, but not for the full price, game wise it's definitly not worth that amount.

Qu'est-ce que ce jeu?
Le principe de base de Sang-Froid est assez simple; les deux frères devront protéger leur sœur contre les hordes de monstres que le diable leur envoie la nuit. Pour ce faire, ils devront utiliser l'environnement qui les entoure à leur avantage et préparer de savants pièges et outils qui leur permettront de tenir une nuit de plus. Passons au travers des quelques éléments qui constituent ce magnifique jeu;


Les deux frères / niveaux de difficulté
SangFroid_Feuille-PersonnageEn commençant votre partie, vous aurez le choix de jouer l'un des deux frères (Jacques "Ti-Jack" et Joseph "Ti-Jos" O'Carroll). Les deux frères représentant les deux niveaux de difficulté du jeu; Facile/Difficile. En jouant avec Jacques O'Carroll (le mode difficile), vous serez un chasseur agile et rusé. Vous devrez faire preuve d'ingéniosité à l'aide de vos trappes et de votre fusil de chasse, étant plus faible physiquement que votre autre frère, la ruse sera votre meilleure arme! En jouant avec Joseph O'Carroll (le mode facile), vous serez un fier bûcheron fort et robuste. Vos coups de hache seront forts et puissants, il est également important de remarquer vous aurez beaucoup plus de facilité à résister aux attaques de vos ennemis. Les deux personnages auront accès aux mêmes actions, objets et arbres de compétences. Cependant, les différences se joueront au niveau de la résistance physique, de la force de frappe avec la hache, de la précision aux armes à feu ainsi que l'agilité de chaque personnage. Tandis que l'un sera beaucoup plus résistant, l'autre devra garder ses distances. Et alors que l'un possède une meilleure maîtrise de l'arme à feu, l'autre devra se préférer l'utilisation de sa fidèle hache.

La phase de préparations (le jour)
SangFroid_Jour-MonstresLe jour, c'est votre période de préparation. Vous aurez accès à une carte détaillée de l'environnement dans lequel vous allez combattre. Sur ladite carte régionale, vous aurez la possibilité de voir des cartes de monstre vous permettant de planifier vos défenses grâce aux prédictions de votre petite sœur, Joséphine. Ces cartes vous permettront de connaître chaque type de monstre, l'endroit d'où ceux-ci débuteront leur attaque, leur trajectoire ainsi que leur but final. Une mission se déroule généralement sur deux tours (ou plus), les prévisions de Joséphine vous permettront également de connaître d'avance l'ordre d’apparition des monstres pour chaque tour.
SangFroid_Jour-Trappes
Pour vous défendre contre les monstres, vous aurez la possibilité de placer des pièges de toutes sortes pour vous aider dans votre tâche; appâts pour ralentir certaines créatures, feux-de-joie pour effrayer certaines créatures, murs de feu pour changer la trajectoire de vos ennemis, trappes-à-ours, et plus encore! Chaque monstre possède ses faiblesses, et ce sera votre travail de savoir quels pièges sont les plus appropriés aux situations dans lesquelles vous vous retrouverez. Pour installer un piège ou une installation, vous devriez utiliser vos sous ainsi que vos points d'action. Après un certain point dans le jeu, vous serez dans la mesure d'échanger vos points d'action contre des sous supplémentaires en coupant du bois.
SangFroid_Magasin-GeneralPendant la préparation de vos défenses pour la nuit, vous aurez également la chance de visiter le village de Val-aux-loups afin de faire quelques emplettes aux différents magasins du village. Vous pourrez y acheter armes, balles pour vos armes à feu, objets de guérison, etc. Afin de pouvoir faire vos achats, vous devrez utiliser les sous que vous aurez amassé au courant de vos dernières aventures. (Vous aurez des sous pour chaque monstre que vous aurez tué, pour chaque mission complétée, ou bien en vendant du bois.)
Une fois que vous êtes préparés, il ne vous reste plus qu'à attendre que la nuit se lève.

La phase de combat (la nuit)
SangFroid_NuitEt la nuit, c'est là que l'action commence! Vous aurez un petit laps de temps pour déplacer votre personnage là où vous le souhaitez avant que la première vague d'attaque ne commence. Par la suite, vous devrez vous assurer que chaque créature a bien été tuée pour sauter à l'étape suivante. Pour ce faire, vous pourrez activer certaines trappes manuellement (pièges de roches suspendues, feux-de-joie, etc.) ou bien attaquer les créatures directement à l'aide de votre hache et de votre fusil.
En combat, vous pourrez courir et sauter, faire des roulades pour esquiver les attaques, lancer de puissants cris pour attirer les créatures au loin ou effrayer les créatures tentant de vous attaquer, attaquer vos ennemis à coups de hache, tirer à coups de fusil, utiliser les objets que vous aurez achetés au magasin ou même tomber en rage quelques secondes afin d'asséner des coups encore plus puissants aux monstres qui veulent votre peau. Faites attention à votre barre d'énergie; chaque fois que vous faites une action physique (coup de hache, courir, rouler, etc.), vous utiliserez une certaine quantité d'énergie. Une fois la barre vidée, vous serez exténué, et deviendrez une proie facile. Il est important de prendre de petites pauses lorsqu'il est possible pour éviter que cela n'arrive!
Une fois que vous aurez anéanti toutes les vagues de monstres, vous aurez complété la mission. Vos récompenses en sous vous seront alors distribuées, et vous pourrez attaquer le prochain jour pour de nouveaux défis. Il est important de noter que chaque nuit apporte de nouveaux monstres ou de nouvelles possibilités/mécaniques de jeu qui vous demanderont de pouvoir vous adapter rapidement.

Qualité graphique, artistique et sonore
SangFroid_ChargementCertes, les graphismes du jeu ne sont pas les plus beaux, et ce, même si vos paramètres sont au maximum. Les modèles utilisés pour représenter les personnages et les créatures font un boulot très convenable et du moins, le jeu n'est pas laid. L'ambiance générale et le style artistique de Sang-Froid nous permettent d'oublier très facilement les quelques lacunes côté modélisation, textures et animations.
SangFroid_Discussions
Malgré le style artistique intéressant de Sang-Froid, le jeu possède une grosse lacune côté doublage. Malgré le fait que les voix francophones utilisent un français d'antan (ce qui facilite l'immersion d'ailleurs), nous avons l'impression que les acteurs lisent directement un livre sans regarder l'animation des personnages. Également, il est important de noter qu'il n'y a pas beaucoup de cinématiques dans le jeu, le jeu utilisant plus ou moins le même principe que les jeux de "nouvelles interactives" où l'image des personnages est placée au-dessus d'une boîte de texte. Seule différence est que chaque texte est accompagné d'une voix, et que l'image est remplacée par un modèle 3D quelque peu animé.

Conclusion
Sang-Froid est la preuve que le Québec est capable de grandes choses dans le monde du jeu vidéo. Le petit studio indépendant d'Artifice Studios a su créer un petit bijou que tous les amateurs de jeux de stratégie devraient se procurer. L'univers utilisé pour le jeu est unique et utilise une époque peu exploitée par l'industrie, ce qui lui donne un charme exceptionnel. La qualité graphique du jeu est un peu basse, mais le style artistique de celui-ci nous fait rapidement oublier ces quelques lacunes. Le jeu ne possède pas de modes multijoueurs, mais offre tout de même un excellent facteur plaisir. Nous vous conseillons de vous le procurer dès maintenant!

*Be advised! This review is made with me only played the very first zone/stage of the game*
As a Sonic fans that have no consoles, any Sonic games released on PC is always a nice thing.
I find the control and stage environment is rather confusing at first, but after sometime playing it, the fun feeling started to emerge. Well, there is no tutorial whatsoever, you start a new game, got to see a beautiful cutscene and then straight to first zone without anything telling you what you can do in this game, not even an Omochao tells you what to do in the loading screen. Probably will be told later as I just played the very first zone/stage of the game.
Multilock homing attack is also kind of confusing as I still don't know how to properly multi lock on enemies, sometimes I lock one, sometimes two, sometimes almost every enemies nearby.
I don't know if this a con or a pro, but there is no rank system when finishing a stage, meaning there is no rank E,D,C,B,A, or S after you complete it. The bright side is that with this you can actually enjoy exploring the stage without worrying the time, instead of blasting through the stage and restart on even just one simple mistake like usual Sonic games before this game.
This review is made with me just playing the first zone and repeatedly playing it until I get all 5 red star rings in that stage, and my conclusion is : Sonic Lost World is fun, might not be the best Sonic game ever made, but I find it really fun to play. And FYI, I didn't get bored a single bit even I played the same stage like almost 5 times straight as there are many paths to choose from to finish the stage.
Definitely going to recommend it to someone, even if they are not a big fan of the blue blur.

I'm going to get this out of the way before I continue;
This is NOT as polished as the Portal 2 base game. There are the occasional graphical glitch or problem, and hiccup here or there. Also I have finished the game as of this review, unlike some other reviews which only have 1.5hrs or less.
BUT;
That being said, for $5.00 (as of this review) this is actually nice for the price. You can call it a mod or DLC or whatever you might want, but it's worth it. You can complain about the price all you want, but if you're ready to shell out money for another TF2 hat, a key for CS:GO or something like that, I think you can drop the cash for this.
Game play:
Basic Portal 2 game play, but with a twist. Instead of using the Aperture Science Handheld Portal Device, you're using a device which allows you to shoot the Repulsion and Propulsion gels introduced in the before-mentioned game. It adds a new element to it and switches it up quite a bit in many rooms. Controls are smooth, no real issues there but the physics can cause problems if you're not careful.
Puzzles:
Some of them are recycled from Portal 2 (which, all things considered, some puzzles in Portal 2 were recycled (either in part or in whole) from Portal 1) but others are new and unique. Towards the very end you'll be scratching your head, but some are frustrating and not in a good way, plus I think I beat Chapter 4, Chamber 8 not as intended) You'll have to shoot gel in front of you quite quickly in some puzzles and while it works, you're going to discover quite a bit of trial and error. But like its predecessors just stick with it and you'll get through.
Unfortunately, the hindsight of it all is that on some chambers your best bet is to spray gel everywhere you can because it'll actually help more then hinder. Plus you CAN and WILL knock yourself out of bounds or into a pit with the repulsion gel. Get used to that now and you'll be a happier person.
I did have issues in Chambers 2, 6, 10 and 14 all after you get both gels available, with one of the issues being what I feel is a programming oversight and the other being a crash. Your results may vary however.
Music;
Surprisingly fits with the game nicely, done in part by Harry101UK of "This is Aperture" fame. No complaints at all... except for one and you'll know it when it shows up. "Why is this even IN the music library?"
Voice work;
Here's where it takes a hit in my book. I understand that it's not done by professionals, I respect and admire them for the work they did. But they tried too hard to make another Wheatly and sadly, while your testing associate does have some clever one liners, he's more of background noise then anything else.
Overall:
I'm going to stress this again, like I did in the beginning.
This is fan made. It's not as polished as Portal 2. You'll get some problems here and there, it'll make you frustrated at times and you'll wonder what the hell they were thinking when they came up with some of the puzzles. But as a twist to the Portal mechanics, it's a nice little add-on storyline that's worth the price, on sale or not.

I'd say the game is aimed at the more serious gamers. You train skills over real time in a queue(so you don't have to be logged in to be training) that is time dependant on your character stats.. It's for those that enjoy a higher learning curve, as very little is straight forward and there is so much to learn and pretty expansive. They do ok with getting you started and teaching you how to start making your first money through missions, that themselves mean nothing and you will get repeats. The higher level the difficulty the better the rewards(money, reputation and Loyalty Points) and harder the difficulty. But beyond that a lot is up for you to discover or research. It is a pretty massive ever expanding sandbox universe, with a lot of micro management things you can get into, to keep busy or zone out to straight farming or mission grinding while waiting for skills to complete to unpgrade whatever your into. End game you'll probably want to be aiming for your skills to set you up for a job you like best in the universe. Either being a fighter, farmer(such as miner, salvager or ruin hunter) a commander for an allaince, a builder, an explorer(probing and scanning, finding wormholes, good resource spots and part of the universe, a transporter, a pirate, a bounty hunter (hunting those ganking pirates as you can place bounties on other players that will build and there is also the most wanted in the universe with of course the highest payout). Play how you love to. Build simple planet mining setups to star bases and huge mining colonies or citadel for your allaince and own your part of the galaxy you may have to fight for to defend or go on conquest and take down a nearby enemy corporation/allaince, in day long battles of epic size for fight and control of a zone. Each zone has a security number with how well guards will protect you, higher being the starting areas, lower being end game free for all, but where the most wealth is with the most resources. Also the graphics themselves are pretty beautiful and incredible. Overall I love the game, it's frustrating while learning different things or how to accomplish getting there, but for me as a true gamer, once you hit that point and learned all the little things that you needed to put together and finally get what you want, is the greatest reward.
