Well, first things first.  I'm not a professional reviewer or anything, just another gamer.  I played the original Prototype all the way through, and I thoroughly enjoyed it.  While it started out easy, it got harder and harder the more time I put into it.  By the end of the game the strike teams could harass me repeatedly, and without careful positioning, they could lower my health to dangerous levels or even kill me.  Groups of Hunters were almost as difficult in the end of the game as they were in the beginning.   I particularly enjoyed the story of the first Prototype.  Alex Mercer's character fascinated me from the moment I learned what he truly became after the outbreak at Penn Station.  You're probably wondering why I'm talking about the first game in a review for the second.  It's to provide contrast.
After I finished Prototype, I moved on to Prototype 2, as I had bought them together.  I was mildly irritated by a few of the default controls, like how the toggle Disguise button is now F, which was the stealth consume menu/military disguise power menu, and how the new targeting button was the old power wheel selection.  I was able to remap the keys to be more similar to the older Prototype's controls, which made the game much easier to get used to.  Prototype 2 takes advantage of its open world much more than the original did, with collectibles (black boxes) and little mini-missions (field ops and infection lairs) that reward you for their completion with perks, like making him repel all bullets, take reduced damage, increase the range of his melee attacks, and power up charge attacks for each of his virus powers.  While these are very enjoyable, they lower the overall game difficulty immensely.  The disguise/stealth system has been overhauled, with the suspicion meter actually moving up based on your actions in front of the military.  It's also much easier to evade strike teams; when you break their line of sight, toggling your disguise makes them stop and look for you, instead of pursuing you to the ends of the earth even if they can't see you, like they did in the original Prototype.  The whole game world also looks more vibrant, with some areas actually looking like a city people live in, complete with angry protestors and anti-military and anti-Blacklight posters and graffiti, while other areas look like the devastated hellholes they're supposed to be, crawling with infected mutants and screaming civilians desperately trying to escape the clutches of bloodthrirsty monsters.  While most of the animations are the same as the ones from the first Prototype, they still look smooth and believable, and still make you feel that the main character is superhuman.  I also enjoyed the new Hunt system (viral sonar), which makes finding targets satisfying and interactive.
Now for the things I didn't like.  I absolutely HATED the new main character, James Heller.  The beginning of the game makes you think that he's a family man gone mad with grief and rage after the avoidable deaths of his wife and daughter at the hands of the second outbreak of the Mercer virus, but after the first few minutes, it's incredibly clear that that assumption is false.  He's more like a walking stereotype, the "Angry Black Man" stereotype to be specific.  He's incredibly foul-mouthed, with each few minutes of the game laced with profanity that sounds like it was written by a middle-schooler.  He lacks the amoral qualities of Alex Mercer, even though he's doing the same terrorist-like activities; most of the time he thinks he's doing things to help people, when really he's doing more harm than good.  It's doesn't seem to be intended, as a quirk of his personality, only lazy writing and bad character personality design.  He feels two-dimensional, like a caricature.  His sole motivations throughout the entire game seem to be rage and anger, nothing more.  He's mentioned his family all of 4-5 times during the entire time I've played the game, and seems to care more about killing random people for random things than actually getting revenge for his family's deaths.  I also immensely disliked the changes they made to the throwing and targeting systems.  It's far harder to lock on to specific enemies than it needs to be; they have to be right in front of you to be able to easily lock onto them, and anything else requires careful positioning and small movements to target anything that's farther away.  Linked with that, the hitboxes of rooftops are larger than they appear, which makes it very hard to throw objects from rooftops unless you have a decently upgraded jump, or the target is positioned in such a way that it's easy to lock on to and nothing is in the way.  Also, so far in the game, the only thing I've learned from the story is that Blackwatch is a horrible organization.  That's about it.  There is no more character development for Heller, just him learning about some atrocity that Blackwatch soldiers have comitted.  The final thing I dislike about it is the overall dumbing down of  the combat system in the game.  I know it's getting more and more common for games these days, but it's just pathetic at times.  In the first Prototype, to dodge you had to hold Shift while pressing a movement key, and during the roll you were susceptible to damage and relied on positioning to be able to set up attacks once the roll was complete.  Now, in Prototype 2, all you have to do to dodge is press Space, and you somersault over them and have a clear opening to their undefended backs.  It takes no skill beyond pressing a button at the right time, and it even tells you when you need to press it.  Hunters used to be dangerous, even after you could grapple them, as long as they were in packs, but now they're barely threatening at all, and even the super-soldiers that Blackwatch sends after you are now only a minor annoyance.  They're supposed to have been designed specifically to kill you, yet after a few damage and defense mutations, they can barely scratch you, and can easily be killed, even when they're backed up by helicopters and tanks and other super-soldiers.  Oh, they also radically change Alex Mercer's personality, which was one of the things I disliked most about Prototype 2.  He becomes incredibly hypocritical and an all-around scumbag instead of an amoral self-serving mutant.  He was hard to like in the first game, but at least he was semi-relatable.  Now he's just as two-demensional as Heller, only serving the role of antagonist with a subpar explanation as to why.  There is little to no explanation as to what caused his rapid and extreme personality shift.  I haven't fully completed the game, but looked up the full plot, since his character was bugging me, and I was about 99.9999% sure of what was going to happen in the end less than halfway through the game.
I know I listed more negative things than positive, but I don't really dislike Prototype 2.  It's just that it feels like it was made by a seperate group of people than the first game.  If you're looking for a game similar to the first, I'd recommend trying the inFAMOUS series for the Playstation 3 and 4 before you try Prototype 2.  It's not a bad game, but it's different enough from the first game to make it less fun to play.  It would almost be better to play Prototype 2 only, or at least first, and just watch a recap of the first game's plot in the menu to understand the events in the current game.  It would probably lessen your disappointment.  Overall, I think Prototype 2 puts in some good changes to the series, but at the cost of overall game difficulty, bad plot and characters, and questionable tweaks to the existing game system.  I think, objectively, it deserves a 6.5 at the lowest, and a 7.5 at the highest.  If you enjoyed the first game, you'll probably like Prototype 2, but you'll have to overlook its obvious flaws in order to do so.

I had no idea this game was being made until it was released on Steam and GOG. This game caught me completely by surprise and immediately won me over with its charmingly cute papercraft graphics and intuitive spellcrafting system - especially with the crazy amount of spell combinations you can make!
Some people have drawn parallels to Magicka in terms of complex spellcrafting, but believe me this game is much different.  The spellcrafting is much more relaxed and much more about experimenting with different combos - Plus there's no "invalid" combinations so out of the 40 different materials you can really start making some incredibly crazy spells!
One I've made, which I've called "Me And THIS Army!", summons a magical turret which fires a volley of bullets that split apart - the bullets themselves do no damage, however upon disappearing or hitting a target they spawn a veritable swarm of little minions who will happily swarm any and all enemies on the screen.
If you're still not sure, give the demo a try and get a feel for the spellcrafting mechanics (The demo allows you to use 15 of the 40 materials, and lets you play 3 missions). You won't regret it!

This was the first musou-type game I ever played, so I think that my review is best suited for folks who are also new to the genre. If you’ve already played a lot of these games, you probably know what to expect. This is also aimed at people who really like One Piece...if you're not a One Piece fan, I don't think this game has much to offer you, and you can safely skip it.
For anyone who hasn’t played a musou title, here’s my impression: Pirate Warriors 3 is definitely fun for a short amount of time, but it loses its appeal before too long. It’s great for getting in a few mindless gaming hours, just bashing away at thousands of enemies and running around a map like a chicken with your head cut off, but it’s extremely repetitive. You fight the same minions over and over, and even the bosses aren’t really all that different. Yes, the bosses have all got their unique powers from the anime, but the strategy is almost always the same…rush them with your best attacks until they die. That’s really about it. There’s nothing deep happening here. It’s like you’re taking a bunch of action figures out of your toybox and whacking them against each other. There’s obviously some appeal to that, and like I said, it’s a blast for a little while. It just couldn’t sustain my interest for the long haul.
So, ultimately, Pirate Warriors 3 is fun in the short term but has no legs and isn’t worth sinking a huge amount of time into. I’m still giving it a positive recommendation…but only if you absolutely love One Piece. This game is a massive love letter to the One Piece universe. If you like One Piece, you’ll get a big kick out of this game. The voices, character designs, special powers, bright colors, music, everything about it…it’s all ripped right out of the anime. You can pretty much play as almost every single major character, both heroes and villains, from the entire history of One Piece. If you’re into One Piece, you know that’s an impressive statement: the series has dozens of characters with their own abilities and personalities and iconic designs. You’ve also got a really long story campaign where you play through a sort of greatest hits version of all the big One Piece story arcs. There’s a ton of content, with lots of story stages, a special mode where you can play through a long series of battles with different characters, and plenty of little things to unlock.
Personally, I'm a big One Piece fan, so I enjoyed my time with the game. It didn't set my world on fire and I'll probably never return to it again, but it was fun for a short burst. I feel like that's worth a positive recommendation from me. That being said, the price is WAY too high for what it is. If you love One Piece and you enjoy beat-em-ups, this is worth a play and it deserves to be in your library, but for the current asking price? No way. I got it on sale for about 10 bucks, and that was fair. If you meet all the conditions that I've laid out and you still think that this game is for you, wait for a good sale, and you'll be happy.

The closest 3D Sonic has ever come to being like 2D Sonic (specifically the Genesis/MegaDrive games), and it's GOOOOOOD. Have this game on Wii U - The port is flawless. 1080p, locked 60fps throughout. Supports FXAA through drivers, vsync is forced in-game by default. Supports XInput controllers, including my own Xbox One controller, without any issues whatsoever.
Now, onto the game itself: It's the best 3D Sonic game, quite simply. Only Sonic Generations comes close to being as good as this. Close, but not quite. Unlike Sonic Generations, Sonic Lost World is more controllable. Sonic's movement has pinpoint precision, which means this game is significantly more focused on exploration and precision platforming.
In a nutshell, this is finally Sonic's break into 3D the way it should have been 20 years ago. Sonic Lost World is to 2D Sonic what Super Mario Galaxy and, to a lesser extent, Super Mario 3D World, is to 2D Mario.

This game has an enemy which can easily perma-stunlock you, and doesn't even do any damage, thus forcing you to exit via the pause menu. Furthermore, your spells all feel incredibly weak (and, in fact, are), with the wand being utterly useless. In addition, the spell part of the tutorial doesn't work properly. You're supposed to set a chain of targets on fire, but it won't happen. As a bonus level of suckage, the dialogue assumes your character is male, even though there are female character customization options.
AND, the level generator can leave you unable to finish the objective by placing the things you need to destroy/get/open/kill out of your reach, clearly under the assumption that the player will be using an artifact or material that allows them to reach higher places, thus not accounting for differing play styles or the like.
So, no, this is NOT a good game.

So, after playing this 7 hours the day it came out and completing it, I can finally write a full review of it.
I have not played the Wii U version, so I can't really say what's missing or changed form the PC version, but it seems like they dropped stuff like the Miiverse stuff, but also the 2 player mode, which is odd.
Also a summary at the bottom if you're interested in that instead.
The game is very different from other Sonic games or just platforming games in general, since you are mostly aren't going on a flat surface. I personally, kinda like this.
There's also a lot more precise platforming than other Sonic games, requiring you to slow down. That's mostly why there's a run button now I guess. The whole thnig with Sonic is going fast, I know, but I personally didn't mind this at all. It still has sections where you go fast and stuff, so if something, it just mixes stuff up.
One thing I really feel is missing is some sort of thing where it would tell you what to do. On some of the bosses I had no idea what I should be doing and died many times over, having to me look up what I actually needed to do.
There's also 2 different types of homing attacks, kicking and the normal homing attack. Then again, some enemies and some bosses require you to do either of them, where doing the wrong one will hurt or kill you and the game never tells you what you should be doing. Just a different icon on the homing attack icon would be enough.
I've only played this with controller. I don't even want to try it with keyboard. I know how bad Generations was with keyboard, so I'm going to guess the same for this. So if you don't have a controller, you might want to get one. If you like these kind of games, you should anyway.
If you have a controller, the controls are great. I feel like I full control over Sonic and that he does what I tell him to. Sometimes, the homing attack can target weird stuff or not at all, but not a big issue.
The only thing I really have to complain about here, since you don't have a whole gamepad, like the Wii U one, to play with, some of the buttons are weird. I kept pressing LS by mistake a lot to open the missions menu, but just smaller things really
Not much to say here, it's Sonic, to what to expect.
The music is really awesome. Maybe not as good as in Generations, but those were just remixes. As far as I can tell here, all tracks are new and no remixes this time.
I also just had to extract the music files from the game itself to load up in a playlist to listen to outside of the game, since I couldn't find anywhere to buy the actual soundtrack.
So, alright, the port. In short, it's just ok. In many way it's worse than the Generations port.
The port still has a Wii U feel to it, there are buttons on screen which is meant to be pressed with the Wii U gamepad etc. and as usual with the Hedgehog engine, the game is capped at 60 fps. This is not a huge issue, but it's a thing.
It also feels like the game is made for Wii U and not for the PC, for example, there are plenty of popping issues, just moving forwards and backwards. It's very noticeable.
All cutscenes are in 720p, they don't look very good, but not a huge deal either really. Keeps the game smaller I guess.
Pretty much all 2D sprites and menus feel really low res. I can only guess this is because the Wii U version ran at 720p and they didn't bother to fix them for the PC port.
The performance overall is fine, I only had 2 small frame drops, but it was up to 60 fps again in less than a second.
One huge issue is the graphics options. They are terrible and very limited. You can turn on and off some thing and the resolution switch is there, finally in the game itself rather than from the launcher, but a lot of options are missing. The thing I was missing the most is AA.
So, overall, the game itself is awesome. It's different than other Sonic games, but I don't mind it too much. There isn't as much of just going fast, but more parts where you have to take your time and sometimes even solve small puzzles.
As usual with Sonic games, the soundtrack is really awesome. For me, this is a huge deal. If a game has bad soundtrack, I can just feel like not playing it.
The port is probably the biggest downside. It's just ok. It has the same issues as Generations, 60 fps lock, problems on some computers etc.
The graphics weren't changed much, if at all for the PC port. Some stuff, specially the 2D stuff, look really low resolution.
The game would get 9/10, but I'll give it 8/10 for the bad port.

This is definitely one of the worst definitive editions I've seen to date. It's quite sad that almost nothing was fixed from the original version of Dead Island.
First of all I want to start off this review that I wasn't able to review the first Dead Island, because I finished after this was released. I played this a few days after launch since I pre ordered it and put it aside since recently I sat down and played through the entire game co op with a friend.
The story of Dead Island is a very cliche tale for a zombie game/movie. You pick from 4 survivors Sam B, Purna, Logan or Xian Mei. They're all stuck on an island of Banoi and after a heavy night of partying they wake up to find the island overrun with the undead and they try to fight their way to safety.
The story itself is abysmal. Most of the story plot points don't make any sense and most of the choices made by the main characters and other survivors are questionable as they put everyone around them in immense danger. The game also really tries hard to make you attached to characters but this doesn't work because of the abysmal voice acting.
Gameplay wise is where Dead Island sort of stands out from other games in the genre. The gameplay mostly consists of melee combat and this is where you learn to fight using everything you find on the ground, like bats, crowbars and planks. You also an craft weaponry which has elemental stats which do even more damage.  There's also a stamina bar which depletes on every attack, once the bar is depleted you are then forced into recovering as you are not able to attack, or run away.
The game is a lot like Borderlands, but instead of Shooting you are using melee weaponry. There's also firepower but it's only effective against raiders and not zombies since trying to kill a zombie with a gun is rather useless.
Graphically this game is impressive in some aspects and absolute trash in others. First of all I wanted to say that this Definitive Edition looks almost identical to the original except for a few very minor changes. The environments all look great, but the character models look absolutely horrendous. Almost all of them look like they're burned alive and brought back from the dead.
This Definitive Edition also doesn't fix a lot of the main issues of the original. Most of the bugs come back again and one of the achievements that was bugged isn't even fixed in this version which is absolutely lazy on the developers part.
Audio design is absolutely terrible. The hacking into the zombie flesh and hearing it being chopped off is glorious, but this quickly ruined and made to be annoying by some audio problems like a massive echo which is produced by critical hits and since most of my weapons were all high stats happened all the time.
The game took me 20 hours to finish Every main quest + Side quest + Ryder White DLC, after that there's some replay value since you can go back and replay the game which each of the main characters which all have different abilities, but for me playing this game twice is plenty and I'll probably never go back.
In the end do I recommend this game ? I really think there's better zombie games on the market. Dying Light also made by Techland is 100 times better than this game and a lot more fun too, so I think you should save up your cash and get that since the game is incredibly boring and not fun to play.
Pros:
+ Graphically Impressive (environments only)
+ Fun to hack and slash
Cons:
- Gets tedious incredibly fast
- Story is abysmal
- Definitive Edition of the game doesn't fix bugs from the previous version
Final Rating:
5/10

Sweet merciful heavens is this game weird.  And I love it.  Sang Froid is a strange beast.  I know it won't be for everyone, but for me, it was pure bliss.  The story is actually fairly unique, taking a different spin on the werewolf lore than the usual and throwing in some native american lore for good measure.  While it is a bit campy, it's fun and one of the most Canadian games in existence.  It has great flavor and atmosphere.
But how is the combat?  In a word, clunky.  The game mixes setting traps, some automatic and some you have to trigger, alongside fighting in third person.  The traps are very cool, but the fighting itself is a bit awkward to get around, whether it's swinging your axe or aiming your gun.  However, if you can get past that, it is a ton of fun.  There are some ingenious mechanics, such as having to take into account how your scent is carried on the wind, the long load times of a musket rifle, and how afraid your enemies are of you.  This, combined with setting traps and planning your battles in the day, and actually fighting at night, makes for an addictive experience.
Comes highly recommended.  I played through both campaigns and loved each of them.

Estranged: Act 1 is a free single-player stand-alone mod of Half-Life 2. Since it's Stand-Alone, you are not required to have Half-Life 2, all the resources that this game uses come along.
It's supposed to be the first part of many more acts to come, to my knowledge. It also allows you to start from any of 3 chapters in the game right off the first time you launch game, not exactly logical thing.
In short, you may think that it's a survival horror. Well, wrong! For being a mod of Half-Life 2, it offers experience of same style, a linear shooter, where half of exploration will be spend on fighting and another one will be simple puzzle solving, while uncovering storyline all along. And it would have been excellent package, if only fighting part wasn't so lacking...
Let's see, first, it tries to be survival horror. The health is limited and the so is ammo. Ammo packs and health don't come often, and what is even more interesting, their placement on the level is actually randomized. Nice! The stamina is limited, flashlight battery aren infinitive. And all while you have to fight zombies, the fast kind of them...
Yet you very quickly find out just how pathetic those are! They easily die, they don't do much damage and their melee attack can be easily avoided by just moving away. (Well, at least they can throw items in their way like HL2 zombies... Which rarely happens here). The ammo turns out to be more than enough to headshot every single one of them. When you will get to SMG with 250 ammo around or so, you will realise that Survival Horror aspect just went to hell. And seeing how player is able to have only one weapon, which is usually given for each certain section, the action parts of the mod become just no-brain shooting range!   ...Until you meet non-zombies. Actually difficult, but with one-weapon limit you don't have to use brain there either.
Yet it still leaves us with varied package with puzzle sections and just exploration, so I wouldn't say that the mod is wasted. Hell, there is some new things not from HL2, mostly interactive HTML computer screen and the chair moment was unique.
The adventure isn't too long, something like 1-2 hours, but you get an excellent half-life-style experience in meanwhile.
The music, like HL itself, playes only once during special event, like when you enter completely new area, after which it leaves you alone in silent envirmoment. It doesn't help a lot to atmosphere, I am afraid, and it isn't memoriable either. I don't remember a single track from it.
Achievemnts were pleasent in this one. No silly "kill 1000 zombies with some gun", thankfully. Just something like "Empty out all 5 vending machines in the game". Oh, wait, HL2:E2 style "bring object from beggining to the end"...
Overall, flawer yet solid free experience that wouldn't waste too much of your time.

Borderlands was a good game for its time. It was unique, it introduced great characters, a new genre and a new franchise. But playing it in 2017 definitely shows its flaws.
First negative was FOV. The game is just way too zoomed in and you have a very narrow viewing angle, but this can be very easily fixed with any of the guides on Steam (make sure to do that before playing). The inventory system was absolutely horrendous. Comparing and selling items could have been done so much better. I also did not like the way enemies received damage. For example if I am shooting at somebody in the distance, I would only know that I hit them if their health bar dropped, there was no other visual que to show that I hit them which was frustrating at times. Also the game still to this day has some bugs and glitches.
But overall the game was good introduction to the series. For anyone that played Borderlands 2 first, this game is a nice addition to the story. Or for anyone that is interested in the franchise, it a good place to start.

There's no doubt that Steam has been flooded, for better or worse, by visual novels as of late.
Now, don't get me wrong, Indie titles are great, but amidst the endless stream of "waifu"-bait visual novels (VNs) you'll see here on Steam, I think you'll be hard-pressed to find many decent stories with an intriguing plot that aren't about getting in a girl's pants for an affordable price. That's par for the course when discussing visual novels, but that's also why I tend to trust VNs from well-known studios/devs, because at least you know you'll get plot while playing VNs of acclaim like
, the
Trilogy, or
in exchange for their premium price.
But, let's rewind time back to 2012, when Gangnam Style was top of the charts around the world and every tween and their literature teacher was dying to see
The Hunger Games. In this archaic age of yore, there were, quite frankly, no good visual novels on Steam, save for one: Christine Love's
. Back then, I wasn't sure how much story ten bucks could really buy, but boy I was surprised.
Analogue eschews all the teenage high-school setting jazz you'll see in 99.9% of visual novels out there. Instead, it opts to tell the fate of a ruined colony ship, the Mugunghwa, in a decidedly sci-fi setting. It does this with considerable polish.
Analogue's presentation is simple, nothing more and nothing less required to tell its story, letting you explore the lore of the ship's mysterious downfall at your own pace as you literally read through logs like the investigator you are supposed to be. At the very least its more interactive than half the VNs on the market, with a very entertaining minigame thrown in halfway through the story.
Now then, you can hold off on impulsively buying those tempting 11 Anniversary Lootboxes in Overwatch since for those same ten bucks, you get a substantial story and can brag to your friends all about the "Joseon" Era of Korean history.
And at the end of the day, what's more important? Getting yet ANOTHER Tracer legendary skin or knowing what "Joseon" means? You be the judge of that question.
Just uh...don't blame me
.
No but seriously. Play Analogue.

Mislead by the screenshots into thinking that this would be a competent strategy game with an artistic flair; couldn't have been more wrong.  Gameplay is, at best, banal and repetitive.  Despite the appearance of strategy elements, the actual gameplay is primarily action-oriented -- that is once you can get past the tedious hand-holding tutorials.  What really drives it into the trash heap is the writing, cutscenes and VA.
Combat is primarily action-based, with a thin veneer of tactics on the surface.  Once you actually have some contol of the tactical aspect, you quickly realize how effectively limited your options are.  Most traps are ineffective and you end up using the same basic traps ad nauseam, in typically the same places every day.  The buildings that you are required to defend are apparently made out of rice paper, because a single wolf can destroy any structure located on the opposite side of the map in a matter of seconds, causing you to fail the night.
I understand the gun mechanic is intended to supplement combat, but it's not enough to save you from the tedium of constantly running around and wildly swinning an axe.  The timing of events in combat is imprecise and slightly unresponsive.  The game is touted as being a variation on Tower Defense, but let's be clear:  Get used to swinging an axe, it's 80% of what you do.
The writing is unbelievably bad.  It seems to be composed of lifeless tropes, clichés and hamfisted exposition.  The idioms are inappropriate and inconsistent with the setting, the characters are dimensionless, idiotic puppets playing out a callow farce.  Even the poor spelling, punctuation and  grammar exposes the lack of education and sloppy QC of the people involved.
You're expected(?) to endure panel cutscenes at the beginning of each 'day' that foreshadow the subsequent combat scenario.  I cannot adequately describe how crass and farcical these scenes actually are, but subjectively speaking, they're awful.  Beyond the terrible writing, you have to listen to even-more-terrible voice acting.  The 'actors' mispronounce words everywhere (to almost comic effect), even inconsistently mispronouncing each other's names.  The characters are native to the story's setting, which is in northern [read: French] Canada, yet they manage still to mispronounce the names of Canadian cities.
Again, the 'actors' cannot even remotely keep their accents and idioms on target -- instead they meander all over the place, ranging from faux-British, to faux-Canadian, to Texan, to Mexican.  The female character central to the story is French-Canadian, pale skin, long red hair and -- get this -- voiced by a borderline-illiterate Hispanic woman.  The two protagonist brothers aren't voiced much better, either.  It's painful to listen to.

You should really play this game.
It was one of those things that just stays with you, and you keep thinking about it the rest of the day after you’ve played it. It’s also not that long– I got 98% completion in, according to Steam, 2.8 hours. So it’s more than worth the investment.
There are two stories here. The frame story is that you are sent as part of your job to go through the records of a recently rediscovered lost ship/space colony that has been gone for hundreds of years. You head over and start sifting through the log files with the help of the ship’s AI. The second story is what actually happened on the ship. The setting is simultaneously a future dystopia and a past dystopia– the frame story takes place more than a thousand years in the future, while the secondary plot takes place six hundred years before that.
It’s hard to describe the game without getting into spoiler territory, but I’ll do my best: the gist of the secondary plot is that on this space colony, some unspecified disaster caused major social and educational regression and an extreme population reduction that ultimately resulted in the establishment of an extremely oppressive patriarchal society in which women rarely are allowed to leave the home and are often married off as young as 12 or 13. A young girl put in stasis before the disaster due to an illness wakes up hoping that a cure has been developed, only to find the world has gone to hell.
The game is simultaneously a reflection on the horrors of the past– a particularly disturbing post-game author’s note lets you know the circumstances are based very heavily on actual customs of Feudal Korea– as well as a warning about where we could head in the future. The girl wakes up and tries to tell her new “family” about her illness by emphasizing how thin and pale she is, but all the men hear is a woman’s whine and all the women hear is bragging about good looks, which would sound extreme if the exact same thing hadn’t happened to me in the past. It’s an examination of the ways women survive in such an oppressive society, and what happens to those who don’t fit the mold.
The final reveal of the girl’s storyline was something I saw coming by the time I got there but was hoping wouldn’t happen all the same.
The gameplay itself was clever, if simple. The navigation was freer than you usually get in a VN, as the interface is of a computer system you can explore more or less however you see fit– as the AI offers commentary– though the AI will dole out information based on how you interact with them so the story itself it ultimately nonlinear. In addition to reading snippets of the ship’s logs and chatting with the AI, there’s also a command input console where you can type in whatever you please to the ship’s computer. I thought the puzzles involving the commands were interesting enough to require some good thought while also logical enough to be solvable on your own.
The weakest part of the game to me was the ending of the frame story. The story itself is somber, serious, and tragic, but the AIs end up flighty, silly, and almost like caricatures. Like, after everything that’s gone on, Hyun-ae suddenly turns into terrible tsundere and decides she’s in love with you and wants to get married? What? The LAST thing she should be interested in after what she’s seen is some kind of weird relationship with a stranger. The tone shifts from torture and oppression to some kind of parody with no warning whatsoever, and it’s like she just forgets what you were looking at. It’s jarring, but also comes off as though the game doesn’t take its very, very serious subject matter seriously at all. “Oprression and mutilation destroy lives. CAN I BE UR WAIFU????” Just wat.
In the same vein, I thought calling the “best” ending a “harem” ending was ridiculously tacky. In a story where women are literally being forced into harems, just what the hell. Is it supposed to be a joke? Why is that something to joke about? Is it some weird attempt at meta-commentary on VNs? Wrong place, wrong time.
So yeah, the last five minutes or so of the game are… bad. They’re just bad, there’s no way around it. But overall? This is an engaging, emotional, tragic story with a message that hits close to home, and I really recommend it.

Analogue: A Hate Story is probably the most hard-hitting visual novel I've ever played, which is saying a lot; I've been a VN fan for almost ten years now. It's short - I completed it 100% in less than 4 hours - but I made a couple save-related errors so I can't claim the game to be even 3 hours of content. But it really doesn't matter, because what the game does with its short story is so impactful that I can't see it being pulled off in any other way.
The soundtrack is good but, as with all visual novels, it can get a little repetitive after a while. There are 5 endings to reach, and while I have my preferences, they're all very serviceable and satisfying conclusions. But the meat of Analogue: A Hate Story is slowly cooperating with an unreliable narrator to unravel what happened on a spaceship that's been abandoned for over 600 years.
Analogue: A Hate Story will have you learning everything about people you will never meet, reading about relationships and conflicts that you can never personally witness, and slowly experience your heart being crushed by one of the most sympathetic AI characters ever written. You will find yourself questioning your own morals, and who knows? You may even end up embracing hate with open arms.

As a Hatred fan (obviously) I was very excited for IS Defense. Now this isnt going to be a bashing review. Im going to give both positives and negatives.
THE GOOD:

-Simplicity, Its a simple game with a simple goal, kill everything that hates democracy.
-The guns and explosions- The gunplay is fun, its a stationary shooter where you get to mow down durkas with a big machine gun and a rocket launcher, the explosions are beautiful and very well animated.
-Repetitive, but a fun kind of repetitive.The goal is the same on every map, kill durkas. Each map has a level of difficulty and  I find myself dying after a short while but that doesnt stop me from trying again because its too damn fun.
-The skill tree has very nice skills that will really help you out in the long run.
-The help you get to call in ( Soldiers, air strikes, Helicopters) gives the game more life, its not just you versus the Isis horde, you get to call in soldiers to help fight and get to call in air strikes to annihilate everything around you (Your soldiers included so be careful).
THE BAD:  theres gonna be a bit of stuff here so bare with me
- The graphics look great but makes my coputer run a little hotter than I like.
-The Soldiers skins arent so beautiful, youll notice that looking at your troops closely show that they look very bland and the skin quality is very low.
-AI can sometimes be very dumb, Ill have friendly troops all the way across the map shooting at durkas from a distance, Enemy cars tend to crash into other burnt cars or just plain crash into your MG nest.
-The animations are a little wonky for enemies and friendlies alike, it seems as if they took the animation from the soldiers in hatred and just pasted it in there and said "Good enough".
-Sounds are great but also have sound clips from the game hatred as well, in my opinion thats kind of lazy.
- The progression system is too fast for my taste. I get too many skillpoints too fast, kinda makes me feel less accomplished if I can 8 skill points in one game.
-Overall the game just seems rushed an unpolished, it looks like it needs some work.
Thats my review, this is still a great game for the price tag and I deffinately recommend you give this game a try.

In Prototype 2 you play Angry Black Man. You can tell this because his name is Heller. He's a part of the military, he has a wife and daughter he loves, and he generally treats everybody like crap.
This is all you ever you will ever know about him.
He get's about 1.5 seconds of character development  during the game that almost made him somewhat human (A later scene with Dana asking her to do something for him, and when he decides not to flat out murder somebody like he normally does).
Mercer is even worse. Since the last game he's done badguy. Why? Uh... don't know?
Since in the last game he's a good guy who's trying to stop the spread of the virus the sudden swithc to deciding that it needs to take over the world is jarring. And they never explain it.
The side missions can be fun, but they're all "find this guy and eat him", "kill these monsters", "sneak into this base and eat him", "drive a tank/helicopter", or the worst of the lot "Run and collect things that fell out of a helicopter".
Sounds like an okay mix, but they get old real quick.
The main story can be completed in one sitting if you just rush through it, and since the story is bizzaro and almost non-existant it's not really worth the effort.
And the ending is really a face palm moment.
**SPOILERS!!!!***
You become some kind of virus god capable of eating all the infected stuff in the entire city.
Because we needed a quick easy way of cleaning up the mess that was New York to make it seem like a real ending.
Like I said, the gameplay is a lot of fun, but personally I'd suggest playing the original.

As someone who has played the game for the first time in 2016, I'd like to write an objective and detailed review that somewhat disregards nostalgia.
Can't say I'm a big fan of RTS games, but this one is really something. The only RTS I remember enjoying this much was Red Alert 2. Developed by the same guys that brought you Age of Empires, this game is going to be a blast to Star Wars fans who played AoE titles before. Because at the very core this is Age of Empires II in the Star Wars universe.
If you're unfamiliar with the RTS genre, don't worry, the game provides a great tutorial on how to do everything you need to know. If you're a hardcore RTS player, do keep in mind that this is a slow paced RTS, you won't be able to rush your opponent with beginner units expecting to win. You'll need to advance in technological levels and upgrade your units before you feel like they have that "Oomph".
With total of six (+2) different factions to choose from (Galactic Empire, Rebel Alliance, Wookies, Royal Naboo, Trade Federation and Gungans), it really spices up the variety of the battlefield. Not to mention that at every upgrade your units receive (0 - 3 upgrades depending on the unit), they gain a different visual appearance.
While units and structures vary from faction to faction, at the basic level, they're more or less the same "type" in a different shell, with some exceptions of course. Yes it can be viewed as a negative aspect but it does give you a sense of balance, so you don't feel like the other faction has the upper hand.
Before jumping to a skirmish battle, take the time to play the campaign missions. Not only they are well made and enjoyable, they also put you in different situations where you learn to play the game better.
Overall, do I recommend this? Wholeheartedly. Is this a breathtaking masterpiece? Of course not, but it's a fun game and that's all that matters.

This. Game. Is. Awesome!
Seriously. There isn't much to the game overall. You are a knight in armor on a horse with a lance, and you basically ride, jump, and joust your way through various levels while avoiding obstacles in your way (or smashing into/through them). There are a lot of game modes including an actual campaign, endless riding, and so on, plenty of upgrades and unlocks, quests, lots of little tweaks and skins, etc...
On the surface, this game seems overly simple, but it is really just pure, simple fun. The physics in the game provide lots of hilarious screenshots, especially the slow motion death scenes, which are abundant and cool looking (both yours and the deaths of your enemies).
This is definitely a game you can play over and over, for brief blasts (30 minutes) or for extended play periods.
This review probably doesn't do justice to how much fun this game really is, but I definitely recommend this one highly. You will appreciate it whimsy and its gameplay.

EVE online.
The first thing you need to do in eve, is make a character, the second one is to pilot a ship. The moment you start flying your ship, or fitting it, or adjusting your ingame char, or,....... You will be drowned in the complexity of the game and its very clunky GUI.
Since its free, I would recommend people to try it, run through the career missions and give it a shot. You will like it or you will not.
Pro's
- It looks good, on a nice pc.
- It gives you a tremendous amount of freedom.
- Space ships, of all sizes, from very small to very big. (with the free account your limited to ships up to cruisers or a special type of battlecruiser (gnosis))
- Free to configure all the ships within the constraints of the ships and your skills.
- Player driven market.
- Just about any ship, fitting, item, rig, drone, ammo, etc, is build by players like you.
- Deep combat mechanics.
- The ship you choose and the setup you choose is the biggest part of what you do and how you do it, be it fighting, mining, hauling, exploring or more.
- Lots of nice and helpfull people in here. (nice community)
- For people who like pvp, willing to invest time and loose ships,.. this is the game for you to try out.
- Skills will train, in real time, even when your away and not online.
Con's
- Graphics are "crap" on a machine without a dedicated graphics card, or when turned up, the game will not run "playable".
- Most of the community is very nice, but this will not stop you from being scammed, tricking, conned out of your money, ships, fittings and more.
- This is a game where its not the question "If" you loose your ship but "When".
- In this game, you are pretty safe"ish" in high security space, but you should never presume you are safe anywhere.
- In low security space, null security space, wormhole space and in high security space in a wardec (only if your in a corp), pvp will come and find you, wether you like it or not. So be prepared or be trembling in a station for the duration of the wardec. (or ofcoarse get blown up a few times xD)
- It takes a lot of patience, planning and some experience, if you want to succesfully pvp in eve on your own.
- Skills will train, in real time, and can take ages to compleet.
Conclusion.
If you like a deep, complex mmorpg, you got a lot of patience and maybe got a friend in allready. Are you both someone who like doing stuff alone and be a team player, willing and able to be part of a team, fleet and/or corp. And can you take a beating in the form of loosing stuff like a ship, fitting or isk. Then I reccommend you trying out this game. You might like it.

Here is my straightforward review of the OSX version:
PROS
+ Being a knight is fun
+ Beheading other knights is really fun
+ Narrowly avoiding death and THEN beheading other knights is an awesome feeling
+ Seriously, this might be one of the best 'experience concepts' ever devised!
CONS
- 15 minutes just to load the game
- The developer has a weird obsession with distortion effects
- My thoughts on what consistute a fatal mistake vastly differ from the game's thoughts
- The game likes to have frame-rate issues when you input commands, which is kind of unforgivable in a game about reaction speed
- Most of the time, the game does not explain what is going on and it's rules seem arbitary at best: for example you can literally explode on the spot if you crash into too much food, and what constitutes too much food is unknown to you.
- Sometimes the enemies 'double up' meaning you get killed by an invulnerable enemy that was INSIDE another enemy you just killed.
- All of the bugs I've experienced have been with all the graphical setting turned down to their absolute lowest. The main problem lies with how the graphics engine runs on OSX and there is no fix for that.
CONCLUSION
This is a brilliant game. Probably. I might never know on my MacBook Pro. Buy it for Windows or make sure your Mac is WAY better than the current system requirements. I enjoy the game, but I have to play it in short bursts for fear of goring my computer with a real lance out of frustration.

So I wanted to play a Warriors game. Couldn’t afford for Berserk, or Samurai, so I found this one on sale. I bought it on a whim, but definitely did not regret it. I haven’t played the past two games of the series, so I can’t make any comparisons. What I can say is that this game was a whole lot of fun and that it earned a spot in my favorites.
One thing that must be known, though. This game follows up on almost all of the One Piece story until now. So if you’re not up to date with the manga or anime, chances are you’ll feel a bit lost. As a matter of fact, Pirate Warriors 3 is pretty much meant to One Piece fans that follow the story close. It is NOT a game you should play if you want to get into the story for the first time. It’s probably its biggest downside, but for people who don’t know One Piece, this game might not be the best choice.
Since I am a One Piece fan, I had a very good time playing through all the story mode. Each  campaign follows one arc of the story, and while it is pretty rushed, they’re all interesting and fun to play through. The battle system, while loyal to the basic Warriors game mechanics, adds a few gimmicks on its own. I personally found the friend/Kizuna system pretty interesting and fun to play around with. Overall, this game made me remember why I used to love One Piece so much.
Pros:
- Very fun and dynamic gameplay. It can easily eat a few hours of your time while fighting your way through the many campaigns available.
- Pretty cool soundtrack.
- Interesting mechanic for skill learning, which awards you for playing and testing different sets of characters.
- All the characters with their unique set of skills, while also being pretty loyal to One Piece. Like Sanji being unable to hit women, people getting depressed from Perona’s moves, or turning to stone by Hancock’s moves… Very cool attention to detail.
- Intense campaigns, with different challenges that can cause different changes. It’s no walk on the park, son.
Cons:
- Not really meant for non One Piece fans.
- All the mechanics and controls took a bit of time to learn, because they just use symbols instead of showing the actual joystick buttons. You might need to take a peek at the controls configurations to check how to do certain things.
- A certain lack of skins. While some characters like Luffy do have different outfits based on different story arcs, others just don’t. I feel there could be a lot more, and not just from DLC.
Overall, this game is pretty great. If you’re a One Piece fan, it’s almost a must buy. If you’re not a fan, but don’t care much for following the story, it’s still a pretty fun game. Well earned thumbs up!

Basically, you have one MMO to play dedicatedly per life. It's too big an investment to play more than one big MMO dedicatedly. If you want a really good one, you can make EVE Online your MMO. Do so if you like serious internet spaceship wars in space, working with other people to have some fun, intensive planning and theorycrafting, an ever changing meta, sandbox gameplay, and large group communication/fleet combat. It's a very, very social experience if you join an Eve corporation, and playing in a corporation is the most interesting way to play the game. If you want quick, fun pick up and play multiplayer stuff like you would get from Overwatch, it's not at all what you'll get from Eve. But amazing stories, great friends, and intense detailed planning and fleet formups are abundant in a well-managed Eve corp.
I played Eve intensively between 2010-2014. I have at least 3000 hours logged, and never used it on steam. If you are going to play it at all, pay for a subscription. It's the only way it'll be worth it.
There's a ridiculous amount of things to do in Eve. The main aspects are exploration, mining, market trading, industry, and the extremely multi-faceted combat that is loadout-based and a sort of single-unit RTS style of gameplay rather than FPS. It's very tactical, and winning needs a ridiculous amount of planning. Additionally, we have four main areas of the galaxy: high sec, low sec, null sec, and wormhole space, that will greatly affect the gameplay you experience.
To put it simply, the main reason to play eve is the PvP combat. PvE is an afterthought, and is more of fuel to drive your PvP experience by giving you more money to buy things for PvP. In this manner, exploration, mining, market trading, and industry are all simply additives to your PvP experience. You have to go into the game knowing this, that it's MEANT for PvP, and you have to WANT to do PvP, for the game to be fun.
The PvE part of the game is grindy, samey, and not all that fun to be honest, it's more interesting to watch youtube and let a ship mine then actually watch the ship mine. Exploration content (hidden sites, scanning down anomalies) is fun initially, but doing it constantly you'll just see the same thing over and over, with occasional new additions to the things you can explore. Of course, you can simply "explore" new areas/systems of the galaxy as well, but unless you do something in these places you won't get anything from it other than some cool stuff to see. Mining is meant to be multitasked, it's not fun at all to do, it's just passive money-making. Market trading can be very fun, if you like playing a stock market-style simulation. Outdo other players and you can make a ton of money, but you have to be very observant. Since the whole game's economy is essentially player-operated, you can easily become a part of it. Industry is pretty fun to, as it drives the economy. But really, the biggest draw of the game is the PvP.
When you fight in a fleet that is well set up, it's one of the coolest multiplayer experiences in gaming. Joining your friends and fighting as a fleet needs intense planning, scouting for targets, and a lot of communication. The entire way of commanding a spaceship fleet has been put together from years and years of player history, it's amazing to see how corporations do it. Setting up your ship in an effective manner is addictive, and theorycrafting what will work well and what won't is the most entertaining part of the game. Then working with your corpmembers to attack another fleet you find is just amazing to experience. It's not easy to set up. Find a good corp, and you're golden. PvP is where it's at, and it really changes based on where of the four areas of the galaxy you live.
High security space is where people are the most safe. Here, the only way you can shoot other players without guaranteed death is by challenging someone to a duel, or declaring war on an entire corporation. Despite guaranteed death upon shooting other players, people sometimes amass ships to destroy expensive vessels in a suicide attack. It's interesting to see these emergent tactics to kill expensive ships. It is pretty easy to avoid suicide bombing though if you know where to go. The combat here can be good, but is usually pretty small scale, and hard to maintain a fleet fight (easy to run away).
Low sec is where I played mostly. In this area of space, there are less restrictions. If you shoot other ships unprovoked, in certain places security guns will fire at you, dealing a relatively heavy amount of dps. In a fleet you can simply tank this DPS, so you are effectively free to attack others. Since it's mostly connected to high security space, it's a good place to find unaware players who don't even know what low security space is. But it's also a great place to have small fleet combat, as it's usually not filled with the giant alliances that fight for power over null sec space. Lemme talk about small fleet combat for a sec. It's the best because each player in the fleet matters a lot more. Flying in a certain direction, keeping warp disruption on an expensive target, running after another ship who tries to escape, it all matters a lot more. You want to matter to your fleet, it's more fun if you can pull crazy moves that help your fleet win a battle. This is why small scale combat is the best.
Null sec is where the giant battes you hear about take place. Giant alliances go at it, warp disruption bubbles are usable, AOE preventing escape of ships, no repercussions for shooting other people without warning, and the ability to OWN star systems in the name of your alliance. It's where you can make a ton of money, and have giant battles. It's dangerous to do small combat though, as you will usually end up with huge backup forces when you attack anyone.
Wormhole space is the craziest, most dangerous part of space. Also probably the most exciting to look for combat in, and the most risky. You don't know where you are in relation to the rest of the galaxy/other wormholes, unless you have communication with big wormhole corporations or those who constantly map out the ever-changing wormhole network. There's no indication of how many users are present in the star system, so you could be attacked by a fleet without knowing anything about it until they are already shooting you. It's an intense place to live, and is probably the most entertaining of them all.
So if you play the game, you need to find a place in space, and a corporation. It's just the way to do it. Looking to play it for 1-player stuff just won't be fun. It's too big a game, and too restricting. If you've got time to invest in this game, you can have an amazing experience. If you don't want to invest hundreds/thousands of hours...i don't recommend playing Eve. It won't be fun.

A must have for any fan of the Budokai/Budokai Tenkaichi Games.
Sagas are abridged, so not recommended as the first introduction to Dragonball.
For fans of the series, there's plenty of nostalgia candy.
Game design choices are hit-and-miss.
Controller Support had no issues (plug-and-play Wired XBox 360 controller)
There's a good selection of playable characters along with different outfits (i.e. Saiyan Saga Vegeta, Goku Ginyu); however, skillsets are locked for the playable characters.
You can use practically every move from the series and some new ones (Yamcha's Saibamen death is even a move); however, some of the best skills require grinding and/or heavy RNG to acquire.
Grind can become an issue for desirable skills, outfits, and Z-Souls. Some items only drop when certain mission objectives are met, and even then they're not guaranteed to drop.
Clothes have stats, which would've been fine if they didn't also have trade offs (+2 to X, -2 to Y).
Really hurts making a perfect look & build combo.
In PvE, Saiyans are by far the superior race to cheese content due to Super Saiyan. During the Super Saiyan state, ki gradually decreases; however Supers and Ultimates consume no ki. Spamming AOE Ultimates remains highly effective throughout the game.
In PvP, it's a bit more diverse, although expect to deal with said Super Saiyan Spammers.
Couple ending notes regarding the Create-A-Character:
You start the game with one character slot, eight in total.
The other character slots are unlocked once you beat the main story.
Your items and skills unlocked are shared across all characters, even if you delete your first character.
The dragonballs can be used to reset your stats or appearance (can't change gender)
Overall, a great game for fans of the series, especially if you ever wanted to put yourself into the world of Dragonball.
In terms of value, wait for a sale. The DLC (specifically Resurrection F) are a nice enhancement for endgame.
Also, some bundles (not the one in the Steam Store) do in fact still have the Pre-Order bonus (Gold/Crystal Battle Armor and Super Saiyan 4 Vegeta)

Telltale's Tales from the Borderlands is a good example of Telltale's ability to tell an in-depth story that is immersive and fun.
Pros
- Very good story.
- Very good audio: Both in music and voice acting.
- This is one of Telltale's longer stories.
- A pleasant mix of Telltale's "action" mechanic and story exploration.
- There is a "comedic" or light hearted side to the game.
- You get to play as two characters.
Cons
- At points this game's "action" feels more like an interactive story as opposed to MW4 or Halo 5 action.
- The story is typical of several Telltale titles in the fact that no matter what choices you choose to make, you reach the exact same ending either way.
- The game's comedy may not be appealing to everyone. It's not bad, but some won't find it nearly as funny as others.
Final Thoughts: While the lack of permanent choices that change the ending can be disappointing, the story is very good. If you're looking for a more interactive story as opposed to an action game, this game is well worth your time.

The music is fantastic and adrenaline charging. Add to that the sound effects and voices of enemy terrorists and you are sure to find this game something you will come back for more and more. The opening movie is laced with video & news shorts from today’s news, and weaves out the projected path of IS threat in the European world. It really makes you think about what is happening around you.
I’ve only had the game a short time, but since many are interested in this game, I wanted to do the review now and lend support to this awesome game. The graphics are great. The premise is simple enough. And, the firepower is great! The card art is something worth collecting as well.
I often say I’m not into fps games, though shooting is something that I can do fairly decently in games. I just normally don’t enjoy heavy combat elements. This one is intense, and you are stationary, making it probably more intensive, as far as fire power goes. You literally mow the waves of incoming enemies down as the suicide bombers attempt to reach you. With the perfect defensive position, your job is to shoot and reload. That’s it. The first level has you on the beach, as waves of pontoon boats are followed by ships with pickups. They all attempt to land a force on the beach and sweep past you. You hear the screams of the terrorists as they wage what they see as a “holy war.” And, you are reminded that war is not always a choice.
The game reminds me of the words of George Orwell, “People sleep peaceably in their beds at night only because rough men stand ready to do violence on their behalf.” If you are like me, you don’t like blaming a group of people nor a religion, nor other non-germane causes for the evil that takes place. But, the IS is not a religion. It is a terrorist group that is as much a problem for the Muslim community as for the rest of the world. If you don’t see the difference between IS and the Islamic faith, then this game may not be for you. Another word of caution; the shooting is intensive. I usually need frequent breaks when playing shooters like this.
I recommend IS Defense for teens and adults interested in current world events and defending their homeland from terrorists.

Borderlands was a good game for its time. It was unique, it introduced great characters, a new genre and a new franchise. But playing it in 2017 definitely shows its flaws.
First negative was FOV. The game is just way too zoomed in and you have a very narrow viewing angle, but this can be very easily fixed with any of the guides on Steam (make sure to do that before playing). The inventory system was absolutely horrendous. Comparing and selling items could have been done so much better. I also did not like the way enemies received damage. For example if I am shooting at somebody in the distance, I would only know that I hit them if their health bar dropped, there was no other visual que to show that I hit them which was frustrating at times. Also the game still to this day has some bugs and glitches.
But overall the game was good introduction to the series. For anyone that played Borderlands 2 first, this game is a nice addition to the story. Or for anyone that is interested in the franchise, it a good place to start.

It was with much trepidation that I decided to feature Destructive Creations second game on Steam IS Defense. My initial fear was that this was just going to be a trash game without  much thought  or effort put into the game. I was expecting a poorly executed political message and one that played on people’s fears and hatred of the Islamic State. I was expecting a game was almost designed to leave a bad taste in the mouths of non-radical Muslims around the world. After all, this is the same indie developer that developed and published Hatred – a game that is banned in Australia and obviously which I cannot purchase from Steam. Hatred has to have been one of the most controversial games released onto Steam in the past couple of years. That they followed with a game where the player’s task is to kill the Islamic State is surely one of the very few ways in which they could have found an even more troubled subject matter.
However, I can say that after playing the game that I believe that my expectations were in fact wrong. IS Defense may in fact prove to be a controversial game and others may find the game to be offensive or in bad taste but I do not believe that this will prove to be overwhelmingly so especially when compared to Hatred. In fact I would go so far as to suggest that I found the game to be a pleasing back to the future type game of some of the games that I have vivid memories of enjoying when I was a youngster. Games such as Operation Wolf, Beach Head, Bad Dog McCree and Dynamite Duke. It is the type of on rails shooter experience that isn’t often made anymore because modern technologies has far surpassed the minimalistic style gameplay available to make games back in those days. In the past the level of controversy featuring such anti-western subject matter (e.g. the United States Vs. Russia, games based on the Vietnam War, etc.) have had some controversy but the majority have been able to ignore it. Therefore I surmise that the controversy here is that the subject matter is so fresh and in our face that some may find it offensive.
Before writing this feature I went so far as to approaching an Islamic friend that I have long had on Steam in regards to his opinion on the game. His opinion is much in the same way as many of the reviews are on the Steam game page. He claims that he is not offended by the material because IS is absolute extremist Islam and does not and will likely never represent true Islam. Therefore he claims that those who claim the game to be “Islamaphobic” are absolutely wrong. However, he does urge that those who consider playing the game to understand the cultural and religious differences between a common non-extremist Islamic person and an extremist. The gulf between the two, he argues, is just as significant as someone claiming to be Christian or Catholic and an Atheist.
I believe that the opening video – which thankfully can be skipped entirely before launching the game – provides a very realistic and somewhat educated viewpoint of the potential IS has over the coming years.  It also does a very good job of setting the game up. Sadly, in my opinion, it is by far the best part of the game. For a full release game that is asking consumers $7.99 per copy you’re getting three maps and some repetitive shooting game play – fire IS troops with your weapon or use a rocket launcher to kill them. It’s very basic but so too were the same type of game decades ago. What is fresh, however, is the nice usage of special effects in the form of explosions and other visuals. The computer AI is hit and miss and not something that I expect will be memorable.  A bit more effort into the development of the game could have turned it into a memorable title but at the end of the day it is the subject matter that is the most memorable aspect of the game.
If you’re looking for a relatively short on rails shooter that deals with potential real world futurism then IS Defense is worth a look in.

As far as gameplay goes it's not a terrible game.
You get to run around feeling like a superpowered god, it's fun running around and doing things, and the missions don't drag on.
The bad news is pretty much everything else. If you've played Prototype then you've already done 90% of what Prototype 2 offers.
Except Prototype 2 has a worse story.
I realize in the first game that Alex Mercer isn't really a dynamic or deep character, but the mystery of the situation and the fact that he generally seemed interested in helping people made him appealing.
In Prototype 2 you play Angry Black Man. You can tell this because his name is Heller. He's a part of the military, he has a wife and daughter he loves, and he generally treats everybody like crap.
This is all you ever you will ever know about him.
He get's about 1.5 seconds of character development  during the game that almost made him somewhat human (A later scene with Dana asking her to do something for him, and when he decides not to flat out murder somebody like he normally does).
Mercer is even worse. Since the last game he's done badguy. Why? Uh... don't know?
Since in the last game he's a good guy who's trying to stop the spread of the virus the sudden swithc to deciding that it needs to take over the world is jarring. And they never explain it.
The side missions can be fun, but they're all "find this guy and eat him", "kill these monsters", "sneak into this base and eat him", "drive a tank/helicopter", or the worst of the lot "Run and collect things that fell out of a helicopter".
Sounds like an okay mix, but they get old real quick.
The main story can be completed in one sitting if you just rush through it, and since the story is bizzaro and almost non-existant it's not really worth the effort.
And the ending is really a face palm moment.
**SPOILERS!!!!***
You become some kind of virus god capable of eating all the infected stuff in the entire city.
Because we needed a quick easy way of cleaning up the mess that was New York to make it seem like a real ending.
Like I said, the gameplay is a lot of fun, but personally I'd suggest playing the original.

As VNs go I feel really conflicted about Analogue. There were a handful of elements I was really impressed by, but ultimately I don't recommend it. It's frustration incarnate; more time invested in it brings the opposite of a sense of reward.
Analogue is a VN showcase of interesting ideas that are never seen through to their full potential. The setting is barebones, any mystery of the events on the lost colony ship doesn't have any real contrast with the experience of the player's blank slate agent; indeed throughout the game I felt the real mystery was finding out what was normality outside of the ship.
Evidently centuries ago there was development of human level AI and the resources to build giant colony ships to a destination so far away it'd be travelling for generations. But the player's character just accepts this as an inconsequential triviality, as though they're walking out to the wilderness to pick up a memory card from a crashed weather balloon a few miles out of town; where the world hasn't changed since the balloon's launch.
VNs without a strong plot or compelling characters reallly don't have much going for them. Analogue doesn't really possess either. Indeed, the bulk of the writing is incomplete logs about a crypt ship. Instead of this being a compelling slowburn of intrigue, many of these logs and letters read like they're all written in one voice, giving little individuality to what's meant to be wildly divergent experiences on the ship.
To make this worse, there's additional UI frustration as actually trying to progress through the VN has no obvious path; it's continually go to a log, then attempt to point it at 1 of the 2 main characters. Here at least there's a sense of individuality and characterisation, but that quickly wilts as there's instead an impression of neither being more than a heavy handed framing device - one is basically parroting a dogma of "Isn't a functional society the most important thing WITHOUT ANY EXCEPTION WHATSOEVER?" and the other displaying both staggeringly unsubtle withholding of information, and a need for continual validation. Both treat any response to any disagreement shockingly poorly, as though that verbal disagreement was the worst thing to ever happen to them.
The bulk of Analogue consists of the following: Trying to find to right log to read, then push at the right character to see if they will either release the next set needed completion or discuss their take on the other character aboard the colony ship, in the correct order. Advancing the storyline in this VN felt like a chore. Instead of a replay bringing revelations and discovering mistakes I'd made in hindsight - different perspectives on the same events for example - it felt I'd covered the meat of the content on the first pass, and later variations were last minute indulgences that never met much scrutiny as to whether they deserved inclusion.
Analogue greatly benefits from Isaac Schankler's music, ranging from mellow slice of life to urgency and impending catastrophy, and I'd say it's the strongest and most memorable part of Analogue. Additionally there was one segment with an element of a looming success / fail state that brought some badly needed focus with clear objectives and a sense of urgency to achievement them to the proceedings.

There are two kinds of gamers in that third group. There are the kids who like all the toony games, like Mario and Skylanders, and there are the CoD kids. They were aiming for the kids who are into the toony games with Sonic Lost World (which, mind you, is the severe minority of the two).
Anyway, enough about marketing. I'mma get more personal.
I liked mario when I was very little and had no game console where I lived. With the market rivalry between Sonic and mario going on when I was younger (around 10 or so), and Sonic being the one I favored while watching those fanimations of the two fighting, I grew to be very biased against mario and more fond of how original and often thrilling Sonic games were. I'm sorry to admit I became a creator of fan characters, but I was in the crowd that liked Sonic's darker, more dramatic plots. I'm not sorry for that. Sonic 06 is honestly one of my favorite Sonic games (but I give it credit that most people refuse to because they don't know microsoft is the troublemaker). The environments were too FF, though, for sure. But aside that game, what Sonic game (just Sonic, not collaborative with other games and characters) wasn't original? Sonic Drift 1 and 2. Anything else?
And the music was always AMAZING. It got better and better and better! Sonic Unleashed is my favorite Sonic game in absolutely every way (other than the night stages, of course, for obvious reasons that need no explaining). The music, the thrills, all of it was just epic.
Sonic Colors was much less thrilling, but still alright. Generations was between the two, but it was fun to see this reference and that detail from way back when.
Sonic Lost World is almost a copy and paste of super mario galaxy. The biggest difference is the pace you can move at. I've actually never played or watched any mario games newer than SM64, so I could be wrong. I honestly don't care. The environments and gameplay had nintendo written all over them, regardless, and being not only biased against nintendo, but favoring the originality and thrills and relative realism in Sonic games' environments and music, I was as disappointed with Lost World as everyone else. Almost offended.
I do still recommend this game, though. Why? It sucks among Sonic games, but I'm also biased with Sonic games being my favorite series. And even though it IS slower and less thrilling than other (fairly) recent Sonic games, it's still faster than anything you're gonna get from boring ol' nintendo. The art sucks, the music sucks, the story is "meh", but I can't say I didn't have a moderate amount of fun playing it.
The thrill and fun of the game, like most Sonic games, is in the long segments where you can dodge this, break that, and keep going without losing much speed (and not in the 2d platforming areas, which was almost the only shortcoming for Sonic Colors). They become more and more rare as the game progressed, and you're usually forced to slow down. No, I'm not one of the people who takes stages slow. I hate standing still, which is another reason I've found to hate nintendo.
The new wisps are garbage. Without playing the game, you forget over a very short period of time that they're even in there. The red "eagle" floats like twice as fast as the green "hover" wisp, but that seriously isn't much. The indigo "asteroid" wisp is a time-consuming gimmick. It does you no favors in the game other than getting you either past a wall or toward a poorly-placed red ring.
Speaking of red rings, Super Sonic is once again achievable by collecting them, and this time, it's even LESS worth it. You're invulnerable, but your top speed is no faster than the spindash. The spindash is simply replaced by boosting, which moves just as quickly and turns just as effectively, but it doesn't require the 60 milliseconds to initiate. And considering how long the transformation sequence takes, you're pretty much losing time doing it.
AS FAR AS THE PORT GOES
There is no instruction manual. You gotta go to your input screen to figure out how to play. That wasn't much of an issue for me.
You might have a hard time believing that the gameplay went to 1080p when you set it that way in the menu, but just get to the gameplay part, okay?
And the cutscenes are compressed this time, sadly.
Further, my IR emitter (that's a device for playing games in 3d, for those who don't know) won't even acknowledge it as a game.
