Analogue is basically a visual novel made out of datalogues.
You are tasked with solving the mystery of what happened on a ancient spaceship, but when you actually get power working things get complicated fast.  You'll spend much of your time sifting through diary entries, trying to search for titles and words that may relate to your pursuit, and trying to juggle the chronological order of events in your head.  Also there are two computer AI's with attitdude that you'll be interacting with throughout.
There are good themes here, the game doesnt feel overly preachy, and there are multiple endings, albeit earning those endings is not very interesting in a game sense.  Not much to say about the music though.
If you enjoy texted based mysteries, and dont mind a very limited visual tableau then you'll probably enjoy Analogue
If gratuitious reading and light game mechanics scare you off, you'll most certainly not like Analogue.

Firstly and most importantly: if you go into this title expecting a "traditional" game, and not a story presented in an unorthodox manner, you are probably not going to enjoy this. Having played two of Christine Love's other titles (Digital: A Love Story, and Don't Take it Personally Babe, it Just Ain't Your Story,) and enjoyed them, I went into this knowing to expect a good story, and one that was quite possibly heart-wrenching.
If you're a reader, or into old feminist works, you will immediately notice the resemblence to The Handmaid's Tale, which is about a society where women are more or less just baby machines, and rather than being based off the Korean Joseon period, it's about a Christian fundamentalist society. I read it as a high schooler, and it was at times one of the most harrowing and eye-opening books I'd read.
Analogue is like that, and it's even more harrowing when you realize it's not far off from what the historical basis was like. It forces you to wonder "why? Why would people even consider doing this?" especially as it grows more and more horrific. You don't know which characters to like or trust, especially as *Hyun-ae and *Mute present very different views of the logs and what happened. Though, keep in mind, *Mute is the product of the Mugunghwa's society, and *Hyun-ae...well, she's arguably a bit more progressive about women, but you'll see the why of it is a bit more complicated. You are forced to question and consider the roles of both AIs and people like them in a society like this, as well as the other women in the logs, and the various men. Nothing can be read in black and white.
You realize that if you grew up in a society like this, what we see as being unacceptable would be what you see as what's right. You may short-circuit a bit, because the actions taken against the society are arguably more or equally wrong.
There are so many elements to this that you note as you play it once, twice, more than that, that it becomes deeper and deeper. The story fleshes out as you hear both AIs' sides of the story.
My only real gripes are these: I wish it was more interactive, and having to go through all the AI commentary on the logs is tedious. At the same time, how sucked into the story I got offset it.
If you're looking for a story that will make you think and even research an old Korean society afterwards, plus cute, messed up girls and a nice pinch of lesbianism, this is your game.

This game could be considered great if we were talking about a single-person developer doing this in their free time.  Why? It is a working multiplayer shooter that heavily relies on usage of superior team tactics to win matches - an organised team with voice chat will outmatch a team of "super skilled pro players" with each player doing his own thing.
That's the good thing.
The bad thing is, that nothing ever happens in term of updates. Every three to six months the developer team wakes up from their beauty sleep, decides what to do for the next hour, puts out massive walls of text praising the amazing new feature (even if it is just a single gun), and then goes back to sleep for the next three months. That would actually be okay if we were talking about a "finished" product, but this isn't a finished product.
The way things stand, I can't see any intention of the developer to ever finish this game and implement any of the features promised originally. If you're okay with that and you want a small-scale, team-based, tactical FPS you can of course still go for it. You can of course have a lot of fun with this game as is. But don't expect the grand plan of the developer to happen within the next ten years...

One Piece is a Musou game ported from PS3 to PC based off the anime. I'm a big fan of Musou, thrown all the way back to my high school days when I poured hours into Dynasty Warriors 1-3 with my friends.
Controls are simple and easy to understand, rich character history, each character is pretty unique with different attacks that you'll love to try out. Every character is unique and fun to try.
Are you a completionist? Then this game will be one hell of a grind. Difficultywise, 100% achievement is easily doable. Does the time justify the hours spent to earn those? You'll definitely feel like you've achieved something, but in my honest opinion, I'd pull my hair out from sheer tediousness.
Pros:
+ Warrior games meets One Piece
+ Follows the story of the anime along the lines, having you to go up from the beginning up to the current ongoing arc. Added bonus of the final level, which is non-canon
+ Great amount of playable characters
+ Long story (20+hours), and even longer if you are a completionist (90 hours in and I'm only 10 characters in on maxed crew level)
+ Simple controls
+ Changed feature from OPPW2 where you can level break and keep progressing your characters
+ Simple leveling system
+ Lots of cutscenes giving you a chance to understand the story even if you haven't read the manga, doesn't quite capture EVERY single detail but does a pretty nice job placing almost everything in
Cons:
- No online co-op,only local co-op available
- Port is based on PS3 version
- As a completionist, I gave up 70 hours in trying to complete the last 3 achievements
- Price
TL;DR:
7/10
Musou game that takes from the anime, simple controls, great variety of enjoyable characters, long game, big improvements from it's predecessor. Lacks online play, is a direct port, a little pricey, and will have to grind hours to 100%.

SWGB is one of those games I keep reinstalling, no matter how much time goes by. It follows the classic format of Age of Empires II with some notable differences - from the cosmetic overhaul to the fact that basic infantry have blasters instead of swords - that make it stand out. These differences allow for a variety of viable strategies, from converting everything your enemy treasures with Jedi/Sith to creating an impregnable fortress and slowly expanding.
The AI is very retro in the sense that it's not metaphorically drooling on the floor. When I set campaign difficulty to hard, I forgot that it would actually pose a challenge and accidentally lost the man I needed to protect. When I set a standard game's difficulty to normal, I forgot that is normal for someone acquainted with the nature of the game and got mauled for being rusty.
There's a campaign for each faction. No, not just a campaign: a
campaign. It can definitely get cheesy, but it's fun nonetheless.
The campaign isn't the main chunk of gameplay, though. It's mostly in the standard mode, which generates a map and offers an array of game modes that can even be played in singleplayer. If this isn't enough and you have a bit of a creative spark, there's an extensive map editor that allows for the placement of every prop, unit, and building in the game. It comes with the tools to make your creation feel less like a handmade map and more like a homemade campaign (such as modifying unit stats, changing possession of buildings, and even setting new win/loss conditions).
So far, all of this has been positive.  It's hard to be unbiased when you grew up on it. However, here's some things I've noticed that were a little offputting:
• The multiplayer matchmaking is long dead.
• Graphics settings are limited, offering low, medium, and high settings and a selection of three 4:3 resolutions. There's no 4K, 2K, or even 1080p support (officially).
• Steam overlay doesn't appear to work.
• Yousa might not be liken hearen da proud talk of da goongan people!
tl;dr
If you haven't played it before and you like classic RTSes and Star Wars, you can't really go wrong with this entry. Just know that this isn't some fancy shmancy HD remaster; it's the same game that came out on November 9th, 2001.

The best Dragon Ball game since Budokai 3. A huge collection of playable characters with their different forms and transformations. An original plot based way in the future of Dragon Ball. Your custom character can be a sayian, namekian, a buuspawn, a frieza-thing, or an earthling. You can also build your character to specialize it, so you could become someone who spams kamehameha, or someone who goes kaioken and beats the crap out of enemies with their bare fists. Or you could just have a balanced build between the two. Of course if you want to play PvP, certain builds won't work as effectively as others. In addition to PvP, there's co-op modes where you take on PvE quests with other people for loot like costume pieces or special attacks.
There's some DLC for the game which adds the GT characters and the new movie characters (golden frieza, blue haired ssj). So to unlock those you'd need the DLC for it. You also can not unlock SSJ4 Vegeta, because that was a preorder bonus exclusive, unfortunately.
The game also has an incredibly good soundtrack, reminiscent of the old Budokai games.
The only disappointing thing about this game for me was the fact that fusions can't be performed in-battle, you just pick the fusion as a character in character select.

Very short, but very entertaining.
It's more of a puzzle game than a stealth/assassination game, and I really think that it does that well.
The controls take a small amount of getting used to, but the pixel graphics ensures you have good precision for your actions.  The music was nice, and there were multiple ways of solving the later missions.  Sadly the earlier missions are rather linear, but they are more of tutorials than anything else.  The game is rather short, but I feel it explores its mechanics well.  It could only really done with one or two extra levels near the end at most: any more and I expect it would have begun getting dry.
There were a number of plot points and things that could have happened differently, and I felt, while playing, that had I have done different things I would have gotten a different ending.  However, unlike most other 'multiple choice' games, at no point did I feel that I should go back to get '100% completion'.  Usually you are choosing between two good – or more frequently, bad – choices.  No one is superior over another, only different.
The replayability of the game is actually a little mixed.  I feel that I would like to replay the story again to see if I could get a different sort of ending, but replaying the levels would be either boring, or an exercise in speedrunning.  These seem at cross purposes.
Overall, it's a great short game, and I think it's well worth your money, even to play through just once.

I wasn't sure what to expect when I bought this game in the hopes of bridging the gap to the release of Mass Effect Andromeda in March 2017. Borderlands was advertised as similarly addictive as the Diablo series, so I thought "Hey, why the hell not?"
Well, it didn't deliver. Really, it didn't. Perhaps I'm playing it wrong (which I'd find surprising since I more or less breezed through it without any trouble worth mentioning), but as far as the single player campaign is concerned, it was a staggering waste of money. To elaborate:
- The "story" - if you even want to call it such - is a paper-thin excuse plot at best, nonexistent at worst.
- The enemy AI is dumb as brick, and since there's no such thing as difficulty adjustments, you can't even do anything about it. Just watch them either stand around in the open waiting to get shot, or charging straight at you waiting to get shot. No challenge here whatsoever.
- The quests are awfully repetitive, all of them: Go there (with "there" being a location you often just came from), kill/fetch some stuff, come back. Rinse and repeat. Sure, most RPGs run on this routine, but they usually have the decency to supplement it with some variety or background. Borderland is not one of them.
- The Fast-Travel System is a bad joke. It doesn't become available until the second act of the "story" and there's most often exactly one access point per dungeon, which means one thing: Backtracking. Lots and lots and lots of incredibly boring backtracking through the entire dungeon. Again and again. Half the game seems to consist of running through empty levels. In the rare cases fast-travelling is a valid option, have fun trying to find the FT spot you need for the location you want to visit; the menu is a catastrophe with less useful information than any tabloid.
- Another insanely repetitive facet: The things your enemies and especially the vending machines have to say. Having to listen to the same half-dozen lines over and over again without a means to skip or silence them had me on the verge of throwing my speakers out the window within the first hour of gameplay. It didn't get better afterwards. At all.
- The bosses. Oh boy, the bosses. Sure, they're big and all (most of them at least), and they're somewhat tougher and deal more damage than the average mook, but that's about it. No special tactics, no special abilities I noticed, no strategies required to beat them. Just keep shooting in their rough direction until either the boss or you bites the dust (usually the boss, since none of them is particularly challenging. Some are even outright jokes).
- Last but not least, if not worst of all: The loot system, considering the 87 bazillion guns available are the game's primary selling point. The randomized loot system isn't much different from Diablo's or similar franchises, granted. Still, it utterly failed to capture me just like the rest of the game. I can't put my finger on exactly why that is the case. Something's just... missing. Don't ask me what, I don't know, but it sucked.
To say at least something positive about Borderlands:
- It has a nice, dark sense of humor.
- The character classes, their abilities and the surprisingly useful NG+ features appear well-made, although not to the point that I feel any urge to continue playing after my first completed run and a brief peek into NG+.
- I heard/read about the DLCs being fairly decent and entertaining, but alas, the base game did far too good a job at♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off for me to give them a try.
I can't say anything about multiplayer since I am and have always been hardcore singleplayer, so go figure.
Bottom line: If you (like me) expect something on the level of DIablo, with guns, IN SPACE!, you're about to be sorely disappointed. Better spend that money elsewhere.

Very well made and well writen, the story is engaging, makes sense and is pretty sad. It doesn't go with the sterotypical cliche of the characters parents being killed when they were young, or that they never had parents. The story is as follows, you're sent on a mission to extract information from a abandoned ship the Mugungwa (I may have misspelled it, it's hard to remember because it's Korean) to see what exactly happened to it. When you reach it you need to access one of the A.I to guide you through the information. You get to choose between two A.Is, *Hyun-ae or *Mute. Both have pretty interesting personalitys and have their moments. Now this is all i'm going to say because I don't want to spoil the entire thing, but I will tell you this. You get to change what outfit *Hyun-ae is wearing, you can choose between things like a scientist, a detective, a maid and other things, it's adorable and I love it. Also one thing to note that it is for adults, a lot of sexual things and violence, however the sexual part can acutally be pretty funny,
If you're looking for an engaging and interesting story, you've come to the right place.
Although i don't quite recommend its sequel, Hate Plus. It's not bad but it has flaws that Analouge didn't have. You play the game in 3 different days to reach earth to do some stuff. Each day you uncover more informations from the Mugungwa's files and uncover more parts of the story. For one once each day is done, you have to wait exactly 12 hours real time to play again, and that's pretty dumb. Also, like Analouge, It has sexual stuff and violence, it even describes lesbian relationship, but that's not really bad, but it did make things pretty awkward. Another thing and *SPOLIERS!!!!!*
At the third day, it's some special occasion and *Hyun-ae will tell you about how much she loves cake before she became an A.I (Yeah, she was a real person and became an A.I... Because plot.) and wants to have a cake, so you and *Hyun-ae decide to bake a cake. However this isn't a virtual cake, she wants you to make an actual real life cake. That's when I stopped playing, I get it that it's adorable and how she's and A.I and you're a person and it's a relationship going on and it gives it more character to make it more engaging, but i really didn't want to put in effort to bake a homemade cake, i'd rather just buy cake mix and do it. And besides, I may be a sad pathetic loser, but i'm not that much of one that I would share a cake with a girl inside a computer.
Case closed, Both games are good, but I prefer the first one over the sequel.

Sang-Froid is an impressively complex RTS, with creative, realistic traps that remain grounded in the setting. Every level requires a careful plan, without a detail of the enemy's plan overlooked. The tension is palpable, as timing is everything: will the wolves finish the bait and move on your house before you've finished killing a werewolf clear on the other side of the map? How long do you have before the bonfire goes out and the pack closes in?
Set in pre-Confederation Canada, the setting feels real and is well-maintained: every weapon, potion, trap and setpiece fits in the world. Even the prices are accurate to the time (eg. A bullet only costs a penny, and to bless them costs ten cents). Budgeting your money becomes another challenge; saving up for a better gun becomes difficult when you still have to worry about affording your silver bullets and spike traps to survive the next night.
As a game, it is quite fun and exciting, but there are some issues with the presentation. The graphics are nothing pretty, but adequate. The music might wear on your nerves, depending on your taste, but like almost everything else, it is accurate to the time. There is one problem that stuck out, and that is the voice acting, which is bad enough that it falls noticably below the standards that every other aspect of the game meets. Despite the obvious setting, the characters do not speak with the proper accent, nor do they acknowledge the severity of the situation in their flat line-reading. My reccomendation would be to turn off the voices, and I'm thankful that the option is provided.
Once the voices had been muted, I had a wonderful time with this game.
After all thesee years, it still rocks, go get it.

I started playing City of Steam: Arkadia mostly due to the fact that it was a Steampunk based MMORPG with the fantasy touch that I enjoy added in. The story at the start was interesting and easy to follow, and it held my interest long enough for me to get to level 20 something as one character - which depending on the MMO you play can range from super easy to down right difficult.
Now, let's get down to the nitty gritty...
/PROS/
* Steampunk, Steampunk everywhere. Glorious top hats, goggles, corsets, and a Steambike!
* The Story - It has a story, I'll give it that, and one that's actually interesting enough to keep me curious about the next chapter.
* Easy-to-get Costume Items - While they do give some perks, via set bonuses or on their own - they are easy to get with daily log on and your 5 free lesser items and your 1 free better item, and if you keep opening those, you eventually can open more boxes to get a chance at the rare set.
* Different Battle Options for Classes. I like this, but at the same time it doesn't really do much when half of your ability to kill things depends on your gear that you're actively using.
* Mercenaries. A good idea, pretty nice at low level.
/CONS/
* Graphics - They're not all that great, but considering it's a Free MMO, there's not too much you can do [aside from maybe polishing it up, I guess?]
* Music/sounds - Music makes a lot of the game for me, and if I have to turn off all sounds just so the game is remotely bareable, then that's a huge issue.
* Auto-Battle - While this could be a good thing, it's not. You can set yourself to AFK level and get through things [if you're high enough of a level and item-set] and never talk to anyone in the game ever. If that's your thing, go ahead.
* The amount of difficulty ramps up /quickly/. I'm all for a hard game, but when you have an auto-battle system in place, you're pretty much saying "Press button to win" and if you're not paying complete attention to how your gear is set up and when you're using potions, you will die pretty fast, even with things being done for you. The dungeons and other areas aren't marked off by level restrictions like most other games, but by item restrictions. If you don't meet them, even by a mere 20 points, you will be killed off.
* Limited Character Customization. This one is self explanitory, but even WoW has more customization in comparison to this game.
* Pay-to-Win - Like I stated about difficulty, it ramps up hard if your gear doesn't meet the requirements. Funny thing - If I remember right, Costumes add to that. You can buy really good costume armor and weapons and just glide your way through a good chunk of the game. This also includes Bike skins, pets that also give you stats, as well as mercenaries that can wreck things.
* Mercenaries - These guys can make or break you too, as /they/ are also figured into your relative ability to kill things fast so you don't die, even as a tank class.
In short - Play at your own risk, this game has more Cons than Pros.

The Hate Series is one of the more popular visual novel series, and for damn good reason.  These games are at once thrilling, soothing, hilarious and heartbreaking.  If you enjoy visual novels, there is absolutely no reason to deny yourself the experience of Analogue and Hate Plus, and I definitely recommend playing both of them in the proper sequential order to get the most out of your experience.
In Analogue: A Hate Story, you take the role of a "space investigator" seeking to unravel the mystery of just what the hell happened aboard the Korean Generation Starship
, which has been floating dead in deep space for several hundred years.  As you read the novel by way of unlocking old data logs, you will be partnered with one of two chirpy AI constructs: either the strong-willed, conservative *Mute, or the adorable and affection-starved *Hyun-ae.  Each AI has a unique perspective on the novel's action, and multiple playthroughs are encouraged to get the whole story from both sides.
Bear in mind: this novel is not for the faint of heart.  There's profanity, sexuality, intrigue, and some incredibly dark undertones regarding the subjugation of women.  Balancing these tropes, however, is a healthy dose of humor and some straight-up, old-fashioned Asian cuteness.
If all this sounds like your idea of a good time, then take the leap.  You won't regret it.

An incredible visual novel that examines what it would be like if society went backwards instead of forwards.
Fully, absolutely recommended.
______________________________________________________________
Told through reading logs and diaries, and interacting with characters guiding you through them, the balance between the plot unraveling as it was designed to and the player leading it in a certain direction is pulled off really well. Discovering what happened on the ship has its fair share of juicy twists and turns. Good♥♥♥♥♥♥👌
The fictional setting draws parallels to ancient Korean culture, in regards to the universe, characters, world view, and other details. (This wasn't localized! It was completely made by someone English. Both the obvious examples and subtle references to Korean dynasties of long ago are super impressive)
Well, technically they are two dimensional, but... you get the point. Don't be fooled by the "A.I." interface. This story is full of people who are undoubtedly human and their development is one of the main highlights of the experience.
The OST is on steam too! The aesthetics aren't just high quality, they also fit really well considering other aspects of the game.
Considering that the game definitely has some emotional impact too. I won't get too into it because of spoilers. There are also 5 different endings. You can save/restore at any point, so as long as you keep a save before any major decisions then 100%'ing is easy peasy. Don't worry, most of the endings don't require much backtracking.
I'm thinking of two of them especially, due to the important plot resolutions that only occur during each individual one.
There is a lot of reading, specifically logs. There isn't as much dialogue as you might expect, although there is certainly enough and it is very effective. Well, that being said... not only the player choice but also the open parts of player exploration are key to the overall experience. It wouldn't work as well if it were a literal novel either. Overall I'm glad the devs chose this format. VN players more fond of bright artsy types with lots of interacting may be a
thrown off though.
Getting one ending doesn't take too long, although it does depend on how fast you read I guess. My reasoning is that between the complex structure, Korean names, and overall captivity the story has, if you leave it for a long while some of the details may be lost when you return. I mean I went to grab lunch and came back fine, but don't get halfway and then forget about it for a month.
I talked about the cultural aspects a lot, because that's what Analogue focuses on. But it could have focused at least a little on the science fiction part of the setting. It takes place on a spaceship! Granted it's a big one designed to send an entire people to start a colony, but this doesn't come up as often as I'd hoped. For the most part you could really completely forget that this isn't actually an ancient society. Aside from an awkward puzzle bit, the game does not explore the futuristic concepts. This also leads to a plot hole regarding AI and humanity, but I got over that pretty quickly.
Now, this one is
but I didn't want to include only one possible negative. That'd be kind of silly. Anyway, I found myself thinking as I played this, "Wow! That's so much different/worse than my own experiences..." While this effect is executed really well, it could have happened on a character vs. character basis a bit more. The cast includes primarily high-society upper class people. The majority in poverty is mentioned, but it isn't explored enough to draw a contrast between the two. Also, aside from one main character (that conflict was handled in an AMAZING way!), society is very similar minded. This is done for a good reason, and the characters are great, varying in personality and niceness and redeemability and all of that stuff, but I ended up hoping for a bit more direct conflict as opposed to the indirect conflicts of people under one worldview.
I'm a bit iffy about the sequel. This one wrapped things up very very nicely, and the different endings left just enough up to interpretation that after it was all over the story had a lasting effect on me. Haven't played the sequel yet though, so don't take my word or anything. Fingers crossed! I can't say much else without spoiling the first one. Sorry.

Hell, if you even want any sort of thrilling gameplay you're in the wrong place (dialogue choices and QTEs for miles, as is Telltale standard).  But if you want a game that takes the good bits of humor from Borderlands (while leaving the drek behind), robot buddies that are actually maddeningly endearing rather than maddeningly annoying, and a story and characters that will keep you hanging off the edge of your seat for both action and dialogue, whether funny or serious, you might be in the right place.
And dear god the title cards for each episode.  I cannot express enough love for how well the title cards are done.  Both the events and music of each title card capture the current mood perfectly.  If they put out a soundtrack that was just those 6 songs (5 title cards + credits music), I would still buy it just for how linked those songs now are in my mind to the events of the game.

I tend to enjoy quirky games, and games that aren't traditional games. This title was a pretty huge disappointment, to the point that I have major doubts about the validity of the positive reviews that pursuaded me to try it.
The game shows a sentence on the screen, and you have as many as three possible responses to it. You click through the decision tree for a bit, then you reach an "ending", and you're dumped back at the start. Then you repeat the sequence, with a change to your last choice to check for an alternate ending, gradually traveling back through the decision tree. There's no indication of any kind of clever surprising game mechanic or paradigm shift, where the game suddenly opens into a bigger, different experience.
It's not funny. The humor is trite: There's a large person next to you on a plane, haha? You go to use the plane bathroom and there's someone in there, haha?
The screen layout is an unnecessary frustration: Reading (and clicking) text is the entirety of the game, but the text is all centered, which makes it feel unnecessarily clunky to read. A screen layout based on left-aligned text would have helped, at least somewhat. Or even better: shrink the sentence and choices to cover the top half the screen, and on the bottom half, show the decision tree you've uncovered so far. That, plus an intelligent warp/skip feature would take away the title's big negative, which is the realization that you're going to spend all your time repeating sequences over and over and over and over to check for alternate endings.
After an entire 4 minutes, it was clear to me that this game is simply not up-to-par for Steam, even at a sale price. I'm requesting a refund -- a first for me.

Star Wars: Galactic Battlegrounds is a real-time strategy game, and was orginaly relased back in 2001.
Almost 15 years have already passed and of course right now game is very dated in every aspect.
It's important to say that developers used upgraded Genie Engine which was designed in order to create first Age of Empires.
After a very short time spent in this game you will realize that it has both - advantages and disadvantages tied to this game engine. Game interface, units upgrades, game balance, units AI, resource managment and even 4-tier tech levels are a clear copy/paste of what we know from Age of Empires 2.
This is just the same game when we speak about it's roots, and the only one diffirence is Star Wars license used during development. Layout has been re-skinned and developers implemented new campaigns inspired of course by Star Wars Universe.
The most important thing you might ask will sounds like: is this game still playable?
The answer is not simple and depends on what you expect. If you loved Age of Empires series and if you're a fan of Star Wars then for sure it will be a very interesting trip.
I still remember how bad this game was when Microsoft relased it. We (RTS fans) had too high hopes and thats why Galactic Batlegrounds was a huge disappointment.
But now? In 2016? It's funny but game became a better experience. Why? Because now you can experience it as a relic from the past, so expectations are lowered to minimum.
One thing for sure - if you still like old RTS games, then definietly you will like Star Wars: Galactic Battlegrounds as well.

Very short, but very entertaining.
It's more of a puzzle game than a stealth/assassination game, and I really think that it does that well.
The controls take a small amount of getting used to, but the pixel graphics ensures you have good precision for your actions.  The music was nice, and there were multiple ways of solving the later missions.  Sadly the earlier missions are rather linear, but they are more of tutorials than anything else.  The game is rather short, but I feel it explores its mechanics well.  It could only really done with one or two extra levels near the end at most: any more and I expect it would have begun getting dry.
There were a number of plot points and things that could have happened differently, and I felt, while playing, that had I have done different things I would have gotten a different ending.  However, unlike most other 'multiple choice' games, at no point did I feel that I should go back to get '100% completion'.  Usually you are choosing between two good – or more frequently, bad – choices.  No one is superior over another, only different.
The replayability of the game is actually a little mixed.  I feel that I would like to replay the story again to see if I could get a different sort of ending, but replaying the levels would be either boring, or an exercise in speedrunning.  These seem at cross purposes.
Overall, it's a great short game, and I think it's well worth your money, even to play through just once.

I'm updating this review so y'all will stop leaving comments asking me to update it. Star Wars Galactic Battlegrounds Saga is now a playable game and I can review it on its own merits. It's Star Wars! It's an RTS that's basically a Age of Empires II mod! It's old as heck so multiplayer needs third-party programs to work, the max resolution is tiny as heck and it's just kinda clunky on modern operating systems. But it's fun, has great story campaigns and the AoEII formula works surprisingly well for a sci fi game such as this.
Anyway the way the game was launched was unacceptable and Disney should be ashamed of themselves. But I got the game for a dollar through Humble Bundle, third party mods got it working within the first week and eventually Disney got it fixed, so that's something. It's no substitute for a version of Galactic Battlegrounds that is in HD, has working multiplayer without needing Gameranger and works on modern systems. That's a fantasy game that will only live in our imaginations, since I can't see Disney wanting to make an HD version. But a girl can dream, right?

This is an amazing game that I have played for a quite a bit with close friends and made friends online from time to time.
The game is probably the most refined open world Space Sim you will ever get in to. The graphics are amazing and always seem to improve. Since i last played there have been amazing improvements just in the opening tutorials alone. The economy is very realistic and you can make good money trading from Low Sec space to High Sec space provided you feel lucky and have the guts to take those risks.
Mining ore is realistic and profitable if you take chances like anything else. Mine is probably one of the more laid back professions you can do where as Military you find your self in combat quite often.This can lead you to a pirate profession should you enjoy the idea of PVP. There are lots of pirate players that make their money off your head.
Treasure Hunters make good money going in to Wormhole, scanning down old ruins and salvaging or hacking instolations to find valuables.
The possibilities are endless.
My thoughts on EVE going Free to Play however is that you will not experience what this game truly has to offer. Coming back I noticed my old accounts with maxed skills have lost their maxed abilities and am subjected to lowering my ship fitting to weaker versions and even using different, or weaker ships unless i pay for a subscription.
You will get very limited enjoyment from the game on a F2P account and will never get to experience some of the more interesting aspects of the game till you pay. You can certainly explore to your hearts content on a free account warping around from star gate to star gate but most likely you will be killed and respawn with a starter ship again. For most, this will become discouraging and they will stop playing almost instantly.
There is the posibilty of purchasing in game a 1 month PLEX to fund your account with out paying real money, how ever the cost on these items have gone way up to the point that you would be grinding for quite some time as a new player before you even see one to play the full version of EVE Online.
I recommend the game to anyone YES, but it’s not good to F2P with the restrictions put in place.

Before taking anything into consideration, one must take into account that there's literally no reason to play this if you can afford to buy Football Manager, as it's better in anything you can think about... except price, of course. This does give Soccer Manager a solid niche as the poor man's football management game, and it does not do bad in that regard.
Now, let's get to the game itself.
Pros:
+ If you ever played FM (Especially up to FM09), you'll be able to navigate quite easily.
+ Extremely lightweight. You could teach Sports Interactive a thing or two in that regard :P
+ Wide league selection. Nothing near FM, of course, but bigger than several not-free football games. *glares at FIFA and PES*
+ The microtransactions are not intrusive at all.
Neutral:
~ I'd take the splash screen out of this version, to be frank. I would simply replace it with some "Login with Facebook" option available in every screen, but not a dedicated screen for it.
~ There is no option to create customized formations, but I can give it a pass. It's not easy (In terms of it being reflected in the engine. If Football Manager can struggle, then why not this?) and... I guess it has to be portable and multiplatform.
~ It's not exactly the most realistic thing in the world. Mostly comparable to FM Mobile. Expect some crazy moves... but it can add in the flavor.
Negative:
- Somehow the game does not look as well at 1366x768 than in 2015. For instance, I have to scroll down in the tactics screen to see the entire pitch.
- There are several interface issues that were not fixed from 2015. Several "intuitive" actions that cannot be done. For instance, you cannot pick players from the squad screen, and you cannot sort players by star rating in the tactics screen. There are others, but I want to keep this short: The number of clicks that are necessary to perform an action should be reduced. And add some kind of indicator for hyperlinks in news posts.
- Some leagues have the wrong format. For instance, Argentina uses 20 teams and no average point system instead of 30 and average points.
- The Copa Sudamericana does not exist, and the Libertadores uses the same format as the Sudamericana.
- The translations are a loooooong way to go.
tl;dr What I said at first - good if you cannot have FM. Stay away otherwise. The story *could* be different on mobile platforms, but I can't test that.

Although I'm not usually one for the tower defence genre, I was happily lured in by the setting of Sang-Froid. What other game takes you to Quebec in 1858? You play as one of two brothers who are both good men at heart but somewhat troubled and not particularly liked by civilization. When your sister falls ill after being run out of town by a two-faced priest, the tiny cabin you hole up in becomes full of family turmoil and the epicentre of attacks by possessed wolves and more. Family woes aren't exactly put aside as monsters come night after night, giving a great feel for the brothers.
Gameplay is a merge of tower defence and third person action. During the day you go to town to buy booze, weapons, and gear and set up all sorts of traps from simple wolf traps to hanging nets of rocks to much more elaborate tools like spring-loaded spikes and ballistas. As is often the case, you unlock more and more goodies and more routes and more places to defend as you rely on a mix of trapping and just beating things with an axe or shooting a musket. Depending on how you spend your skills every level can also help out your preference of play.
So with a unique setting, variable gameplay, a great soundtrack, and enjoyment all round, if you remotely like tower defence and/or third person action, Sang-Froid is a must!

Sang-Froid appeals to me in a huge way, there is very little that I actually dislike about this game. The game is very creative and also innovative for games in general; adding interesting mechanics and ideas that are difficult to find in any other game!
Simple things like having enemies able to fear you, smell you and hear you, make this game stand out from anything else you could find.
What I like:
- Great progression - The game is constantly adding new mechanics, enemies, traps and weapons, so it never becomes stale.
- Planning - Allowing you to set up traps and decide what to defend during the day, and setting the plan in motion at night is a brilliant idea, and feels so rewarding when you accomplish the level.
- The Lore - I usually don't pay attention to the setting of the games world, but Sang-Forid makes me care about the folk history, the overall aesthetic to the game is really amazing.
- The Music - The music appeals to me in EVERY GODDAMN WAY POSSIBLE, simply fantastic. It is also very fitting for the world it is set in!
What I dislike/ could have been improved:
- The story/ Dialogue - I am interested in the story, but due to the fact it was made by french developers the translation from French to English can sometimes come off poor or cheesy, not all the dialogue is bad though and most of the voice actors are actually quite good. It is sadly just not as strong as the rest of the game, but the fact that the developers were able to pull it off in the first place is a positive in my opinion!
If you haven't guessed it already, I adore this game and would recommend it to anyone and everyone!

I wasn't sure what to expect when I bought this game in the hopes of bridging the gap to the release of Mass Effect Andromeda in March 2017. Borderlands was advertised as similarly addictive as the Diablo series, so I thought "Hey, why the hell not?"
Well, it didn't deliver. Really, it didn't. Perhaps I'm playing it wrong (which I'd find surprising since I more or less breezed through it without any trouble worth mentioning), but as far as the single player campaign is concerned, it was a staggering waste of money. To elaborate:
- The "story" - if you even want to call it such - is a paper-thin excuse plot at best, nonexistent at worst.
- The enemy AI is dumb as brick, and since there's no such thing as difficulty adjustments, you can't even do anything about it. Just watch them either stand around in the open waiting to get shot, or charging straight at you waiting to get shot. No challenge here whatsoever.
- The quests are awfully repetitive, all of them: Go there (with "there" being a location you often just came from), kill/fetch some stuff, come back. Rinse and repeat. Sure, most RPGs run on this routine, but they usually have the decency to supplement it with some variety or background. Borderland is not one of them.
- The Fast-Travel System is a bad joke. It doesn't become available until the second act of the "story" and there's most often exactly one access point per dungeon, which means one thing: Backtracking. Lots and lots and lots of incredibly boring backtracking through the entire dungeon. Again and again. Half the game seems to consist of running through empty levels. In the rare cases fast-travelling is a valid option, have fun trying to find the FT spot you need for the location you want to visit; the menu is a catastrophe with less useful information than any tabloid.
- Another insanely repetitive facet: The things your enemies and especially the vending machines have to say. Having to listen to the same half-dozen lines over and over again without a means to skip or silence them had me on the verge of throwing my speakers out the window within the first hour of gameplay. It didn't get better afterwards. At all.
- The bosses. Oh boy, the bosses. Sure, they're big and all (most of them at least), and they're somewhat tougher and deal more damage than the average mook, but that's about it. No special tactics, no special abilities I noticed, no strategies required to beat them. Just keep shooting in their rough direction until either the boss or you bites the dust (usually the boss, since none of them is particularly challenging. Some are even outright jokes).
- Last but not least, if not worst of all: The loot system, considering the 87 bazillion guns available are the game's primary selling point. The randomized loot system isn't much different from Diablo's or similar franchises, granted. Still, it utterly failed to capture me just like the rest of the game. I can't put my finger on exactly why that is the case. Something's just... missing. Don't ask me what, I don't know, but it sucked.
To say at least something positive about Borderlands:
- It has a nice, dark sense of humor.
- The character classes, their abilities and the surprisingly useful NG+ features appear well-made, although not to the point that I feel any urge to continue playing after my first completed run and a brief peek into NG+.
- I heard/read about the DLCs being fairly decent and entertaining, but alas, the base game did far too good a job at♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off for me to give them a try.
I can't say anything about multiplayer since I am and have always been hardcore singleplayer, so go figure.
Bottom line: If you (like me) expect something on the level of DIablo, with guns, IN SPACE!, you're about to be sorely disappointed. Better spend that money elsewhere.

An excellent game, if not quite what I was expecting.
Going in, I imagined that it would take more work to discover what had happened to the ship than it actually does. I also imagined that getting that out of the way quickly was the right way to do things, and then I could go back and and fill in some more background details and side stories and whatnot. As it turned out, I hit a certain turning point very early in my gameplay, picked a side without really realizing what I was doing, and just sorta got to an ending, with a pile of logs unread. It had been intriguing and interesting, but I felt like I missed most of the game. So then, of course, I immediately started it over again. And that's when it really became great.
The characterizations of both AI characters, first of all, is excellent - not just in their backstories and interactions, but in the fact that they're both kind of annoying and they're both kind of wrong. It's refreshing, and it makes the game's atmosphere really 'work' - you're not trying to find the 'right answer', you're trying to find the truth. Really, one of my few complaints would be that I want to experience more of the world (the setting is established, but most of the game is character-focused), but that's hardly a fault, and if Hate Plus serves that purpose as I suspect it might, it's no fault at all.
The one quibble I do have is that the console screen creates expectations that aren't met. The fact that you're past a certain turning point is only indicated by a vague-sounding error (since you can still shift power around and such) that initially made me think I had done something wrong, and I spent quite a bit of time trying to carefully manage that situation to accomplish something that it turns out is simply impossible. This isn't helped by the fact that the 'copy' command, as far as I can tell, doesn't ever actually serve any purpose.
Regardless, though, the dialogue, the characters, the story - all of that is very well done, and since that really is the heart of the game, any issues beyond that are fairly trivial. It is a fairly short game (7.5 hours for 100%, and that's spending probably the last hour tracking down a block of logs that's only unlocked by asking *Hyun-ae a question I had assumed she would respond badly to), but it's absolutely worth experiencing.

Having to piece together all the political aspects and the motivations of all the characters by reading the logs was very different from everything else. Interacting with the Mute and Hyun ae was solid and really helped to flesh out their characters and their beliefs. This story takes itself seriously and really doesn't go in the direction I and most likely anyone who has played this game thought it would. The game as a whole can be very unnerving and will cause you to pause as you read certain sections, making you feel for the characters and even though fictional, calling into question what your belief systems are and making you wonder just how far would you go if ever crippling hatred caused you to break.
So far i've only gotten endings 2 with 87% completion on my first try and ending 4 with 63% completion but I am definitely going to look up a guide to getting all the endings.
So I guess it all comes down to this.....Do I recommend it?
Well....yes, yes I do.
The game as a whole when it comes to visual novels has a rating of 8/10 from me. That is hard to achieve in my book and I don't rate all games at that level. If it had been easier navigate which notes could spark a conversation with the two female characters in the game it would have gotten an 8.5 from me.

If you enjoy multiplayer games like Counter Strike: Source and Battlefield you may be in for a treat. This game has a heeping helping of class based units on either the Allies (American Army) or the Axis (Nazi Germany's Army). Each unit has a very specific loadout. I enjoy shooting granades with my M1 Grand as a rifleman for Allies. However, equally fun is heaving around a panzshrek on my back while toting my favorite pistol the "Broom Handle" (aka the Mauser) as a German. Either way, multiplayer is every bit as fun as you can imagine for a WWII First Person Shooter (FPS).
However, there are some drawbacks. Unlike Counter Strike: Source where if you feel more like a relaxed game of practice with some AI bots (computer controlled enemies/teammates) this game does not offer such a thing at all. No bots at all actually! Which is a huge let down when it comes to how many times gamers like to chill after a tough fight, especially if a sniper dominates, yet they still want to play too. A more relaxed offline game with bots often times left me with a built up enough confidence to get back into the fight with human players so I can give my best again.
Also, the clunky controls for aiming and moving are a little lackluster. Some weapons do not even let you aim down the sights. This is a disappointment too. The game does compensate for such things, like the soldier carrying a Thompson may only fire from the hip, but he carries a pistol, one frag grenade, and one smoke/flash grenade. Each unit actually has there own loadout which in of itself may prove unique not only among their teammates but even between both armies. This does help keep things fresh and provides each character with more of their own advantages.
Machine gunners and snipers seem to be the heaviest of hitters as they both rack up a lot of kills. Though a very skilled marksman in this game with a sniper rifle is the deadliest opponent yet! Rifles are ok and allow aiming down the sights. While smgs are strictly hip fire these pack a wholop at close range, which make them ideal for clearing a room but not good across open space. Bazookas are Bazookas. No shotguns can be found, but they are hardly missed.
The matches are usually about capturing positions. Whichever team controls all the flag posts wins. Pretty straight forward and fun. Should you spend $9.99 on it? Well honestly if you have no problem with only playing online with people, love FPS games, and love the era of WWII then this is the game for you. If you do not fit into any of those, do not buy this game.
My opinion is: It is worth checking out, but I would recommend waiting for a Valve publishers sale because it offers little in terms of offline (because no computer opponents/teammates to play with). If that is not a problem, then buy it today.
Overall verdict: 8/10 [Cons: -Clunky controls -No offline (bots not included); Pros: -Good FPS -Brings CS:Source to WWII era -High Replay Value for FPS and/or WWII era fans]

This one is sadly hard to recommend.
Goods:
- The graphics are gorgeous.
- The loading screens are amazing.
- The level design blows my mind. Especially the early levels in the game are incredibly beautiful and wide. Filled with interactive elements, that help you kill the enemies.
- Really like how the glass in windows break.
- WW2 shooter, but every second level is supposed to be stealth level, which is nice change of pace.
- The German soldier banter in stealth levels is fun and adds to the world building.
- Interesting additions, like throwing  stones to distract the enemies, or taking hostages.
- Interesting noise mechanic, that allows you to shoot enemies and remain in stealth.
Bads:
- For some reason the game likes to take control away from the player in order to close doors, look a certain way, etc. Gets annoying.
- Clunky reload mechanics. During a reload, if you cancel out of a reload animation at the last milisecond, you've cancelled out of all the reload (does not matter, that the new magazine has been inserted into the gun).
- Clunky stealth gun mechanics. After taking a shot, there is a lengthy animation, that you cannot cancel out of. So if you mess up, it's curtains for you.
- No bullet drop down. I know it's not a must, but it kept weirding me out, especially with snipers and rpg launchers.
- Stealth take-down animation is so long, that it's way faster to take the enemy as a hostage and kill him that way.
- The story and lead character are meh. Kind of understand why they did it the way they did, but it's a bit hard to keep the suspension of disbelieve.
- BUGS! Oh dear, this game didn't get enough time before being pushed out:
-- Game crashed to desktop twice.
-- Fell out of the world once.
-- Mission failed to progress after killing all the enemies. Had to kill myself to replay the mission again.
-- Some scenes are very  badly choreographed, so you can make the audio pay way before the animation.
-- The world geometry is very unpolished, and it's easy to get caughed on it. Had a stealth attempt fail, because I couldn't get out of the door.
-- Had a stealth attempt fail, because enemies saw me and killed me through solid walls.
So, even if I've started in high spirits, after just a couple of levels, my will to continue was on the floor. It's a shame - the game came out during the WW2 shooter famine, and could have been something special. It's clear a lot of work and love went into the game, it's baffling they did not finish the game before release.
What killed this game the most, is that they added all these stealth mechanics, and yet, tha buggines and lack of polish punish the player so hard for trying the stealth route. I've just ended up going and mowing everyone down with a machine gun.

I liked the first Prototype. The combat and movement mechanics were fantastic, while the world felt full of life. It had an uncanny sense of complete chaos, like as it was hard to see the difference between civilians and zombies in the crowds. The second game builds on the world design from the first game and creates an even more believable sense of bewildering chaos. It’s so much that it’s hard to take in if you just stand and look at it all. Any ideas you might have of avoiding collateral damage quickly go out the window. You just can’t help killing crowds of innocents when dealing with the military or monsters in the city. The city is just too dense for combat.
Prototype 2 is a wasted opportunity. The world design is the perfect stage for any post-apocalyptic game. It’s teeming with details and history. The art department really went all out in creating a believable world. Even the sound design is impressive. It’s subtle, and has a carefully designed wide dynamic range. It’s full of details, like car tires squealing when an NPC slams the brakes to avoid hitting you. It’s a competent studio pulling out some of the best work of the generation. And it’s all ruined by the story.
I don’t know what they were thinking when they signed off on the script. Did someone high up decide that this was fine, because “it’s just a game”? The story and characters are about as shallow as they get. Nobody has anything resembling a personality or a story arc through the game. They all look different, but the way they speak, their motivations and their roles in the story is all devoid of texture or depth. It’s just flat and boring, and as a result you can’t get engaged in anything going on. The mechanics are all great, and the mission designs are acceptably good. But there’s no excitement to see what happens next.
Despite the abysmal story and characters I still had a good time playing the game, thanks to everything else being good. But make no mistake, this game is instantly forgettable. You barely know what’s going on even as it’s happening, because it’s all flat and monotone. It’s like going on a nice sightseeing trip through a nightmare vision of New York. But we’ve already seen plenty of those, so that might not have much novelty value. I wanted to play the game after playing Saints Row 4, because SR4 basically copy-pasted the game mechanics of Prototype. For the €5 I paid Prototype 2 was worth it, but I can’t get over what a wasted opportunity this was. Every other component is here for a phenomenal game, but they decided that players don’t care about story and that this level of ambition is fine. And it just isn’t.

When this game was announced and it was hyped as hell I actually got interested into it.

I dont get it why they dont make a new Budokai Tenkaichi like 3. This would be amazing and a must buy for me. Just make it Namco. Budokai Tenkaichi 4 or whatever you have in mind. Maybe just make a cheap BT3 Remake with some new characters and Sagas like Golden Frieza. I dont even need a completely new developed game. Also do it for PC though!
Well, after that was said it should be obvious that I didnt really enjoy Xenoverse.
Yeah, I did not. It was one of the better DBZ games but none which I would like. Maybe I expected it too much to be like Budokai Tenkaichi, because its not at all like Budokai Tenkaichi. For me the gameplay feels boring. Its actually like a MMORPG. And since I dont like MMORPGs this game falls flat for me. People who like MMORPGs and DBZ will probably have the time of their life. I dont. The main story is actually well made! How it was implemented NOT. In fact you had to level up your character to do the Story. Also the difficulty is sometimes too easy and sometimes too high. The devs werent really able to make something between. Thats the burden of a MMORPG I guess. Also for me nearly all fighters played the same. There was nothing really unique to them. Beside that their super attacks were extremely boring made. Thats what I love Budokai Tenkaichi for. Every player feels unique especially with all their transformations and super attracks. It was interesting though to create your own fighter. This was one of the, for me, very few good aspects of the game. Also for some reason the armor and clothing aspect is stupid because it gives you extra stats. Like that everybody is forced to use something specific and not just what he or she likes.
The PC Version is quite good, not perfect though. The fact that any sort of Anti Aliasing is absent is horrible because the game just screams for Anti Aliasing. There is a way to force it over Nvidia Inspector with a Anti Aliasing "hack". AMD users have bad luck though and have to live with horrible FXAA. Also what annoyed me to hell was the waiting times to connect to the Xenoverse server, even if you just wanted to play Singleplayer. This is nearly impossible by the way...
The devs also released several DLC packs for the movies and DB GT and stuff. Those are totally overpriced though and should have been in the game for free. Money milking at its finest. To this comes a Pre Order exclusive character. There is no other way to get this character without Pre Order. And another horrible implementation... To this comes now the dropped support from the devs. Probably they are doing Xenoverse 2 which will just be like the first. Sadly it got a trend to make always the same game with maybe a different story but the rest is the same. Naruto is one of the glory examples of this. Those games sadly developed into the same♥♥♥♥♥♥that CoD is nowadays. Always the same boring crap filled with DLCs and after a few months support is dead and the next is on the line. People still buy it though. Which I will never understand. People will buy it anyway and even Pre Order to get unique characters. I will definitely not buy Xenoverse 2 and rather wait for a new Budokai Tenkaichi sort of game, if we will ever get one again...

Interstellar Marines has been one of the most entertaining games I have played, despite the fact that I am not a huge fan of the FPS genre. Zero Point Software's vision of creating a Sci-Fi tactical shooter is incredibly impressive, as is their work on the game so far. The game is highly detailed, incredibly immersive (in fact, it can be quite terrifying at times for that very reason,) and its multiplayer experience is actually pretty good as well. In order for your team to succeed in PvP, for example, you must work with your team to be successful; trying to be a hero and throwing yourself in the middle of dense firefights invariably gets you killed, and denies your team an otherwise valuable asset. Co-op is also quite interesting as well, and provides a formidable challenge in its own right. Playing the game on your own is not quite as enjoyable as playing with others, but do bear in mind this game is meant to be a multiplayer experience, rather than a campaign-based shooter.
Interstellar Marines, in my opinion, is an excellent game as it is. It does, however, suffer from a nagging problem that many early access games suffer today -- it has been, and still is, largely in its infancy after many years of development. The ZPS team is small and incredibly limited -- anyone who has been paying attention to their development knows this. It is for this reason I urge people to cut this team some slack. However, I also believe the way ZPS went about marketing this game was not smart. If I could give a piece of advice to ZPS, and I say this as a hobbyist developer, it is this:
Do not publish your game on Steam, even on early access, until you have achieved your game's primary goals. If this means keeping it off Steam for three years, so be it. You'll be able to focus on building your game as opposed to (expending resources better spent making a finished product) supporting an active community. Furthermore, Zero Point Software has lost hundreds, potentially thousands, of players over the years as people lost interest in a title they would otherwise be enjoying if it had been released as a finished product. By publishing this game to Steam before it was complete, Zero Point Software lost a large chunk of supporters.
Am I suggesting taking IM off the shelf until it is complete? No. It is far too late to take IM off Steam, as it would upset the few people still enjoying the game. If this game were finished before being put on Steam, I have no doubt it would be
half as much a hit as TF2 for a good while.
So, do I suggest purchasing this game? No.
if you appreciate the ZPS team's work and wish to see development continue, I
recommend supporting these developers as they persue their goal of completing this game. Make donations, and to those who already own the game,
provide plenty of feedback. They have put a lot of effort into making what you see before you, and it would be a heartbreak to see this opportunity wasted. I hope it's not too late for this game to see a resurgence.

Amazing story driven mix of stealth, platforming and puzzle mechanics. Art style of this game is pixel but simple and clean (its very important in 2D stealth games) and for some (me included) can be appealing. Range of Conway's missions are not very big, in fact almost always we have only one task: brake into the building and hack targeted computer, but it doesnt bother much, because how we do this breaking and what we will say in conversations between missions counts most in this game.
The only problem i have with this game it its length. Finishing main storyline will take you 3-4 hours tops. I definitely see some replayability value (different choices to make during conversations+different tactics to use during missions) but its not much. Few more mini side plots or contracts could be great.
In the end i very strongly recommend this game. Its funny, interesting, sometimes challenging indie gem crafted with love. If 7 euros for 4 hour gameplay bothers you, just wait and pick it up on a sale. But pick it! In the end Richard Conway thanks to his gadgets and skills is far more better and effective spy than 007 XD

I got this as part of a Humble Bundle a while back. This believe this game was in the $1 tier.
This is not your typical VN, but it was a very refreshing, albeit short-lived, experience. While there is an acceptable amount of dialogue to be had between both the AI characters you interact with, the bulk of the game's story comes in the form of journals, logs, letters, and diary entries that you read through. Additionally, actually having to use a computer terminal for various functions makes the novel more involved with the player's direct actions, but the novelty of the mechanic can wear off on subsequent playthroughs. If anything, I wish that the game expanded upon this a bit more, and perhaps with a bit less hand holding.
There is a LOT of reading required in order to grasp the story fully, so should you play this game I highly recommend making sure to pay close attention to what you read to get the most out of it. If info dumping is not your thing, this game may be lackluster to you. Having read all of the logs in the game, I found myself enjoying the story and drama from those moreso than my interactions with either AI. This is not to say that I didn't like the AI characters. Both had enjoyable quirks to their personalities, but I found myself wishing for more dialogue with them by the time I had finished.
While this game is NOT an eroge by any means, there is an element of romance in the game, and certain logs and entries you read through are mildly explicit.  It is not without plot significance, so just be forewarned. Minor context spoiler:
My only real issue with these logs, which I do not fault the game for, was minor difficulty in name recognition. While there are in-game resources to assist with this, all of the game's character's are Korean, which I had difficulty putting to memory.
It took me under 5 hours to sub-optimally get all achievements in this game. Playtime is short for a VN, but minor complaints aside I was plenty satisfied with my game experience. For what effectively was a single evening of plot dump, I would be very hard pressed to pay a full $10, but if you see this game on sale and are looking for an entertaining story, consider picking it up.
There is also a direct sequel to this - Hate Plus. You can play the story as is, or carry over your save file from this game. Something to keep in mind.

This game isn't all that complicated - mostly reading logs, followed by brief conversations to unlock new logs. Mostly.
The content of those logs, though, is wonderful. The game's story emerges in a nonlinear way, and depending on which set of logs you happen to unlock, your conclusions at the game's end might be quite different. For a game this short, the characters are complex and well-developed.
Be aware - it will take multiple playthroughs to find all of the game's content, especially some of the last few logs. I've spent about 24 hours of total playtime with this game and I think I've seen most, if not all, of the content. Beyond that, replay value is pretty limited.
If you have a few free days and like somewhat-dystopian sci-fi (or just a good visual novel), this game is worth your while.

I'd like to start with that I love and hate this game, and that this will be a long review. For those who want the short version of this long review, skip to the bottom where I will have a TL;DR section.
My biggest issue with this game has got to be the main thing this game is based upon. Let me explain...
There is this really cool system that is used to randomize a colonists traits and attributes so that no one person will be alike, so that each colonist will be unique and different. Excellent! I like how Sanji can't fight fires because she's a pyromaniac, and I love that Tony is addicted to drinking. However, it seems that the negative traits are more likely to be randomized in as opposed to the... how shall I put it... not so annoying traits?
As much as I enjoy seeing that some people prefer to be up during the night, and other's can't use weapons, it gets increasingly annoying as the game progresses. Having colonists who can't contribute to the colony is incredibly annoying! And yes, you can kill them, or banish them, but then the rest of your colony becomes upset even though Bryan couldn't cook, mine, craft, smith, tailor, haul, clean or research. So where is the winning in that? I've had to sacrifice my food and time to keep Bryan breathing even though he was incapable of everything.
The problem really is that no colonist is a "good" colonist. Every colonist has some kind of negative attribute that is bound to ruin your colony at one point or another.
And I know. That's the game. That's how the game is challenging and rewarding, right? Not entirely.
If dealing with annoying colonists isn't enough, then comes random events like extreme weather or pirate raids. Imagine being attacked by a band of pirates but Nyx and Stu won't pick up a gun because they are incapable of violence. And your colony is on fire because of incendiary launchers but Sanji won't put them out because she's a pyro.
What I'm trying to get at is all of the randomness is almost too much randomness to make it fun (sometimes). I understand what the Dev's were attempting to create with this game, but there's a fine line between fun and frustrating that this game really throws at you.
TL;DR
Pros:
- Unique colony every time you play
- Random series of in game events
- Cannibalism
- Base building
- Resource gathering
- Micromanagement
- Multiple difficulty settings
Cons:
- Catastrophic world events that will leave you crying
- Annoying colonists
- Mechanoid invaders
- Randomness that deviates between fun and frustrating gameplay
- Bryan literally couldn't contribute to my colony
Despite all of my complaining, I really do recommend this game for anyone who enjoys a base builder and survival game. I wish it had a couple of things tweaked but the bright side is: there are an incredible amount of mods for this game that take a lot of the annoying aspects out. If you like just building and harvesting then there are other AI options to include that will allow you to do just that.
10/10 would have Bryan as a colonist again

In Enemy Front you are a journalist covering WWII in Poland.  You fall so deeply in love with the Polish people that you become an unstoppable Nazi killing machine, taking on the world's most dangerous missions using some pretty rare weapons and your wits to defeat legendary Nazi tactics such as "Stehen im offenen" and "Verstehe nicht abdeckung". Overall it's a good game with stealth options, even if it feels somewhat bland at times and has a non-sensical plot.
In terms of style this game feels like a mix of the Far Cry and Call of Duty series.  You have your standard tools such as suppressed weapons, bolt-action and semi-auto rifles, the venerable Panzerfaust, mounted machine guns and different grenades.  Some sections give you noise cover with lightning or annoying annoucements so you can snipe freely when timed right.  You also have magical binoculars that help you track enemies and their states (idle, or alert).  You get mostly Russian and German arms to use, but there are some rare British weapons as well as the occasional Polish weapon.
The graphics are pretty good, although there is a bit of artistic blur and overuse of bright washout in areas.  You get to see a variety of areas so this does put the CryEngine through it's paces.  There is an all-knowing mini-map present, which detracts from the challenge and gets in the way of artistic screenshots.
The AI are in some ways better than other games and in other ways much worse.  I appreciate that AI sightlines are closer to real life; the AI can spot you from pretty far away if you are in their line of sight (excluding incredibly lazy troops in guard towers that can't seem to see you standing on a hill).  You have an omniscient detection meter that shows when you are starting to draw attention.  In most games AI are relatively blind compared to this game. The AI starts to fall apart once you are noticed, though, as out in the open combat is a repetitive wack-a-mole game.  The AI usually find a spot they like and will send soldier after soldier to the same spot, especially during "defend" portions of a mission.  Every once in a while they will lob a grenade at you, but they mostly sit around, waiting to be slaughtered.
The level design is somewhat open, you have options at least.  It isn't a corridor shooter, you can move through at your own pace for the most part.  The controls have a couple issues.  First, some actions use "E" and some use "F", which is confusing after switching from other shooters that use either "E" or "F".  Ammo is overly plentiful so it is hard to run low on ammo.  Each level has a few collectibles in it as well, so if you want to collect them all you can explore the levels, although there really isn't all that much to explore.  In terms of historical content and lore this is a little light; the setting isn't much other than the framework for killing Nazi fodder.
Overall it's a good time.  Get it on sale and enjoy a good, A class shooter.

So I got this for a buck on the Humble Bundle, along with two other games I don't care about (but hey, .33 cents per game ain't a bad deal). Gunpoint looked interesting from the start, compared to Steamworld Dig (a more boring version of Motherload, a free online game) and some other game I cannot recall the name of, but it's medieval/fantasy. The main point of the game is: You're a spy, you're contracted to gather information/steal♥♥♥♥♥♥ and you make your job easier by crosslinking electronics so that you could, say, make a lightswitch open a door, or make sure a camera doesn't set off an alarm, but instead turns off all the lights on two floors. It looks simple, it plays simple, and I really don't have much to complain about as far as gameplay goes. It has a story, and the story is the main driving force behind most of your missions, and the story works. Yep. There are a lot of nice upgrades to get, like making your landings silent, or breaking through windows without making a noise, or rewiring an enemy's gun to be activated when you do something like lightswitch -> light -> door that has another enemy behind it -> first enemy's gun so he shoots his friend. There's an achievement for that. Also, you don't really get a gun until late in the game, and you don't really need it, so the name of the game is pretty eh, and the Dev recognizes that with yet another achievement. There's also about 8-ish achivements for how you decide to finish off the final "boss" of the game, though he's not really a boss. He goes down as simply as the others.
I will not make this review entirely based on fellating a simple game, so I will say this: Do not buy it yet. I got it for a buck, and I feel it was worth the price. In my first playthrough, I managed to beat the game in about 2 hours, and then I played through again to get the achivements I missed, so that was another 2-3 hours. If I did not bother getting all the achivements however, it would just be a 2 hour game, and the price for Gunpoint right now on Steam is 10 bucks. That is ridiculous. You're paying 5 dollars for every hour if you only play through the game start to finish (or two dollars if you bother with all the achivements like I did). If you want to buy it, wait until it's 50% off, at the minimum. But I can still recommend it, just not at its full price.
Edit: I just noticed that it says I got 6 hours. That was with playing with the level creator. You should not say a game is worth a high price if the base game is bare minimal, but includes the ability to play other levels.

Since I don't know what to put here, let me give you a recipe for Japanese rice balls.
You will need:
1 lb short-grain rice
8 servings of umeboshi (dried plum)
8 servings of nori (dried seaweed)
Directions:
Cook the rice.
Keep it warm, but let it cool enough so that it won't burn your hands.
Cut each nori sheet into 9 strips.
Wet your hands and sprinkle them with salt to prevent the rice from sticking to them.
Mold a handful of rice into a triangular shape with an indentation in the middle.
Press a piece of umeboshi into the indentation you left.
Wrap the rice and umeboshi in Nori strips.
Serve immediately or save for later.
