To look at Dead Island Definitive Edition in a purely comparative manner to the original, there wouldn’t be a whole lot to talk about, at least not in the same way comparing Resident Evil and its remake would for instance. Besides, the original was done so well as to firmly cement itself as cult classic, and secure a flock of affected souls such as myself who become emotionally distraught every time there’s a delay announced for the sequel. Great games last the test of time, and I suspect that Techland and Deep Silver know this very well because there aren’t too many titles that you could ask people to pay more money for without adding any extra gameplay. But just like thousands of other hopeless Dead Island romantics, I somehow justified doing just that, to play a game I already own... I still don’t quite understand why, but I’ve chalked it up to paying for the motivation to invest another hundred hours of my life into what is arguably still one of the best zombie games on the market.
There is something to be said about survival games that primarily rely on the use of melee weapons, and five years on I still haven’t played any that make using a rusty pipe or the humble kitchen knife to fight your way through hoards of undead, such a visceral and satisfying experience. Don’t feel like busting heads with an oar? You could just punch, kick, and stomp your way through hours and hours of content, and I bet you’d still be just as satisfied every time you hear the popping dislocation of a neck, or the splatter of wet brain every time you moosh a head with your feet. Whatever approach you decide to take, Dead Island has something for you. If you absolutely MUST have guns they are in there too, you’ll just have to play through about a quarter of the game before you can really start slinging bullets, and I have to admit that some of the modifications you can get for your guns are a lot of fun too.
Controls are a usually a pretty big part of whether I can just jump into a game and start enjoying it. I feel as though having to complete tutorials that teach you how to do basic things like jump, run and crouch are a waste of content, especially if you’re made to do some silly training exercise or other activity that prevents the game from making a bold statement straight off the bat. If your FPS game needs to have a tutorial to show people how to do simple things, then you’re making it wrong. Dead Island, however, is made properly. You wake up in your hotel room and it’s go time. All the key bindings are customisable if you want to tweak something, but essentially she’s plug and play, no tutorials, just straight into the story.
The backbone of Dead Island is Techland’s own Chrome engine, which is excellently suited to the multiplayer aspect of the game for multiple reasons. Some are integral to enjoyable gameplay, others are a little more subtle but no less important. Firstly, Chrome is able to cope well with multiple players being spread out over large areas, and when vehicles are involved, that’s very important. But it’s the way that Chrome handles online play that really stands out to me. Dead Island is a big game in terms of quests, side quests, and just exploring the map; It’s highly unlikely that a team of four players who aren’t at a LAN party are going to finish even the main quest line in one sitting. So what Chrome does is to allow players to drop in and out of the host’s game as they please, and providing that they are up to the same point as the host in their character’s single player campaign, whatever progress they make while playing together online, will carry over. If the host drops out, no worries, the next player in the queue seamlessly takes over as host without any halt to play. This might seem like a pretty straightforward and logical feature, but it’s one that is surprisingly uncommon in co-op games.
If the lengthy main quest, or staggering number of side quests aren’t enough to keep you occupied, Dead Island has some huge and colourful environments to explore. There are some awesome opportunities for screenshots, and Easter Eggs galore to keep you searching every inch of the map in order to find everything that is crammed into this game. If colour isn’t your thing, then you can hold off for the dank tunnel systems, or the gritty streets of Port Moresby. There really is something for everyone in this game. With the remastering of the Definitive Edition, Techland have honed the lighting and motion effects. This not only adds extra life to the different environments with lens flares and the like, but also adds another layer of detail to combat. The first time I was grabbed by a zombie playing the remaster, I was genuinely impressed by the extra detail they have been able to squeeze in. I am very unhappy, however, that I can’t kick beach balls like I used to.
Dead Island Definitive Edition is certainly not, “Just another zombie game.” Dead Island is a cult classic. There are moments of brilliance in this game that are unforgettable because they are so ridiculously over the top, but then might be followed up with something that strikes at the core of your being. And that’s what I love most about Dead Island - it’s a game of paradoxes. The weapons, the accents, and the borderline nudity, leads you to think that it’s all pretty light-hearted fun like an 80’s horror film; but then BANG, you’re hit with, “The Pool Scene”, or a man begging you to put his family out of their misery. It’s a perfect balance, and one that keeps you guessing about what you'll encounter next.

First off, I really enjoy this game, it's great. But all the reviews are painfully outdated, just like the game.
It's not worth buying. The only way to right this is probably a free weekend followed by a sale.
Cons
-No one plays anymore. It is VERY hard to find a duel with someone at your skill level, no one plays ranked, barely anyone ever plays co-op. Even at Peak NA hours, or right after school for kids, or weekends, I've tried them all lately and seen a max of 10 people online.
-The game was designed as an MMO, unlike other DBZ games. Right now with no playerbase, the party fighting system feels pretty clunky to solo the game with.
-The grind. It follows a normal MMO-grind system, if it was at release; you had people to party with for the quests making the grind seem less. But you don't anymore so you are forced to play with:
-Absolutely terrible AI. You won't notice it at first, but after you start getting more skilled at the game and learning mechanics, you'll see just how terrible the CPUs are. They don't break guards, they don't dodge super abilities with charge up times, (Think kamehameha- while you charge, they just sit there, dont even block). And generally they have the reaction time of potatoes. This was okay, because the game was designed to be played online, with other players, to quest together- but no one is left to do that.
-Stat modifiers are tied into what outfit you're wearing. So, wanna fire badass kamehameha's? Don't equip Goku's Beerus Gi, it reduces your Ki attack modifier by the maximum. ChiChi's world tournament outfit helps that stat more.
-Certain abilities are still IMBA as hell. Regeneration's tick rate in the game is determined not by time, but by your FPS. So if you have 100+ FPS with regeneration skills, you're broken.
-Price still $50.00
+Redeeming features
+Gorgeous manga style game
+Really good original story
+Combat really makes you feel like your in the original series
+Character creation is really nice, There are 5 races, each with their own racials, mostly balanced
+Height, weight, and even gender effect a characters balance between health, speed, Ki, and striking techniques
I was late to the party. I really enjoy the single player story but without people to play a game that was designed to be an MMO at its heart, its dreadfully boring. Imagine playing world of warcraft without players, and you get the idea.
If you think $50 for a single player beat-em-up with a grindy level system set in the Dragonball universe is worth it, I'd still recommend it. But I expected to be able to have online matchmaking at the very least.

Sang-Froid is a terrific game which unfortunately suffers from not being particularly well known. The story won't have you on the edge of your seat but the key players are well written and likeable. As for the gameplay, it's an interesting blend of tower defense and a sort of hack and slash. Defend your buildings from the wolf hordes for as long as your traps hold out and then wade in with axe and rifle to finish the job. It's a terrific concept that consistently feels fresh with new traps and enemies unlocked every so often. Combine fantastic gameplay with two playable characters who play very differently from each other and some basic RPG elements to make the two even more unique and you have a very entertaining, very enjoyable gaming experience.

Against:

I played the heck out of the HL1 mod and got pretty good at it.
Bought DoD Source and found out it took away a bunch of the weapons and made a bunch of the dark corners super bright.
It's kinda fun still, it's tainted by campers and very likely people who use aim bot, but for the most part it's pretty solid and if you can manage to find a populated server it's still very playable, despite its advanced age.
I do miss being able to play as the British from the HL1 mod, and a lot of the weapons are absent like the M1 carbine, the M3 grease gun, the FG 42, K43,  Lee Enfield, and the Bren gun, and the Source version doesn't have quite as many maps from what I remember. I do like the alt-fire modes on many of the weapons, and the weapons feel nice and punchy like I remember, but compared to some more modern trappings, if you're looking for more realistic weapon behaviour and functionality like in Red Orchestra you may be left wanting.
Ultimately, it's still a fun nostalgic romp from a time where you'd be surprised at what you remember if you used to be a player, but you'll also be reminded why a lot of modern FPS innovations are taken for granted these days. End up on a server against people who haven't stopped playing since this game came out and you'll probably remember why you stopped playing in the first place.

Christine Love is... an interesting developer. Her first big game, maybe her first in general, was Digital: A Love Story, and it used a creative format to make a very linear story feel very open ended, and a simple premise feel really unique.
Her second game, which I can't be bothered to remember the whole name of but is something like Don't Take It Personally Babe This Just Ain't Your Story, is a comparatively unambitious Ren'py VN that has some interesting ideas married to poor execution and unlikable characters. It's not a bad game, per say, but coming off of Digital, it's attempts at moral quandaries mixed with mediocre art and a dumb cast are at best quaint and at worst cripplingly mediocre.
The good thing about both these games, however, are their status as freebie games, and their short run times.
Gameplay wise Analogue resembles Her Story, only less interesting and more traditionally minded. The affection mechanic for the featured anime girls is underdeveloped to say the least, and while her exploration of feudalism and gender politics are actually beat, God dang if this game isn't a chore to play and not enthralling enough to push through that.
If you're wondering, I did complete this game, via a walk through because midway through the endless periphery text no longer held surprises, I just wanted to get to the end to see if there was a point. Instead I got a harem? What? If this is about gender politics then why do I end up with two digital women on my analogue schwanz? It's not a conflicted message per say, it's not wholly unexplained, but golly gee I just can't say this game had any good take away for me.
If you're interested, instead try Digital. I'd skip Hate Plus, as well, and to be honest her newest game sounds like a train wreck.

I just finished the first episode last night. If you like Borderlands then you should like this one. It has the same art style, kind of on top of Telltales engine. It works pretty well. The writing is very reminiscent of Borderlands. It definitely feels canon to me.
You play as two different people (at different times obv). One is a Hyperion corporate ladder climber who was supposed to get a promotion, but was overtaken somehow by an evil corporate stooge. So you get smashed back down to janitorial. Of course now he wants his revenge. Go down to Pandora to do some stuff and meet up with the second player character – a street con[wo]man. They are both smart in their own ways. The guy has an eye implant that can scan things, though I haven’t really come across much of a real purpose for it. The girl has a family in the thieving business. Her sister and an older mentor. You only play as the two, but the others are frequently there. There are many bandits and bad guys (including epic bosses, I think from BL2) mixed in. There are occasional appearances of Vault Hunters (so far just ZeR0). It’s clear that to them, you are just a minor sidecharacter that doesn’t at all matter. Which is pretty interesting seeing a vault hunter from that perspective. People don’t really like them.
Gameplay – it’s a typical Telltale game. It’s definitely more of a slightly interactive movie. You get the occasional dialogue choices, which really only change the story so much. There are occasional bits where you actually control the character, but they are generally pointless. There are quicktime events where you die and go game over if you fail. All the sorts of things every telltale game has, which I don’t mind, but it’s not for everyone. I’ve kind of played this as my cool down game, when I need to calm the brain before bed.
Guns (a very big part of any BL game) are all but missing. One of the sidecharacters has one. The main guy does not. The main girl has a one-shot derringer that you can choose to use or not in different situations. But the characters are not gung-ho shooters like Vault Hunters anyway, so it’s fine…I guess. Guns are a lot of fun in the BL universe.

I was surprised by how much I enjoyed this game.  More important, I was surprised by how much I enjoyed the concept.  The game is spent going through dairy entries that are gradually unlocked with the assitance of a couple of AIs.  It's a visual novel so you shouldn't expect too much of gameplay mechanics, but the game does ask you to navigate windows as if you were really remotely accessing the ship, and that little bit of immersion (along with the mid-game "crisis" effects/gameplay) goes a long way in helping to tell the story.
Without spoiling anything: the story's setting is a bit weird, but it allows us to explore a more traditional, confucian society from the perspective of a more modern woman, along with how the various peole around her respond and their perspectives.  It's interesting and, at times, heartbreaking.  The storytelling is really well done so a lot of elements of the game (including the endings) can be interpreted differently.
It's short and enjoyable. Give it a try if you enjoy visaul novels or just enjoy good stories and have a couple hours to blow.  10 dollars is a bit more than I would pay, but if this is your style of game or if it goes on sale then give it a go!

So I got this for a buck on the Humble Bundle, along with two other games I don't care about (but hey, .33 cents per game ain't a bad deal). Gunpoint looked interesting from the start, compared to Steamworld Dig (a more boring version of Motherload, a free online game) and some other game I cannot recall the name of, but it's medieval/fantasy. The main point of the game is: You're a spy, you're contracted to gather information/steal♥♥♥♥♥♥ and you make your job easier by crosslinking electronics so that you could, say, make a lightswitch open a door, or make sure a camera doesn't set off an alarm, but instead turns off all the lights on two floors. It looks simple, it plays simple, and I really don't have much to complain about as far as gameplay goes. It has a story, and the story is the main driving force behind most of your missions, and the story works. Yep. There are a lot of nice upgrades to get, like making your landings silent, or breaking through windows without making a noise, or rewiring an enemy's gun to be activated when you do something like lightswitch -> light -> door that has another enemy behind it -> first enemy's gun so he shoots his friend. There's an achievement for that. Also, you don't really get a gun until late in the game, and you don't really need it, so the name of the game is pretty eh, and the Dev recognizes that with yet another achievement. There's also about 8-ish achivements for how you decide to finish off the final "boss" of the game, though he's not really a boss. He goes down as simply as the others.
I will not make this review entirely based on fellating a simple game, so I will say this: Do not buy it yet. I got it for a buck, and I feel it was worth the price. In my first playthrough, I managed to beat the game in about 2 hours, and then I played through again to get the achivements I missed, so that was another 2-3 hours. If I did not bother getting all the achivements however, it would just be a 2 hour game, and the price for Gunpoint right now on Steam is 10 bucks. That is ridiculous. You're paying 5 dollars for every hour if you only play through the game start to finish (or two dollars if you bother with all the achivements like I did). If you want to buy it, wait until it's 50% off, at the minimum. But I can still recommend it, just not at its full price.
Edit: I just noticed that it says I got 6 hours. That was with playing with the level creator. You should not say a game is worth a high price if the base game is bare minimal, but includes the ability to play other levels.

I played the first Prototype (and enjoyed it) on the PS3 few years back. I thought the first game was good for the time and was hoping for a second one to be released. When I saw the advertisement for the Prototype2  I just had no reaction to it and decided to add this title to my maybe pile for the future. So when it came up on steam deals I toke a chance and got it. The game is very similar to the original in both good and bad ways, The combat feels the same which if you didn't like the first game then you won't like this. The story is mediocre at best (compared to modern standards) with no real connection with the main character, which could leave most people possibly disinterested on following the game till the end. However James Heller is a badass character himself and they could of created a much better back story for him. This may seem like I'm ripping on the game but, it falls down at most of the points it needs to hit. There are some features of the game which are original and with work (possibly in a Third Prototype game) they would have chance to shine. All in all if you liked the first one then pick this up (on a deal of course).

Having played this game already on the PS4, I knew the game was mostly excellent. The niggling issues like missing assets (outfits that had clearly been programmed but not made available) or underutilised opportunities (your hair doesn't change shape when you go Super Saiyan) are generally overwhelmed by how cool it feels to get to make your own character for the DBZ universe and the plot is pretty good at making you feel like your character belongs there.
Your silent protagonist seems just a little too unexpectedly silent at times, but I suppose this is a result of being given some 20 or so voice options: they couldn't record 20 full storyline protagonist scripts. The RNG grind for the items that *have* been included (that you need to make your character look right) varies greatly from "it's a fun little 2 minute mission, I have no problems running it 20-30 times over the weekend to get that set together" to "it's a twelve minute mission, why the fudge can't it drop these friggin' gloves for Christ's sake?"
Luckily the PC version has mods (that fix up missing clothes and Super Saiyan hair) and save editors do allow you to skip the grind for clothing if you find you tire of it. This doesn't excuse the design decision entirely, but it does ameliorate its effects for PC players.
Coming from playing on PS4, the community here (since my recent switch) seems astoundingly dead. I rarely, if ever, can find a "room" to join for a co-op mission and people seldom join my rooms. The lag is astoundingly bad for said co-op with 50% of randoms I do join and manageable for the other 50%... But when you don't have to pay $20 a month for PS+, it is pretty hard to find yourself genuinely bothered by that.
When this game goes on sale, buy it. The core mechanics are pretty solid, basic combat using the right kinds of characters is extremely satisfying and you really are made to feel like you've been invited into the DBZ universe. Just don't get your hopes up about the multiplayer.
Finally, try and buy this game with the DLCs on sale too. No way I'd say they're worth an extra $30 with the community in its current state; but if, like me, you manage to snag the full game with DLCs for $30-40, you will likely consider yourself a very happy customer.
Pro-tip: get into online parallel quests as early if you can if you can find yourself a buddy. It is a fun way to do the parallel quests (especially if they live nearby) to gain experience. The difficulty curve of the game can be pretty sharp if you're not doing enough of the parallel quests to level up.

From Destructive Creations, creators of Hatred, comes IS Defense. An on-rails wave survival  turret shooter.
---- Plot ----
In a politically-fictional setting, the year is 2020, ISIS controls all of the Middle East and the North African region through their conquest of world domination. They're next major step? The invasion of Europe.
You are put into the boots of a NATO stationary machine-gun operator whose task is to stop the assault by any means given.
---- Weapons and Skills ----
You're only given two weapons here, a M240 Bravo (at least I think it is) and a rocket launcher. At first starting out, your weapons are fairly weak. Over time, when you start leveling and gaining skill points, your two weapons can take out ememies and vehicles with ease with the upgrades you can earn.
With skills points you can make your MG shoot faster and deal damage harder, etc. Give your rockets the option to shoot incendiary rockets, bigger blast radius, reload faster, etc. Better support help like "Special Forces" which gives your infantry more health, make your chopper fire rockets. There are quite a bit of skills to put to use here.
---- Enemies ----
ISIS, duh, but in three varieties. Basic rifleman that will shoot at you. Suiciders that will rush your pillbox in an attempt to kill you. Technicals and stolen Hummvees with LMGs on them that deal little damage if you tackle one. In pairs or more, they'll shred your health if you not careful.
---- Support ----
Supply Drops - refills your health or rockets
Infantry - helps handle ground targets
Artillery Shelling - handles ground and vehicle targets
Airstrikes (my favorite) - drops bomb payloads onto ground targets and vehicle targets like artillery, but more damage
and lastly, Chopper - does everything the others can do.
Each one can be upgraded in some way with skill points earned.
---- Overall ----
This game reminds me of Boom Beach, and other rail shooters. Great game to spend time playing to see how far you can last against wave upon wave of fighters. If you unlock all the skills and plan accordingly, you'll be almost unkillable. This game was a side project for the devs and lasts maybe 2-3 hours ..ish and for $8. All in all, I had fun and some memories of the old rail shooters I've played.

Well, to start the review, I think it's important to say I'm not experienced at all with visual novels, but the premise of this one made me interested enough to try.
And it was worth it. The huge amount of text and confusing names you have to go through sounds overwhelming at first, but eventually you begin to understand the story behind it all, and it's a very satisfying feeling. I only wish the game had more freedom in how to discover the plot. As it is, the sequence of reading a letter and showing it to the AI becomes kinda repetitive.
But, well, the most important part is the story itself, and on that front, the game does not disappoint. The setting created is very interesting, with this fusion of futuristic and medieval, and the themes the story present are well-developed. The revelations in the end are dark and heavy, but adequate to the tone of the story.
However, some moments were not - some of the dialogue becomes too much like a dating sim, and it's kinda jarring. To choose the ending I was most comfortable with I also had to pick a not very intuitive sequence. The binary system of choices is used to good effect at parts, but it fails at others.
All in all, it was a very, very worthwhile experience. The investigative aspect was well done, and the story and writing were worthy of being found out.
While this game never received the dev support it deserved, the community continues to keep it alive. It has certainly shown its age, but I continue to enjoy the team play required to do well.

After a long time spent simply being fascinated by the "Make your own choices" kind of games and dying to try one, I finally got the chance to put my hands on this tiny jewel.
Ever since The Walking Dead episodes came out years ago, I've always been interested in the Telltale Games, and I was very happy to experience Tales From The Borderlands to give these guys' products a shot.
With tons of hours under my belt spent on every Borderlands game, with mostly all the DLC's and whatnot, my expectations were quite high. And in complete honesty, I was not disappointed.
Tales From The Borderlands truly has pretty much all those elements that might have made you fall in love with the original franchise.
Same ol' sense of humour, puns, priceless dialogues, unforgettable characters, those amazing Pandora skies, tiny psychos, ferocious skags, and a main quest that keeps getting delayed because, ya know, the bad guys never sleep.
We all know how it works when they try to make something new out of an existing game. We're always expecting the tragic result around the corner. (With good reasons, usually)
But not this time. Not with this game. Not once throughout the whole experience you will stop and think "Man, they just milkin it". Tales From The Borderlands is plain and simple a pleasant and welcomed addition to the Borderlands universe we've presumably already been part of.
The new characters, together with their stories and their backgrounds, are all quite charming. Whether they're the heroes or the enemies, in a way or another they're gonna hit somewhere there right in your feelings.
The plot is quite in the classic Borderlands style. There's some clichés, but it's overall enjoyable and interesting. Although some parts of the story are going to be decided by what the player wants, the game doesn't lack surprise elements and unexpected events, which keeps it captivating and riveting, and always leaves you wanting to know more.
As for the soundtrack, needless to say it's a real treat for those who have played Borderlands before. A huge part of the game features the same musics and themes as the original one. A fight sequence against bandits with music from Borderlands 2 in the backgroud? Sign me the F up.
So, if you're looking at a Telltale Games series, you probably already have a general idea of what the gameplay is like. Obviously the cool thing about this kinda game, is that you get to make choices. Whether it's just a badass cool line you want your character to say, or a life-or-death decision, it's all in your hands. This means that it's not your regular videogame, but rather a movie-ish, interactive experience. In fact, there is quite a few quick time events that will require your attention at several points as well. And you should probably keep your fingers ready because in some occasions these QTE can become pretty tense, and pressing the right keys at the right time might just become a slightly more articulated process than you would expect from this kind of game.
Generally speaking, this game is like icing on the cake for the Borderlands veterans. So many of the features just bring you back to your old, dear Pandora. The attention that was put into the details is just astonishing. Crates open with that same exact sound effect you'd hear when you looked for loot in your games, the characters use the same items you'd pick up and shoot with the same guns you'd find lying around after a fight, just to mention a few.
These things and many more, which a real Vault Hunter will surely notice, truly take you back to the atmosphere you've loved and experienced with the original Borderlands games, just this time you're going on a new adventure.
The one thing I have to criticise, is the impossibility to change language. Unless you're ready to change your whole system default language, you're going to have every dialogue in English, while all the rest that's written anywhere in the game is gonna be in the language that is set on your computer.
Because of the dialogues being in English anyway, you still get to have a pretty cool experience with the game. But I personally believe that in the translation a lot of meaning and side concepts get lost or left behind, which is pretty sad.
Despite this, frankly I can't say that the game loses any particular value. A bit of an annoyance, but it's still completely worth it.
Hopefully Telltale Games will repent and fix the mistake for the next series.
If you've played the Borderlands games over and over, and you miss that unique world, this game is your chance to jump back into everything you've loved before, from a new and enjoyable point of view.

You can play this game for free, and it will only take two or three hours of your time.
In many ways, it feels like a love letter to Valve games, but does enough original things to have its own identity. The design of the environments and atmosphere will leave you constantly looking out for something and checking behind you. The artificial scarcity of health and ammo plays into this as well. There is no difficulty selection as far as I could see, but the more resources you end up needing, the more you will find along the way. It keeps the flow of the gameplay going smoothly without making the player feel like there's too much going in their favor for there to be any real danger, which is something I think this mod does better than Half-Life 2, which threw health and ammo at you like confetti. Only give this game a pass for now if you're allergic to cliffhangers, because this mod does end rather abruptly, with absolutely no clues as to where it could go from here. Having played several f2p-based MMOs over the years, I was eager to try out EVE Online once it went f2p. However, if you have never played EVE Online before, you may be in for a shock.
Most MMOs have a system where if you die, you return to a respawn point and possibly have to repair any damage done to your equipment. Not so with EVE Online. Oh yes, you have a clone that wakes up and picks up the story where you left off... but any ship/enhancements/cargo you had prior to dying is permanently gone. There is not even a warning up front about this. Considering that most ships in-game are being sold at very inflated prices (even with "ship insurance" which is good for only 12 weeks) this can be a very painful surprise.
Yes, EVE Online is mainly a PvP game. Yes, "ganking" is allowed. Yes, even players running (some) scams in the game to trick you are allowed. CCP insists that it is all a part of the story's harsh atmosphere. However, having new players taking a major loss and grinding their way back to playability only to face having the same thing happen to them all over again is not a good selling point for this game.
What complicates matters more is that there is no "official manual" for the game that you can just sit down with and read. There is EVE University which is meant to "teach" you how to play EVE Online... but that too, is not mentioned up front in the game. If you get ganked and lose everything, the fans of EVE Online (usually the ones who did the ganking) will immediately argue that "it's your fault" for not doing your own research BEFORE playing the game. This is not to say that the EVE Online community is all bad. Some veteran players will warn the newcomers up front... but this really should be mentioned by CCP in an official game manual.
I still play this game because I love the genre and would recommend it IF you have no objections to the risk of incurring significant losses from the gameplay. But DO NOT play this game thinking that you can just dive in. Learn the game, play smart and trust no one.

This game is pretty good. It isn't supposed to be this good. I mean it's web based (although that doesn't really mean anything nowdays, since html 5, and unity web player), runs on a potato, and needs like 60 MB hard disk space. But it's suprisingly fun!
The graphics look pretty good! The models are detailed, textures aren't that blurry, I can say it looks the same as WoW. It's just much more fun!
You can play in TPS style, or in "2.5d" (kind of like Neverwinter Nights or Baldur's Gate). Plays much more like an actual crpg, than any other mmo-s i have tried. The character development system gives you much more freedom over your character. Your choice if you want to have more accuracy, more health or more armor.
The actual gameplay is like in similar mmo-s, you have your skills, that you can upgrade, some of them are aoe, some of them are cc, you have seen it before. There are pets, you have a steambike you can upgrade (and even change the looks of your "mount", like to a mech). There aren't many customization options at character creation, but after that, you can have like a hundred different steampunk clothing pieces, and accessories. Also there is a pretty interesting mercenary system.
Crafting is there, but that only upgrades your gear in a variety of ways. There are events constantly, like boss killing, clearing dungeons for rewards, asynch pvp besides normal 1v1 arena, and of course the hillarious golden egg smasher event.
Oh yeah, rewards. You get a sh*tload of rewards just for playing the game, xp, money, crafting materials, you name it.
You get rewards for being online, you get rewards for being offline, you get rewards for everything!
So is it pay to win? Well if there are still games that are pay to win, this game is the complete opposite. You get shop currency as rewards (bound electrum), only a few items can be bought with paid currency (unbound electrum), and you can get that, if you manage to sell something on the market, without spending a dime. You even find subscriptions as item drops.
I have only one problem with the game. The dungeons (especially the early ones) look boring, and they aren't that long either, however you can always go deeper, where stronger monsters wait for you.
The developers did a pretty good work on this game. If you are looking for an mmo, with original ideas, and not something along the line of WoW, just give it a try.
I absolutely recommend this!

You have the option to eat an old lady, steal her identity and use it to butcher countless hordes of innocent civilians/incredibly evil mercenaries. Any game in which you can sprout swords from your very own spaghetti flesh deserves a reccomendation in my book.
You start off in the least screwed up area where it sets the stage to show you just how cartoonishly evil Blackwatch are (see slaughtering autistic child for no discernible reason). It also allows you to hone your wallrunning old lady killing Blackwatch disgruntling skills. Rimworld is mostly a colony survival/management simulation game. As per the design, the emphasis is on "stories": how the different colonists interact/affect each other, how they respond to the challenges of the world (raids by rival factions, natural disasters, etc). Replayability is very high: one can use different bioms to settle, one can migrate over to different places to settle abandoning the current colony, one can have very different chemistry between the colonists in the various playthroughs, the colonist might have very different traits themselves, etc. The game is pauseable and supports various running speeds, allowing for a chilled or mode action-packed gaming experience.
I really like this game. It combines the management aspect with survival and actual fighting. The balance between the two is very good! Some games fails is this respect, but RimWorld does it well. There is a natural ending for your colony by leaving the planet via a spaceship, allowing for players who pursue some "real" ending to their campaigns to satisfactorily finish the current one and start a new campaign.
Overall: the game succeeds spectacularly to be the kind of game it promises to be. If you like the synapsis, I highly recommend RimWorld to you.

TL;DR - The game started off quite fun, with a decent variety of enemies, weapons, and pretty terrain / locales.
Unfortunately, about half way through (the moment I moved from the City to the Jungle) everything fell apart, quests became mind-numbingly tedious, and now I'm just playing because I hate not knowing how a story ends.
Visuals - 8.5/10
Audio - 9.5/10
Combat - 8/10
Vehicles - 2/10
Story/Plot - 4/10
Characters - 1.5/10
Also, ignore the playtime, sometimes I pause games and alt-tab because life happens and I'm not the only person using this computer.
---------------
Long version contains a few minor spoilers
---------------
Anywho, I wanted to like this game, and will still finish the playthrough I am on (I used the Asian girl, because swords).
I even paid the extra couple of dollars for the "Definitive Edition" so that I could see / enjoy the best possible version of Dead Island, since I hadn't gotten around to playing the "original" yet (sorry if you were looking for a review clarifying the difference between the two).
However, now that I'm about 80% done the main quest, and have completed every side-quest available thus far in order to obtain their rewards, I can honestly say this game just wasn't enough fun for me to justify going back and trying out the other characters and their weapons / fighting styles.
At first I was able to ignore the occasional bug or annoying game mechanic (such as not getting any weapon mods for bladed weapons until almost halfway through the main story; the camera / view inside of vehicles making it very hard to navigate the roads; the movement / control of the vehicles being a cross between a shopping cart and a tank, what a joke; or the GPS being utterly useless half of the time and markers disappearing once you're within a certain distance of the objective: especially with regards to the mission in the city where you need to activate speakers on the rooftops).
I even enjoyed the learning curve of getting better at using different combinations of weapons, taking on bigger crowds of zombies and learning to predict how different enemy types will behave.
Until I left the city and headed into the jungle.
Seriously guys, what happened?!? It was like night and day.
At this point, the plot narrative went to crap, I ceased to feel any emotional connection to any of the characters and thus any real reason to complete objectives aside from getting the markers off my map and earning money or weapons.
I don't know if the devs budget ran out, the writers quit, or maybe they had an encroaching deadline to meet, but this DOES NOT feel "definitive or remastered" in the slightest.
At one point, everything (and I mean literally EVERYTHING except for safes and weapon boxes) I searched was always empty. Was this the dev's version of ramping up the "difficulty", so that I would have to STOP WHATEVER QUEST I'M IN THE MIDDLE OF and return to an older area in order to collect parts for my weapon mods?
That's just lazy game design.
At least have the decency to remove the search option from this area / chapter, so I don't keep thinking "Maybe that was just a weird load up glitch, and I'll start finding batteries and bleach and stuff any minute now!"
Nope. None for you. But we sure made ya look again!
Because everything that USED to potentially render loot, still had the option to be searched, which is just rude and visually clutters up the play area.
I may be wrong, but on numerous occasions I felt like characters and settings were put in place with a larger / longer role in mind, but then at some point in game development they were just given up on, and they tried to compensate / cover it by being like "Oh crap, that guy is a lying backstabber!" or "Oh no, everyone here got killed by the zombies and now there are no NPC's and you don't need to / can't come back here anymore".
You can only do that so many times in a game before it starts to form a predictable and unpleasant pattern.
Speaking of cop-outs, let's just make all the cutscenes and dialogue about all 4 characters, so that the story is impersonal and generic, even if you're playing it solo!
And don't even get me started on the "Natives" of Banoi, they were like a bad mashup of 20 different ethnic stereotypes...

Though the games interface may lead you to believe it is a visual novel, aside from from the lovely AI companions who assist you throughout your investigation, the game is a interactive, heavily text-based storytelling experience in which you attempt to unravel the mystery of how the dystopian society that called the lost starship Mugunghwa its home suddenly collapsed.
It may seem difficult to get into at first if you have a short attention but before you know it the story, which you assemble based on the letters and diaries of the ships residents, really pulls you in. This is broken up with conversations between you and your AI companion that build character and affect your relationship with eachother in a way that can sometimes change the ending. There are also some challenging text based puzzle elements.
It's definately one of my favorite interactive novel experiences and I would recommend it to those looking for an intruiging (and often heartbreaking) story with a lot of replay value. That being said, it also may not be for the faint of heart as it touches on some very dark themes.

I purchased and enjoyed the original game when it first came out. I was already considering playing through it again whilst waiting for Dying light 2 to come out, and then they released this Definitive Edition. The promise of improved graphics and the cheap price for existing owners sealed the deal for me.
I've completed the main game now and am about to finish the Ryder White DLC. I can't tell without a direct comparison whether the graphics are any better, but the lighting is improved and the game looks great, if a little contrasty. I've got much more powerful gear and a 40 inch display this time around and so that makes it better anyway. I do however notice that some of the zombies look different.
The Definitive version is basically the same game as the original but with loads of bugs. There was nothing that ruined the game for me, but there are bugs aplenty. The most irritating bug is the invisible barriers that pop up all over the place. The funniest was when I was blowing the textures right off the cop models in the hotel. Even so, I still enjoyed the game and recommend it for anyone who likes Dying Light and hasn't played these earlier games.
I can also point out just how much better Dying Light is overall. The sound, script and voice overs in Dying Light are all dramatically better then in this game. The player sounds and taunts are just laughable and do their best to ruin the otherwise successful immersion. Techland clearly improved every aspect of their production to deliver Dying Light.
Other bits – It would have been great if one could remove the ugly UI and adjust the difficulty in some manner. I never used the fast travel as I find that ridiculous. I also did not use the fury feature as that seemed equally silly. The slicing weapons and a couple of guns are all you need.
The game is surprisingly large with many locations. The best part of the game is Moresby. The city is very atmospheric and finding one's way around without all the parkour from DL is good fun. I fouind it a shae how easy many of the bigger zombies are to kill. One grenade on anything kills it. I ended up avoiding using the grenades just so that I could have a bit of a fight.
The Ryder White DLC is much more intense, and more similar to Dying Light. It throws zombies at you and you really have to charge along to get anywhere. The only drawback is that the prison is not a very interesting location to have to go around a second time.
Get the game if you have a thing for zombies… good stuff!

Despite the rough graphics and voice-acting, despite the hack & slash being lacking, it blends together with a rich atmosphere, capable RPG elements and ingenious strategic compentents to come together as a deeply clever and immersive game that has no equals in a genre it has created all by itself: Which I'd like to call Strategic Action Defense.
In essence, the game is a unique, ingenious bland between a rudimentary third person hack&slash and a clever (tower) defense game in the most strategic sense possible. Anyone would be excused for thinking of isometric Multiplayer Online Battle Arena (MOBA) games like LOL or DOTA, or Orcs Must Die where the combat is hectic, constant, fast paced and deals with hundreds of mindless mobs marching towards your side, but Sang-Froid is not. Instead the action is tense, tactical, clever and far more personal.
Every game, you start off with a top down perspective of a pine forest through which snowy trails wind towards your cabin. They're paths taken by an onslaught of wolves out to tear it down. This is the planning phase. At first, you just need to defend the cabin where your sick sister lies, but soon the barn, mill, church and more buildings get added to the community under your care. Your sister is a special kind of sick however. She can see from where the wolves are coming to attack those buildings and what routes they'll take, through visions.
This is where the first difference between the game and others like it become apparant: It's personal. When you choose to leave the planning stage and enter the world, the third person hack&slash ensures that your character is the most versatile weapon you have and there really aren't that many wolves, especially in the beginning. Its just that the wolves are capable of coming in from anywhere and your character is just one man with a tiny bar of stamina that can't possibly cover the large stretches of space between buildings AND safely fight more than a few wolves at the same time. And when you do choose to engage, the wolves aren't fodder either. They really are characters in their own right.
Personal combat is involving. Should they have all pounced at once, they would have torn you apart, but a complex system of fear and intimidation, using roars, fires and actions, will see them circling while you deal with those few who manage the courage to take swipes at you. You are are armed with axe and rifle, but the axe will quickly sap your stamina and your rifle is an antique that requires 10 seconds of loading. Tougher foes arrive by themselves or in pairs, but these are often so durable that they take just as much time as any one of those packs.
Combat is a long process against worthy foes then, but time isn't something you have as more packs all over the map close in on your buildings.
This is where the traps come in, and a good deal of patience and savvy from you. Using the planning phase ahead of the third person action phase, allows you to not only prepare your own community through the purchase of gear, but to prepare a strategy for dealing with all of these packs at the same time. And instead of just placing down towers that splash the occasional damage, these traps are of the visceral, personal kind, suited to dealing with a foe that would have given you so much trouble in melee.
Bearclaws will instantly kill the four legged wolves. Bait attracts and slows them down, giving you precious extra time. Placing nets with an avalanche of rocks in them high among the treetops, will bury werewolves when timed right. Place kindle in certain passages and set it alight to redirect packs.
Some of these traps work automatic. Others are far more involving. The net trap for example, needs to be triggered by a shot from your rifle, preferably after luring the werewolf underneath through the use of deception: Bait or a shout to lure it there.
If there's one thing the game does exceedingly well, it is to establish the relationship between hunter and hunted, or making you feel like a rugged outdoors man triumphing over nature through wit. You are keenly aware of just how frightful and tough a werewolf can be in combat, so seeing it carried off through the air on the sharp tip of a ballista bolt after you've personally set it off and tricked the wolf in the right position is a gleeful moment. The transfer between planning phase where you control the map, and action phase where your control is limited to the range of your gun is a disempowering one. The map is tidy, but on foot, the mill is a world away. All you could do is set some spike traps around it, only to realize you couldn't do the same for the werewolf you are about to face for lack of cash. There's only a bonfire for him, to keep him back. "Will it work?" You will wonder.
In such a moment, a sudden swish-click-yelp sound in the far distance of the frozen wintersky, will make you smile as you keep warm around the lit bonfire.
Other than this, the game itself has charm too. Its not a looker, with somewhat decent animation and bearable graphics. Sometimes, the voice acting is cringe-worthy too, with a cast of would-be native Americans barely able to manage the accent. But a cast there is however, with cutscenes and a story too that - although not particular exciting - perfectly enforces the atmosphere of being a Canadian lumberjack on the frontier of a dangerous wildernesses. The mythology of werewolves and Canadian folklore is handled with careful respect and soon you'll be facing creatures from both British Canadian Christian fables and Native American Folklore. Even items are carefully described for their history in logging and Canadian history. I don't even mind the completely outdated method of clicking on individual buildings when going to town to buy gear. It adds to charm. The sound and music make up for a lot and once you manage to see past the outdated looks, you'll appreciate the cartoony feeling and the perfect v-shaped broom closet that is your main character.

I enjoy it when a game designer approaches a pre-existing genre from a new, flavorful perspective. For example, I think it would be neat if we could get rid of the zombies in a lot of these survival/horror games and instead put the players against mummies in Egypt.
So how did I react when I saw that Sang Froid was a tower defense game, set in the Great White North, where you must protect a house with an axe and a musket from waves of werewolves sent by the devil? My reaction could be summed up in one word: SOLD!
Sangfroid (pronounced san-frwa) is a french word for “the ability to stay calm in difficult or dangerous situations.” This game requires exactly that.  Most games give you relatively fast recharge time or a clip for you gun rounds, so you can afford to miss shots occasionally.  In Sang-Froid, you have to reload your musket after every shot.  In many instances, you have to stall the wolves while you reload your musket, and you have to build that time into your gameplan and make every shot count. You have a lot to do and a short time to do it, but the key thing is that you keep calm and carry on.
I once heard this genre referred to as a “boots on the ground tower defense game,” and I think that’s an apt description.  It reminds me a little bit of Brutal Legend; I even remember thinking during one mission “this does to tower defense what Brutal Legend attempted to do with RTS, but it does it right.”  After reading other reviews, I have seen the game compared to Orcs Must Die and/or Sanctum.  If they are anything like Sang Froid, I am excited about giving them a try.
While Sang Froid requires timing, I wouldn’t call it a twitch game.  That said, it is one where you have to remain alert to the larger danger while keeping your attention on the specific task at hand.  The stages were hard, but satisfying.  whenever I finished one, I felt like Hannibal from the A-Team. ("I love it when a plan comes together.")
The overall flavor to the game is light, campy, with a good story and just the right amount of cheese.  The game constantly changes graphical styles between game play, cut scenes, and dialog. If I wasn’t such a fan of Ralph Bakshi’s animation I would likely find this quite jarring. I wouldn’t be surprised if other people found this annoying.
The digital storytelling technique used in the game serves as a reminder that it is a low budget title, but I think that added to the overall charm of the game.  The characters appearing and disappearing during dialog reminds me of the dialog from Guild Wars 2 or Aqua Teen Hunger Force. The folk-style soundtrack makes me think of what country music must have sounded like before country music existed; it keeps the player in the moment, but remained light enough to keep it from feeling like a horror game.
Sang Froid is an excellent tower defense game with a lot of charm and an interesting story.  Give it a try.

You will play as a space explorer who was hired to investigate the wreckage of a long lost space ship whose disappearance has been a mystery for ages. The ship is inhabited, it's crew is long dead. The only remnants of life are two AI programs called Hyun-ae and Mute. Together, you will dig through the archives, records and digital letters from old members of the crew trying to piece together where and why everything went wrong.
If you're a fan of Visual Novels with deep plotlines, I definitely recommend you to give this dramatic masterpiece a try.

Sang-Froid - Tales of Werewolves combines tower defense with wilderness survival horror and a little resource management/trade, and achieves this hefty little combo with style and panache.
There are some truly original mechanics in the game, such as the "fear factor" that pits your own character's fear (or bravado) against that of the blood-hungry beasts of the night - when the werewolves pluck up enough courage, they will attack; this passing of time is represented by a meter on the HUD.  This mechanic can create some really tense moments as you frantically struggle to reload your flintlock rifle, or try to get away to a well booby-trapped spot on the farm before the hairy hordes close in for the kill.
From historically accurate weapons and equipment to an easy to access resource management element, there is plenty to keep the player engrossed in many hours of werewolf bashing.  Oh, and did I mention this game has possibly one of the best (and most fitting) soundtracks I've heard?  Great fun, and at the time of posting this review a great price too.

One Piece: Pirate Warriors 3 is an entry on the collaborative game series between Bandai Namco and Omega Force of the Dynasty Warriors fame. This game is supposedly a downgraded port of the PS3 version. Even without playing the console version, it is obvious that the PC port has several issues (namely missing several textures and blurring during cutscenes). Regardless, the game is still fun to play and the optimization is good.
If you've never played any 'Warriors' game before, this game is best described as one-man warrior versus army of many. During battle, you use one main character literally battling thousands of enemies while being helped by assist characters. Each character has different abilities, making them unique from each other. The gameplay also feels fluid with combos and assists alike.
Other than the ~30 hours long Legend Log (Story Mode itself), you'll find most of your time playing the Dream Log, a mode to unlock a majority of stronger characters from the One Piece universe. Too bad the battles in the Dream Log are usually 10 minutes long and don't differ much.
Fans of Dynasty Warriors series might notice that Pirate Warriors 3 is similar to the DW Empire series, as both of them has territories that can be taken over by depleting their fodder armies and defeating the enemy captain guarding the territory, if any. Special missions called 'treasure event' are also available, providing additional in-game events when cleared. Overall, Dynasty Warriors fans will feel right at home when playing this game.
Ah yes, the graphics. Don't get me wrong, the cel-shaded graphics style itself fits with One Piece. However, even without playing the PS4 version, it is obvious that there are several glaring issues that exist in this port. First, several Logia characters (Crocodile, Eneru, Smoker, etc.) have missing textures, making their in-game model see-through when they use their Devil Fruit abilities. Sometimes, they just disappear from the screen for several seconds before reappearing again. Second, the cutscenes have blurring issues. Whenever a cutscene uses blurring, the supposedly focused models are just out of focus for no reason. Lastly, the game is notorious for its bad draw distance. While personally I don't feel these issues make the game literally unplayable, they still do drag the quality of the port down.
The music is great. It's made up of a mixture of 2 different genre, orchestral music and rock music. Overall, they fit the game pretty well.
Albeit the story of the game covers the Shells Town Arc up to an original version of the Dressrosa arc, the story is best considered as a highly condensed version of the original story. Quite a lot of the important details are skipped. Nonetheless, as far as game standards go, the story is still good, as the game still manages to capture the feelings of several major events quite well. Several moments still give me the feels even after reading the manga for 10+ years already.
+ A lot of playable characters with unique abilities to choose from.
+ Time Skip and Pre-Time Skip versions of several characters.
+ Gameplay feels fluid
+ Fitting art style
+ Quite long in length
+ Good soundtrack
+ As far as frames go, this port has good optimization. A 4GB RAM laptop is able to reach a constant 59 FPS on high settings.
+ Steam Trading Cards and Achievements
• Japanese dub only
- Sometimes may feel grindy and tedious.
- No Steam Cloud support
- Online Multiplayer is removed
- Second player is forced to use the keyboard.
- Several graphics issues found in the PC port
- Most levels in the Dream Log lack depth
- Limited resolution options
It is obvious that games like Pirate Warriors 3 are not meant for people who are tired of the Dynasty Warriors formula. However, if you're looking for a great One Piece game to play, then this game is for you.

So, IS Defence. Islamic State. Dieties bless you Destructive Creations. First you riff Postal with "Hatred" which was a decent enough attempt at Postal, it wasn't -great-, but it was good enough, and despite all the controversy, it was a good enough "shoot everyone" game much in the same vein as Postal. It was a bit clunky, it was definitely cheesy, and much like Postal, it is almost certainly going to be one of those interest pieces that lots of more progressive media pieces chew over and fill their virtual birdcages with down the line on slow news days.
As if that wasn't enough, now you're going to riff Beach Head, another classic game, except this time for the controversy angle you're throwing Islamic State into the mix. I mean, fair play to you, you're based in Poland, so the chances of someone running at you with a suicide vest isn't exactly high, but this is a bit like throwing a red rag to the bull here. The people you're aiming this one at aren't exactly renowned for their sense of humour to put it lightly.
That aside, is the game actually good? Well the answer is "mostly very, and for what they're charging, absolutely"
Put this in an arcade cabinet with some appropriate controls, and this thing would eat your loose change like no tomorrow. Seriously, it's hard, really hard. The first map will take a good dozen attempts before you secure a good foothold and get the hang of what's going on, the second map will throw a whole new set of problems at you (such as your friendly Islamic State militants deciding that a sea only approach is a bit last year, they can now come at you over the road an on the roof of buildings), I'm working on unlocking the third map but there's a good likelihood that'll add even more verticality and yet more difficulty into the mix. This is not by any measure a game where you can autopilot your way to victory. You need to prioritise your targets, get rid of the most dangerous threats, and keep an eye on what's going on at all times, as well as call down your various cooldowns as they become available.
On top of this you have a simple meta levelling tree that offers a nice solid selection of useful upgrades (which in turn make the later levels much more viable), and the ability to fully rotate the turret on it's "rail", which is important for dealing with flanking actions. Graphically at max settings it looks pretty, not jaw dropping, but pretty, with everything represented well enough, and the enemy soldiers flying through the air when the explosions begin the light up the scenery (as well as the beach surf turning red once enough of them die on the first map, that was pleasant!).
Sound effects are passable, not amazing, but passable, in fact a lot of the game can be said to be much the same as Hatred, it's not going to win awards, it's not going to be the high watermark of any particular area, but this is good, solid entertainment, and as a remake of the original Beach Head, without any unnecessary frills or spills, it achieves what it's set out to do, and it does it with a solid level of competency. Most importantly, it's priced at a point which places it firmly in the "impulse buy" area, which means that if you're hesitant, you've really not got too much to lose in giving it a whirl.
Destructive Creations are getting a rep for taking old concepts and remaking them very competently, first Postal and now Beach Head, and controversial slants aside, both of these have been executed with decent skill. Neither have been exemplary in either case, but they've been solid entries in the catalog, if these are opening entries in what Destructive Creations can manage, and in time they come up with bigger and better things, then this is a good sign of things to come. As for this one? If you enjoyed Beach Head, well, for the price asked, it's a gimme. If this kind of game isn't your bag, you can safely skip it, it's not going to sell the unconverted.

It's short, longer than the amount of time I'd like to spend on a date prior to going back to the bedroom though and certainly cheaper than said date which is great.
It's simple, not in a bad way, similar to the kind of girl you meet in a bar who has a few badly done tattoos that are just visible enough to prevent her from getting a job without being sufficient for her to be an alternative model - she's a simple girl but that's what you want in that situation.
It's fun, really fun. Great stress relief. Much like the result of meeting that girl in a bar but with violence as the fun instead of bedroom entertainment. Again, while it's short, it also lasts longer than I do in the bedroom and I don't have to deal with waking up thinking "what the ♥♥♥♥ did I do last night" afterwards.
So onto a better review (skip to the bottom if you just want pros and cons). You can forget there being a storyline at all. You're a big♥♥♥♥♥machine gun with unlimited ammo (though you have to reload until you unlock the chain feed skill) and you have to mow down things attacking you, you also have a rocket launcher attached but this has limited ammo, the machine gun does not. These things attacking are infantymen, trucks and humvees which can attack from 360 degrees and have a range of armour values (the humvees being the most heavily armoured, infantry having no armour and die with a single bullet as far as I can tell). There are 3 maps which can be viewed as easy, medium and hard. The difficulty level is not linear, the second map is a little more challenging than the first, the third map is immensely more challenging than the second.
The enemy design is pretty basic, the humvees look like stolen US military ones, the white trucks look like the beat up toyotas you might find on the sands of the middle East. I do like the touch of them flying IS flags, it's nice to be mowing down hundreds of enemies and feel like you're doing the world some good. There are also small boats and large transporters which carry enemies and can be destroyed prior to landing, though the transporters require 2 or 3 rockets for destruction (but they carry around 6 soldiers and 1 or 2 vehicles)
The graphics are surprisingly nice, solid framerate too, I guess Unreal 3 is to thank for that. The level designs are pretty good, fair. I like the second map the most as it's a good mix between open areas and covered corners that the enemy can attack from. The first map is far too open and gives a lot of chance to destroy enemies before they can attack you as it's a beach and the third map is a little chaotic as enemies seem to come from literally everywhere and have cover until they are relatively close.
There are a series of skills to unlock. You can make the gun more powerful and accurate, you can make your rockets more powerful, you can boost your survivability/health and you can increase your "assistance" power. The assistance is a perk system where within each map you earn experience that can be spent on CPU help in the form of:
supply drops; health crates and rocket crates,
infanty support; a group of soldiers who shoot at the enemy with you,
artillery support; random sustained explosions knocking out enemies around you for a while,
air support; a group of jets bomb the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the map and
helicopter support; a chopper hovers around the map shooting♥♥♥♥♥♥for you.
The downside is, the difficulty level seems to be tied to the number of skills you have unlocked and to how many forms of assistance you request in each map, or maybe it's simply rated against the XP you're earning in the map. I might be wrong on this but I lasted longest when I had fewest unlocks though.
I also found that the rocket launcher is a bit of a gimmick, due to the limited ammo and my resistance to wasting experience points on supply crates, I found I didn't use it much as the actual power of the rockets is negligible compared to the fully upgraded gun.
It would be far improved by the rockets slowly respawning as you play every 30 seconds or so rather than requiring supply crates, or even having that as one of the skill options.
The CPU support also kills the infantry you request when using artillery or airstrikes, to the point some airstikes wipe out all my infantry. Helicopters do not stack, you can only have one at a time. Infantry does stack, but I'm not sure what the limit is. The infantry also tends to run very far out and it's easy to mow them down with enemies once they've expanded away from your area too much. This can be pretty annoying as by 2-3 minutes in each map, CPU support becomes necessary. The helicopter and airstrikes can save your♥♥♥♥♥ while the infantry often take a lot of the heat off you by eliminating the smaller targets.
You can unlock all the improvements and defeat the map challenges (certain kills and vehicle kills per map) within about 3.5 hours. Considering the game costs as much as about 2 beers here which might last 1 hour at a push with a bunch of friends talking rather than drinking, I'd say that equates to pretty damn good value for money! I'm 4.4 hours in as of writing this and I've killed 16000 enemies - there's an achievement for 30000 which looks like it might be the most difficult achievement in game, along side the last 20 minutes on each map - I think my top survival is about 11 or 12m.
So:
Pros:
+Explosions
+Killing Terrorists
+Stress Relief
+Surprisingly good graphics for the money (thanks, Unreal 3)
+Entertainment
+Value for money (playtime vs cost)
Cons:
-Only 3 maps
-Not much replay value outside of stress relief
-Inability to turn off improvements once unlocked despite increasing difficulty
-Unpredictable and non-linear increase in difficulty level during play
-Fairly short gametime before "completion"
Summary:
Buy it, it's cheap and fun, you wont regret it. There's also a potential for mods in the future (hopefully more maps) so that should extend it some in the end!

tl;dr: A true survival roguelike RPG set in a very deep and detailed world.
This really IS a
game.
You cannot just go somewhere and attack a wolf with your sword to gain 50 xp.
First of all, you more than likely won't have a sword - they are hard to come by and you will have to gather many boards, furs, leathers and food to finally get enough value together to trade in for a sword.
Also, good luck finding a wolf. In all my hours so far (of which I spent quite a few hunting), I did not encounter a single one. You do hear them, though. And hope they stay far away...
Oh, and if you do find one, it will very likely be deadly. Combat in general is deadly in this game. Even small game like a wolverine might already cause a wound that can kill you if unprepared. And even if you start out with good combat stats, you will be lacking in other stats and have a hard time surviving.
Of course, you will not have to worry about a single wolf. As is realistic, they hunt in packs. A single bear is more deadly than a wolf, of course, but I don't see how anyone but a perfectly equipped seasoned warrior would be able to bring a pack of wolves down.
And finally... you won't get 50xp as this game has no XP or even a level system. You have skills and they improve by using them. And since combat is very deadly... well, let's just say it would be a good idea to train a very long time before setting out for trouble.
As of writing this review, I spent about 25 hours building a hut next to a lake to survive the winter.
By falling trees, cutting them into logs and boards, building all those walls and floors and of course the fireplace.
All of that while having to catch fish to eat, hunting and trapping game in the wilderness to skin and tan the hides (a multi-step days spanning process), taking care of my wounds because a crazed wolverine attacked me and almost killed my poor reindeer companion and continuously trading whatever I could to afford better tools, weapons and dried food for the winter months - because I do not yet have a smoking cabin, nor is it winter to dry my fishes.
And the best part: Every single step listed here is governed by skills that you create your character with and that will slowly improve over time. So not only a true survival game but also a true RPG.
Oh, and all those things I mentioned do not even cover half of all the mechanics of this game.

Its been almost a year since my adventure began. Since I struck out from my home village where I had lived my entire to experience the greater world. For months I desperately scraped together a meagre existence, fishing, hunting rabbits, trapping foxes and when desperate enough, stealing from villages under the cover of darkness. My mind casts over all of my numerous near death experiences. Ive been tracked by a pack of wolves, fallen off a cliff, butted by a bull elk and wrestled by a fully grown bear.
My most dangerous foe however, a lone poorly armed Njerpez raider, half starved and half frozen. It was a savage affair, arrows were notched at range, spear struck sword in close combat and countless blows were exchanged. Strike after strike after strike. Our weapons had been lost in the struggle, we drew knives. Blade bites flesh. We were exhausted, both bleeding from a dozen wounds. Our knives were lost too. We wrestled like two worn out boxers. He collapsed and I fell on him like a spider. I lifted a heavy stone and brought it down on his face, over and over. He finally lets out one last rattling breath. I collapsed in the snow beside him and woke hours later unable to walk. It took me two days to drag myself back to camp eating roots, weeds and a frozen bird carcass to survive. I saw things in the woods at night.
But that was then and this is now, its different you know.
Im standing tall at the edge of a river, a Njerpez camp lying empty in my wake. Im wearing skis, thick furs, a battered iron helmet and gauntlets aswell as thick mail shirt. I feel like a giant, no man can fell me, my long axe has drank the blood of many Njerpez today. I begin to stride across the thick ice of the frozen river.
I am a different man than the one that set out all those seasons ago, in the thaw I shall use the waterways to travel far and wide to seek out other figthers to test my mettle agaisnt, yes, I will be a warrior of the greatest renown in all of the Unrea- *Crack*
Is the ice as thick as I thought it was?
*Splash*
Swimming in freezing water is hard, swimming in freezing water wearing fifty pounds of iron armour and over laden with battle trophies is impossible. Exhaustion and coldwater shock set in quickly. What a way to go. Perhaps the spirit of the waters have something agaisnt hubris?

This is a really interesting game. As an action tower defense game you can't avoid comparing Sang-Froid to Orcs Must Die. However, these games are very different in gameplay and layout. In Sang-Froid you prepare all your traps before starting the level in contrast to OMD where you start the level and then place traps. In that manner Sang-Froid is a little more slow paced and not quite hectic as OMD, but enough with the comparison. Let's focus on Sang-Froid alone.
The story isn't the strongest side of Sang-Froid and the same could be said about the voice acting and cut-scenes. On the contrary the music is really great and it's a perfect fit for the game. The surroundings and the environment also suits this game nicely. I really like the cold, snowy lumberjack theme. The game evolves around one single map which you play every mission. It could let you to believe it would get boring quickly, but the map changes enough along with the objectives that it doesn't feel boring.
The traps offer a good variety of different killing possibilities. You can upgrade weapons and traps for the fur you sell after killing wolves or werewolves. You could also buy potions and other useful item between each level.
What I would like to have seen is that when you play the game the second time with the other brother you know all traps, how the map works etc. but you have to listen to how to use the traps again. It would have been nice to have these things unlocked after you beat the game once. Also, a co-op mode would have been a nice feature. Perhaps in a sequel? Or as the story in this game turn out, a prequel would be more fitting...
All in all, I thoroughly enjoyed this game and it was well worth the money.

This game is true brilliance, it might look like a simple- plain game, but the AI of the animals is just.... Incredibly good. I'll describe it to you quickly, since this is one of the many things that really made me mindblown.
I started out with a Kaumo (There are cultures in the game), basically maxed out his fishing/spear skills and dropped myself near a lake on the east side of the map. I luckily spawned next to a fjord, a fishermans heaven. I started fishing and soon i was stocked for the upcoming 5 days. Used those days to explore for villages. When i came across the cabin of an old kaumo man, I sneaked behind the man and planted my spear in his rear-skull, stole his kota material (kota is a fur-tent) and his food. Then i wen't off to live near the fjord. After i put up my kota it was time to hunt some elk. I looked near my campsite for some elk, and found one. Mostly one elk means there COULD be a herd nearby so i wasted 3-4 days building a trap fence of 3 hexes. During this peroid, i was strongly convinced by the amount of traps that there was atleast a herd of 3+ elk nearby my trap fence. So, i waited for 2 days and my trap pit was filled. With only one elk. This elk made so much tracks that i really thought that there'd be a herd of 3+ elk. I was really annoyed, and just slitted the elks throat with my edge of my spear and let him bleed out to retrieve him the next day.
Now for the finale, when i made my kota, i attracted the attention of a wonderful lynx. These critters are 9/10 times more afraid of you then you of them. Luckily this was the case. But this small lynx was too quick to catch so i instead i placed a trap pit and threw in some bait hoping he'd take it.
He did not, take the bait.
I think he was maddened by the fact i underestimated him, so his time to take revenge was begun.
This fierce predator encircled my kota looking for a entrance to bite me to death while i was asleep. I woke up in the early morning with a thigh wound, then a gruesome hand wound, and then i found out the critter was finishing me off in my sleep! Quickly i grabbed my spear and tried to stab the c*nt but he quickly ran out my kota before i could do him any harm. After that, i feared for my life and crawled to the wooden cabin from the old kaumo man i murdered before. I literally slept next to the rotting carcass of this old man for 13 days straight.
After that it was time to also slit the throat of this forest critter, i wen't back to my kota in the fjord (Still wounded) and camped the entrance of my kota. I knew that our little house cat saw me enter my kota. And then, two hours later he steps in the kota, sees me camping, and sisses at me and tries to leg it. I manage to hit him in the skull but it isn't enough and he books it into the woods. Fun fact the cat is still visiting me every day. And he just won't get trapped by all the trap pits i have laying around. He just memorises all the traps i have build and reminds himself not to go near that area.
The AI is wonderful in this game. This game deserves a 95/100
