Naruto Shippuden: Ultimate Ninja Storm 3 Full Burst is perhaps the most extreme example yet of Namco Bandai's attempt to appeal to the converted and only to the converted. Here's a game not simply for any old Naruto fan, but for Naruto fans who are completely up to date with the story and characters as they currently exist in the anime/manga episodes and are seeking a new way of experiencing previously explored plotlines. If you're not up to date, then not only are you going to struggle enormously with the story as depicted in the game's early stages, but you're going to ruin what you've not yet seen of the TV series. Unfortunately, due to gameplay that is as unwieldy and bloated as its title, Full Burst is not an acceptable way to get yourself up to date with this franchise.
his may be a beat-'em-up, but the primary Ultimate Adventure mode features so little gameplay in comparison to cutscenes and dialogue-heavy exposition that you'd be forgiven for thinking you're sitting through a barely interactive (albeit combat-heavy) soap opera. It feels as though developer CyberConnect2's plan was to create a condensed edition of the anime in which fight scenes are playable, rather than create a game in its own right. This leads to an experience that features such haphazard and irregular pacing that your principal cause for intrigue rests in trying to work out just how long it's going to be before the game asks you to pick up the controller again--and even when you do, the core combat is a shallow, button mashing affair that requires little in the way of skill. While there's definite and worthwhile value in repackaging the events of a beloved series in a new format, there's also value in a game giving you something to do.
There may be a lack of interaction in story mode, but that doesn't hold true for the package as a whole. Including all of the downloadable content released for the original Naruto Shippuden Ultimate Ninja 3 release, the volume of content on offer is gargantuan. Chief among the additions is the extra Ultimate Adventure chapter, which sees Sasuke and Itachi Uchiha take on the nefarious Sage Kabuto, a segment that is so phenomenally difficult in comparison to the rest of the game that all previously learned tactics become essentially redundant. The same Sage Kabuto is unlockable as a playable character if you have the patience to jump through the numerous hoops to unlock him, and there are also some new costumes to swoon over.
he biggest, but certainly not most interesting, piece of extra content comes in the form of supplementary challenge missions. One hundred of these have you beating an opponent in a fight while handicapped in some way--removing your ability to jump, for example, or setting a limit on the number of attacks at your disposal. While these missions do add some welcome variety to the combat, they primarily serve to highlight just how shallow the core mechanics are. Without these externally shoehorned twists on battle, fighting suffers from an overwhelming shallowness that sees you engage autopilot once the basics become second nature. Only during set-piece boss battles are you asked to do something out of the ordinary.
To compound matters, the most members of the enormous character roster plays in the same way. You swap between characters regularly during Ultimate Adventure, but this is done predominantly to facilitate the narrative rather than to spice up gameplay through variety and diversity. Granted, significant and impressive visual flair is achieved by switching often between characters with attacks that are literally out of this world, but that aesthetic quality doesn't remain interesting long enough for the combat inadequacies to be forgiven. Clearly, this is not a game with the remotest desire to cement its place in the bastion of hardcore fighting game legacy, but that doesn't excuse the fact that there's so little meat to the gameplay that you're essentially feasting on elaborately painted bones.
Similar problems exist with Ultimate Adventure's role-playing-game-lite elements, which allow you to roam around a number of different environments with a view to collecting and buying items to use in combat (health potions, strength buffs, and so on) and optionally talking to loitering non-player characters. At times, these moments provide a welcome break from the cutscene/fight/cutscene pattern, but more often than not, they feel designed to artificially lengthen the game and trick you into thinking you're playing something with genuine genre-blending aspirations.
The closest comparison to this format is Asura's Wrath, another of CyberConnect2's offerings. However, where Asura's Wrath succeeds in this style of storytelling thanks to its short length and ferocious pace, Ultimate Ninja Storm 3 suffers from attempting to cover far too much ground for the core mechanics to handle. If you do classify yourself as a Naruto aficionado, then simply having another medium through which to consume the narrative is potentially going to be enough to satisfy you. Without a doubt, everyone else should look elsewhere.

To start, I will say this:
is addictive fun for any fan of the
series. However, to those who either aren't fans of the series or aren't fans of
, there's nothing here for you. Move on.
The game is standard
fare, except with characters from the inexplicably long-running series
. As you may have guessed, I'm not particularly a fan; the writing, though never superb, has plummeted to levels comparable to the execrable
. Fortunately, there's only one mode that forces you through the story. Unfortunately, that mode is also the mode where all the Free Mode stages and some character unlocks come from, and it regrettably glosses over some of the best stories in the whole series and then, later, dwells on some of the absolute worst, reaching a nadir of saturation comparable to other well-known series like
.
Some of the mechanics of gameplay seem designed to frustrate; anything that you can do, your enemies -- no matter what level -- seem able to supersede any action you might take. If you should hit harder, they somehow will manage to outdo you every time, even grunts. You also can't jump at will in this game, which is a personal pet peeve in action game controls, but I will admit that it has fairly little impact overall on gameplay. There is a certain grace, a certain balance to achieve, but it's remarkably hard to figure out for a rather fundamental aspect of a game.
It doesn't help that the game is buggy (not Buggy, n.b.) and at times will be outright unfair to the player due to serious glitches. For example, in some (thankfully few) stages where you're required to prevent enemies from reaching a point -- or the stage ends in defeat, often inexplicably -- it will register them as having reached the point even when they aren't anywhere close, or you've already defeated them. There's no real explanation for this, and there's no solution for it but to learn the stages and act faster than the automated events.
However, the game does have a lot of fun to it. The characters each feel different in terms of play. The game itself doesn't feel like your usual
game either: it has distinct controls that are unique to each character. It feels more like a proper
game taking advantage of an experienced studio to realize it, which is a definite advantage. There are also multiple costumes for most characters already in the game, so it's not something trying to pressure you into buying DLC ad nauseam. The costumes are there, and you can grab them if you want to. But they're just costumes, and as for the stages attached to the packs, they're not really super special. The game does, at the very least, offer plenty of variety and enjoyment for those who like this sort of thing.
And there are so many characters! It's a bit confusing why some characters were playable and others weren't, though, especially with them being in the game but strangely not able to be played. It's also unfortunate (unless there's some way to do it that I don't know) that you can't equip someone with specific support before going out to a certain stage. You're stuck with whomever your allies happen to be on any given stage. Boo. It's especially unfortunate that particularly important characters like Vivi aren't even given in-game representation, but far less significant characters turn up and sometimes are even playable! What's up with that?
But
is not without its problems, and these are typical problems for the more modern crop of
games, especially the ones attached to series and franchises. Like
(but perhaps not as much a chore to play),
really should be considered before purchase. Watch some videos. See if you really mesh with its gameplay. Some of the characters are a delight to play, like Ivankov, and others seem to have been programmed by someone who hated them. There's a tremendous imbalance to them, and it's to the point where characters who aren't good against certain opponents (I'm looking at you, Sanji) are pretty much useless to the point of being unplayable.
It's a fun enough game, obviously, but if you're not a
fan or a
fan, you will not enjoy it. It's just not solid enough to have a broad appeal beyond its twin fanbases. And that's a shame, since even though I don't think much of
at this point, I can usually find enough to enjoy in a

I normally don't expect a whole lot out of anime games, but Pirate Warriors 3 blew my expectations away. I have played plenty of other One Piece games but none of them capture the spirit of the series quite as well as this one does. Being able to plow down massive armies of enemies while unleashing unique devil fruit powers is what One Piece is all about! There are a ton of playable characters and most of them have very different play styles.
I wouldn't call the graphics amazing, but they fit the style of One Piece well. The story is told through both cutscenes and "talking heads." It's pretty cool to see the familiar story unfold in game format, and they have faithfully recreated many scenes from the series in 3D (even right down to some of the more memorable manga panels).
The music is decent and it seems to fit the style of One Piece, but it gets a bit repetitive and doesn't hold up to the soundtrack of the anime. (There is a way to replace the music so check out the forums if it's something that's really important to you). I was also very happy to discover that the original Japanese voice actors from the anime are present, so that really adds to the experience. Clearly you won't grasp the full 900ish episode story line over the course of the game, but it covers the basic plot points well and I think even people who don't follow the series super closely can appreciate the story.
Outside of the main story mode, there is also a 'Dream Log' that gives you more freedom in your character selection. It has different scenarios for you to complete and it adds a ton of replay value to try and unlock all the characters. Think of it as being in the same spirit as Event Mode from Super Smash Bros.
Overall, I would highly recommend this game. If you are a fan of One Piece or Musou games, this will be right up your alley. It is one of my favorite anime games and the best video game representation of One Piece that I have ever found!

A beautiful meld of 3rd Person Action and strategy set in early 1800s Canadian woods, swinging heavily towards strategy part. Main goal of the game is to defend various buildings of importance from the attacks of wolves and werewolves during the night by setting up traps during the day. Selection and placement of traps is incredibly important, it's almost like a puzzle game. Game doesn't force you solve every puzzle perfectly though. When things don't go the way you hoped you can always let your axe do some of the work. You can also customize your character with unlockable skills and items which opens up different solutions.
Story is rather interesting, presented almost as a graphic novel. Really nice soundtrack and probably the best musket action I've seen in a game. What's also worth noting is how well the enemies and combat are balanced. You won't be facing generic tower defense creeps which die by the dozens when you sneeze at them. Game really makes you respect the enemies here as even a single werewolf can make you sweat if you mess up your traps.
Overall, anyone who's into one of either strategy, tower defense, puzzle or resource management will really enjoy this game.

"A great and unique trap-based spin on the tower-defense genre" is the best way I can sum up Sang-Froid with.
What does it have going for it?
- Two characters to choose from.
- Character development, both in terms of equipment and skills.
- Good enemy variety, which will force you to adapt and evolve your strategies.
- An interesting story.
- A compelling artstyle.
- Catchy "folk" soundtrack.
What could be better?
- The fighting system variety, which could be better.
- Performance, which weren't great on my system, but still good enough to beat the game two times.
- The English voice acting for some of the characters (the best voice is definitely the Devil's, though!)
- The experience system, which is pretty basic in what it does while it could be much more.
- The weapons system, which could use less straightforward upgrades and more sidegrades to choose from (similarly to the trinkets, where you only have 3 slots but have multiple useful things to choose in between).
Overall, aside these minor issues, Sang-Froid is an absolutely entertaining game, deserving to be played at least once per character to experience both difficulties provided... and to prepare yourself for Tome II.
I still believe in this game more than I believe in Jesus.

My dad and his dad fought in WWII and as time passes and we get further away from these events and the immediacy of their impact I urge younger gamers to continue to acknowledge what happened by reading and viewing documentaries of WWII.   And of course even some games such as this can help stir your imagination.
This production shows a lot of effort in bringing to life an earlier era, in part by capturing the visual style of architecture, locations, uniforms, gear, vehicles and so on.  It is fair to say that the Polish developers took some pride in the visual recreation of images of the Warsaw uprising.
Picking this up for a bargain, there's no reason to bash this game because it shows a bit of age, or because "multiplayer is dead", but I do recommend that for whatever war games you choose to play, augment your experience by a bit of reading and reflection on the history of true events.

Life got you down?  Could you use a good power trip?  Want to play a character that can throw cars, run up buildings, leap and glide long distances, devour your foes then disguise yourself as them to infiltrate their world, and turn your arms into powerful weaponry?  Look no further than Prototype 2.
One warning: this one's definitely not for the kiddies - this game is full of mayhem, and the main character uses cuss words liberally.
Prototype 2 is open-world, with a main story, many branching side-stories, and lots of bonuses to earn you more POWER!  You start out incredibly powerful, then proceed to ridiculously so - run up a building, leap from the top to the combat chopper that's blasting you, chuck the pilot out the window and take it over yourself, or just leap out and glide, watching the chopper drop to the ground.  Or, after devouring (with tendrils) a biowarfare scientist spreading the plague, run through the city in your lab coat, chucking cars at the Infected monsters.  You have definite missions along each story path, but a lot of freedom on how you want to do it - do you disguise yourself and quietly infiltrate, or decorate the walls?  Do you protect the public to the best of your ability, or drive your tank OVER rush-hour traffic?  You're not forced to be a good guy or a bad guy, though overall your goal is to end the bioengineered plague spreading throughout the city, turning people into monsters.
Now that I've also played Prototype 1, I can say that 2 improved upon the gameplay greatly, and the beginning catches you up on that story.
This is a great game to play when you've had a bad day.
P.S. I defeated the game and earned all the DLC rewards I could on the PS3 before my YLOD ended that - I've only just begun on the Steam version, and it's even better!!

You're a hero summoned by Shenron who fulfilled Trunk's wish of needing a hero who is powerful. A group is rewriting history and it is up to you and the Time Patrol to correct it.
I know we all remember those older Dragon Ball games that had 2D fighting elements, but the graphics were 3D. In Dragon Ball Xenoverse that all pretty much changes. What's even better is, you get to create your own warrior and change his clothing and level him up. It is essentially a RPG. You have the ability to change your character's special moves, buy items, clothes, and skills. It's fun to trick out your character by buying the best gear around. More than just looks, this gear actually adds attributes to your character, and can make him better in certain categories.
You can find NPC's around Toki Toki City called: "masters". These masters can teach you moves that can't be bought from a skill shop. These are very powerful moves, and when you progress with your master all the way, you can use a Z special move, that calls in your master during the attack which makes it even more powerful. You can also switch to different masters and not lose progression, but the Z-special move will no longer work unless you have the active master for that move you're using.
Dragon Ball Xenoverse, looks beautiful on the PC, and doesn't have a frame rate cap that takes away the fun. It controls really well too with a gamepad; i'm using a Steam controller. The game is also challenging, I would argue more challenging than any DBZ ever released. Which for me is a good thing, I like challenges.
There are things about this game however that makes it feel pretty annoying at times. In Toki Toki city for instance you can only jog around, and you can't fly for some odd reason. This makes moving from place to place to buy items feel like a chore at times. And trust me, you will be needing items during these fights that have to be replenished. NPC's also disappear from the city from time to time. If you were looking for someone you wanted to be your teacher, you would have to do missons or quests and hope that person shows up, while you jog slowly around the city trying to find him.
Also, the game only has voice acting during cut scenes, a fight, or dialogue for an important quest. Even though there is voice acting before a quest, there is still a caption box at the bottom and you have to press A to make the dialogue continue. This is pretty much given to the fact the game is not that much space, it is about 9GB. Seems to only have voice animations taken from the Japanese version. The lip movement doesn't at all match the voices.
The last thing I found pretty bad about the game, that doesn't make much sense. Is how when you're fighting and win against an opponent during a story mode quest, when you return to the next fight that is supposed to be a continuation of the last fight, you may end up in a totally different location than you were, and it isn't explained how you got there. It's not a plot hole, because it doesn't necessarily effect the story.
Online multiplayer is Peer-to-Peer, my first time playing I was disappointed. The other person had a good connection, yet he was lagging all over the place.
you can't dodge moves unless you're locked onto your opponent, and when your stamina runs out you are helpless if you get hit.
The good outweighs the bad, the customization and RPG elements will make you feel like you're actually a Dragon Ball character. Hours of fun and enjoyment. You'll enjoy leveling up your character, flying around, and maybe even playing online, if you have a good connection to the host. And maybe hear a few cheesy jokes while you're at it. Great game that feels similar to older Dragon Ball games, while still adding many new features. Dragon Ball has aged very well.

A short visual novel where you are sent on a job to recover information about what happened to an old ship that was found drifting in space. You find that its crew is dead and only the ship's AI is remains to keep you company.
As you play through the story you discover information about a woman called the "Pale Bride" who was forced into a patriarchal society and the downfall of the crew as a whole as a result of it. The story is told mainly through text logs that show letters, diary entries and such with some input from the AI personalities that exist within the computer, *Hyun-ae and *Mute, both representing opposing views on the matter of how the ship's society operated. *Hyun-ae is the woman who hates the ignorance and cruelty of the men and women who blindly accept the traditions and world views forced on them, while *Mute is the maiden who sees no problem with the world and happily agrees with and is very protective of the old gender roles.
The themes are quite mature and depressing, much more so than what you might expect looking at the screenshots. The people described in the logs are mostly awful people, if not by choice then by simply not understanding the opposing point of view, and reading through their entries was really painful at times. I could practically feel my stomach churn as I read the final log.
As for the VN itself, the way it tells its story is quite interesting, as it's mostly you simply investigating text logs. Most of the story takes place in the past and you are merely reading about it as an outside observer, not as a participant. This also makes it that much more painful when you realize that you could do nothing to stop the events that unfolded. The one complaint I have would be regarding the reactor malfunction part, which is somewhat infuriating if you just came for the story. Outside of that, the story and presentation is fine and unique enough to set it apart from most other VNs out there. There isn't as much artwork as most other VNs as it all takes place inside a holographic interface, but I'm fine with that. After all, the story is the important part and not the graphics, but what little there is of it is pretty good. There are multiple paths to take and I would strongly suggest you explore them as well just to get a bigger picture and see how the viewpoints of the two AI personalities conflict.
I'd recommend this VN to people who are a fan of the medium and maybe even those new to it. Just know that the story is a bit darker than the initial impressions would have you believe.

Wasted many hours of my youth with this game long before it ever showed up on Steam.  I've purchased this game 3 times now in one form or another and I don't regret the purchases one bit, the developer more than deserves the money for the time he's poured into this game.
What a lot of roguelikes miss out on is having a balance of complexity, challenge and fun.  There are too many survival roguelikes that are an ocean wide but a puddle's depth, this is not one of them.  This game throws you right into the unforgiving wilderness and you're meant to survive right from the word "go".  Surviving isn't an easy task, food will be hard to come by, but when you actually successfully hunt wildlife you really feel accomplished because it's not black and white simple, more times than not you're going to have your target outrun or outsmart you, or even at times outfight you.
All of your survival skills are stat-based, everything from building shelters, crafting traps, animal tracking, fishing, etc.  and the more you use them the more proficient you become in those skills.  Also beware of hostile creatures or Njerpez warriors roaming the wilderness that will make short work of you early-game.
There is lots of depth here with this game, almost complex at times, especially with the confusing sub-menus within the skills and far-from-optimal UI.  But with enough time you'll soon memorize what all they hotkeys are for each skill.
The game is absolutely unforgiving.  Your first few attempts at it expect hunger to be your biggest enemy, in which you'll need to figure out the best way you'd like to gather food.  Personally I like fishing while laying some snare traps around just outside of camp to try and keep me well fed, but a high foraging skill and enough luck (and proper season) will keep you going as well.
All in all, a fantastic game if you like wilderness survival games that don't stray far from the realm of reality.  It feels quite authentic and I enjoy that.

For a visual novel that has only 2 characters you can interact with, it surprisingly has a lot of depth and characterization than most other visual novels.
The 2 characters do not even do much to establish themselves, all the information about them comes from the logs other people made. The logs, in my opinion, are both a good and bad design choice. It’s good because it’s up to your imagination to process what is going on. On the other hand, it feels like I’m reading a history book all over again! Maybe it’s all the dates and charts that makes me feel that way, but I think it could have been handled a little better.
The game did not need player choices since the backstory mattered more than the characters, but it was neat that they included that. One player choice in particular had such a good and elaborate setup that I consider it most memorable moral choice in any visual novel I have played so far. I’m not going to spoil what it is, but you’ll know it when you see it.
Overall, I recommend this game to both visual novel fans and people who have not played a visual novel before.

THE ROGUELIKE THAT ALL ROGUELIKES SHOULD ABIDE TO AND PAY HEED.

I do recommend you to buy this game, despite it being available for free since 201X in the developer site.
I do recommend you to donate to the developer even after purchasing this game on Steam.

I would say it's worth $5.00 but until the huge bugs are addressed, not worth the full price.
Some reasons why I love this game (which may not be exclusive to the Definitive Edition):
- The graphics are incredible. All of the environments are rich with detail, interesting sights and engaging.
- The world is very open and unrestrictive. You can do pretty much whatever you want, whenever you want.
- Loot respawns, making scavenging always rewarding and worthwhile
- In-game challenges encourage a variation of play-styles and give you okay EXP rewards
- Lots of suspense and surprise. I was downright terrified at a few points in my first walkthrough
- I consider it a decent storyline which is actually based on a real rare virus (although the ending is just terrible imo)
Weaknesses:
My first playthrough, I specialized in throwing sharp weapons and found that zombies disappear too quickly and take my weapons with them. I've lost about 5 of my strongest weapons (at the time they were lost) due to this. I also lost 2 more sharp throwing weapons due to zombie bodies falling into awkward places and not being able to reach the body to retrive the weapon.
Occasionally I died due to ridiculous causes. Once, I was standing behind a door which someone opened. I guess they opened the door so hard I was smooshed against the wall and died. I also fell through the floor on an airplane, died, re-spawned in the same spot, so had to reload my game from last checkpoint.
I don't know if this is different from the original game, but when you beat the story and start over, the rewards when completing campaign quests are not scaled to your level. I'm getting 500 EXP for completing a quest and I need over 600,000 to level.
Occasionally, invisible force fields seem to surround some POI's like cars, buildings, bars... the way may appear clear but you can't move forward, which results in backtracking and taking a different route to get to your destination.
The quest tracking and pathing on the map does not always work or is not clear.
The audio is strange in some aspects. As an example, if an infected is running at you (and screaming) from behind, you won't hear it.  When you turn slightly to either side, it will be quite loud, so the direction of sounds heard needs some fine tuning.
I would like an actual save feature rather than having to rely solely on the checkpoints to save your game.
Overall I think it's worth the cheap price that it's at now, but expect the developer will address the commonly reported issues.

I will begin my review with a disclaimer. If you are uncomfortable with harsh topics such as abuse and alcoholism, this game is not for you. As well as that, if you are easily frustrated or frightened, this is not the game for you. The Archetype, while having an end-goal, offers no explicit objectives beyond 'explore' and will not hold your hand in the slightest. It can be scary, it can be confusing, and that is the point. It's not just a standard game, it's bringing you into the world of this scared young boy with multiple mental issues.
Having finished the Archetype last night, I am very excited for Chapter 2's release (episodic format). The moment the game began, I could feel the dread and very quickly got my first scare. Note that this is not a game that relies on jump-scares, but rather a well-crafted and atmospheric game with the occasional nasty surprise in store.  Nine  year old schitzophrenic Archty, who also suffers from Generalized Anxiety Disorder, is home alone except for his alcoholic father. I admit, while loving the idea of the 16 emotional bars and how they affect Archty, I was skeptical before buying this game. Many works have included schizophrenia and yet portrayed people with schizophrenia poorly, either by making them automatically cloudcookoolander or exaggerating them. This work treated the subject well, as well as including another condition, General Anxiety Disorder. All of this felt treated respectfully and accurately, which is a well done to the developers.
Recently I emailed the devs. and discovered a lot of the aspects that I thought of as bugs were actually features, added in such a way that they're not-obvious, but clear once you think about it. Of course, when you're running in fear, you can't exactly stop to think, which acts to that tension. As well as this though, the devs are extremely respondent to player wishes. I've read online several mentions of changes that have been made due to player wishes before I bought this game, and there's already talks of further updates. This game isn't early access level, but it is still being refined.

Analogue is a visual novel with a lot of choose-your-own-adventure aspects and a touch of dating sim, maybe. In the game, you are investigating a generation ship that disappeared 600 years ago and has just been found. You’re tasked with finding out what happened by reading through the ship’s logs. The ship has two AI which can help you with your mission, though they aren’t particularly reliable narrators.
Gameplay mainly consists of reading through the ship’s logs and asking the AI about them, who may then open up new logs for you. The main interface for accessing the logs is slick, attractive, and very easy to use. There is also a Linux console interface which you use to perform certain actions on the ship, such as enabling or disabling the AI, or downloading the log files. As someone who has never used Linux I found this interface a bit puzzling at first. It’s the first thing you see when the game starts and it took me a few minutes to figure out what it was expecting me to do.
The most exceptional part of the game is the writing. The logs, written as diary entries are enthralling. There are multiple authors and each one has a clear and distinct voice. They paint a picture of a spacefaring society that has somehow regressed into a medieval patriarchy. You don’t get access to all the entries though, and often get things out of order, so you need to piece together the story for yourself. Depending on which AI you have active, you may learn some parts of the story but not others. It’s quite well done.
As for the interaction with the AI though… ehh. One AI is a giggly, cosplay-loving schoolgirl. The other is a casually misogynist and homophobic security program.  If I had known nothing about the creator of this game, Christine Love, I likely would have written the game off as sexist drivel and quit before I got too far in. However, I assumed that there was probably going to be a bigger point or message to the game, so I continued.
I haven’t played a ton of visual novels before, the most similar experience I’ve had to this was Long Live the Queen. An aspect of the genre I find hard to reconcile is that I want to see multiple endings, but the process of replaying and trying new things to get to those endings is exceedingly tedious. Careful use of saves can reduce the amount of repetition, but it’s hard to know exactly when the important branches take place and I find myself mindlessly clicking through things I’ve already read/seen way more than is enjoyable.
Verdict: Recommended for those who like the genre. The writing is strong and the story is compelling. While I personally don’t enjoy the repetitiveness required to experience all of the endings, I think this game will appeal to fans of visual novels.

This game was reviewed using a code given to me by the developers for that purpose.
It's worth noting that this game is about 25% finished; It's not in early access, but the only playable chapter as of this review is chapter 1. (Of a planned 4)
Okay, I'd like to be able to recommend this game. It has some interesting ideas, especially at the intersection of gameplay and story. However, at this point, I just can't. I think the devs are taking player experience into account, and have already made a few changes to chapter one. So, I do plan to come back to this game when the next chapter is released and see how it looks. I will edit this review when I do so.

Upfront: I did not finish the first chapter. I haven't figured out how to progress very far. This game can be very obtuse, and there are no clear goals. I think that's in large part intentional. In this chapter you're playing a nine year old with mental issues. The confusion and lack of clear direction make sense in this setting.
Personally, I'd appreciate a little guidance, but people who are better at this kind of game than me might not have the same sort of issues.
One of the interesting gameplay//story decisions is to unlock the mouse cursor from the viewing mechanic. The game gives you the reasoning for the decision, which I appreciated, since I originally thought that it was just an un-squashed Unity bug.
I have a real problem with this mechanic, however. Since I have more than one screen, it's trivially easy to mouse out of the game without realizing it, and then when I click outside of the game, the game minimizes and I drop to my desktop. It's incredibly annoying, and I can't imagine that it's an intended side effect.
Basically, it's a really interesting concept, but the execution just makes it frustrating.
Next design choice: You can't save your game. (Once more chapters are added, you'll be able to start from any chapter you've reached.) This means that short runs at this game won't do much for you.
Not my favorite thing, but I don't mind this too much; it seems to be a stylistic choice, and I can't really argue with it. I don't particularly appreciate how it's implemented, however.
Condescending menus just aren't necessary, IMO.
There are no in-game options at all. (The unity launcher gives resolution + full screen choices)
The lack of brightness choices is intentional, made for atmosphere, but I think it's a misstep. I've pulled up a few gameplay videos from other places, and there systems are
brighter than my system. I can't make out half of the details in my game that I could see in those videos. I don't want to have to change my monitor settings just for this game :(
There are also no options for sound. This isn't a complete deal breaker, but it seems silly to have to drop to windows to use the system volume controls just so I don't go deaf.
The movement isn't satisfying at all. As a child of nine, I expect quick, smooth movement. Based on my movement speed and the Foley for that movement I feel more like a tired dockworker than a child, no matter how depressed.
The stats are interesting, and they serve as much as a teaser of what kind of stuff you might encounter as anything else. Not sure how some of them are going to be used, but it could be kinda interesting.
There are a few glitches I've run into: sometimes onscreen text runs over itself to the point of complete illegibility, and I've been chased down and killed by a human that was already dead. (not like a zombie, this character was killed, and the model was splayed out on the floor. then it started following me and killed me while I was trying to figure out what was going on.)
This review, as I re-read it, focuses heavily on the negatives, but I don't meant to say that it's terrible or anything like that. It has potential, and it interests me quite a bit, but there's not a lot I can say - in part because of how far I got - without being really spoilery. I also want to point out the problems, because I think they're interesting AND important to notice.
To sum this up, I can't recommend this game now, but I hope to be able to in the future. I can't assign a number grade, but it's not far below positive for me.

Alright so this is my first legit game review and I’ve put a lot of thought into it. I would like to say that on a whole, I really loved this game. Hands down, it is possibly one of my favorite games that I’ve played in the recent years. That being said, I want to break down the pro’s and the cons and I’ll go into a little bit of detail about them. Starting with the cons.
Con- The Animation.
While I think that some of the cutscene animation was done well, I feel like it was lack luster most of the time and that it detracted from the feel of the moment.  There are times it gets very, flaky? I’m not entirely sure what the proper word is, but it seems very rigid and choppy.
Con- The Comic Panels
There are times when in the cutscenes, the comic panels work against the story. Like times when their mouths are just agape and it really detracts from the scene. I don’t really feel like it’s a major con, but it’s something that pulls me out of the world and the moment.
Con- The feeling that every map is just kind of the same.
It’s basic cookie cutter beat em up. That’s not VERY bad but it’s still, after a while I would like some kind of change up. The Dream Log was a nice addition to try and get out of the beat em up monotonous grind, but it just felt like more of the same after a while.
Now for the pro’s.
Pro- It felt like One Piece.
It really did have this grand feel about it, even though it could get repetitive, I loved the feeling of being zoro, or luffy or anyone else of the series. Their powers felt like something deserving of their titles. Like Whitebeard’s ability to basically flip the world on it’s head. It all felt very satisfying.
Pro- The Art
While I think there are times the cutscenes can detract from the moment, when it get’s it right. It get’s it ♥♥♥♥ING right. I loved so many of the scenes where the cutscene was full animation and it felt like how a One Piece game should be and I was so excited and sad and just… it was really well done and well executed.
Pro- The Characters
The unique cast that it offered and just the sheer number of characters with their own unique styles and everything just made this game much more fun to play. It gave me a nice goal to try and unlock them all so I could see all their amazing powers and how they interacted with the crews during the kizuna rushes. I really wanted more and more from them.

Please find the full game review here:
The game design structure is unbelievably well-managed and fortunately, the game is a neat example of "How one can execute their ideas into the virtually living entities!". From the theoretical point of view, the game follows a simple tower/hero-defense pattern : During the daylight, get prepared for the nocturnal attack of the Werewolves; buy weapons; set traps; use the gathered skill points to equip your character with perks and yet you're ready to start a nightmarish night! But in fact, practically, it's not that simple at all cause there are really plenty lot of important things to take care of before embarking on the Werewolves killing adventure. Ladies and Gentlemen, please be assured that "every" game design element will effect your performance during the night! You're not about to face a game, as said, "with minor RPG elements" as the game provides a magnificent hierarchy of character power-ups that reminds you of classic old school RPGs while at the same time regards the fact that the game is being represented to post-modern gamers. And that means the hierarchy system avoids any sort of sophisticated rules of choosing this ability instead of that. The player's first,second even third mistake is not their last mistake as the game gives you the opportunity to think over your strategy once again.
...
In addition to the strategy planning, "Sang-Froid" is also a 3rd-person tactical p.o.v. which make you confront with the enemy with melee or ranged weapons. During the 3rd-person experience you'll have to protect the playable character while defending specified buildings or areas and that's when two style of game-play, tower and hero defense, are mixed up with each other in order to give birth to a brand new mechanism style of survival-horror.
...
By the first glance, the story may seem like a simple "Tale of Werewolves" but as the narration progresses, other twist will save the story from being a linear tale to multiple story lines told in parallel channels in order to add a deep sense of suspense and excitement to the core tale. The story is often narrated by cut-scene in the form of two/three-personage dialogs and sometimes by illustrated cut scenes all of which are empowered with charming voice acting.
The music is perhaps a part of game-play as it won't let you down during the night battles. It's so motivating to hear a well-chosen merry  Celtic/Francophone-Canadian Folk* songs during a face-to-face battle with a Grand Werewolf as it brings hope into your heart letting you chop the Wolf fella in two. That's not the only thing one can mention about the voices in the game. Perhaps you'll admit this after you've hear the warming voice of the tutorials narrator. The sound effects design of the game will make you feel yourself in a real forest of frozen maple trees, near a hut with a smoking chimney, under the pale light of the full moon playing hide-and-seek as the dark clouds pass by and eventually a cry of a wolf in a distance...
...
To conclude, I'd like to state that fortunately "Sang-Froid : A Tales of Werewolves" is based on a great story-line which is followed by appealing presentation, making the excellent game-play a much better experience.

This game has some wonderful atmosphere and tons of pluck.  I have followed it's development from the get go, and have watched it's evolution and how this small team has overcome some legitimately substantial obstacles in the name of getting their game out in the world and breathing on it's own.  I love the steampunk vibe this game has, and they have crafted a world and backstory that could well be the fodder for a good novel.  The races are all distinct with cultures and quirks (Though at last play, i noticed the simplified character race descriptions were gone from the character creation screen.  Likely a bug.. (There ARE a good few of those, though they are always working on it.  Indie - you know how it goes) The gameplay is pretty standard MMO fare, but its also very easy to pick up and run with.  The city itself can be rather overwhelming when you first enter.  It is much more than a traditional games faction hub - WoW's Orgrimar or Dalaran look like roadside tomato stands next to the shear scope of the city here - and with good reason - That city is where all the action is.  You adventure into old ruined quarters, forgotten sewers, and things of that nature instead of ventring off over the hills...  There is a lot to see, and the different districts all have pretty neat style and flavor.  If you like steampunk stuff, you will likely spend good time just admireing the design quirks and details in the different districts.  Combat is fast paced, and generally fun though I do have a gripe concerning the fast monster respawn rate - perhaps owing to this games roots as a browser based program, and the limited instancing, monsters continuously respawn - you clear out an abandoned courtyard, turn around to kill a thing in the alleyway, and turn back to find 4 more monsters in the courtyard.   Makes it feel like a meatgrinder, and eliminates the "Room Clear - move on!!" element of a dungeon crawl in a typical game.. (In fairnes I havent played for a while - this may have been fixed.  I need to dive in and see, but this is the way it was, at least.)  Gear is neat and varied, they have a crafting system, spells are cool enough  and the whole thing is lightweight enough to run on pretty much anything.  (Big point.)  The only other real  talking point i want to bring up is the whole "Arcadia" element.  Originally this game was simply "City of Steam" Published by another company that had a small stable of MMO type games.  That company started to do badly, and the folks at Mechanist really wanted to save their baby, so they bought the rights back, and self published - no small achievement, and also part of how it came to Steam.  Now, presumably due to copyright issues or licensing things they needed another name.  That led to City of Steam: Arcadia" being born.  Along with the new name, they added this Arcadia realm where you can participate in games and fish and do other powerup related stuff.   Problem is, for me at least, it seemed tacked on, and sort of pointless.   I thought the game had better feel without it, but all told its not that big of a deal.. Bottom line, this game has a lot of charm and character - it is original, while still incorporating a lot of the stalwart features you would expect from a big money developer.  It's a little rough in places, but this isnt Blizzard.  This is a few guys from (Canada/UK - dont remember) who moved to China to found a small studio to build the game they wanted to build.  This is an indie studio and the game is their labor of love.  For the size of the team, what they have created is astounding.  I would very much recommend you give it a shot!

I rather enjoyed the first Prototype game. It had its fair share of flaws, but few games let me feel as gosh-darn powerful. I could leap tall buildings in a single bound, bash a tank to pieces, run through a crowd of zombies leaving bloody chunks in my wake... what's not to love? So despite the mediocre reviews the sequel received, it was a no-brainer that game would end up in my library as well. And you know what? I'm glad it did. Like the original, it's not perfect but it's a fun - if gory - superhero fantasy adventure (or maybe super-villain).
The developers went with a more traditional method of storytelling (although they did go a bit heavy on the cut-scenes. but fortunately they are all skippable) and by the last third of the game the adventure does become somewhat repetitive. But the powers are still great and the controls have been streamlined since the original iteration, so it's even easier to become a weapon of mass devastation.
If you're looking for engaging story telling as well as plenty of EXTREMELY cringy/hilarious(depends a bit on the consumer here) moments, this game's a steal with a discount.

This game exceeded my expectations by a lot. I kind of expected it to just be a casual arcade style game but I was pretty far off with that one. The game has a suprising amount of depth and gave me hours and hours of fun for a pretty low price.
Pros:
1. Lots of content
-After playing the game for about a month there were still new things I was discovering that I hadn't known about before. The easily integrated mods really help this a lot too.
2. Difficulty
-The game is very challenging, even on the easier modes. This was something I had mixed feelings about, but mostly saw as positive. You really have to think things out and constantly be aware of what is happening in your settlement or else you could end up having pretty much all your colonists suddenly die, which happened to me on many occasions.
3. Depth
-This game is very unique because not only does it take into account the characters skills but it also gives them a personality that can sometimes affect things even more. You can have a character who is very physically strong rendered useless because they are easily scared when injured and likewise you can have the weakest characters be mentally tough and endure even when all the other colonists are dying around you.
4. Characters
-This is sort of continuing off of my last point, but it was easy to become attached to your colonists. I think if they were to keep adding to the game expanding on the peoples personality traits would be a great idea because it already is such a great part of the game.
5. General activities of the game
-Things like constructing, crafting, mining, growing, etc... allows you to customize your society and is pretty fun for the most part.
Cons:
1. Graphics
-It's not that they're bad really, it's just that there are a few things that are kind of annoying. For example, the fact that you can't see the colonists pants and they look naked when not wearing a shirt...kinda weird. Also, the body shapes of the people could probably be differentiated a little more. There were only like four options and most of them looked kind of odd. Not a big deal, just something they could fix.
2. Slow settlement growth
-I found that if you play the classic stlye mode where you begin with three settlers it's very difficult to increase the size of your colony. You rarely get new settlers and usually for ever colonist you gain one of them dies some horrible death. I recommend changing the scenario so that you start with at least six colonsits. If you're like me and are stubborn and keep trying to build a colony with the classic mode you'll probably spend a lot of time on a colony that's going to be whiped off the mad once you get up to only 5 colonists.
All in all, very solid game. I strongly recomend you get it, and try out some of the great mods for it too.

I started playing Fallout Shelter at the same time as I started this game and I can easily say that Fallout Shelter is ten times more fun than Enemy Front. I am here to tell you a story. A story that will torture your thoughts by day and poison your dreams by night. And though I will do my best, there are no words that can be written, nor brush strokes laid on canvas that can describe the stark and utter horror of the night that Blair decided to absolutely smelt our rations to the floor.
It was a rather frigid cold snap in the quadrum of Decembary. Our food was running low as scarce amount arctic animals existed in my temperate forest, and not a single plant would grow. The ideology behind my greenhouse failed, as a blight took over at the same time. As our food ran low, I had no choice but to feed my colonists artificial food grown in tubes. However, the colonists didn't understand why I did this. They started to get progressively more upset with me. Colonists fought each other day after day until one day a single colonist decided she had enough.
Blair set our rations to ashes. The person who was set to only cook and clean had enough of the tube food and cold and burned what little prosthetic nutrient paste we had and went on to the nearby hallway. I awoke Tommy from his sleep and did what had to be done. She was now to be thrown in jail. I did allow for the chance to re-recruit, but she was rather upset with us for jailing her. To add on, with no one that actively cleaned even when set to only clean, the colonists grew even more upset.
However, now we had no food.  More fights broke out in the colony of Blanket.
"Get me out of here", and, "Make it stop... make it stop..." were frequent thoughts from my colonists. They were all starving, cold, and angry with the filth they lived in. Every time I butchered and cooked an animal, the food was immediately demolished. Eventually a colonist named Michael took it upon himself to eat dead animals raw, as he didn't find it necessary to cook his food. Many followed suit.
They were fed, but getting sick and were sad that they were eating raw food.
"Why not just take 10 seconds and cook your food?!" one would ask. Well, the hyper-intelligent AI decided that it was time for bloody beef. Cold beef that is full of bacteria. They would rather eat decaying corpses than cook something for once.
I watched in terror as my colonists ran outside to scavenge through the few dead, frozen animals that had accumulated throughout the winter. Eventually I did learn how to get rid of blight, but it was too late. Food poisoning was just a daily thing at this point.
With all of my colonists malnourished and agitated, the final straw was the mechanoid invasion. As the robot-like creatures obliterated my turrets and animals I knew my colonists wouldn't stand a chance. However, I had forgotten. Blair was set to recruit. Luckily, Brandon, with his high Talking skill, recruited her at the last moment. The mechanoids were already hurt deeply but no one was physically able to take them down. Brandon immediately stepped outside the prison cell and got gunned down.
It was up to Blair to save the day. I made her pick up Brandon’s weapon and charge the Mechanoids. There were three of them. Two Scythers and a big ol’ fat guy. The fat guy went down first, and the Scythers were missing shots left and right. One Scyther down. Blair, thankfully, had a near max Shooting stat.
Something happened next that I wouldn't wish on my mortal enemy. Blair started to set our house on fire as the Mechanoids were still raiding. I could only watch as my house burned down while no one could stop Blair. Blair went down with the house.
I wept.

As a Dragon Ball/ Dragon Ball Z fan, I love the games that come out of the franchise, and this one was no exception. This game is a pretty well made game, except for a few things. This game is based around more of an RPG aspect, with a leveling system, customizing your character's skill set and attributes, etc. Then there's the A.I. which is rather crap. Your (NPC) allies don't do much but shoot measly ki blasts, that ultimately end up screwing over you, or mess up your combos. They will fight, but they don't do♥♥♥♥♥♥for damage, meaning it's your responsibility to take out the enemy, and if you don't, the NPC (mainly any form of Goku) will steal your kill.
Next we have the Parallel Quests. A good way to level up, but when it comes to getting skills, clothing, etc. it sucks. You have to milk the quest dry before you get what you want, and sometimes it takes longer than that. I've had to do a quest a good 15 to 20 times before I got what I wanted, and for someone who doesn't have a lot of patience, that's saying a lot.
Then there's the part everyone loves, the CaC (create a character). This allows you to choose your race, and cutomize his/ her look to your liking. You can choose from either Majin Buu, Saiyan, Earthling, Namekian, and Frost Demon (Frieza Race). The only thing I wasn't a fan of about it was the selection. I felt as though there weren't too many options, so it didn't really feel like "my character," if you get what I mean.
Overall, this game is good, but not great, it has some flaws and that's to be expected. So if you're a gamer looking for a fighting game, this isn't for you. Like I stated earlier, this game is more or less an RPG, with some Fighting game aspects. If you look at this game from an RPG, you'll have a lot more fun with it.

I've always been attracted by this title but the review rate kind of made me suspicious. Luckily I've bought it in a digital store at a ridiculous price (about 1 or 2 bucks) and even though this is not the game of the year I don't regret the purchase.
Enemy front is an FPS set during WWII using the (always heavy) Cryengine 3. That's all you need to know about the story. You might want to know that you play as Robert Hawkins, a journalist that joined the resistance in Poland, but the narrative structure is filled with flashbacks and sometimes there's also a flashback in a flashback so it might be a bit confusing.
What really matters about this game is the atmosphere. Cryengine is really powerful and full of possibilities and even though it hasn't been used to its full potential the game still delivers nice locations, forests, castles, sieged cities, roads and military bases. The game is definitely not a Triple A production but you can see the attention and inspiration for the locations.
All of this is pleasantly accompanied but a beautiful and inspired and dynamic orchestral soundtrack, made of slow paced movements during explorations and faster arrangements during firefights. Beautiful tunes with an appropriate orchestra for a WWII game: perfect.
What about the gameplay? Well, here you can notice the good and the bad of the game. As an FPS you can obviously go full Rambo for most of the situations but some mission will have mandatory stealth situations. I've read many reviews about it complaining "the stealth mechanic is broken" and so on. I don't think so, you just have to be careful not to be seen by anyone as there's no FOV cone with a ridiculous 10 meters range (MGS, anyone?). As a matter of fact I had absolutely no problem at all with any stealth situation I've been into (there are also a couple of silenced weapons you can run into) infact, except for sieges or battlefield situations, my first approach was always stealth, and IF I fail then I can go full Rambo. The real trouble in the game lies in the enemies AI, as the will just take cover and keep their position, or just run toward you. Very simple, very mild... Except in battlefields where numbers represent a real threat... Unless there are other NPCs on your side that will hold their attention allowing you to take down all enemies like flies...
And it's a real pity because even though the game is a straight tunnel, the fact that you can face most of the situation with your guns or stealthly is a very good thing, not to mention the chance to choose between different paths in few situations... very few actually.
I don't know what to think, it seems to me they've been investing most of their time and resources with the artistic aspect of the game, and the remaining wasn't enough to develop a properly polished gameplay. This doesn't make this game a horrible and lame game, but a game with some raw unpolished gameplay mechanics. I've honestly had my fun with this game, so fully aware of the problems it has and considering the good it can offer I still recommend this game.

I've played this gem of a game for nearly 9 years and I can't even estimate the amount of hours I've devoted to it. I purchased several version licenses during this period prior to it being made available for free and now it's finally obtainable on Steam. I primarily purchased it here to support Sami and Erkka while also giving it a review. The game is still being updated regularly and it appears it'll continue doing so for the unforeseeable future. The developers have refined this piece with commitment and dedication for 25 years which is downright amazing.
It's a very slow paced game where one's choices has ramifications and over time you'll begin to feel an obligation to contemplate every decision you've made and intend to make as it could end up being the last for your character. The unfathomable depth of detail in this game makes it incredible for immersion. The fear of death greatly enhances this and the longer you survive, the greater the anxiety and dismay. Your character actions are based on realism, so consider wisely whether you should fight or flee when stumbling upon a pack of wolves or if you should risk your characters life hunting a bear for that well needed fat and calories for winter. I've always thought it's worth to progress in a sensible manner. Although as such, UnReal World does require a lot of your time. There's also quite a steep learning curve for the controls, but once you've adapted, you'll have it in your muscle memory and it'll become intuitive. The satisfaction you'll feel after setting yourself up to a task and finally completing it weeks later is monumental. While also making it heart breaking when you fail. This is a very difficult game for beginners and death is almost guaranteed. Even the most experienced players will have challenging moments that may end up with their characters dying. However, don't be deterred by the game having permanent player-character deaths. It adds so much to the game and the replay value is immense.
I've loved and hated this game ever since I got it. I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys the earlier generation of games. As well as those who are considering giving them a try.
Posting your own experiences with UnReal World whether good or bad assists potential newcomers in making their decision in whether to purchase the game or not.

Unintuitive, challenging, old-school, and absolutely unforgiving. You need a good imagination and some patience to enjoy this game, and a bit of experience with older, clunkier games will help. I have to disagree with other users - I haven't found the game experience to be "unfair". Yes, sometimes an enemy will get a lucky shot and get you in the head with an arrow, and you'll die. Yes, it is hard to kill bears. Yes, you can work all winter to build a nice cabin, only to absent-mindedly fall through the thinning ice carrying too much gear and drown. In all of these cases, I felt that the challenge was fair, and I could recognize the mistakes I made that led to the death. I felt each death was meaningful and I learned a lot about the game each time, and I am still learning.
Once I got over the initial learning curve, this has easily been one of the best and most immersive experiences I've had with a game. I can't quite describe it, because it looks pretty underwhelming at a first glance, but there is some magic in this game if you are willing to hustle a bit for it. The game constantly challenges you to make tough decisions and manage your time carefully. My favorite part is the wound system - ripping off a piece of my fur cloak and dragging myself to a branch on the ground to splint my broken leg just feels perfect. The animal AI makes hunting a constant challenge, and the wide variety of traps, weapons, and hunting strategies keeps it fresh even hundreds of hours in. On top of that, it just has this indefinable charm - it's a loveable game.
I can't recommend this game to impatient players or those looking for a "smooth" experience. Nor can I recommend it for those looking for a quick couple hours of fun. If you're like me and love simple looking games with unbelivable complexity under the hood, pick it up!

Fair warning. I was able to play the game during development and became friends with the developers, so I may not be the most objective reviewer.
This is a very ambitious game. The overwhelming majority of Steam first-person horror games are virtual walking simulators with perhaps an enemy or two to run from.  This game goes beyond all of that with a lot of interesting mechanics and also a story that is more than just written on notes that you find lying around.  You're an actual character living out a story that goes far beyond the "waking up with amnesia in a haunted house" thing that's been done to death.  You truly feel for the protagonist.
One very interesting mechanic is a full psychological system that tracks every facet of your mood.  I would give examples of how this impacts you, but I don't want to give away any spoilers.  Let's just say you need to be cognizant of your mood as you play as it could take some control away from you and limit your options.  Overall, it's a very smart system that I enjoyed quite a bit.
The scares are pretty solid.  The sound design is okay to above average and provides a good, spooky atmosphere with the occasional, well-done jump scare.  The graphics are excellent and put together extraordinarily well.  This is certainly no asset flip as you see so often.  The enemies are literally scary, particularly the second one you come to, not just random monsters walking about.  Overall, I'd say this is all quite well done.
There are some things you need to know, however, in order to make an informed decision.  Personally, I love the game, but I know how picky some people can be, and there may be things here that will turn you off; for instance, there are only 2 resolutions, 720 and 1080.  There is no brightness setting.  The mouse, by design, is detached from the screen (you are supposed to be psychotic and have a difficult time with everyday acts).  Additionally, there isn't always much in the way of direction on what to do.  Also, there are bugs here and there, but I'm confident those will be worked out by the devs.  Overall, the game could use a little more polish, but is still a great experience to me.
Also, I should point out that the game is being released in four chapters, with only the first being currently available.
If you are a fan of complex horror and aren't afraid of the rough edges, I'd say this is an excellent buy.  You can certainly feel the love that was put into this game in all the little touches here and there.

I want to love this game. And there is so much to love about it. But 20 years of game development seems to have helped it little in the way on being fun for the player. I have played and enjoyed so many other rogue-like games such as Dwarf Fortress and Cataclysm DDA, so I'm fairly used to "so unfair its fun," but often Unreal World seems unwilling to indulge the user in fun.
Combat is infuriatingly unfair. It is not difficult, per se, rather, your opponent has unseen and unfun advantages. I can accept that a highly trained red cloaked barbarian can easily take down my peasant forester. I cannot accept that I can sneak up to the red cloak, hit him with three arrows, stab him multiple times with a spear, and then get one shot and die instantly. The dev believes the game to be balanced, as late game armor and weapons make fighting trivial. But early and mid game, fighting is deadly for you. The dev also claims that NPCs do not have any unfair advantage. Tell that to a bear I shot in the head, whose wounds was "badly bleeding," and who was fading in and out of conscienceness (literally passed out twice), yet was able to run to me in one turn of combat, and proceed to kill me within 2 more turns.
"The world will surely teach one; if nothing else, than to walk slowly." Upon generation of a new character, you're greated with this Finnish proverb. And quickly, you realize how much the game wants you to act upon this proverb. The game is a slog. That may sound bad, but I love the thought of slowly working through a cold, rough game of Unreal World. I want to get to planting broad beans, crafting tonnes of trading goods, making friends with the locals, buying animals, and exploring the giant world. But at times, I find myself wanting something... more. Part of me wants to be self-sufficient in the world of Unreal World. It feels like it was meant to be so. Yet you are desperately tied to the small towns who are your only supply of metal tools and fishing nets (beside those you spawn with). Fustratingly, after 20 years of development, nets cannot be made, and the best tool you can create is stone. Salt, invaluable for curing food, must also be traded for. Seeds can either be spawned with, or traded for, but never found. All of these tie you to the town, which is fine, but limiting.
I want to spawn in Unreal World, get lost in its woods, build a cabin, and create a life for my character all my own. In many ways, I want to lose myself to the Finnish woods. But instead, I find myself losing to bears that cannot be killed with head shots, enemies that can run faster then the flash (yet be "crippled") and controls that cause physical pain in my hands. Unreal World is so close to being a masterpiece, a true icon of video gaming. But I can't reccomend it without warning. The past 20 years have brought about many innovations, and some have yet to pass into the Unreal World.

(Please keep in mind that this is only ONE QUARTER of the total game.)
Whatever horror games, or “emotionally responsive” games you’ve played, you have not played “The Archetype”. Many games advertise “No Handholding”, but I don’t believe it’s ever been so true before. Certainly not in any game I’ve played. If you find something, or accomplish something, or learn something, it is significant, and very rewarding. "The Archetype" provides few hints of any kind.This is a game where you learn from failure, and can expect to play over and over, getting a little further each game (or not.) Quite possibly you will have at least 10 hours in "The Archetype" before you ultimately succeed in the first chapter.
You are Archty, a nine-year old boy with severe emotion and mental issues. Your father is a violent alcoholic, and your mother and three siblings have arrived to your father’s creepy, dark mansion where the two of you live. And, except for your father, they all promptly disappeared. That is ALL you know.
But that’s far from the sum total of Archty’s troubles. The house is also inhabited by some sort of demon(s), and they do nothing to calm Archty’s anxious mood. So, Archety must attempt to stay calm while searching for his family (or whatever happened to them), evading his bat-wielding, drunken father…and avoiding demons (and worse!). All in real-(game)time. And almost everything upsets the poor child, quite understandably.
A dozen psychological traits are constantly monitored in “The Archetype”. Traits such as anger, jealousy, sadness, and nine more. Also, four more significant issues: suicide, neurosis, homicide and psychosis (I think that’s correct.). If any of the four pass a score of 50 (on the way to top out at 100) Archty’s world becomes very troubled, and those issues must be addressed. Medication can be found occasionally, but can’t be saved in inventory. And if any of the four reach 100……..
This is the first of four chapters which take place throughout Archty's life, and they should each be released about two months after the prior chapter.
There is one aspect of “The Archetype” that is unique in my experience; the cursor. It isn’t dead center, it floats on the screen based on the movement of Archty, and how his POV changes. It’s an interesting choice, but in a game this dark (figuratively and literally) it becomes frustrating to locate the dark cursor against a dark background, with only an edge lit for contrast. Easier with time and practice.
There are some aspects of the game potential buyers of “The Archetype” need to know. First, there currently is no means by which to adjust screen brightness, and that’s deliberate (and significant to the atmosphere.) This is so significant that the DEVs actually recommend that the game ONLY be played in the dark. Since not all gamers have this option, it must be considered sooner, rather than later. It also might seem to fail to take into consideration different PCs baselines, the changes in brightness when playing with battery power, and differences in vision (such as with age. I have one game with eight settings for colorblindness alone), but perhaps not, as the DEVS seem very deliberate in all things. There have been discussions about a slider to compensate for these numerous variables, as is commonly used in games. ("The Archetype" has only been out for a matter of days at this point, so do doubt numerous positive changes are yet to be made.) On a separate topic, please be aware that there has also been an issue concerning a genuine 911 call used in the game WITH PERMISSION. That is no longer a concern, as a suitable replacement has been made.
The first time one tries to save “The Archetype” gamers will learn that the feature will not be available until a certain point in the game is reached by the player, and that will likely be after a minimum of an hour of game time. I’ve played 3 - 4 hours (offline, mostly), died 6 – 8 times and haven’t reached that point yet. Also, at this time there is no PAUSE feature (though it is being discussed), so the game will continue while you answer the door or check the baby. At some points in the game the issue is minimal, at others, significant. (Again, in discussion.)
But “fear not!” (except where appropriate, of course), the DEVs of “The Archetype” are very attentive and concerned about their game. Even in just a few days, the number of ideas and suggestions from many gamers that have been responded to is quite reassuring. There have been updates EVERY 2 - 3 days. There seems to be an excellent possibility that “The Archetype” will turn out to be a very special game.
EDIT: Having completed Chapter One, I can say that in retrospect, it's fairly simple (except for one action that I don't believe is in any way intuitive, and is counter to every other similar action in the game, but can be found in the correct Youtube walkthrough.) And there seems to be no means of saving, only of completion, which I presume counts as a "save" for the complete, four-part game.
(As with most Steam games, offline game time is not tracked.)

You may be wondering why I'm about to give this game such a glowing review when I have under an hour of play time on Steam. That's because it's free. It's been free on the internet for ages. Unreal World, developed by Sami Maaranen, and Erkka Lehmus, is a low fantasy roguelike set in Iron Age Finland. Of course, you know that from the description. To get to know this game, you need to immerse yourself in the world. And it's a big, complex world. URW has been updated regularly since its release in 1992. That's 25 years of frequent updates. The most recent version is 3.40, which just left alpha this year. I bought this game to support the devs, and it was worth every penny I paid for it. I'll do a quick rundown of pros and cons.
Pros:
+Small game file - Since it's a simple roguelike, URW doesn't take up much space on your machine. You could probably run this on your 1990s IBM ThinkPad if you wanted to.
+Better graphics than your average 1992 procedurally generated roguelike - Seeing as Sami has been updating the game for the past 25 years, it makes sense that it would look good. It's no Witcher, but it's better than Zork, or ASCII games.
+Great skills system - Skills govern everything from weapon skills to dodging, skiing, sneaking, building, cooking, trapping, fishing, forestry, and agriculture.
+Depth - The game is deep and complex. The game comes with its own encyclopedia (F1), and it's easy to sink hours upon hours into the game, discovering all the little secrets. For example, just yesterday I learned that sometimes, villagers who you help out will tell you the approximate location of buried treasure. That's better than 2 squirrel skins' worth of traded goods.
+Rich world - The world is procedurally generated, but with geographic features like lakes, rivers, rapids, crossings, mountains, hills, seas, cliffs, and forests and swamplands of all kinds, you're unlikely to grow bored of your environment, or run out of space to explore (The game world is huge!) Each culture has its own spheres of influence surrounding their villages, where you will meet people of that culture. (Different cultures are good at different things. For example, the Koivulaiset are good farmers and trappers, but poor physicians and herbalists. They are handy with flails.) You can learn all of this stuff over time just by playing the game.
+Seasons are awesome and add a great degree of "Freshness" to the game - Things are easy in the summer. Food is plentiful, and you can grow what you can't catch, hunt, or trap. It's easy to walk around, and you're in little danger of extreme temperatures. Winter is another story. If you haven't prepared for the long snows by the time the first flakes are falling, you may be doomed. The temperatures drop low enough to easily kill someone who doesn't have enough furs or shelter, the snow is so deep it slows you down and tires you out (Skiing is faster, and makes you less tired), and animals are rare. You probably won't stray far from your cabin. Winter really switches things up, and forces you to manage your time in the summer.
+Mods add additional depth to the game - The game isn't perfect. Sami and Erkka are just two dudes, so they can't put everything they want in the game (Though they always have plans to add more content.) This is where mods come in. 3.40 is very new, so people might still be tweaking their old mods to fit this version, but I can let you know what I play with. Buiodda's Crafts (Which includes some of the mods of Rain, another amazing modder) adds ironworking, bowying, clayworking, and weaving (courtesy of Rain.), among other things. Budz Brewing adds beer and berry wine to the game (It has mead, but that may need another mod to work, because I haven't seen any bees or honey.), as well as barrels, which are great high-capacity containers. For a list of some of the mods, visit
.
+Just try it. - It's free! What do you have to lose? If you love the game, like I did, you might support the devs, so that they can keep working on this incredible project. Link to the official site below.
Negatives
- Not easy - This isn't really a negative, but something which players should keep in mind. At least, it isn't easy to a disgusting casual like me.
- I honestly sat here for quite a while trying to come up with something which I actually don't like about the game, and nothing came to mind. I don't know whether that reflects on URW as a game, or on me as a reviewer.
tl;dr: Incredible game, great creators, great mods, just challenging enough, free from Sami's website, please pay him on Steam if you like it. Please.
