The Archetype is a tense and dark psychological thriller placing you in the shoes of Archty Tolomei, a 9 year old with general anxiety disorder and schizophrenia, who is trying to find his mother and sister’s in his father’s house, after they “vanish” following a fight.
Currently only chapter 1 is available and I have played through part of it. The camera and controls are a bit wobbly to presumably simulate the mental disorders our protagonist is suffering from. You start out in a dark room and the game leaves little direction to the player, letting you explore the game world on your own. An interesting mechanic this game introduces are the psychosis and psychological meters. As you explore the game world, certain objects trigger feelings and emotions in Archty that increase these meters. For example, watching a bottle drop will frighten Archty and increase his fear level, and finding a painting by his mom will increase Archty’s depression/solitude meters. As these meters increase, gameplay will drastically change to reflect the changes in Archty’s psychological condition (for example, controls become inverted, you hear other sounds/hallucinations etc).
This game shows a lot of promise and I recommend it to anyone who enjoys horror atmospheric games.

The Archetype is an episodic indie horror game that puts us in the shoes of Archty Tolomei, a 9 years old boy suffering from several mental illnesses (schizophrenia, for instance), emotional and physical abuse from his mother and father (respectively). Each episode will contain a piece of Archty’s life, ranging from his adolescent years to his last moments on Earth.
Right now, I can only discuss chapter 1 since it’s the only chapter available at the moment. This review will be updated as more chapters are added.
In Chapter 1, we explore Archty’s childhood home. His mother and sisters have vanished mysteriously while his drunken father locks himself in his room, leaving Archty to fend for himself. With nothing to do, we begin searching around and uncover the truth of how the rest of his family vanished so suddenly. The story is mostly told through the notes scattered in his decrepit home and several side comments made by Archty when he encounters objects that either frightens him or bring about memories from the past. I like the story and following Archty’s tale might be an interesting adventure.
The game’s main feature is controlling Archty’s mental health and stabilizing him when he approaches anything that rattles him. Displayed on the HUD are 8 emotional traits: fear, despair, anxiety, envy, jealousy, sadness, anger, and guilt. The other 4 are libido, aggression, depression and solitude (I’m separating these 4 because they’re not exactly emotions.) These 12 influences the 4 main mental statuses. Archty can become suicidal, neurotic, psychotic and homicidal. Each are given a numerical value (0-100. 0 being neutral and 100 being, dangerous…we’re stepping into the…danger zone).
For example, at 100 anger and aggression, I observed that Archty’s homicidal tendencies are brought forward. If you disturb Archty’s father in his room, at this condition, Archty is allowed to pick up either a gun or/and an axe (both are openly found in the house for some reason) and repel the father (btw Archty has a hell of a throw if you use an axe to “take care” of the father.) There are other ways to influence Archty’s mental statuses but it’s up to the player to figure that out for themselves.
The mouse cursor is also detached from the camera, so the cursor doesn’t always follow the camera. You might be turning the camera to the right but the cursor is at the bottom of the screen. This is added to simulate Archty’s inability to focus very well due to his mental issue. This feature is annoying at the beginning and I simply had to adapt when interacting with doors and items. I wish this is optional because I just want to click “E” to select stuff. The HUD can be messy to look at with all traits on the screen at once but that is easily fixed by hiding it.
So far, the game isn’t scary but there are times when the situation shifts its direction and becomes more unsettling. Namely, when Archty is experiencing his psychotic episodes, he begins to hear whispers (random voices playing backwards). He will start hallucinating (the screen will start shaking, coupled with bright lights and impaired vision. I cannot say in confidence that this represents what a person with Schizophrenia would see through one of their episodes, however, I’ve worked with a couple of children with Schizophrenia, and some of the symptoms these kids have experienced (hearing voices that aren’t their own, clicking, visual hallucinations) are present in the game. The developers attempt to mimic them.
The two hostiles in the game, the mother and father, aren’t as threatening as you would think, with the dad wielding a bat, and the mother being a ghost, these two turned into the comic relief of the game. I say that because while I was playing, their AI was exploitable because they would not attack when I was near them. Giving them a bear hug is fine but walking away from them hurts their feelings so much, they want to kill you. I believe this will be patched but I found this glitch hilarious.
There is a scavenger hunt in the first chapter, in a form of gathering ingredients for a ritual to destroy a clingy apparition and I needed some time to gather them all. It took me about 5 hours to finish the first chapter. I got stuck for a bit.
The graphics is nothing to preach about. They’re pre-made assets from the Unity asset store so most likely, you’ll recognize the environment. Also, besides from the configuration menu that comes along any Unity game, there are no other graphical options. My small problem with the game is that there is no way to turn up the brightness. There is a flashlight but in my opinion, the throw of the light is terrible. I found myself squinting at times. That’s just me though.
I have no problems in turns of framerate drops and crashes but I’ve witness several non-gamebreaking bugs that ruins the atmosphere at times. I have read people reporting of crashing during start-up and I am unsure if this has been resolved. The developers are responsive and I’ve already brought to their attention several problems I have with their game.
All and all, chapter 1 is an okay start for The Archetype. It’s enough for me to want to see what happens next.
TL;DR
Pros:
- Interesting story
- Intriguing game mechanics (controlling Archty’s mental health can be difficult to manage)
- Might bring some awareness to the mental illnesses mentioned in the game
- Atmosphere can be unsettling at times
Cons:
- Buggy
- AI is exploitable
- Interacting with doors and items can be irritating
- Game is too dark (needs brightness option)
- Bare graphical options
- Reported crashes from a few players (not sure it’s solved yet)

MY OLD REVIEW:
What a shame to have to leave a negative reveiw for this. It should've been the best game ever. A tribal-ear survival game with minimalistic graphics and over 25 years in development, with great depth accumulated over time? Yes, please! I really wanted this game to work out and was willing to forgive it a lot, but it just fell flat on its face because, apparently, it looks like in those 25 years nobody bothered to put any time whatsoever into a more intuitive and convenient UI or just improve the gameplay experience in general, other than adding more to the game's amazing depth.
It started out with technical issues right off the bat. It took over 2 hours of research, manually installing VC++ distributables  of various versions to even get this game to run (apparently if anything goes wrong during the game's original distributable installation, it never tries to install them again and just crashes on every start without giving you any errors; not even deleting all game files and redownloading/reinstalling fixes the issue).
Having gotten past the technical stuff, I was excited to play. To say the user interface is clunky is to say nothing. You can do almost nothing with the mouse and menus. You're supposed to remember all the key shortcuts in order to play this. Want to drop something? Can't just go into inventory and drop what you see from there like a normal game would. You have to press "d" on your keyboard, then mark the item(s) in the resulting drop menu with "ENTER" and then when you are done selecting press "SPACE". Want to craft something? Press "s" for skills. Want to put on your mittens because they game tells you your hands are getting cold? Press "W". Pay attention, that's upper case W, because lower case w is reserved for selecting your weapons. The only way it could get worse is if you had to type in action words a-la 1985 games.
The game does a poor job of informing you of what's happening and stopping time accelleration, leading to unfriendly outcomes. The tutorial guided me through felling a tree and building a fire and, after giving me a fresh pike, asked me to cook it. The pike will be cooking for a few hours, it said, so why don't you go try crafting something? OK, I went to the felled tree, selected the woodworking menu, and tried to make some boards. No indication how long it will take, time accelleration kicks in. Three times through the process a bird flies over, and the game helpfully asks if I want to stop what I'm doing. Well, no, I have no bow and so no way to interact with it, so I keep going. Then, in very quick succession and with no indication other than pale text in the game log, I get hungry, the pike starts to smell like it's burning. I frantically cancel the action manually and go pick up the pike. It hasn't burned, but it has spoiled. How on Earth does a fresh fish spoil in the middle of grilling?! Whatever, let's eat some food we started with instead and go finish those boards. Time accelleration starts again until without any warning you collapse and eventually sleep. Wake up in the morning with fully depleted hunger and bar, and a red state of "malnourished" barely able to get up. This, after eating full the night before, right after the game tutorial told me I can go without food for a couple of weeks. Thirst, which the game warned about was critical, didn't even rise past half in all this time.
Now, I'm willing to put up with a ceratin level of junky UI and buggy mechanics from a game I like, but let's also not forget that this is a rogue-like. A bug or a dumb outdated UI decision can be the undoing of your character. As somebody on the forum wrote, they spent months building a house, then built a fire close to it and it just burnt down, leading them to rage-quit and abandon the game for a while. I can see stuff like that happening a lot in this game.
Now, it's undeniable that the game has a loyal following, so there must be a way to get past all this stuff and see into the good sides of the game if you invest enough time and effort, but in the time I got while still being able to refund, all I saw was a buggy, poorly designed and unplayable mess that belongs in the '90s where it crawled out from.

I was able to try this game pre-release during a live-stream, and while there were some bugs here and there, the devs were awesome enough to hotfix on the fly, so they're definitely attentive to any problems that may arise, which is a definite plus!
As far as the game itself goes, I've had a great time with it.  I feel it gives a great, creeping horror kind of feeling, which I get a lot more enjoyment out of than constant jumpscares, which tend to wear thin after a while.  The disconnected controls can sometimes make things a little difficult to focus your view on, but with what Archty has going on in his head...well...it just ends up adding something to it.  It starts to feel like a disconnect between your hands and your mind, which actually ends up being a pretty effective way to express his instability..It's not easy for him to focus on things, so why have his focus be locked to the center of the screen? It ends up disorienting you, forcing you to focus more on what you're trying to do, so that when the game does unleash one of its scares on you, it catches you completely off-guard because you'll glimpse something out of the corner of your eye, question whether you saw it or not, then get hit in the face with it when you go for a second look.  So I can see how it can be frustrating, but thematically I feel like it really makes sense.
Now that the game's released, I definitely plan to start going through and seeing how various things affect the different states, there's chances for a lot of things here, and for it being a first game from a 2 person team, I was impressed.  Definitely can't wait to see the effects the events of Chapter 1 are going to leave on Archty in the coming chapters, especially as the team hones their skills to the fine point of an ice pick, to bury in our mental states.

I am mad. Sure, this game is good - sort of. I enjoy playing it, and have spent many hours playing it, but there are a few glaring issues which still make me so horribly upset that I cannot write a positive review.
The first, and foremost issue, is combat. In a sentence: Wow, it sucks really badly.
Let me be clear: the system itself for combat is quite cool! It uses body parts, different attack types, bleeding, various injuries... It's extensive, and very fun! In theory. In truth, trying to fight literally ANYTHING that isn't completely subdued in a trap is as fluid and balanced as Niagra Falls - which is to say, not at all. Unless you get a lucky strike early on in a fight, you are doomed to die as the AI lands nearly every attack (with at least glancing blows) and will eventually kill you or knock you out, whereupon you also die OR lose all your stuff. Let me give you a recent example. I made a character, high stats all around, good Strength and Endurance and Speed and Agility, good Sword, Spear, and Block skill, and chose the Bandits! start. I began with a Broadsword, which was brilliant! I waited, baited the bandits to a bottleneck in the trees, and combat began.
Only two attacks in and I had landed a solid blow on his neck with my broadsword. 'Huzzah!', I thought, assuming that would be the end of him - except, he kept attacking me. Yes, you heard that right - a man whose throat had been slashed (not a glancing hit mind you, a 'solid strike' with the Edge) by a SWORD continued beating me with his stick. He then conked me on the head with what is the equivalent of a god-damn mother ♥♥♥♥ing BRANCH and I was instantly unconscious. He took all my things and left me for dead in the wilderness.
What?! Are you kidding me? And that's not the first time! I have been MASTER level upon character creation with weapons, been given said weapons, and then tossed into the fray only to die to the first combatant I encounter (Human or Animal, it matters little to this worthlessly lopsided combat system) and be forced to re-start. I barely land any hits that are more than mere grazes unless the person is previously completely incapacitated, and even when I do they miraculously shrug off serious injuries or the fear of death and beat me like a punching bag. It's horrendous.
This is the main issue with this game, in my opinion - and with it being the only way to ever gain new items without literal in-game weeks or even months of grinding (hello, Craft Wooden Bowl option!) or what essentially boils down to RNG (here's lookin' at you, Trapping and Hideworking! Better hope you can find 12 OTHER Bear Hides that aren't Ragged or Harsh!), it's horrid. It's like soggy porridge laced with gravel, scumming up what would be a fine brunch otherwise.
Tl;DR? Combat sucks because the AI hits almost everything and despite your skills and stats you are a bump on the log.
And don't even get me STARTED on how crass the food spoilage is. Yes, food spoils, this is true and by no means do I mean it should be removed. But, unless you are a hunting or trapping G O D, fishing is the only sustainable way to stay alive and gain food in the entire game, since Smoking, Drying, and Salting are arbitrarily hard and un-doable until certain requirements are met (Smoking requires you to have built a home or use an already-built home in a village, which is wildly inconvenient, Drying requires it to be WINTER SPECIFICALLY, and Salting means you need to trade the Driik (( yes only one tribe can provide salt )) and they charge you like it's their god-damn lifeblood). This leads to a life spent almost always with the 'I want to be a Fisherman' start, as to guarantee a Fishing Rod, as even large take downs like Elk and Bears will still spoil in a few days regardless of how quickly you eat. And once that's gone, well, good luck finding more, you poor sod!
Update: As I was writing this, I tried again on the combat thing. After landing two hits to the head (one even being a 'perfectly executed thrust to his skull!') of an enemy, I proceeded to never hit him again for literally 30 turns of combat as all my weapons broke in quick succession, he never died or fell unconscious from blood loss as getting a SPEAR TO THE HEAD WOULD DO, and I died. And then, after trying AGAIN, I missed an attack on an Unconscious opponent. What?

Having put over 400 hours into the game and bought nearly all of the DLC, I can recommend this game, but I would like to outline some things in regards to the game's previous seasons and the direction I feel they're taking.
I deeply enjoyed season 2 of this game, and I feel that the wave system was not actually a bad idea -- I feel that it could even be re-implemented in the form of another mode.
Since then, the maps and art design have changed to a system where enemies have to be individually encountered, which isn't a bad thing, but the accompanying levels have taken a hit in terms of atmosphere.
The randomized levels aren't a bad idea, but when you go back and look at the overall feel of Act I - I or Act VII as a whole back in season 2, it's honestly disappointing to see that the current levels come off as a mashup of tiles and nothing else; there's nothing intriguing about the locations or the direction the hero is supposed to be taking in terms of the plot progression.
This isn't even taking into account the actual gameplay, which in and of itself is a roller coaster of quality.
Early game stays interesting because of discovery, both of all the different locations and your character's talents/abilities.
There are also various pickups like potions and relics which can give stat bonuses, special abilities, or can even act as weapons themselves, but these become useless late-game due to the effects being proportionately minimal and not scaling with your character as you level up.
The problem with the characters themselves is that a lot of characters have abilities that are near useless, and so you spend most of your time working toward a build similar to what everyone else has rather than something that would accomodate your preferred playstyle with the character.
Even worse, there's a cap on the amount of points you can put into a character's individual ability, so that is where the runes come in, which increase your character's abilities or stats.
The rune system is fine, and there's nothing wrong with higher value runes being more rare, but there is absolutely no reason that there should be a chance-based system in upgrading runes when the cost of upgrading gets higher every time using a currency that's semi-rare to begin with (especially keeping in mind that gold is useless outside of buying wormhole keys).
Also, there's now a strange bug with the equipment, where several equipment names have been taken out in exchange for very generic names, so most characters will have a golden amulet, charm of the witch, heavy boots, steel gloves, steel armor, and skull cap as opposed to mythril armor or charm of the gladiator, etc etc.
This, in addition to lower drop rates and lowered item level scaling (and taking out enemies and locations in wormholes), has made this season terribly grind-heavy and monotonous, actively discouraging people who are getting into the game.
The player should always feel a sense of progression, and while I can understand wanting to level the playing field, having to stop every few wormholes to farm for hours and hours and get 0 drops from bosses on the hardest difficulty (with some creating impossible-to-dodge situations like Anubis chain lightning + meteor strike + electricity field or Damien spawning 20 flies that rush you and bodyblock you + detached head chasing you + blood surge in addition to the numerous unfair enemies with traits like waller + arcana or reflection + teleport in a game where most hits take anywhere form half to all of your life even with the best equipment), it's honestly difficult to recommend this to others, having known what the game was and knowing what the game could be with some effort.
In closing, it would be nice to see more enemy/level variety in wormholes, level design equivalent to season 2, better talents to encourage variety in builds (and to keep melee classes reasonably playable), currency that's actually useful, a scaling system to keep relics/potions worth obtaining, and, provided the item level scaling won't be changed, a higher drop rate from act bosses (or better drops from ancient monsters).
Even just focusing on the aesthetics can keep players entertained and willing to play for longer, but that shouldn't detract form the rest of what I've said.
Regardless of the game's current shortcomings, I believe the devs have what it takes to make this game into something great, especially seeing how far the game has come since season 1.
All things considered, I rate this game in its current season (4) a 6.5 out of 10.

The controls are very easy: WASD to move, arrow keys or LMB to shoot. The game generously shows which key to hit to do a certain thing like opening your skills menu for example. Navigating through your inventory is a bit weird and I still find it awkward to use. When playing the game, you should be comfortable for the most part since most of the action keys are in the same area (number keys for using skills, Q for potions, etc...).
First of all, this game lives up to the bullet hell genre! When you don't have a weapon that has 10%+ HP on hit, you better be a god-tier dodger. The game wants you to be challenged. Just when you thought you were doing good at the game, you get charged by five enemies while simultaneously having your shots getting reflected back at you, resulting in your abrupt death. When you do die, you lose all of your relics that you worked so hard to obtain. There are a lot of different bosses with a lot of different kinds of tricks. There are also a lot of different effects that happen too. For example, on toxic difficulty, there are random volcanoes that pop out of no where and will destroy your health. You step on pink goo that worms deployed and you get slowed and killed. Hero siege has a lot of different tricks and surprises for the players to encounter and experience.
The game is pretty balanced. The items that drop from enemies scale with the difficulty chosen and the act you are in. The Rune levels also scale, the enemy toughness scales too. It matches with the amount of other players there are with you too. You might think that the bosses are difficult when you just start, but you have to keep in mind that this game is meant to be challenging.
Sure, this game has in-game purchasing but the extra classes aren't essential to the game. I find that playing default classes like marksman or pyromancer will still be incredibly powerful to play with.
The graphics are pleasant to look at. The objects, items, enemies, bosses, characters, etc... all match with everything else. The sprites aren't bad-looking and the artists of Hero Siege did their job well. You can also customize things! On your character, you are able to purchase hats with crystals that you find while playing the game. There is a plethera of options to choose from. You can also customize the HUD, I have mine selected as the cheese one.
The sounds in the game are pretty well-done. The music in almost any area is creepy and ominous in a way. The voice of the shopkeeper matches well with how he looks. The sounds of the arrows being fired from my bow are consistent and not delayed, the sound of gold being picked up is satisfying and the sounds after beating a boss makes you feel relieved and accomplished.
The community of Hero Siege is quite small and private. Most of the games are people in private servers by themselves or with friends. Occasionally, there will be people looking for players to do
with. From my minimal experience with playing with other people, I can say that the communtiy isn't the worst. There's not really anyone being rude and there are some friendly people talking in the lobby periodically.
For the most part, Hero Siege is fun and challenging. The experience can be enhanced by bringing a few determined friends along and fighting your way through waves of monsters and bosses while obtaining items to help you along the way. The game can easily get boring alone which is why I don't play the game so much. The small community along with my lack of friends leads me to not play this game as much. However, I did have fun playing this game for a while. When there is an update, the population of this game increases so, upon the release of an update is the best time to play Hero Siege.

This is one of the best visual novels I've ever played.
The premise is simple, yet compelling. You are a nameless, genderless, ageless space investigator sent to read the logs of the long-dead in order to understand what happened on board the generation ship, Mugunghwa. You do this with the assistances of two AI, *Hyun-ae, a young woman, and *Mute, the ship's security system. They are the powerful personalities that make this game worth playing, and if you're anything like me, you will fall in love with them both.
Warning: the logs deal with physical and emotional abuse aimed towards children. It also explores homophobia, speifically towards lesbians, misogyny and classism. Forgive me if I spelt any of those words wrong.
Analogue's gameplay is entirely text based. You will be reading log after log after log. Initially, the logs aren't that interesting, but very quickly, I was drawn into the game. The GUI is sleek and actually does feel like a futuristic computer. It's simple and easy to use, and it's unlikely you'll ever get lost. The most confusing it gets is when you need to prompt the AI to search for more logs by clicking on logs written by the particular person you wish to investigate.
(I hope that sentence made sense).
The real focus of this game is the AI, although Analogue focuses more on *Hyun-ae then *Mute. (*Mute's game is Hate Plus, the sequel to Analogue, which I also recommend you buy). I won't spoil anything, but through these women, you're confronted with some serious moral ambiguity. Actions and beliefs that are objectively terrible are rationalized, and suddenly you're not sure what to think.
The minor characters are basically every person you'll read about in the logs. They all serve their purpose; no-one is focused on so extensively that they over-shadow everyone else. Moreover, they all feel like real people. The logs are well written and feel genuine...although I do feel the lesbian sex between too women was written in more detail then strictly necessary.
Your choices matter in this game, btw, particular when you're finally given the option to stop being a genderless and ageless entity. Whether you select male or female will influnce one AI significantly.
Overall, this is a very good game. It's heart-felt, its well-written, its fascinating, and its cheap. Give Analogue a go, you won't regret it :)

The devs while struggling through tough times have managed to keep this game alive for many years and while progress is slow, i'm sure the end result will be worth it.
This will be a coop game at heart with multiplayer integrated in with it.  ZPS decided to first start with the player mechanics, so multiplayer was the first thing being developed.  While there are not a lot of people on it, you can still get games going and i've had fun in the Wargames mode known as hell week.  There are still enough people in the game to get into intense firefights with.  While the game is barebones as of now, I believe there will be major progress once this game gets a publisher.  I have the patience to wait and love the game and want to see something truely capture the feeling of a sci-fi first contact scenario.

-The weapon play(Even with only 3 weapons being available)
-Art and character design

And now for the one negative:
-Lack of content (This is understandable though because of the current state of the dev team and lack of a publisher)

Was overall quite an interesting visual novel with unique aspects. Haven't gotten around to the second game in the series at the time I wrote this post, so my review is based on only this first one and what I've completed of it thus far.
Graphics: 8.5/10
For a low priced VN (9.99) the graphics were pretty amazing. I wasn't expecting the graphics to be were they were, so it was very nice to be surprised by this.
Gameplay: 8/10
Probably one of the most interesting things about this VN. It is a VN, so don't expect 3D action, but man were some of the puzzles and choices intruiging. The puzzles were not hard, but not necessarily easy. One of them even gives an alternate ending, which is interesting. I also like the computer aspect where you have to type in the information via the keyboard. Over-all. it was an interesting style and I would love to see more styles like this.
Characters: 7.5/10
The characters were also quite interesting. Both girls had their own unique personality, making you either hate or like them (I liked both personally). The design for both of them were also nicely done, adding more to the uniqueness of them. I didn't rate an 8 due to the fact that only one of the 2 had a in-depth background while the other was given some, but nowhere near as much as the other. (Might change after getting rest of trophies)
Story: 7.5/10
The story was really, I mean really. interesting. It took place in a spaceship out in space. You have a possibility to end up with 1 of 2 girls (or both if you get the harem ending) or obtain the bad ending. This much is common in most VNs, but the uniqueness of this one is the files and history. Both the files and certain options you make will give detailed information about the past of the game's story. Then there's the fact that the story of the second game is determined by what ending you got in the first one, a little twist not seen in most. Put simply, a wonderfuly (but short) storyline with interesting twists.
Over-All: 8/10
I would most certainly recommend this to both begginers and advanced VN readers.  =(^,.,^)=

Enemy Front keeps a solid 60+ frame rate the entirity of the game - I often exceeded 100 FPS. The game looks good while doing it, though the shadows on faces can be pixelated and the ragdolls of dead enemies looks as goofy as any other game with ragdoll effects.
You play as a field reporter, who decided to get his war stories by fighting in the war himself. The game takes places exclusively in Europe, mostly around Poland and Norway. This means the main campaign contains mostly Non-American weapons, until the bonus Saint-Naizare mission. All the weapons feel pretty good, except occasionally sniper rifles that "miss" even though your reticle is right on them. This seems to be an issue in certain points - at one point my shots didn't hit the enemies, but they didn't hear them either, possibly due to a bug or scipted event issue. Thankfully, you can carry two weapons (the silenced bolt-action De Lisle is awesome!) and a pistol. Speaking of bugs, there is a lengthy bug thread in the Steam discussion forums that unfortunately has not been addressed by the developer. Outside of the ragdoll weirdness, the only true game breaking bugs are two moments I was stuck in place being not able to move and enemies being invincible in the optional bonus mission. The enemy AI feels fairly stupid as well, making the Expert difficult a breeze for experienced FPS players, except for the fast player deaths. It's relatively easy to flank enemies or take advantage of the classic "wait until they pop up their heads and shoot them" tactic that was popularized by shooters like Call of Duty. Allied AI is largely useless, other than being distractions for the enemies that the newspaper reporter will eventually kill - because that makes sense.
=============================
Sometimes when I play a game, I will make notes that I will use in my full Steam review. I left them here below for anybody that might be interested in the points that got my attention.
Review notes:
- Solid "classic Call of Duty" clone. Doesn't do too much wrong, but nothing spectacular either
- solid framerate on my machine at highest settings - It looks good and "plays good"
- Highest difficulty will make enemies kill you relatively quickly, but not as fast as the hardest difficulty in CoD games. Enemies can be killed quickly, so even hard mode is easy, without being annoying, if you're decent at FPS games
- Enemies have partial ragdolls, resulting in some amusing deaths, or annoying animations that give you the appearance of an alive enemy even though he is dead, almost like Goldeneye 007
- One level features the De Lisle, a silenced bolt action rifle I've never seen in any WW2 FPS. Impressive by WW2 era standards, but unremarkable by todays standards, it has near instantly become one of my favorite WW2 era weapons because of this game
- Multiplayer is dead, though what I saw of it on videos looked unimpressive.
- can hold two primary weapons and a sidearm (including a silenced Welrod in some levels). isn't this already more than what you get from most CoD games?
- NPCs can be janky, getting stuck on things, nearly flying of into space, teabagging your corpse when you die, are some of the things I've seen. Check out the Community hub screenshots and gifs for more funny and odd examples
- On more than one occasion I have become stuck in place. I got lucky to get out, but you may have to reload the checkpoint or game to restart the game to fix it at times.
- Gnarly, pixelated shadows on in game faces sometimes
- Second/DLC campaign is glitched? At some point during the first mission, the enemies could not be hurt by my bullets

Overall: 7/10 Has good level layout and weapon physics with massive graphical issues that require turning down the settings just to see what is going on. Also the story is just a series of random missions to highlight how much Hawkins is really BJ Blaskowitz, but not enough to get sued over.
I played through the campaign and bonus mission on Casual difficulty. I recommend only playing on that difficulty because the game has the Elder Scrolls 4: Oblivion effect; everything is glowing, oversaturated, and unrealistically affects the player's vision. Due to the terrain glowing all the time, it's very difficult to see the enemy while they are AI and don't require sight to accurately shoot you. I can only imagine the hell multiplayer would be where anyone who wants a chance to succeed has to turn off all the graphics just to spot somebody.
Some missions were completely bugged like the snow mission where the snowstorm effect blurred over the entire screen and I couldn't see anything past 5 feet of the character. It wasn't as intended because every now and then while aiming, the filter would clear up and I could see it was a mild blizzard. That and two crashes during my playthrough.
The actual story telling was well done when they bothered to mention the story. The gist of the game's plot is Hawkins, the main character you play as, is helping the Poles during the Warsaw rebellion in WW2. He is helping just to get front line access to great photographs and first hand experience on the scene. Helping to save lives is a byproduct of his career and they make about three attempts to highlight that throughout the campaign. The only downside to the story is the game doesn't really do anything with the missions. They are there to tell you how amazing Hawkins is, nothing more. Also, the first five missions have no transition scenes and progress the timeline drastically with no explanation. It's weird pacing altogether, but has some cool scenes to experience.
There's nothing terribly wrong with EnemyFront, but to it's fault, it's so bland to recommend to everyone interested in a FPS. I liked the game though and would recommend people give it a try just to experience the presentation.

-The campaign has a decent length (around 15 hours) and the environments are varied enough. Warsaw, the French countryside, a prison camp, the V2 facilities...

A very fun 'Beach Head' inspired type of game, which actually delivers great chaotic action.
You have 3 maps, each one that has to be unlocked by meeting the requirements of a map in order to move to the next one.
You also have a level up system, which makes your gun stronger and faster, support (like artillery or infantry) more useful, health upgrades and finally rocket launcher upgrades.
The first map starts pretty slow, but this made me underestimate the time i could take to shoot the boats one by one, so i was suprised when they launched a full blown counter attack from my right flank and quickly overrun me. It quickly turned into a big chaotic battlefield.
You can see limbs flying off, IS soldiers crawling their last moments towards you, suicide bombers can be shot to explode their entire squad, machine gunners run out of their vehicles before the vehicle explodes. Great little details which make the game so much better.
Graphics are pretty good considering the amount of craziness going on in the battlefield, i'm suprised my system can hold up (optimization is good).
Replayability is great too, because you have global high scores, achievements and a level up system.
This on-rails, but don't let that deceive you, because this game is worth every cent.

"During the winter of 1858 something happened in lower Canada, near Wolvesvale.
No one truly remembers what happened, but rumor has it that the DEVIL came to town...
...and that two lumberjacks hunted down his minions every night.
They were, the OCARROLL BROTHERS!
With solid PLANNING during the day...
and cold EXECUTION at night...
...they became FEARLESS!"
That's how the devs summarized the game in its trailer, and there's really not much to add to it. One of the best games I've ever played, worth every penny. Only downside I could think of is the lack of local and/or online co-op, though the devs were thinking of it for a possible sequel...
This game is a great mix strategy, action, rpg and tower defense genres where you take the role of the O'carroll brothers, who are being besieged by Devil's minions, which are composed of all kind of wolves, werewolves and other mythical creatures.
To protect each other and their cabin, they will have to plan during the day the strategy to follow at night, using their sister's foretelling powers to determine the number, type, wave and initial spawn point of the enemies that will attack during the night.
With that information you will have to set up the traps for them, and even go to town to buy guns and items. But one must be wise spending their money and/or action points in doing so.
Night starts as a tower defense game where you have to avoid enemies from destroying your buildings, though you can(and must) take direct action and activate some traps manually, or kill the enemies which haven't fell on them; since the game also features wind, which can render useless all your setup if you are detected when least expected.
As for the rpg part, game features a complete set of skills to customize and develop your style by improving your character and traps in the way that fits you better.
Have to say that game can be very, very punishing with poor planning and/or execution and stealth. It's actually quite challenging since you will have to set up your traps, then memorize the enemies, waves and spawn points in order to pull it off correctly and quickly under pressure and against the clock(not an actual timer, though the game is quite fast paced)...
Last but not least, game's atmosphere and music are really sublime.

A four-pack was purchased for family multi-player use in a mixed Windows and SteamOS / Linux environment.  On my Linux system, Online Multiplayer was not possible.  The game reported "Steam connection failed. Please restart steam".  Restarts had no positive impact.  All the techniques I use to get games like Terraria (which is working through Steam), Minecraft, etc. did not fix it, and frankly, I'm not interested in fiddling with it for hours to figure out what the problem is, since spinning it up in single player shows a mob spammy game that easily overwhelms if you're not used to two handing a dual stick game on a keyboard... I'm new to Steam, and the last thing I want to do is have to figure out how to fix Steam right off the bat.  Not only that, but the game doesn't work with a Logitech F710 controller on Linux... though a friend's XBOX controller seems to work just fine on the same machine.  In fact, going into the in-game controller config screen in the game locks up the game so you can't exit the controller configuration.  I thought the point of Steam was to provide a platform that "just works" for games that might be otherwise hard to get running on some random hardware platform.  In summary, I couldn't get online multiplayer to work on at least on Linux system, and could not get the Logitech 710 to work in this game (deal breakers), though after seeing the game up in single player, its hard to imagine I want to jump in pools full of mobs that you have to just crazily run around to avoid while only being able to shoot up/down/left/right with two hands on the keyboard - one hand to move, the other to shoot.  I guess a lot of people would find that fun, but not me.  I do like N64 / GameCube Gauntlet games, and did enjoy games like TOME, so its not like I don't care for the genre, but the very open maps with hordes if mobs just waiting for you to over-steer while engaging other mobs kills it for me.  Mind you I only played normal, and not the more insane modes!  I'm not a fast player and much prefer sniping techniques and what not.  Even so, I'd probably not have returned the game if it was just the gameplay issues and not the multiplayer and controller issues, because my kids aren't so intimidated by the fast pace games... so hopefully you can get a feel for why I don't like it, but you might not have issues with it.

This is a very original mashup of several different genres - a tower defender, an rpg and a TPP masher to name a few. If I had to name one game that is similiar to this one it would probably be Orcs Must Die!, but it is still very very different.
Sang-Froid's setting is enough to make it stand out from the rest. The story being told takes us back to the times where the northern american settlers lived aside native indians. The player plunges into the role of one of the two O'Carroll brothers, forced to fight for the life of their ill sister and their own as well.
Game consists of two distinct parts - the 'tactical' phase, taking place at dawn and the 'action' phase where our tactical plan is being put to test. Would you expect Orcs Must Die ! clone, you'd be up for a big suprise, a selection of deadly machines that chew, chop and incinerate mindless hordes of enemies is replaced by simplistic traps, overhang nets filled with stones and baits that only slow down your enemies. Most of the traps are disposed after being used and aside from a handful barely useful tools, they require to be set off manually with a painfully slow reloading rifle.
Well, the game is difficult. An easy setting (represented by Joe, the burly O'Caroll brother) turns out to be nowhere near easy. On the other hand failure comes free-of-charge and you can repeat and rethink your tactics infinitely, as long as you're not satisfied with the success. There's nothing cheap about the challenge, not Borderlands 2 half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥design or numbers ridicule. It takes a bit of thought to survive each night, but it's both satisfying and rewarding once you make it.
Obviously the game is not perfect. A little rough round the edges, some animations could be a tad more refined and so on - but that's nothing you wouldn't expect from an indie game coming from a very small studio. My biggest gripe is the awful voice acting which does nothing but hinders the story told. I'd glad with no va at all, in favour of the subtitles, unfortunately the option isn't there. On the other hand the folkish score is loveable and really adds to an already great package.
Bottom line: buy it, these guys deserve your support. It's definitely worth it's current price-tag and getting it on sale is a no-brainer.
If you like games that cost 5 dollars and can entertain you for an hour at a time, get it.

The main character of Prototype 2 is James Heller, who is out for REVENGE! And won't stop telling you that every 5 minutes. He's also very angry. We can tell he's angry because he keeps saying f*@! every. Single. f*@!ing. Sentence.
The game does a good job empowering the player with interesting and visceral mutations, which are gained by killing mutants that have powers you want. Power and ability progression is dealt with quite well mechanically and employing the various powers is rather fun. However, press the wrong button or take slightly too long to interact with a quick time event, which boss fights are unfortunately made of, and all that empowerment is stripped away for one jarring moment as the game remorselessly punishes you by stripping up to a quarter of your health away. Despoite the fact that you can punch helicopters out the sky and kick tanks to death.
The story is an unfortunately flat follow up to Prototype 1, where Alex Mercer (the player character in Prototype 1) is suddenly, inexplicably, mustache twilingly, top hat wearing, puppy kickingly EVIL. He wasn't a nice person in the first game, but the sudden change in character is very jarring and poorly executed.
"How do you know I'm EVIL James Heller? Because I will tell you so while twirling my mustache! Mwa ha ha! Let's take over the world together."
"No Alex Mercer! Mutants killed my fambly! You are a mutant so I shall kill you too. You f@"!ing emo."
The best character interaction Heller had was when he called Mercer emo. Which was unfortunately during one of the worst QTE fuelled boss fights I've had in years.

Many ATI Radeon users have experienced a memory leak that has made Prototype 2 unplayable. This fix seems to eradicate the issue and locks the client at 30fps, almost perfectly stable.
1. Run Prototype 2 and disable Anti-Aliasing in the game client
2. Download and install Radeon Pro Preview
a. Create a profile for Prototype2.exe by searching in steamapps/common/prototype2
b. On the "Tweaks" tab:
VSync control : Always on (Double VSync)
Dynamic Framerate C Keep up to : 30 FPS Max
c. On the "Advanced" tab:
Flip Queue Size = 1 (Set to 1 and Check to Enable)
3. Right click on the profile your created in RadeonPro and click "Apply Now"
4. Ensure RadeonPro is running and start the game normally.
5. Play the game and enjoy!

I don't like strategy games. I don't like top down games, because that type of view draws me out of the story. I don't like simple graphics, either, because I like putting my gaming rig to good use.
Above all else, I ESPECIALLY hate colony managers.
With that said, this game took me in and kept me there. I don't plan on leaving anytime soon, as it's one of the deepest, most fun games I've played in years.
Why is this, you may ask? Well, the truth is that it isn't a colony manager; it's a story generator. A dang good story generator at that, and one where you, the player, will variably take full control over an efficient and happy colony, or watch helplessly as your emotionally unstable, "colonists," murder each other, or binge hard drugs in a fit of pain and anguish.
The simple, top down style and text-box backstories/personalities provide just enough information to guide us towards a story, but they leave enough to the imagination that we can effectively fill in the blanks with something far more awesome than anything which graphics could depict. This is a balance which is rarely seen in video games, and makes Rimworld play like the most advanced choose-your-own-adventure novel ever written.
The combat and strategy is deep enough to feel realistic and stressful, but simple enough to pick up with reasonable efficiency after a few failed colonies. If you don't play smart, your colony will die, but that's half the fun; watching a miserable, dark story of a dying colony unfold, as each of your members dies off due to stupid, preventable mistakes and their own quirky personalities.
On that note, I sincerely suggest that you NEVER, EVER save scum when playing this game. You will have 10 times more fun working through the problems, rather than reversing them until you get a perfect solution. I've gotten stories of pacifist medics, rushing through the fire of a burning house to grab a burning gardener, and failing at the last moment to patch his bleeding wounds. But, because I don't save scum, the times when I route a whole army of tribal attackers using only thrown together turrets and superior strategy feel AMAZING! And, sometimes, a little bit disturbing.
Why do I say that? Well, here's a catch: Everyone has a personality. EVERYONE. Every raider, every colonist, every random visitor- they all have a detailed backstory and unique personality traits, with certain popular psychology mods pushing this even further. So, even when you win, you can't help but feel a little bit forlorn as your dazed and weakened colonists limp over the field of dismembered bodies, trying to put out the flames so that they can give that headless, dismembered, 14 year old artist a proper grave.
I could say more but, honestly, I don't want to spoil anything for you. This is a game best learned on your own. So, I'll leave you with this:
This is the best colony manager ever made. Buy it, play it forever, watch your time slowly go away...

Dead Island: Definitive Edition is an upgraded version of the original Dead Island, featuring improved visuals and all of the available DLC for that game.
Other than the better graphics the Definitive Edition plays identically to the original title, so expect the same blend of visceral zombie massacre, fetch quests, skill tree upgrades, bad voice-acting, and weapon-building that you experienced the first time around, either by yourself or with up to three other people in co-op play.
If you didn't like the original Dead Island or were only mildly impressed with it, the Definitive Edition won't win you over since it's essentially more of the same. The Definitive Edition *can* be safely recommended to hardcore Dead Island fans, and to those who like loot-heavy action RPGs like the Borderlands games.

I played this for many hours with the free version before it came to
. At times I feel like this is a slightly more 'zen-like' experience than many of its dungeon-crawling brothers, simply because there does not
have to be a clear-cut goal of getting to the bottom of a dungeon or escaping something. In exchange for dungeons, you get the great Finland outdoors. Sometimes you just chill out and exist. But don't get me wrong, the learning curve is still quite steep and you will 100% always die on a long enough timeline. This is
for the hardcore (I write that with a loving nod to
).
This does not play or feel like anything else out there, as far as I'm concerned. It can't
be described as just some sort of 'different angle' or 'take' on another game. The obscure mixture of old-school artwork with, well, old-school real life images is weird, but after a while it becomes alluring. The text is well written. I like the 'online' in-game encyclopedia and deep lore.
This is a classic roguelike that is a pillar of the community, and deserves recognition as such. The controls are awkward at first, for sure, but quickly you get used to them and actually like them (plus there are options for traditional roguelike controls). Like any roguelike worth its weight, you will explore, die, learn why you died - and repeat to hopefully make it further. You will have a good time.
You won't regret it.
It's as if CoD4 had a child but no one's quite sure whether the father is Skyrim or Fallout 3.

Like Fallout 4 but feel like it's "meh" due to it using Skyrim's engine/ just being boring at times? Have you played Destiny but absolutely hated its looting system engrams and want a better version of its loot system? Do you like goofy over the top jokes with crazy characters? This game is for you! Well... maybe. Borderlands is a great game and it takes time to get through, it doesn't feel like a game I could take bite sizes of and play here and there, it feels like a sit down and play whole title. This game leans heavily on its writing and characters, and without them, it would have utterly failed imo. This was a single player play through, so this is a review written by a lone experience. Here's some pros 'n cons!
Pros:
- Interesting cast of characters that are rememberable and unique.
- The game will break the 4th wall but tastely and not rip you from the immersion. Great writing, and plenty of jokes that will actually make you laugh out loud, no lie. LOL
- Looting weapons is great and it's nice to find some badass epic or legendary weapons not given by bosses.
- Unique skill tree building will allow you to build your unique vault hunter the way you want to play them.
- Does a great job making sure you feel like you're in a trashed planet with a bunch of scum bag bandits who can't write nor barely speak proper English.
- Fun unique DLC that came w/ the bundle I got was fun and fairly more entertaining than the original game.
Cons:
- Long treks back 'n forth from quest boards to waypoints on the map.
- Game is not fully optimized for controller support. All interactions will specify pc UI/button usage, and unless you've figured out the buttons and usage through the menu, you'll have a bad time.
- This same Wasteland is nice, but also bad? It would have been nice for a change of scenery to be honest. Most of the game makes you feel like you're stuck wading through trash piles and barren, lifeless and dry/dead plains just to hope that the quest you've been treking across the map to get to will be fun and exciting.
- by the 3rd quarter of the game weapons are unique in nature and have some cool effects, but the weapons you may have looted hours upon hours back are better than legendary loot? Kind of makes it feel like you're stuck with the same  ♥♥♥♥ for the rest of the game's experience. (Even the DLC)
- Claptrap never SHUTS THE  ♥♥♥♥ UP ABOUT HAVING NEW QUESTS AT QUEST BOARDS OR PERSONNEL! More than half of these extra tagged on quests are lame, agrivating, and annoying to do. Mainly the ones where you have to build weapons from scattered parts only to cash the quest and get a  ♥♥♥♥   ♥♥♥ gun you'll vendor 2 minutes after cashing.
- Menu for quests sucks in its organization and is hard to use since it doesn't work hand in hand with your map to figure out where you have to go.
- No mini map.
- Vehicle gets stuck one every little  ♥♥♥♥ing rock you accidently run over (or guard rail) and you are forced to get out, blow that stupid  ♥♥♥♥ing piece of  ♥♥♥♥ up and run your  ♥♥♥ the rest of the GOD DAMN WAY TO THE QUEST MARKER. UGH.
Anyways, yes, this review had many faults to pros, but I honestly enjoyed this game. I'm currently still playing some of the DLC before continuing my venture in BL2 which imo is far better than the first in almost every way. If you start w/ BL2 I don't blame you, the first can seem boring, but not uninspired. The game lacks much, but if you play the second, trust me, you'll love the characters so much you'll want to play homage to the first game. On a scale one 1- 10, I'd give this sucker a 7/10. Good game, even great at times, but not without its set of issues. Good luck out there Future Vault Hunter! :D

After playing through the game once, I can safely say that this title does it's job when it comes to atmosphere, be it through the well placed bodies and buildings, to crawling through tiny places, your heart racing in both the game and real world as you peek around corners to see what's up ahead. This game has so much potential, and I hope that more acts come out in the near future.
However, I do have a small complaint, mainly a personal one. The very little combat and the small threat there is in the game. I understand this is an atmospheric game, but when you decide to put any amount of combat into a game, any threat, you expect it to be a bit more in volume, and slightly spread out through an act. The majority of combat is dealing with zombies at the start with a very accurate pistol that can easily get headshots if you time your shots carefully. For this case, it gives you a great deal of ammo as well, arming you up rather effectively for alot of combat. I was able to kill most every enemy in the game and still have enough ammo to fire pot shots at the enviroment with no real guilt. The creatures wern't a real threat, but when other humans started hunting you down with automatic machine pistols, sidearms, and one with a shotgun, you tend to loose health rather quickly, no matter how good you are in a fight. But again, atmospheric game, so it's mostly a small complaint.
I highly recommend this game for all kinds of players, fresh out of the water, and seasoned veteran alike. The story is fantastic, and the pacing is almost spot on from what I'd expect from a game like this. It's free as well, so there's no real reason not to give this a shot.

His goal is to corrupt the town's priest by bringing him your sister, whom he attempted to force himself on starting the events of this story.
The music is very fitting to the setting, old fiddle music like you might've heard in an inn or bar back in those days, and the weaponry is very reminiscent of the olden days. No run and gun here, you have a flint lock rifle and reloading between shots takes time, a lot of time. You have to plan, you have to think on your feet, and you have to survive against all the monsters that hell can throw at you with nothing but your axe, your rifle, and your wits. The voice acting could be better, but otherwise this is definitely a game I could recommend.

Novel contains explicit adult contents, and the plot is deep and dark. Therefore it is not suitable for children and early-teens.
There are 2 distinctive AIs that plays the role of narrating and advancing the plot for you. These 2 AIs have totally opposite personality, and such they reveals 2 different plot-lines for you to read and understand the history and mystery of the "apocalyptic" event that happened. This "unreliable narrator" mechanic is what makes a visual novel so much more interesting and entertaining than conventional book novel.
The first few entries aren't that exciting, but as I uncover more story along the way, they gives me the urge to continue on. The logs are so carefully crafted, that almost every entry contains a mystery that tickle my curiosity to find out what happens next. The plot are mostly dark and sad, full of love and hate. The few happy moments in the game helps to further contrast the rest of the sadness.
There are a lot of waifu moments in the game. I am not a big fan of waifu games, but I do find them quite entertaining in this game. They serve as great timeouts in-between reading, helps me clear my mind and combat read-exhaustion.
There are a few occassions that you need to type some unix-like commands into the ship's console. There is also a timed-puzzle event in the game, which is very easy to solve if you're a gamer. In my opinion, these puzzle elements are completely unnecessary and breaks the mood for novel reading, but they do enhance the unreliable-narrator mechanic and further establish the 2-distinct personality of the AIs.
The background music is very nice, a mix of Korean-Asian styled theme played with clean modern-futuristic digital music. The music also blends nicely with the mood of the logs you are currently reading, as well as the personality of the current active AI you are interacting with.
There is one thing that I struggle in this game: I find it very difficult to remember Korean names. I had to re-read many logs to fully understand what's going on sometimes.
If you do not hate reading, this novel is definitely worth a try.

Highly recommended. What I liked was that the game doesn't take very long to complete, even with the branching storyline, and it's a well written story. There's only one traditional "adventure game"-type puzzle, which is the nuclear reactor, but it's easy to solve. The real puzzle is trying to see all of the log files and getting all the endings, to try to get the best picture you can of what happened to the spaceship and its inhabitants. Normally, in any one playthrough, you would not be able to see everything, but in a metanarrative sort of way, since you can go back and start over, you can combine your knowledge from different playthroughs to put everything together. Another game which does this is "Nine Hours, Nine Persons, Nine Doors."
Most of the game is spent reading. Once you've played through once, you can skip reading the log entries that you've already done, and you can skip any dialog with the AIs, making it easier to get to the other branches. This game is a visual novel, but instead of showing text in a small 4-line box like most Japanese VNs, this game uses the full screen to show text, which I liked.
As for the story, I liked it. The inhabitants of the spaceship, in the years covered by the logs, live in a society based on a historical period of Korea. There's a real struggle for the main character, who is really like a time traveler from today's world, to be understood and to try to live in this society. The only thing I wish is that there were more written about what happened on the spaceship. You only get a glimpse of the lives of a few characters, momentary fragments in time in the form of letters, diary entries, or other notes.
Overall, an excellent game.

This is a really hard game to review.  A visual novel based around Korean history where you progress by showing documents to cute AI women is probably a concept that either appeals to you or doesn't.  However, it's well implemented, and the story it's telling is a lot more interesting than it first seems.  I only have two problems with it: Firstly, the opening is hopeless.  The initial set of documents you get are some of the most aggressively boring in the whole thing, and the most interesting story arcs it has are hidden away and unlikely to be found in a first playthrough.  Secondly, it feels a bit reversed.  The sequel has logs from before the logs in this one, but takes place after it for the purposes of the 'you romance cute AI women' subplot.  Thus, they feel a bit 'chicken and egg',
But overall, it's pretty good.

"Telltale should do more comedy games"
This is my first thought when thinking about this game, the comedic writing skills of the team that made this game really shines through and keeps the player interested in this grand adventure.
The main characters of this game are Rhys and Fiona, they are used in a certain way, Rhys is more of the straight man, he is a fish out of the water on Pandora and thus more of an avatar for the player. Meanwhile Fiora is a Pandora native so she's more in tune with the Borderlands universe weirdness, you could say she might be an avatar for the Borderlands games veterans.
You don't have to be a Borderlands veteran to enjoy this game, you just have to know a few stuff like: "Who is Handsome Jack?", "What is Hyperion and the other companies?", and "Pandora has a lot of crazies"
You also don't need to be a fan of the Borderlands brand of humour to enjoy this game, the humour is entirely different from the main series and I'd actually say that this is one of the few games that is genuinely funny and knows how to do comedy without feeling like it's trying to hard.
The adventure also feels like a real adventure, thanks to changing settings, fun companions and the roadtrip like opening segments that each episode has. I don't want to spoil anything but I feel like thise game really balances having a fun time and having emotional heavy segments, which I didn't expect of a Borderlands game before playing it.
In my experience this game was also plagued less with technical problems than most other Telltale games I played, I never experienced any slowdown or misisng sound effects.
All in all I would say that this is my favourite game Telltale has made and I'd definitely recommend it to anyone who wants to play an actually funny game.

Konung 2 is weird. It's an open RPG with a little bit of unit management.
The game is pretty complicated with lots of unorthodox  features.
Yet the devs decided not to include a tutorial whatsoever, leading to players fumbling around inside the game.
The funny thing is that the first game has a pretty comprehensive tutorial.
Konung 2 is an open game. You can go wherever you want and do whatever you want.
Do some quests? Or killing monsters or maybe even killing all of the villagers.
Another aspect of the game is you can own a couple of villages and by doing so you can earn money from daily tributes.
You can also make you villagers to be stronger by dispatching one of your characters as a trainer to train them or as a blacksmith to make the villagers have better equipment.
You can train them up to trainer's level + 1. So you also have to train your "trainer" lol.
This is because your enemy will constantly sending a raid party to attack your villages.
So they have to be able to protect themselves lest they become occupied by the enemy.
All NPC on an occupied village will not interact with you. And you will also be attacked by enemies patrol as they see you. But you can free them by killing every enemy's patrol on the village.
Now onward to battles.
Battle in this game is very hard. The enemies always swarming together so you have to make a big party of your own to fight them on event ground.
The lowest enemies levels i've seen is 5. so before you can fight them you will also need to level up a couple of times via doing quests too.
The bad news is Exp from completing a quest will only be granted to your Main Character. Any other characters have to earn it via battles.
And even worse Exp in battles only given to THE CHARACTER THAT DEALT THE FINISHING BLOW. Making leveling a chore.
The worst is the enemy raiding party is also getting stronger. And they are getting stronger very fast. Faster than you.
So you will soon face a situation where you can't protect any of your villages at all. Bad game design.

I honestly did not pay attention to the story because I was having too much fun playing it. I did eventually read some of the dialogue that takes place before each mission and it put a smile on my face as it is humorously written and its nice to see that even in game. Smashing guards through windows, remodeling their faces through means of punching and causing general prankster shenanigans feels rewarding in a strange way.
Most missions will task you with stealing some data from a computer in a secure (or so they thought) building with guards, locked doors, security cameras and such devices. But once you've reached specific points in the building, you can hack it all. Hack the guards gun to fire when you flick a light switch, make a wall socket buzz out electricity killing a guard when another guard walks through a motion sensor one floor above... its all possible.
The fun part is, you can ignore it all and do it your way. All levels can be beat without any guards noticing you were even there - the true spy way. You can go in, kill everyone and make Rambo proud or just have fun hacking everything you can. It is a puzzle game as its core, it can be as tough is you want it to be - killing everyone will generally be easier than going in sneaky peaky like.
Its worthy to mention the soundtrack is fantastic and blends with the game nicely. I wouldn't penny pinch if I was on the fence about getting the special edition. The main story will take about 1-4 hours to complete, depending on how you play and how bad you are at puzzle games. It does come with an easy to use level editor and steam workshop support where other people's levels are shared. This potentially gives countless hours of replay-ability.

only when the last river is polluted;
only when the last fish is caught;

This game is clever in ways most modern 3D survival games can only dream of. Sure, the graphics are dated and controls might feel overwhelming in the beginning, but behind the first impressions hides a truly spectacular survival experience in the forests of Iron Age Finland.
Unreal World utilises the mechanics that 2D world offers over 3D to give the player more realistic survival setting. 2D world can speed up the world around you when you perform tasks much more naturally than any game done in 3D could, and the game takes full advantage of this. The days in UrW are 24h, the year is 365 days. When you plant crops they aren't full grown in the next morning. There's also full 4 seasons in a Finnish year. During summer it's warm and the nature is blooming, but after a few months of sunshine it starts to get cold. And it gets really cold. If you are not prepared the winter can freeze you to death in a day and roaming in waist deep snow is exhausting. But even winter has its benefits. Animal tracks are easier to spot in the snow and food lasts for months before it spoils when it's -20c outside 24/7.
Animals in the Unreal World are dangerous, but not like in many other games where you'll be beating them off multiple times a day with your fancy swords. In Unreal World even the most dangerous animals, the bears will flee when they spot you 90% of the time, perhaps even more often. They might get curious, smelling your roasting food and stay nearby. Come night they might try to sneak in and steal your food. Specially foxes like to do that. Or they might eat your livestock if you have any. But most of the time they will attack you only after you have provoked them by chasing them, cornering them or by surprising them, sneaking too close. Almost any animal will attack you when cornered, an elk might kick you to the head if you give it no chance to escape.
Combat is terrifying. Any time you are attacked there's always a real chance your game will end there. This might sound like a bad game design choice. But in my opinion it makes much more sense this way. The player is not a super-human who could beat of 10 other people with ease. And if you lose in combat you will not wake up in your bed the next morning or something like that. You will be staring at the summary screen of your characters life, that has ended. Some special cases might leave you alive after you lose a battle, the robbers and friendly villagers. Robbers will take all your valuables and villagers will take away stolen property by force if you try to steal from them.
Unreal World is the most complete survival experience I have come across, ever. And the best thing is that the author still has ideas of what to add, even if the pace might not be the fastest.
Here's a few ways to end your life sooner rather than later in Unreal World, try to avoid:
-Throwing a rock at a bear when you are not prepared for battle.
-Walking on thin ice in the spring.
-Swimming with all your stuff
-Fishing with poor skill or poor tools
-Eating funny looking mushrooms or plants.

If you enjoy inmersive roleplaying within a game, and making up your own story, and letting your imagination take over in place of visuals then this game is for you.  However, if you need animations on screen, rigid questlines, and giant battles then you will not enjoy Unreal World.  It plays very close to the adventure mode in dwarf fortress (just not with ascii graphics) and Im sure some inspiration definately came from dwarf fortress.
When starting the game you create a character through stats and choosing a tribe/ cultural group.  If you explore the help manual with the f1 key then you can find some more information about each tribe.  One thing I really enjoyed was that most of the native tribes (the northern tribes) aren't especially fond of warfare, but are very much in touch with the land and the spirits.
After creating your character you get to pick your starting "story" which is thr scenario your character will start in.  Most of the time I end up using the unfortunate hunting trip scenario, very revenant like, but I did not survive being mauled by the bear.
What Unreal World lacks visually it makes up for in depth.  The survival mechanics are managable, but it is too possible to not realize that you hadn't packed enough food to last a migration south to warmer climates for the winter.  Also, combat is much more unforgiving (just as it is in dwarf fortress (can you see a theme yet?)) And what seemed like an easy fight can go wrong with a lucky blow to the leg.  The hunting system is my favorite by far!  Tracking, stalking, mix and repeat.  Very realistic, and Im speaking from experience as a hunter myself.  In other games you go look for an animal, you shoot it, and you have enough food for a little while.  Unreal World makes you earn it.  So you found an elk, got close enough for a shot with your bow?  Great, you have mortally wounded it, but it still ran away.  So you will spend the rest of the in game day following blood trails and tracks, and hopefully you find it again.
If you do not enjoy creating your own experience in a game then Unreal World is not for you!  End of story.  If you like dwarf fortress, or other survival sims than you will get many hours of enjoyment from yhis game.

First, the positives:
1)  Original and historical setting
2)  Excellent atmosphere
3)  Interesting and deep combat mechanics
That's about it, really.  There's a lot of negatives when compared to similar games.  But I have to give it a positive review for being so original, especially considering the time in which it was conceived.  My biggest gripe is that for a game that's been in development for about 30 years, there's surprisingly little content when compared to other survival titles that are flashier and prettier to look at.  The development is absolutely glacial in pace (puns, heh...).  Released to Steam in Feb 2016 and it's received only 1 sizeable update if I remember correctly.  While this isn't exactly a roguelike, one of the strengths of the genre is it's ability to do so much with so little.  I feel like UnReal World doesn't capitalize on this asset.  With that said, the game still feels complete and worthy of a purchase, but there may be better survival games out there.  At the rate this thing is being made, I wouldn't be shocked if the developer dies before he ever realizes his ultimate vision for it.

Writing a review before the inevitable ♥♥♥♥♥torm some of the game media website are bound to stur up.
Its obvious the dev team choose what on the outside looking in would be a 'controversial' topic. Thing is ISIS is a ♥♥♥♥ing abhorrent terrorist organization and perhaps the most pressing threat to the first world/western civilization making them an obvious antagonistic force not just off their own 'power' or ability but much of the sympathy they seem to be getting from people within the very nations they would sooner see burned to the ground. If media outlets are shilling this game out as racist or islamaphobic just remember that nearly 10 years back CoD4 did about the same thing over the course of its campaign and is still lauded as perhaps the last 'good' call of duty.
The game plays well, for a 5 dollar game on steam you could definitely get much worse, less polished, and typically perpetually stuck in 'early access' game. Compared to those IS defense is a godsend.
