This is ultimately what happens when crossing Diablo with Gauntlet; you get hordes of monsters, hoards of loot, and you build your character half by stats, and half by skills. Your skill tree is four passives, four actives, for a total of eight skills, which will gain bonuses according to your statistics. All in all, it's really nothing spectacular or unique. The zones are what you'd expect, and are randomly generated battlefields for your perusal so that two runs don't feel too run-together. You use one set of keys to move, and your other set of keys (like ABXY on a controller) will shoot in one of the four cardinal directions. Like Gauntlet (and not Diablo) this means action is basically constant. Like Diablo (and not Gauntlet) you will find that a lot of the action is sort of passive but it's very liable to suddenly occur that an enemy is some manner of elite or boss, and just absolutely dominates your sorry hindquarters. So, in short, again: Diablo met Gauntlet for a crazy night of video game.
I guess it's not bad. 'Recommend' is a really strong word-- the company doesn't appear to have too much involvement compared to some titles that have been around longer and still experience substantial, game-changing updates. The devs are either comfortably working on something else, or else figuring out how to renew the life of Hero Siege. It's certainly not bad at all and if you're a fan of Gauntlet (like the NES Gauntlet game or Gauntlet Legends), or you're a fan of Diablo 1/2, you'll find a lot familiar here that makes you feel at home. But I've found that this game falls into 'kill or be killed' patterns very quickly; I've had a lot of difficulty on every character except the Samurai, who can stand in one spot and clear the screen like that. Gauntlet lacked class dynamics, and Diablo's class dynamics were just that everyone was terrified of Gloams.
It's got polish issues (the Shaman DLC does not possess a sound for his attack is my favourite one to harp), it's got consistency issues (random bosses can either be a total joke, or a complete savage) and the classes start to run together (most melees just have an AoE, some AoE passive procs, and a damage reduction; ranged classes enjoy some more variety though); four active skills means your class pretty much does one thing and completely linear skill trees is a huge issue when replaying because you'll start to recognize trends quick (dump a stat > take most effective scaling skill > don't stop casting that skill).
There's probably some high-tier meta in the deep endgame/postgame that I'm missing, but so far my experiences with Hero Siege leave me to say: grab it on discount, and don't expect something complex. It'll mulch a couple hours and it'll make you remember good times with Diablo. But if you're after digging into an itch, I don't think Hero Siege will scratch it. It just lacks the kind of depth or polish that big names like those have, and you're better to find your hours in a game like Path of Exile or Torchlight 2; where Hero Siege is concerned, this is probably better on a co-op kind of thing to burn a night or a weekend. It's worth checking out and it's worth paying for. I won't name names, but boy howdy, I've seen some games charge 99 cents and that's still too bloody much for them. This isn't one of them, and full price is no scam by any means, but you might feel better spending 40 or 50% off.
Just don't do the local co-op. You aren't capable of discerning that kind of nonsense off of a screen. Stick to online and you'll be fine.

After finally finishing this game, I've decided to give it a more proper review.
Set in the mid 19th century Canada, the O'Carrolls brothers, Joseph and Jacque, have to protect their sickly bedridden sister, Josephine, from wolves, werewolves, and other nasty creatures that dwell in the forest.
If you have played
then you should be familiar with this type of defense game: lay down the traps, create detours, and if need be get into the fray. But there are a few differences that set it apart from
.
First difference is that there is more or less one map. But that map grows and evolves as one progress through the campaign. Rivers freezing over or a section of forest being cleared opens up new paths for enemies to attack your buildings, but it also means more ways to delay those enemies and  more fronts to ambush them as well.
Second, trap placement emphasizes location and combination over sheer quantity. One can only place traps at dawn and cannot be moved once the night begins. This means one must take the time to consider enemy paths (and later on, wind direction), when placing traps so that one may effectively deal with each wave of enemies. In addition, traps often work best when used in combination with other traps. While an explosive barrel may take out many enemies that just happen to pass by, bait can placed near the barrel so that enemies bunch up in a small area, thus greatly increasing the kill count.
Finally, fighting feels more intense and personal. There are relatively few enemies per level, but that only means each one of them poses more of threat. Melee attacks share the same Stamina resource used for sprinting and rolling, so one can only chain up a limited number of attacks before leaving one open for a counter attack. Ranged weapons are reflective of the time period, so each shot must be used effectively as the weapon only hold one bullet and takes several seconds to reload. But thankfully one can intimidate enemies so that they hesitate to attack, thus buying precious time to replenish stamina and to reload.
Overall, I recommend this game to anyone who is looking for game that test one's planning skills as well as anyone who is looking to experience a new setting in videogames.

I've only played for about 11 and a half hours thus far, but I can already tell you that this is a great game.
A little background. I've been playing RPGs for over 20 years. It is my favorite genre of games. That said, Konung 2 is a bit of a mix between a simulation and an RPG.
Don't get me wrong. There are plenty of RPG elements to sink your teeth into here. There are 6 unique heroes with their own backgrounds and stats, stats to customize upon leveling up, a bunch of skills that impact gameplay in different ways, inventory management for every member of your party (yes, it is party-based. You can have up to 8 other characters join your cause.), magical items to find and an extensive loot system, a bunch of side quests, treasure hunting, a bunch of maps to explore and more! It's a very meaty RPG if that's what you're looking for.
As for the simulation side, it's well done in that aspect as well. You control various villages and can build them as you see fit. You can collect tributes from the villages, build blacksmith forges, shipyards, a barracks, etc. You can find people to work these jobs and they will do them based on their various skills. Eventually you want to build up some strong villages so you can recruit some fit warriors to help your cause.
Overall, this game is a hidden gem. I'm very surprised it's as good as it is, given there is little information about it online.
Oh, one final thing. Do not play this game if you want fast-paced action. This game takes a high level of patience to get the most out of. You won't be slaying hordes of enemies right from the start. You've really got to spend some time to work your way up the ladder to become a respectable hero and leader of men. In my 11 hours, I've barely killed anything, that's how challenging the game is thus far. But I've still loved every minute.
Highly recommended for something a bit different and for lovers of RPGs.

Length: Took me about three hours - after going back, getting some multiple endings and tropihies. I have the game at about 84% completion. It did take me about 30 minutes to get into the game.
Gameplay: It's a Visual Novel -- its a wall-of-text detective game. Read the clues, note if there is some additional information, read the new clue. Layered on top of that you have a "discussion" (approve/disapprove option) with the AI's which has story consequences. If you're looking for anything more exciting than that, move on. There is one more exciting sequence that uses an DOS style interface to interact with a mainframe computer, but FEAR this is not.
Storywise: Solid. It's pretty upfront about what big mysteries cannot be solved, though it does suffer from an overbundance of side characters (once I gave up on trying to remember who was who I enjoyed the game much more. The ones that mattered stuck with me). That said, it is exploring a cacooned society on a space ship through diary entries, and things may be trigger-y for some people, and is definitely created from a feminist perspective.

And here we go with Alliance of Valiant Arms (A.V.A.).
This is one of the most know MMOFPS. Why? Because it's Free To Play so everyone can play it.
Let's start saying that A.V.A. is a game published six years ago (2008), but it was released on Steam in 2011. Well, it's not a "fresh game" but it's still a good game.
And now let's talk about the GAMEPLAY!
1.) CLASSES
Well...Yes... before you ask, this game isn't only for players with skills.
When you join a match you will choose your team (UE Forces or the NRF) and one of the 3 classes:
- Pointman (Weapons with high rateo, good aim but low damage)
- Rifleman (Assault rifle with a balanced rateo, an higher damage and unlimited ammo)
- Sniper (Classic man with a sniper rifle)
2.) MAPS
The maps in this game are awful. Let me explain: the most of the maps are tiny, little, short... that may cause an overcrowding and random deaths of players. Some of them are untreated and bugged.
Surviving isn't that simple and it's accentuated, also, by the low speed of your character. You can't roll, you can't lie down, you can't lean out from the shell. The spread and the recoil of weapons may be recalibrated a bit. The game isn't that special but and it's still a canonic FPS free.
3.) GAMEMODES
Luckily... there are a lot of funny gamemodes. For example: Infection (A player becomes an infected with more stamina, speed and a lot of more life and he has to hit the enemies to infect them.
4.) GRAPHICS
The graphic is pretty good for a free game that use the Unreal Engine 3.
5.) CONCLUSIONS
The game entertains the player, but it can't be said that skills are needed to play this games. Aim neither. It's a great pastime where you can kick back, but, absolutely... it's NOT competitive. There is a huge shop in the game that sells powerful weapons. The game is commercial and flat and there's not innovations.
NOT RECOMMENDED: If you want a competitive game.
RECOMMENDED: If you only want to have fun.

Having... never really played this game before and having been told it was free to play by a friend, I decided to give it a go and see what all the fuss was about... in terms of the game's sound, it's nice, but a clear (and I mean clearly pointed out in game) way to put subtitles early on would be way more helpful for people with noisy backgrounds who want to play the game. ... Unfortunately, the CONTROLS and INTERFACE is where this game REALLY let it down for me in a very bad way (I am suffering a headache from just trying to PLAY the game and I'm in no way a dumb person). From the get go, you are given instructions by Aura, your ship AI, in what to do to move around, to fight and so on. However, in my time playing I found that half of the actions she was asking me to do simply weren't working or even AVAILABLE to do. Being told to approach a target, lock on and then orbit, then shoot is all well and good but if you can't easily select to approach or lock on to a target, it really makes playing difficult. What makes it worse however is just trying to MOVE your ship. You get told pretty early on to double click to move your ship where you want to go, however the game likes to interpret where you click as somewhere completely not where you click. What's worse is that rotating your camera requires clicking and holding, then dragging your camera around to rotate, and if you do that on ANYTHING you can interact with, you get a menu instead. This makes trying to turn your camera to look at enemies who have come to start shooting you in the rear end with missiles completely a nightmare, even worse if you're trying to lock on to shoot at them at full speed while they are doing the same!
You'd think I was just griping for the sake of it but it gets worse... it gets so much worse. Several points in the tutorial alone tell you to make alterations to your ship or even get a new ship which involves traversing through about 6-8 different interfaces JUST to set up the new ship, have the required skills to fly it and equip it with what the game tells you to equip to it. Then you get pulled into a giant fleet battle after the game gloriously shows you all the ships you could be flying and you're presented with the nightmare fuel of trying to fight multiple opponents while trying to focus on a key target while fighting THE CAMERA ITSELF to just play the game. Then the game throws a curve ball by throwing you into a 'but thou must' death scene and puts you to setting up ANOTHER ship with MORE items and go get a career?
... Yeah. At this point, I plain just gave up. If you like RTS games and can handle a million and one interfaces and possibly one of THE WORST control and camera systems I've ever honestly seen in a video game... and you're a real big fan of space exploration, mining, giant fleet battles and the like, I can recommend this game, it'll be right up your alley (and all the credit to you. The latter part interested me but...)
For anyone else who isn't into that or prefers controls and camera systems that are easier to use (like myself) and gameplay that doesn't require a million interfaces to just give your ship a loadout, fly around and deal with what you need to deal with... AVOID this game. It sounded good, it looked good, but in the end, the gameplay was the one department that made my playing just some scrap floating in new eden.

Also the indoor combat magically turns your keyboard and mouse into a Dvorak keyboard and a ham sandwich, respectively. They become that useless. Indoor combat consists of attacking where you think something should be maybe but you don't know because your camera has fallen in love with the wall and it'll be a cold day in hell before it turns away from that beauty to look at whatever stupid crap you want to look at.

Taking the time to write an actual new player review. Honestly, take a few minutes to read it, and you'll likely enjoy the game much more, save about 90% of your time, and start with 3-4x the money.
I'll preface this by saying, the game looks amazing, I love the complexity and potential, and the customer service over the first 5 days has been almost scary fast, like, write a ticket and have a moderator respond with a solution sometimes within 2 minutes fast. However, I know this because after 5 days of playing, I couldn't progress in the mission lines for 3 of those days, and had to contact customer service to fix bugs.
Also, I'll outline a few things they don't tell you in the game I wish I knew prior, just to save time doing nothing while you figure out, what is a great, but incredibly confusing interface (mostly due to the game not having a real tutorial, which is also nice, not to be forced to waste time on dumb stuff). The game says to right click everything, regardless of it being a right or left click, pretty easy to figure out. To travel to mission locations, right click in open space to open the location menu, the game never tells you this and it's the only way to travel to mission locations. The "tutorial" is actually composed of agent missions, which you can find by docking at stations (right click on the station). You can basically train in every skill, unlike some mmo's where you pick one or two, and each of the 5-6 agents, I forget how many there are, explain different game mechanics. After the tutorial, grind around a bit, but the best learning area I found was the first epic quest called the "sisters of eve", best to google it, I forget who you talk to to start the mission, but she's in your agent folder. INSURE YOUR SHIPS!!!! right click on a ship and pick which level you want to insure it at, for battle based ships, you're going to use the best one, and it will explode, over and over likely while you figure out all the weapons and shield systems, with the cpu, energy consumption, shield, armor, hull, propulsion, buff and debuffs and all the combinations (there are about 10-15 per category, each with around 6 options at 4-5 different levels, and around 8 types of dps units each using one of about 10 different types of ammo again at 3 levels, all in 1/4 different types of slots, litterally tens of thousands of combinations).
This game is HUGE, the star map is insane, to go from the starting area to the sisters quest is around a 25 minute travel through jump gates. However, and this isn't told either, while you travel, if you click on the genome button second bottom on the left, there's a mini game to play while you travel to advance and make money. You identify mutagens and it's not time sensitive, so you can watch tv and just click and look when you like.
There is a station based "spawn" for items, which is really interesting. Basically, when an item is purchased at a station, it becomes more expensive (excluding the player sale market). So from time to time, you'll find ammo, shields, even ships at insanely lower prices from one station to the next. But be careful, some stations are in pvp type zones, or have what seems to be npc type guards, whatever they are, you'll die, instantly, one shot. The game warns you before you warp into the zones saying "may not be safe", but it's an understatement. I learned this fact after traveling about 20 minutes to get a ship for something like 20000 isk (money is called isk) that was 2.5M isk at another base. BUT, and they don't tell you this again, in the market if you filter the item by cost, and look at the jump location (more jumps = longer travel time, around 2-3 min per jump) you can right click on the item, bringing down a menu to look at the item info, but the last option is location, and you can look at the location info. Each location is rated by security, basically, nothing is "safe", but they have a general warning level, 1.0 being basically safe, and I assume 0.0 being pvp (I've only got to a 0.4 so far). So 0.6 is safe, 0.4 is not, this can save you, a tonne of time by looking at before you buy something and try travel to the location. An example being a location that is 12 jumps away, at 3 min per jump, and a round trip, is roughly 45 minutes)
Anyways, on to the negatives. day one, intro mission glitch, not sure exactly how, since I'd been playing for about 15 minutes at that point, but I blew up my ship and ended up in a base, with no ship, no mission, and no money. Not a big deal, just started a new character, you have 3 slots. Oh, side note, the character creator is pretty good. Anyways, day two, still not sure how everything works, again since the interface is huge and not really explained at any point, so I spent about 2 hours trying to figure out how to get to activate the next mission, how to get there, and didn't know it was a bug at the time, about an hour and a half scanning the same area for the mission requirements, having it not show up, warping in and out and rescanning, later finding out if I had just restarted the game it would have been there. After finishing the agent quests I googled what to do next, because you're just sort of done, nothing prompts you to do anything, and started the epic quest line. Really fun for new players, you are gifted about a dozen ships during the "tutorial" quests, and have enough money to equip the ones you will use. The quest starts a long way (20 jumps, or about 40 minutes) away, which is kind of lame for a starting quest, to just do nothing for half an hour while you travel to the location. Anyways, mission 47 I think, of 50 in the line, you have to talk to a guy, not at his location, but at a mission spawn point. The game glitched and thought I had accepted the quest when I hadn't, so the character spawn wasn't there. So I looked for it, and looked for it and looked for it.... I travelled to his space port, which was 12-13 jumps aways (about a half hour back and forth) 4 times, but kept getting the message I had to talk to him not at the base, but at the spawn, which wasn't there. This was my first ticket submission, about 2.5 hours of doing nothing but looking for this non existant spawn. The mod replied and had the quest rebooted in about 15 minutes, but it happened again. I had just taken to heart the message I just had to warp to his location, but it wasn't there again, so another half hour of travelling back and forth, I re-submitted the ticket, it was refreshed, and the second I left the docking station, the guy was there. Again, not a big deal, if I had known I could submit the ticket and have it fixed in 15 minutes I would have saved about 3 hours though. Anyways, the mission is significantly harder than the previous ones, and you have to beef up your ship, which is good, you have a bunch of money, but if you haven't been training your skills up constantly, you can't equip the stuff you need to win, these total around 50 hours of training, but you can que 24 hours in que, which runs passively either on or offline. But to train the skills, you need the skill books, which are easy enough to get, but the books at the location cost around 1M isk, while they cost around 50k at the ports close to where you start, and you need about 20 of them and only have around 10M total isk at this point, so another half hour to travel to the ports to get the books you can afford (and remember to check the security on the location, since people put the books really cheap in pvp areas trying to get newbs to warp there so they can one shot them). Anyways, not a big deal, but if they told you this at the start, you could que up all the skills during the first agent quests and save yourself 50 hours of training time that prevent you from moving forward. cont.

While Unreal World is a pretty hardcore roguelike, it's also very enjoyable once you understand how it works.  The game is set in Iron Age Finland, and you must face the hardships that living in such an environment entails.  Your character has a variety of skills such as hunting, fishing, farming, foraging, running, swimming, woodcraft and firemaking as well as skills in various weapon types.  You'll need to use them well if you want to survive as long as you can as it's all too easy to find yourself running out of food because you didn't catch enough fish or you let that elk escape.  You can also trade with the numerous villages in the game world, but as there is no currency, you can only barter, so you'd better hope you have something they want.  Building a log cabin which will become your base of operations is something else you can, and should, do.  As this game is meant to be as realistic as possible, you'll find building it to be a time-intensive grind as you fall trees and haul them to the construction site, all the while keeping an eye on your hunger bar.  You'll be grateful for it once winter rolls in though.
Unreal World is a game that requires a little patience, though there is a reasonably detailed tutorial.  If you enjoy survivial games that reflect the gritty grind of primitive life, you will enjoy this.  The game is still in development, although updates are not very frequent.

I'm a sucker for WW2 shooters and I've played a ton of them. MoH, CoD, BiA,Sniper Elite etc. What makes Enemy Front different? Well, nothing really. And I think that's the biggest flaw of this game. If you played any of the aforementioned shooters, you've played Enemy Front before. Is that a bad thing though? Nah, not really in my case. there's still a lot to like about Enemy Front. It uses the CryEngine so it looks amazing. The levels are pretty large and give you some wiggle room on how you approach them. The levels where you're going across the French terrain were especially cool to me. The voice acting I thought was very nicely done and the gunplay overall was very satisfying. The flaws? Remember the wiggle room I told you about? It's very slim. If you want to sneak around levels, good luck. You'll eventually end up gunning your way out. The story? You won't really care.  The mission variety? Eh. Pretty standard WW2 shooter stuff. THAT SAID. I enjoyed Enemy Front quite a bit. I believe I paid $3 for it and I felt that was more than worth it. Was it groundbreaking? No. Was  it fun? Absolutely. 7.5/10 from me.

Don't let the graphics and outdated controls set you off. The creators of this game reached the epitome of wilderness survival.
You are allowed to start off as a member of several northern european tribes, excluding the raiders that are situated far to the east. From there, you are pick one of a dozen or so scenarios to start from, ranging from starting in a half-built house with tons of lumber and building supplies, to waking up on the ground injured, hungry, with only your knife to help you.
From there, you can do whatever you want. You can live as a hermit, fishing and trapping game and crafting supplies. You can be a wanderer and travel between the numerous villages on the continent, where you can buy skins, food, supplies, tools, or even livestock and dogs. You can spend days at a time tracking and hunting animals, hoping that you'll manage to get a new pelt by the end of the day.
I have never felt more free in a survival game. There is no lack of things to do, and due to its difficulty, you are always working, trying to get enough firewood for the winter, or getting enough pelts to make that new overcoat after you had to turn the last one into bandages.
The game runs entirely on keyboard commands, which can take several hours to get used to, but once you get through that, you are bound to have a gritty, stressful, frozen, and wonderful time in the far north.

IS Defense is a modern take on the old Beach Head games that were popular in arcades all around the world.  The premise is simple:  Man an MG nest and destroy everything that comes your way.  You have two weapons at your disposal--an MG and a rocket launcher--and numerous support abilities, ranging from supply drops to air strikes, that you can activate once you've attained enough kills.
Although the gameplay is rather simplistic, it's also highly replayable.  There are several "hooks" to keep you coming back like persistent skill trees, unlockable levels, leaderboards, and end-level statistics that show how many enemies you've killed, vehicles you've destroyed, and whether or not you survived longer than your previous best time.
Graphically, IS Defense is pretty impressive.  Thanks to epic explosions and ragdoll physics, blowing up incoming landing craft and technical trucks never gets old.  There are also lots of graphics options to tweak, including a much-needed FOV slider.  Best of all, the game performs quite well on my rig even in the later stages of invasions in which all hell is breaking loose (i7 4700, 8 GB RAM, GTX 970).
Overall, if you're looking for a simple, yet fun shooter chock full of explosions and carnage, IS Defense is a no-brainer for 8 bucks.  If you enjoyed the Beach Head games, I'd go as far as to say it's a must-buy.

I was skeptical at first. Most Telltale Games are about choice and consequence which boils down to one thing: "What sort of person do you want to be?" (with limits) And many of the other games already have their premises and worldbuilding from the orginal material, making them more foreseeable in what to expect. The Walking Dead and Game of Thrones push the drive for survival (a very messy kinda of survival), Batman and the Wolf Among Us challenge the pursuit for justice. The wheels are already in motion for "Whose a friend? Whose your foe? Will this help later on?" And that last question, "Was it worth it in the end?"
Borderlands is an action world of guns, blood and laughter (and maybe some friend losing because of that one piece of loot if that's how you roll). I couldn't really see how they could make a story out of this. But foresight is overrated.
Tales From the Borderlands is an adventure, the kind that invokes all that nostalgia from 80/90's adventure games. It's a story I've seen before somewhere of sorts. But, and this is the beauty of the Telltale formula in general, is that you control the choice. For example, I'd curse the protagonist for shaking hands with the devil in many a story and game so when my own chance came, I spat in his face. (it was actually a bluff)  But soon, in all good time, I found that I too, had choosen to hold that same devil's hand. And as such, I found that this was my adventure. (one that thousands of other people already experienced, but still, MINE)
Suddenly, it wasn't about the long run of what could be, and instead I was on the wheels and grease of a jounery. And that when I knew this game was everything I didn't realize I wanted.
The humor of Borderlands is well implemented and very can be very flavorful if you keep your eye out for it. This humor is also reflected in your choice of words. The game has many a moment where you can choose to crack a joke. Or the game cracks a joke on you. It may vary. Characters, without giving anything away, are amusing, charming, and many complement each other well. An interesting thing about the dual protagonist bit, is that you can directly influence how they treat each other.
All in all, tale to be retold again and again. Sit back, enjoy and catch a ride.

I picked up this game early on in it's release. I was sold by the (seeming) progress that had been made when it went EA, The compelling dev interviews, the pretty strong stylised aesthetic and the promise of Rainbow 6/System Shock in space. It did not seem like a tall order at all. The concepts were there and the game already had a lot of cool ideas implemented. Put in the ideas, polish the rough edges and we would have had a winner. A few months later and it then seemed the devs wanted to turn it into a strong multi player focused game which was not what I wanted, but the devs said that they would build up the player base and use the MP to balance the game and tweak single player. Ok, sure.  The audience wanted to help the devs achieve that premise through feedback and support. This game generated a lot of hype and people trying to build a community they imagined would exist and grow like the Arma and Rainbow 6 crowds. Fanart and groups were created.
A year later and I am fighting stupid cannon fodder super accurate robots with the same weak feeling weapons and it feels like a multi-player game with a tacked on single player rather than this amazing single player campaign we had been sold. Incredibly shoddy AI and zero noticable improvement. It was pure lip service paid to the original premise on which the game was pitched.
Here we are another year later and it looks like the game is going to be dropped. There is practically no hope for a fraction of what was promised and the worst part was that it was not an insurmountable task. They had a neat framework to hang some great original gameplay and ideas and they did not even come close to trying to be as innovative as they originally seemed to intend. The game will go on that long list of black listed steam games that are remembered not for even being failures, but for the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ behaviour and cowardice of the dev team. They did not fail because they never really tried. If it wasn't for games like Prison Architect, Satellite Reign and Nuclear Throne, I would never bother with EA.
The only reason this game is still in my library is the fact the devs are teaming up with a publisher. In a year's time this review may be completely wrong and I get to eat my words with a big spoon. I doubt it, but I hope so.
Edit: I just checked back in to see if there was any progress with the game. (There is not)
I noticed that the price is about half what I paid. Now the general idea of some early access games is you pay less now so the devs have the capital to make the game. This rule is by no means applied across the board.
But it's a kick to the teeth when when you paid twice as much for an early access game than people jumping on board now, knowing it's dead in the water. But then again, thats EA and half of nothing is still nothing. This game is dead. The devs should have the decency to announce it and bury it.

My overal rating for Interstellar Marines: 50/100
Disclaimer: This review contains only singleplayer experience. Multiplayer will be updated after reasonable amount of time.
This game looked very promising, but after a desperate amount of time, it still looks promising. But that is all. Few new implementations, boring gameplay and super-sniping enemy robots are what destroys this action sci-fi shooter focused mainly on co-op. Lets see in a detail, what went so wrong and where Interstellar Marines (IM) scored. I understand, that the game should be focused mainly on co-op, but in case of singleplayer available, it should be balanced and attractive, which is currently not.
GAMEPLAY
+ Interesting HUD
+ Atmosphere
o Weapons do pretty much the same
- OP enemies?
- no save system, ridiculous checkpoint system
Tutorial was a piece of cake. It prepared me for something not existing. Actual missions are a horrific experience and gameplay is very frustrating. There is some quest indicator, but basically you end up wandering through halls, fighting randomly spawning enemies, and sooner or later getting killed. Sangfroid is an action-tower defence game, like Orcs Must Die, but with more emphasis on tactical planning. It has some neat ideas that provide a fresh experience within the genre. You're a 19th century Canadian lumberjack, and your home is under attack by werewolves and other mystical creatures. Each level is split into two parts, day and night. During the day you can see which enemies you'll face, and which path they'll take. You can place traps, spend XP on upgrades, and visit town to buy weapons and equipment. Then you fight at night, using your traps and 3rd person combat. You can't place any new traps, your gun reloads slowly and melee attacks reduce your stamina. But this is good, because it really forces you to think ahead and carefully plan every move. The difficulty curve is nicely balanced. The story is good, but sadly the voice acting is awful, and graphics are not fantastic. Its very stable, and I got 9 hours from one playthrough, so I'm happy with value for money.

This is in my opinion one of the best visual novels available on Steam and maybe one of the best ones ever made. The UI and graphics are very thematic, fitting the sci-fi setting and nature of the storytelling very well. Most of the game consists of reading through messages and logs of the ship, databases of which you’re exploring as your main mission. Be prepared for a bit limited interactions and a lot of text, but I think all of it is written well enough and offering such an engaging story, that unless you’re super-impatient you’ll never feel bored – especially because there’s a bit of investigative element to it and it’s quite enjoyable to put all the pieces of the puzzle together. This is one of the worst horror games I have ever played.
The game has no story, and the game asks you to perform tasks with no reason why. For example, the game asks you to find a way to turn the power on, and that kind of makes sense, but why do I have to turn all the lights off? So a jumpscare can come at me? That is poor level design.
The monsters are some of the most pathetic I have ever encountered in my life. There is this witch that is the color white all over and has absolutely no texture. Her animation is robotic and parts of her body clip through the floor. The fact that she looks so hideous (in a bad way) eliminates all fear from the game. There is a swamp monster sticking his head out of the water that you can clearly see, before he jumps out and tries to chase you. Was it really that hard for the developer to stick the monster just an extra few feet under water?
The game even stoops to freaking you out with pictures that look like were downloaded from Google images.
It tries to scare you by having random unexpected jumpscares occuring throughout the game, yet without any tension build up, the scary encounters are an absolute joke. The game goes the Silent Hill route by having surreal encounters like a giant baby walking in the woods, but do not think for a second that it does this game any justice, because the game grabs random elements from other horror games and just throws them in here, and there is no consistency.
The environment is big yet not worth exploring. There is little of interest, the levels are drab and boring and look like trees and bushes were just pasted on without attention to detail. There is a dog, yet there is no owner. The fridge just has one banana in it. You can pick up picture frames, yet there is no reason to do so unless you want to drop them on the floor. The person who made this has no level design expertise.
To be fair, the only reason I bought this game was because it was on sale for 74 cents on Steam. I have had scarier experiences playing free horror games, and they are much more well done and executed than this game.
Bottom line: I want my 74 cents back.

With 152 lbs of freshly cut human meat, I returned to my shelter on the nothern coastline and started to recuperate my strenth. Months later, I now have an arsenal of armor and equipement, and an established cottage on a lone island where I maintain relations between myself and the lake spirits that guard the area. The zombie paradise has been revamped to meet the standards of current gen graphics in Dead Island: Definitive edition. The original devs "Techland" once again return to the Dead Island series, porting gaming assets and implementing new textures/effects under their latest "Chrome Engine 6" in which their succesful 2nd open world zombie rpg "Dying Light" runs on.
What's New ?
The main highlight in the definitive edition is the brand new updated graphics of course. The oddly clayish, gritty, blurry, and faded atmosphere that was once in the original Dead Island is now crisp,more detailed, and vibrant which suits the tropical theme. Even models such as npcs got a geometry/texture boost which gives them more detail and artistic personality whether they're living or infected. Not to mention, various new effects such as the lightining technology used in Dying Light has been implemented. The new lighting system vastly improves the over-all look of the world. On a side note it seems that techland added some new tweaks to their lighting technology as it includes hazy rays that can also be visible through indoor areas or just in general everywhere sort of like the early versions of Dying Light in which the retail version lacks. However, despite the new graphical changes the gameplay is pretty much the same and some new minor technical bugs exist such as chrome blood,or weird physics that makes zombie ragdolls fall even faster or the fact that you can't kick a beach ball. This is expected as the game itself is being ported to a brand new engine. On the bright side, the game seems to run smoother than the original and it seems that the major bugs had been tweaked that once plagued the original.
PROS
- Great updated/enhanced graphics
- Fun gameplay
- all dlc's included
- smooth gameplay experience
CONS
- some new technical bugs
Verdict
Dead Island: definitve edition is a true remastered game unlike other games such as "Sleeping dogs" or "HD remakes" for example. Like it's original, it is fun and thrilling especially with online players. The graphics are way better than the original which makes it 10x pleasing to venture around the zombie infested island. This is a "remaster" not a "Reboot" so don't expect new gameplay elements. I recommend this for those who are fans of Dead Island or those wanting more dead island content while waiting on the devs "Sumo Digital" to reveal new information on the upcoming sequel "Dead Island 2"; also if you never played Dead Island or Dying Light then give the definitve edtion a try. Plus the price discount is generously low for all content included.

This game is a PERFECT example of developers taking a game that pretty much perfect and absolutely ruining it. No, I am not saying that to just exaggerate it. They literally had the game's core worked out and all they had to do was just add more content(Weapons, maps etc). Thats it. It was that simple and they had it.
Instead, they decide to mess with the core gameplay and perfect progression system and as a result, they butchered it. I do see the devs say things like "Oh yeah your feedback matters, we care" but they actually don't. I mean, when the game is almost constantly going down hill, you have the real answer.
I'm sure anybody could just call me out on not knowing what the game is like these days because its been years since I touched it, but I do look the game up every now and then to see whats up and it still looks just awful compared to what it used to be.
>No pilot seat
>Self healing
>Respawning(I believe this might be for a certain game mode so I can give it a pass in that case)
>Selling/Trading/Sharing Bots
>Progression isn't like a tech tree where you unlock and work towards what you want(I hear its lootboxes now lmfao)
>Multiple weapons(This is iffy. Back when I played, I wanted this but it also seems like it would get rid of roles that people might fill)
Now, I don't put this here for the developers to see because they don't care and won't do anything. I put this here to let the players and possible new players know what happened to this once amazing game. Want this game to be good? Roll it all back to how it was but keep new blocks and maps that were added. Its that easy.
EDIT: And its a shame that it turned out the way it did. I look at some of the gameplay footage and there are a lot of blocks and stuff that I would love to play with, back when I played, the newest things were those tesla blades and the spider legs or whatever you want to call them. It genuinely looks like it would be such a blast to go back into it and build new stuff but lootbox progression is absolutely stupid and ruins all of it. Having no driver seat also rewards you less for having a good vehicle design(I had made a vehicle that never lost in a one on one). Myself and the friends I got into this game also all quit because of the direction it went, but I would be very happy if the devs would make Robocraft the great game that it was and I would definately come back to play it.

So. Before, I had a very, VERY negative review of this game, when it was full of hackers and everything was dead. That was then, this is now. It's far better, had many of the modes and maps restores, the hackers are all but gone from what I've seen, the permanent weapons are back, everything is GOOD again! Play it, please, I promise it's not nearly as bad as it used to be. The only reasons it has so many negative reviews, from what I can tell, is the people that came for the TF2 knife and only the knife, and the people that played it when it was bad and never looked back. Now, time for the pros and cons!
-Nobody in the mid-level channel, so you have to play with all ranks in PvP/QuickMatch/Etc. channels.
-Stupidly overpowered paid and temporary weapons.
-Some temporary weapons.
-The AKs, mostly 47 and its variations (Gold Snake, Blood Monkey, etc.) are OP as ♥♥♥♥.
-Dated graphics (Who cares, though?)
-Not many people in a few certain gamemodes, but that's rather irrelevant.
+A lot of maps, and a decent number of gamemodes.
+MOSTLY well-balanced weaponry and classes (See above cons about weapons)
+Generally nice playerbase, if not a bit detached and confusing at times.
+Adequate tutorial.
+Properly-priced weapons, for the most part (So, really, no absolutely massive grind to get a single weapon, usually)
+Pretty fun gameplay.
+Not insanely hard to overcome the more powerful, temporary/paid for weapons, in general, most have, at worst, some form of Achilles Heel you can "abuse." (Say, a very large spread, so just snipe the prick.)
So, overall, play it. Now. At least, if you like not-very-realistic shooters and can deal with the random paid-for god here and there. If I HAD to try to give this a rating out of ten, I guess... 7.5/10? I don't like number ratings for games and such.

Analogue: A Hate Story is a visual novel that takes place as communications between an information salvager and the AIs of a long-forgotten ship. As you read through more and more of the ship's logs and see what they reveal about the people who once called it home, you become engrossed and utterly invested in the stories of their lives. As you know the fate of the ship's inhabitants from the beginning, you know, in the vaguest sense, how the story ends. But as you keep reading and asking questions, you find yourself wishing and hoping that things turn out alright for the people of the ship. It is like watching a snow globe fall to the floor in slow motion: a self-contained world slowly meets its doom and there's nothing that you can do to stop it. All that's left is to pick up the pieces.

This is definetely the best MMORPG I've ever played. The controls are simple in the steampunk world, mostly the same as any other in the genre, but this game brings more to the table. With a very simple and unrestricting story line, you are free to play any way you want. Whether you play for the PvP and make your way to the top of the leaderboard, or you play a story based game, or you just mess around with your friends, the game is always exciting to use. I have played for almost 300 hours now (mostly AFK since you get rewards for being AFK) and the whole game has been constantly rewarding. The game has so many rewarding features that no other MMORPG has, and they all make this the greatest MMORPG I've ever seen.
There is also NO need to purchase anything with actual money in the game. Everything can be gained with a little elbow grease and time. Of course though, this game should not be so sparing. If you had to pay for a subscription in this game, I would do so gladly, even more gladly than games such as World of Warcraft and ESO. This is a have to have for anyone who wants a new spin on the the repetitive MMORPG genre.

As it's largely about reading through the logs of a Korean starship, it's initially extremely confusing to Western eyes, as it's very hard to keep straight who all the characters are.  The logs are written like you're just overhearing a few other people's conversations, and so it's often filled with references to people who never appear in the logs again, or are important, but at the start, it's hard to tell what is or isn't important.
If you bear through it for a few hours, however, you find it's largely focused upon a tiny handful of individuals, and is an extremely personal story.
The funny name of this game is an inversion of Christine Love's first (and available for free) game, Digital: A Love Story. (Get it? It's a love story, but it's written by someone
Love, so it's also a Love story! Ha... ha... Anyway...) While Digital was set in the past, and its themes were about how people looked to the future, Analogue is set in the future, and about a society that wants to send itself back to its past.
The author, Christine Love, has, and puts in everything she makes, strongly-held and strongly-expressed ideas about women and lesbians in particular.  Korean (and by extension, Chinese,) traditional patriarchy clashes brutally with these themes.
Inversely, the AIs the player deals with are almost too colorful and anime-esque for the drama in front of which they are standing.  The 'real' action is long since passed, and the player really only has a choice of taking one or the other (or why not, take both!) along with him or her.  It's a minor issue here, and a much worse one in Hate Plus, but the story in the logs has an entirely different mood and themes than the one the player actually participates in with the AIs, which is far more about describing yourself and your point of view to the AIs.  In essence, if you took out the log reading, it's just the player flirting with girls in a standard Visual Novel with an unusually large number of choices.

I found Analouge: A Hate Story to be kind of boring and uninteresting.
In the beginning, you're an individual sent to find out what happened to a ship who's entire crew died. You do this by accessing a terminal and going through the logs and diary entries. You have two A.I's who guide you through it on your quest to discover the truth and what happened her. However the question of "How did everyone die?!" gets wrapped up surprisingly quickly within a few minutes after talking to a new A.I you obtain named *Mute, and then switching back over to the other A.I to question them about the new information. Basically at that point you just need to use your imagination and "boom" you know what happened. At least, if you're keeping an open mind to how this happened. You'll figure it out long before you find the truth which is very disappointing.
The game revolves around a family drama on a marriage dispute and the personal life of a specific person. Also about how women are treated in this family.
I found this really uninteresting and boring. I didn't care to remember anyones name except the Pale Bride the drama was about, because I wanted to know about her life. She was the only person I had any interest in and needed to know the truth about. Everyone else was faceless, mundane, shallow, boring, obnoxious, idiotic and moronic.
I think that the logs could've been easier and more fluid and interesting to look at and switch between. Because this game is all about reading the logs and pressing questions on the A.I you're currently partnered up with. Because sifting through the logs got really messy as I progressed through the game and the overrall reading screen presentation was really boring as the screen was just deadpan text.
Anyways, the music was nice in the game. I think it kind of lacked the functionality to cue perfectly for emotional and important logs you read. But the music was nice to listen to and sort of dragged on sometimes. But either way, didn't really mind the music, could've been more emotional/better though.
There's times in the game you have to enter commands like
>enable_ai *Hyun-ae
and
>power_control enable core1
And things like that. Those parts were kind of fun actually since I never really get to mess with those kinds of things and the game made a pretty nice puzzle segment on the terminal commands. And I thought that was pretty good and fun.
Anywho, after I learned about the Pale Brides entire life and how the entire crew died. I immediately quit because there was absolutely nothing interesting left in this visual novel for me. I didn't care about getting the 5 endings and I honestly only spent roughly ten minutes with *Mute. I didn't like her at all and she was gossipy and annoying.
They made Hyun-ae constantly try to fall in-love with you over the game and I found that annoying, I get 'why' she was doing that. But I still think the game could've been more mature and just cut that bit out. It was obnoxious and didn't really provide and depth to the story or the A.I's character
All in all, Analouge: A Hate Story I found to be an okay experience. I personally couldn't find any reason to bother playing/reading after learning about the crews fate and the life of the Pale Bride. Maybe you will enjoy whatever else this game has to offer.

I don't always review games I play on Steam, but when I do it's something I've consistently enjoyed and kept coming back to for more than a decade.
URW is a survival roguelike set in fictional iron age Finland. The emphasis is strongly on realism, with a few light magical elements in the form of rituals and animism. The pace is slow, and unless you get ambushed by the occasional roving bandit or the game's faux-Novgorodian Njerpez warriors, fighting can generally be avoided. Trouble is easy enough to find if you go expressly looking for it, but combat can be brutal and strong armor and weapons are not easy to come by. Death is permanent, as tends to be the genre standard, and the world is not persistent. There's nothing permanent to unlock across playthroughs either, so unless you're cool with manual "save scumming" it's straight back to square one when you kick the bucket.
Technically the game ticks a lot of the usual roguelike check boxes. There are quite a few keystrokes and commands to learn for various actions, as well as menus and stat screens to master. Graphics are a mix of simple but decent-looking pixel art and photos, and apart from small objects (such as arrows from missed shots) sometimes being difficult to spot in the middle of a thicket, they get the job done. The soundscape consists mainly of birds chirping, wind rustling through the trees, water splashing and other such wilderness ambience.
In summary, if you enjoy epic questlines, clear objectives and lots of mysteries to discover, URW might not be for you, but if roguelikes are close to your heart and you're ready for a more down-to-earth survival experience, you should give it a whirl. If you're unsure, you can even download an older version for free from the game's website
.

I've played quite some competitive team based shooters in my time but Day of Defeat will always remain a special place in my heart. This game is quite underrated and extremely enjoyable to play, there are a few reasons for that.
First of all, it's an easy game to pick up and play for a while. Nothing to fancy or complex to deal with, you play on maps and capture various objectives by standing around. Sometimes you might need to defend some objectives or plant explosives on them but that's about it. You have enough classes that provide variety and offer different playstyles, furthermore the weapons are all extremely satisfying and have a distinct feel. It is always a joy to defeat multiple hostile targets or survive an intense gunfight.
Another great aspect are the absolutely nicely designed maps. All the maps are rich in detail and are extremely well balaned except for a very few ones which are obviously intended to be imbalanced. The maps always have certain spots and places that might give you a major view on various places, but there are always alternatives routes and ways to flank a position. You seldom have positions that allow you to camp for an extended period of time or give you advantages. This is extremely pleasant as it keeps the game moving forward and you always have to watch out.

I paid just under £7 British Pounds for the Definitive Collection and I have to say, having spent a few hours in Dead Island DE, the first of the two full games included, it's the best purchase I've made so far this year.
Techland understand a thing or two about never taking advantage of their customers and they've come up trumps again. This is not just any old 'remaster' - this is a complete port of both Dead Island and Dead Island Riptide into the latest Dying Light game engine - and boy does it show. Three hours into Dead Island DE and I'm constantly blown away by the gorgeous visuals. Now I understand what Techland envisaged for Dead Island the first time around - but only now can their game tech truly do their vision justice.
It's hard to over-emphasise just how impressive these games now look in their new forms. I understand some people have reported issues but I have to be honest and say that even on my six year-old PC (running a lowly GTX 760 on an i7@2.80GHz with 12GB RAM) I'm able to max everything out (no compromises) and the game has, so far, been rock-solid for me. I can also report that Techland have done a solid job with the PS4 version of DI:DE, as I'm fortunate enough to own that, too. Both versions look spectacular and run without complaint.
The actual gameplay remains as hokey and yet strangely enjoyable as ever. It's Dead Island, after all, and although it may wow with it's swish new game engine and stunning lighting and vistas (and the views really are lovely), the gameplay is largely unchanged from tne originals. Menus look better organised and work perfectly well with the 360 controller on PC (my preferred way of playing). In short: if you enjoyed the gameplay of the originals you'll get exactly the same thing here, but it will all look several magnitudes better than those original versions ever did.
Well done to Techland for doing this right. They weren't lazy; this is not a cash-in and the developer should be congratulated for its efforts and for its sensible pricing.
Highly Recommended. Really, this sets a new benchmark for re-releasing games - more publishers should take note.

Essentially a tower defense game with some bells and whistles, similar to Dungeon Defenders. The game is two parts. Part 1 is planning for the wolf attacks at night in which you are able to see the waves, which enemies are attacking, and which paths they will take to a variety of buildings you are charged with protecting. Losing any of the buildings results in a failed night in which you must redo. Each type of wolf/werewolf has different stats, strengths, and weaknesses. You have a variety of traps that can be as simple as a bear or spike trap, or more complex, like a hanging net of rocks that you must shoot at when your prey is underneath. Each trap has either an Action Point cost, money cost, or both on it. These are the costs to set them on the map and limit the amount of things you can plop down on the gameboard. Leftover AP can be used to chop trees once you unlock the mill, thus providing you with more money for unused resources. Keep in mind though, once you do this, you can't use those points to buy extra damaging traps that can help you in the next mode. Once you start the night, you play Part 2 which plays out live action. You can pause the game in map mode, but as soon as the map drops, the wolves are coming.
In addition, there are some interesting features in the game. For instance, you have a stamina bar. Of the two weapons you you start with (axe and rifle), you must be careful as to not tire yourself out. Running uses stamina as well. Also, when you run, you make more noise. Wolves are alert and can hear you the more noise you make. So, firing your gun obviously can alert them. You can also shout, which will call wolves to the last spot you shouted and (if they are close enough) cause them to fear you. Fear is an interesting feature in this game. Wolves will pace around while their fear wears down and then they attack you. You can yell to increase this, but eventually, the pack will attack. You can ward off wolves by building fires - they tend to not like these - and stand near them.
But not for long. Fires wear out. You can take pot shots at them with your rifle, but reloading it requires you to tamp the shot with powder packets, so it's not like you're using a machine gun. Obviously, you can't do this under duress.
After a successful night, you are graded on how many creatures you killed, the skins or parts you took from them (which gives you money), and how in tact the buildings are. XP and money is awarded (you also get money per kill in the game while playing in the live action mode). At this point you can go to town and buy more bullets, better weapons, gear to wear which gives effects, or potions and blessings from the local church on your items. You can also spend skill points in between levels in which you level up. Skill points accentuate your abilities, allowing you to rage for longer (an ability you naturally have while swinging your axe successfully), increase damage from weapons, set better traps, or reduce the time in between loading bullets. There are many skills to improve.
The game has some flaws though. Firstly, the voice acting is really not all that great. The story isn't necessarily bad, but with poor voice acting, it really takes a back seat to just the gameplay.. which is fine. But it would have really brought the entire thing together to have a solid voice cast like in Bastion. The cut scenes are also pretty shoddy. I don't mean just in an amatuerishly drawn sense. Some of the models don't even look finished, especially when you look at how their fingers and hands work. When you play in the game, you don't see any of this. It's grossly glaring in the cut scenes however. And there were some minor annoyances, such as not being able to sell my starting gear once I improved it (it just stays in your inventory.. haven't figured out how to even scrap it). And, I have to travel back to my house to swap out new gear, then go back to town to sell it. I can't seem to do any of that in the buy/sell screen or in town. Minor frustrations.

A continuing evolution of the Tower Defense + OTS Combat genre, Sang-Froid strikes an amazing balance between so many different gameplay elements. A dark and well crafted story weaves the campaign together and keeps you engaged from start to finish.
During the day you can examine the types of monsters that will attack during the next night and the routes they'll take. You then use your time units and money to place traps. Leftover time can be used to generate additional funds, which can be spent in the town on weapons, ammo, trinkets, and consumables.
By tying money and time together, Sang-Froid forces you to make tough decisions when planning your day. It's a balance between putting the bare-minimum of traps down so you can afford upgrades without getting yourself killing the process.
Combat at night is fun and tense, with good controls and a variety of monsters that need special tactics to take down. You'll find yourself juggling defending different objectives and, once again, your greatest enemy is time as you fight to clear one attack as quickly as possible so you can make it to the next objective in time.
Over-all a great game on many levels, and a must-buy for anyone that enjoys Tower Defense, werewolves, or strategic OTS combat.

"The moment I dread most is having to explain what EVE is when asked about games I play"
I've been playing EVE since 2009, (although I've only recently been able to use my old account on Steam, because of the introduction of the new launcher), and I don't think I've ever had more hours pooled into any game in my life.
EVE is essentially a close-to-no-rule sandbox multiplayer game, with all of the goods and bads (goods) that come with that.
EVE is also an extremely complex game of details that makes the Clausewitz engine games look weak.
Still though: it's not hard. It's brutal, without a doubt, but not necessarily hard, and it's equally brutal to everyone.
EVE doens't have safe zones (besides the interiors of NPC stations), although there are systems of crime and punishment, and law enforcement does exist in the areas refered to as High Security (HiSec) space.
Rather than having NPC merchants, EVE uses real resources produced and products manufactured by real players, which are then marketed or used by, you guessed it: players.
Everything from the ships flown, to the structures in space built (excluding the aformentioned NPC stations found in HiSec and LowSec space) are sourced from real people, meaning they have value you won't find in other games.
Every ship (and structure) in eve is highly customizable, with extremely few limitations.
PvP in EVE is probably the most rewarding experience I've ever had in any game. Period.
PvE is a nice break from the stress, but can also be extremely exciting if done for high reward (and high risk).
Mining isn't my cup of tea, but I can see the appeal. Great for people who like numbers and low stress situations (until you blow up).
Industry is very fun in my opinion, despite lacking much interactive content; It's what I do, but I get my inputs from blowing things up and picking up the parts instead of shooting space rocks. Something about pressing the "Deliver Order" button is super nice.
To be honest though, I really don't think I can properly explain this game. Just give it a shot, and brace yourself for something...
If you need any assistance or have questions, feel free to hit me up ingame at Aetran Molou.

Honestly, This game is in a league of its own. North of 4000 hours in, and I'm far from being tired of it, which is quite the achievement.
You could call it a "space MMO", but lumping it in with other MMO's is a disservice, quite frankly. What makes me say this?
Well, lets start off like this: Space is big. Huge. Mindbogglingly vast. You have all of this entire star cluster (and a second one) to explore. Conquer. Do whatever you want, literally; you can build stuff, blow stuff up, explore, scam, trade on markets, heck, make a T-Rex your mascot and go around spamming memes if you want.
Market PVP? Check. Industrial PVP? Check. Good old-fashioned ship-to-ship combat using missiles, lasers, antimatter blasters, and artillery cannons? CHECK!!!
And the fact that it's all single shard means that whatever you do affects everyone. None of that instanced BS in parallel realms that you find with other MMO's - If you go out and blow up someone's space station, you could legitimately throw the balance of power off between the ingame player coalitions in that region, if not on a larger scale. The story is entirely player-driven, and you can interfere with developer-driven-events if you so choose - for example, the leader of one of the NPC Empires was chosen by a player tournament, and at the ceremony, other players were noted for their support/opposition of the proceedings, and all of this is now official lore.
And, of course, the hundreds upon hundreds of possible ships. You like fast small ships with missiles that fly like X-Wings? Check. Big lumbering battleships that tank for days, and have slow-tracking turrets that will obliterate something when they hit? Check. Something in-between? Guaranteed it's there.
The F2P model does lock out capital ships, and advanced hulls (cloaky ships, interdictors, covert ops). But having played with a restricted character as well, I can safely say that you don't really need those either, as the meta is currently focused around cruisers and destroyers (read: fast kitey doctrines), and generally trends towards making the most out of the least expensive possible hulls. There are exceptions, but those are used by niche groups that don't generally take on newbies.
Recommendation: Play it. It's free to try out(!!!), you can do 95% of the ingame content as a free player, and once you get the hang of it, upgrade to a subscription if you want to try those 5% things! The game can be quite unforgiving of mistakes, and is a very tough nut compared to most other games, but I can safely say it's worth the time, and likely one of the easiest games to get sucked into if you have a love of science fiction.

Also, you could make them go out and slap a boomalope a few times. Same thing. Quicker. But same thing.

[Everyone died from plague]
Don't want toxic fallout to rain from the sky?
Hide inside until it passes to avoid poisoning.
Or F that and force your colonists to do what you gotta do.

Crap! Raiders!
No, wait. Capture and convert them (or release them for brownie points with factions so they stopsending raids, but keep in mind that will end your semi-steady supply of converted voluntary workhorses).
Yes! A distress signal. Someone needs my help on the world map (that's a free colonist). Hustle to get there. Return to base. Red flash. Oh, a raid. The two colonists I have left have 3 shooting/4 melee skill between them. ♥♥♥♥ this colony, then.

- Beam battles (spinning the analog sticks for the stronger beam)

This is a pretty decent game that is free to play for the first episode.  The audio (especially during the first sequence) is pretty cool, and the atmosphere is set well very early on.  However, the game seems to devolve later into something that has been done before (and better) many times.  I'm sure there's more coming, but I was disappointed to discover that this is little more than an FPS with some simple puzzles.  The combat element was MOST unsatisfying; there's a certain sluggishness to the controls that seems to make it all the more difficult.  Tweaking some settings didn't seem to resolve this issue.
Overall, the maps (what I've seen thus far) are reasonably straightforward, and functional.  Enemies are dull, but there was one moment that inspired some real anxiety- really good work there.
Try this game.  It's a bargain at the price, and it looks like there's more episodes coming, so hopefully the depth of the game will improve.  At this point, I would be hesitant to purchase further episodes, but I reserve judgment until I've completed the first.

Warning: This review may be slightly influenced by my love for DBZ, so be advised.
Now I've played through this game three times, each time just as enjoyable as the one before. I highly recommend this game, but theres some things I should mention.
Pros!
This game is a great fighting game, and as with most fighting games this one is best with a controller rather than mouse and keyboard. Why I suggest using a wired controller for this is because of the way this game works, most of the time you'll be in the air fighting rather than on the ground. Without a controller it takes a bit of getting used to manuvering while flying, like rising and lowering your altitude to get closer (or further away) to your target. This leads me to another reason why using a controller is supreme. Ultimate and Super Attacks. I have to say this was probably the most fun to experiment with when your playing XENOVERSE, as your ultimates and supers can pretty much make or break your character depending on the way you go with character customization (I.E: using a ton of melee based supers when doing a Ki based character) I suggest you mess around and have fun getting your ultimates the way you like it. Now I can go on for a while about the great things in this game, like character customization. But theres somethings you should know if you plan on playing Xenoverse.
Cons:
*Sigh* This game is really awesome, but some of the features can ruin your fun. Lets start with least favourite feature of this game...
Random Number Generator... Oh where do I begin with this pile of crap. RNG is used for the drops in this game, which can lead to hours or days farming for a super, ultimate, item, or a piece of armor. This is probably what♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off the most in this. I spent hours farming for Super Vegeta 2 (one of the transformations) and still haven't gotten it. Even though I've gotten Z-ranks almost every time I did the mission it was on. So I spent upwards of eight or nine hours farming for it, and at some point gave up on farming for it. So if your playing through this and hoping for a certain item be prepared for either really short or a really long farming state.
Partner AI is another bad part about this game, sometimes they'll just be useless and at other times they'll be helpful. I honestly couldn't figure out how their AI works, but be prepared to revive them a few times. This brings me to my next subject.
Some story missions in this are annoying as heck at times. I'll give an example, theres a part in this game where your character has to defeat 20 enemies. Sounds simple, right? Wrong. You have to constantly protect Gohan and Krillin from getting killed, 'cause if they're killed its an instant failure. Oh and the missions don't have checkpoints, which makes this tedious along with their horrible A.I.
Okay I can go on for a couple more paragraphs on the good things and bad things about this game. But overall, the good outweighs the bad. So what rating would I give this game? I honestly would give this game a 8/10. I went into this game wanting it to be my GOTY for 2015, but I found it in my top 10 of the year. This game would be a 9/10 if it wasn't for some of the annoyances with the Parallel quests (Due to their occasional repeating of objectives), RNG, and partner A.I. If you're going to get this game I'd suggest getting it with a friend because its much better with friends, I also suggest waiting for a sale and getting the Resurrection F DLC along with it. Now go, have fun with this game. I know I did. :D

This reminds me of my first HL mod in the late nineties. The levels and buildings have layouts that don't really make sense. The story is dished out in an odd way, and the enemies aren't fleshed out as well as they could be. We use to call this "first time modder syndrome". This creates a game that simply doesn't flow well. This is often cured by experience though. We get 2 small, and I mean small, snippets of story the entire episode. I never really got pulled in. There were a few nice moments and use of the source engine that are fresh, but these bits are too few and far between. We will probably have to wait at least 6-9 months for the next episode to drop,  but by that time, with not enough story to draw me in and no real sense of purpose in what the main character is supposed to be doing, combined with a confusing cliffhanger ending.. I doubt by then I'll care.
Still, I'd try it, just for those nice bits. Just don't expect to remember this game exists even a few months from now.

One Piece Pirate Warrior is already a well-known smash-da-buttons game series and loved by One Piece fans. This game is my favorite part of the whole series as it leads you through all important stations of the Straw Hat Pirates' stories. This is in fact a good reason for gamer who haven't watched or read One Piece yet to get a good insight and maybe get interested in starting the actual series.
The player has a wide variety of characters to choose from which is in my opinion always a great plus. As a smash-button game, it has to be an easy-to-learn game which is totally the case here (it could be a bit harder if you ask me).
Besides the story mode the player can start the "Dream Log"-mode where you have to conquer all islands by beating bosses to a pulp. It's funny, trust me.
A huge minus is the lack of multiplayer-mode, something that was fun to do now an then in the previous games.
I was actually kinda sad when I realized that there is no multiplayer-mode, but it didn't stop me from enjoying the game at all.
After a good couple hours you will have picked your favorite character(s) and know how to deal with all kinds of enemies so be ready to hunt the Steam Achievements.
If you're done with the latter, the game will get boring and you may play it once in a while for fun.
So keep in mind to enjoy the game as long as possible!
